Śrī: A Catalogue of Ancient Manuscripts in the National Library of Nepal.
This is the compendium of the essence of the characteristics of the foundation for one [of them].
The first volume, extending up to the eleventh chapter, under the editorship of Paṇḍita Buddhisāgara Śarmā.
Edited by Vedācārya Dāmodara Śarmā and revised by the editor, Vedāntaśāstrī Paṇḍit Bābū Kṛṣṇa Śarmā.
Published by the National Library of Nepal:
Śrī Atha Pratiṣṭhālakṣaṇasārasamuccayaḥ.

It begins: *Oṃ namaḥ tasyai*, [in manuscript *kh*: *oṃ namaḥ śivāya* is not present], [to her who is] the three principles, the triple fire, the three qualities, and the three marks (or, according to manuscript *g*: the three bodies).

Having prostrated before the Lord who bears the trident, whose body is the three goddesses of the three worlds throughout the three periods of time, and who belongs to the lineage purified by the descent of the triple-pathed river into his three eyes; || 1 ||

Having extracted [the material] from the traditional scriptures (āgamas), I shall compose this compendium of characteristics (lakṣaṇasaṅgraha), which is straightforward, concise, complete, and filled with the installation of all [deities]. (2)
It is free from doubt, clear in meaning, and bestows dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation;
it is for the benefit of those of dull intellect and for the recollection of the wise. (3)
In some places, certain limbs are clearly described, yet not all limbs are present in a single source;
therefore, having examined many tantras, they are written down here in one place in a systematic order.
Thus, in the Śiva-āgama proclaimed by Śiva, the characteristics of the *siddha-liṅga* have been described. Now, in accordance with that scripture, I shall explain the *liṅga*. (5)
That from which all this has arisen— the three worlds with their moving and non-moving beings—
and wherein it dissolves at the time of dissolution, that is called the Liṅga.
That which is formless and immeasurable is threefold according to the measure of form;
from that, through the ritual offerings of the worship of Śiva, the accomplishments (siddhis) such as the inferior and so forth arise.
Having abandoned the conceptualization of material substances, one should always worship with devotion that Śiva-tattva—
the omniscient, all-bestowing, pure, and giver of liberation.
The principal world-protectors, beginning with Brahmā, as well as the ṛṣis, Vasus, Rudras, Gaṇas, Yakṣas, Grahas, and Uragas, attained perfection through the mantras proclaimed by Śiva.
The Daityas, Rākṣasas, Siddhas, and others have attained the state of supreme sovereignty;
therefore, that [Supreme Being] is worshipped by men and others in the form of the Liṅga.
The sight of the Linga is meritorious; its touch destroys sin.
Worship bestows great sovereignty, and meditation grants liberation. (11)
Whatever fruit may accrue to those performers of a hundred times ten thousand horse-sacrifices, that fruit is certainly doubled by the proper installation of even a single *liṅga*. 12.
Whatever merit would accrue to a king from a palace adorned with gold, jewels, and the like,
that very same merit accrues to the poor from a dwelling made of grass, mud walls, and so forth, provided it is done without deceit.
(3) The form of a man is not at all the characteristic for that which is to be installed by gods, asuras, and serpents.
Now, the characteristic for the linga, the temple, and so forth, shall be explained with respect to men. (14)
That [liṅga] is of three kinds, according to their respective order: the unmanifest (avyakta), the manifest-mixed (vyaktamiśraka), and the manifest (liṅga);
as well as the face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga), and the male, female, and neuter. || 15 ||
Hara is pervasive, like fire always consuming fuel, residing in the house of misfortune (the *vipadgṛha*).
Viṣṇu is in the eight-sided figure of the Sun (*sūryāṣṭāsraka*), and the omnipresent Brahmā is in the four-sided figure (*vedāsraka*). (16)
Through the conjunction of these three, the unmanifest *liṅga* comes into being;
when joined with the head and other parts, it becomes manifest, and possessing both forms, it is called the "manifest-unmanifest" (*vyaktāvyakta*).

The manifest (vyakta) is to be known as fivefold; likewise, that which is called the manifest is sevenfold. That which possesses a dual nature is said to be tenfold; everything is twofold, being either mobile or immobile. (18) The unmanifest (avyakta) truly bestows liberation, while the manifest bestows worldly enjoyment.
That which bestows both enjoyment and liberation is the mixed [type]; such is its nature. || 19 ||

Whatever constitutes the nature of the *liṅga*, its ritual action, and its measurement; that which brings about swift accomplishment, and that which pertains to both desired and undesired results. || 20 ||
The examination of those materials and the characteristics of the preceptor, as well as the artisans, the image-makers, and the procedures for the forest procession and so forth. (21)
The mountains and those who rule over them, the rivers and the trees and so forth;
the classification of sacred sites, the acquisition of building plots, and their worship. || 22 ||
As it was before, so too is the sacrifice (adhvara) consisting of the jar (kalaśa) and the door-union (advārayoga) as previously described;
likewise, there is Śiva, the ritual of the linga (liṅgavidhi), the sacrifice, and everything up to the banner (dhvaja). (23)
The temple is likewise endowed with the five types of installations;
it is such that it serves as a refuge for ascetics, and its consecration is fivefold.

The conjunction of seasons and constellations, as well as the day, the zodiacal sign, and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana); and whatever requisites are required for the installation—this entire process is now described. (25)
One should fashion the liṅgas of these two from gems, clay, wood, stone, or paintings;
for one desiring minor powers, it should be made of metal, while that born of gems bestows many accomplishments.

An image made of clay serves for the attainment of all desired objects, whereas one made of wood bestows swift success. An image made of metal or wood should be established upon a stone pedestal; however, an image made of wood is perishable.
That mountain bestows both enjoyment and liberation, yet it brings disease when located within a house.
Furthermore, the *liṅga* should be known to be of two kinds: mobile (*cala*) and immobile (*acala*). (28)
That made of coral and gems is said to be mobile; that born of minerals is both mobile and immobile.
That which is golden bestows stable prosperity, and that which is silver grants a kingdom. (29)
Copper increases progeny and enhances eloquence, vitality, and lifespan;
bell-metal causes enmity, and that made of brass destroys enemies.
A linga made of lead brings disease; one made of iron destroys enemies;
and a linga made of the eight metals (aṣṭaloha) brings about the destruction of leprosy and consumption.

A liṅga made from the three metals (triloha), which bestows the power of invisibility, should be fashioned by a craftsman; having coated it with beeswax and clay, he should heat it and then remove it [from the fire]. (32)

One should fill the cavities with wax, increasing the amount by one digit (aṅgula) at a time according to the sequence starting from the modification (vikāra), the sun (arka), and so on; [using] gold and lead respectively, along with silver, copper, tin, iron, and bell-metal.

Having rubbed mercury with the juices of *dhūstūra* (thorn apple), one should place that gold—which possesses its foot—along with wood, and then grind it firmly on a stone slab together with sand. (34)
That paste should be ground with the juice of *jambīra* and sea salt;
the wise man should apply it with that [paste], combined with water saturated with salt. (35)

Then, having pressed and struck with the thumb of the hand using the pelvic cavity (*koṣṭhikā*), one should gradually and slowly bring about equanimity by means of the "child-key" (*bālakuñcikā*). (36)
Having repeatedly subjected it to the heat of fire until the threefold mark is stripped of its essence,
one should then diligently polish it with a gem and with *madanāmbu* waters.
Furthermore, having drawn out from the fire the linga of threefold form,
the artisan should immerse it in copper and then in very fine gold.
Red when heated, white when cut, and the color of saffron when rubbed on a touchstone; heavy, lustrous, and soft to the touch—gold possessing these six qualities is beautiful. (39)

One should fashion [the image] from metal or earth according to the rules with mantras; that which arises from minerals has been fully described. Now I shall speak of that which is born of jewels and so forth. (40)
That which originates from diamond is known to bestow long life; that which arises from pearl removes disease;
that produced from ruby brings happiness; and lapis lazuli destroys the pride of enemies. (41)
A ruby bestows prosperity, an indranīla grants fame, an emerald brings nourishment, and a crystal fulfills all desires. (42)
Liṅgas arising from great jewels bring prosperity, while those originating from minor jewels bring other results;
one made of coral is for subjugation, and one made of emerald is for the purpose of killing enemies.
That which arises from the *pulaka* plant produces knowledge; *rājāvarta* removes enemies; that born of the *jīvaka* plant bestows strength; and *ṭaiṭṭibha* crushes foes. (44)
That which is made of pearl causes enmity, while that which is made of conch-shell bestows happiness.
These are the characteristics of the materials for the pedestal; hereafter follows the measurement of their purity.
The linga born of jewels is of two kinds: the fashioned and the unfashioned.
That which is constructed by artisans from wood and such materials is known as the fashioned linga.
That which arises from its own nature, that which is pure, that which is born of jewels, and that which is uncreated—
this should always be worshipped with effort by kings who seek both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should discard a linga that is accompanied by a drop (bindu), is fierce (raudra), has a pointed tip like a trident (śūlāgra), is flattened, or is thin;
likewise, one that has faces upward and downward, is elongated, thick at the base, or lacks luster. (48)
(7) A stone that is of mixed color, lacking limbs, broken, previously used by a deity, perforated, cracked, worn away, pierced by a thorn, or abandoned by a god; || 49 ||

That which is cast obliquely or downward should be avoided as inferior; one should likewise avoid what is situated in the middle, as well as kingdoms, lineages, people, villages, wealth, friends, and sons.
They destroy crops, vehicles, armies, kinsmen, and servants;
likewise, they bring about disease, defeat, agitation, public hatred, and strife. (51)
It would intensely bestow exile, suffering, poverty, and death in succession;
however, if it is free from defects, firm, glossy, and radiant, that [result] shall occur.
Experts in the scriptures have thoroughly examined [the materials] from the parts of the body down to the size of a grain of mung bean;
one should always worship with that which is a great jewel, of high value, and endowed with excellent qualities. 53.
From worshipping it, victory, peace, health, abundant prosperity,
great majesty, fame, and long life shall belong to the king for a long time.
From a great jewel, a great accomplishment arises; from a small one, a small one is produced.
A jewel that is not artificial—whether blue, yellow, or white—is praised. (55)
The deities of the thunderbolt are Varuṇa, Vāyu, Viṣṇu, Indra, Agni, and Yama;
[the mantra] resembles a conch and crystal, possessing the luster of the hibiscus flower and the leaf of the plantain tree.

That which resembles the juice of turmeric, or is like the color of a hare or a conch shell, or has the luster of a washed face—these yellow and reddish-yellow varieties are fit for the twice-born and for kings. (57)
For a Vaiśya, [the marks] are green and yellow; for the fourth [caste], they are grey.
That [mark] which has a trident extending both upward and downward and a thunderbolt is of the nature of Śiva.
That liṅga leads to the increase of lifespan and is the destroyer of all diseases. (58)
White, red, yellow, black, and auspicious crystal—this [lapis lazuli] is considered by some to be of four types, arising respectively from Śakra, Agni, Yama, and Mitra. (59)
Waveless, endowed with qualities, brilliant and pure like a white lotus,
resembling an autumnal cloud, transparent, glossy, crystalline, and beneficial.

One should discard that which is variegated, marked with spots, rough, cracked, of altered color, containing internal cavities, accompanied by ripples, or dense yet emitting light (or, according to another reading, "emitting light and then released"). 61.
It should have a wound, be provided with a peg, and have a tip like a trident, but be devoid of a disc [or, according to Mū., A., K.: devoid of a face].
It may be thick or long, or it may be short, thin at the middle, the beginning, or the end.
One should discard a gem that is covered with frost-like spots, one that is completely filled with internal cavities (or filaments),
one that is attached to another species, and one that is pierced, as these are terrifying.

One should worship the crystal Liṅga, which is beautiful, endowed with mental concentration, characterized by the defining marks of the scriptures, and which grants desired objects, conquers death, and fulfills all wishes.

An image endowed with all the auspicious marks, even if it possesses some slight defect in certain respects, is traditionally held to be like the perpetual *agnihotra* fire; when worshipped, it does not cause harm to men. (65)
(9) If there is a beautiful parasol, there will be a kingdom; if it is slightly on the head, there will be gentleness.
Through a depression there is always success; if it is high, it is elevated; if level, it is equal. (66)

In that regard, the Ratnalinga is declared to be of two kinds: the *sarvasama* (all-equal), which is the most excellent, and the *yavamadhya* (barley-shaped), which grants boons; these are produced from their own pedestal (*svapīṭha*) and from a mineral pedestal (*dhātupīṭha*). (67)

But that which is born of minerals, situated in its own source, bestows both spiritual accomplishment and liberation. The mobile liṅga, auspiciously composed of mineral gems, should be fashioned in two ways.
A liṅga made of gold and so forth should measure between three and five finger-breadths;
likewise, one made of small gems should be of that same size according to its own measurement, while one made of excellent jewels follows its own standard.
For those of the highest caste, it lasts until the end of the lunar day (tithi); for kings, until the end of Indra;
for Vaiśyas, until the end of Manmatha; and for Śūdras, the limit is twelve.
In some cases, the characteristic mark of yakṣas and others is twenty-one [aṅgulas] due to modification;
above that, the mark of the gods is twenty-three aṅgulas.
One should worship that which resides in the temple; therefore, these are indicated as stable.
It is immovable, situated in the sky-like space, and remains until the end of the hand [or until the final dissolution]. (72)

The unmanifest (avyakta) linga is up to nine cubits in length, while the manifest (vyakta) is fivefold; the mixed (miśraka) linga is sixfold, and it is not desired to be stable when exceeding these dimensions.
The stone image should be nine cubits in height, or sometimes three cubits if made of metal;
the wooden image should not exceed six cubits, while the earthen image is always like the stone one.
p. 10) "It should be nine cubits or ten cubits; this is the [standard] for a human liṅga.
However, in some cases, it may be [of that size] for Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Asuras, Vyālas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases. (75)
For the Kinnaras and Siddhas, it is fifteen cubits; for the gods, however, it is twenty-one cubits in both circumference and height.
That which pertains to this world (aihika) is three finger-breadths in height; that which pertains to the realm of fragrance (gandhabhava) and so forth is not higher than that.
However, the image made of flour (paiṣṭī) and other materials, as well as those made from fruit, should be according to their own respective proportions, measuring five finger-breadths.
The Gāndha-liṅga bestows good fortune, while the Paiṣṭa-liṅga grants worldly enjoyment;
these should be worshipped on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or in a mandala during initiations, installations, and other such rites.
For those desiring success, other [types of rosaries] made from a single year’s growth are prescribed here;
the conch-shell rosary bestows honor from masters, while that made from elephant tusars cut by an army [bestows victory]. (79)
The Kūrmaka-sikā, when produced, bestows upon men the accomplishment of the netherworld (pātāla);
it arises from the lineage of men such as Aṇimā and others, perpetually through the mutual half-months.
There are eight types of flour-based [cakes], known as *saṅgri-kṛṣṇaka* (or *sadbhikṛṣṭaka*, or *saṃbaddhakṛṣṭaka*).
That which is produced from the flour of *śāli* rice leads to nourishment (*puṣṭi*), while that made from *ṣaṣṭika* rice increases nourishment (*puṣṭivardhana*). (81)
Wheat destroys wind-related diseases; barley-born food bestows strength and well-being; mung-bean flour causes dissension among enemies; and that produced from *śyāmāka* grain grants women.
Sesame paste bestows the earth; wild rice (nīvāra) destroys fear;
butter brings happiness; and cow dung destroys disease. (83)
Food is to be known as bestowing longevity; liquor made from molasses increases affection.
A *liṅga* fashioned from various fruits grants various desires. (84)
Sand from a riverbank bestows many virtues; that from Lavana brings good fortune;
sand from a desert is for the purpose of eradication; and that from a mountain peak brings about the destruction of enemies.
That which arises from bamboo sprouts brings about the increase of the lineage;
that which causes agitation in the city is for the citizens, while asafoetida (rāmaṭha) produces ferocity. (86)

An image made of clay mixed with *sārja* and *saiktha* is considered effective for attracting enemies and bringing about their death; one produced from a clay mold yields desired objects, and through its application as an ointment, all prosperity shall arise.
From the incense and so forth up to the seed-syllable (bimba), these are neither stable nor moving; having worshipped them for that duration and then dismissed them, who would cast them away? (88)
Having ground cow-sugar into a fine powder and mixed it with the kernel of a ripe tamarind fruit, one should boil it, smear it upon a cloth, dry it thoroughly, and then polish it. || 89 ||
The linga on cloth and other materials should be drawn in three ways using chalk, lac, kuṣṭha, nīlī, realgar, collyrium, mineral pigments, and liquid extracts.
Madhurā and Citralekhā should indeed be depicted with symmetrical joints;
they always rely on strength, transformation, shadow, vision, and emotional states.

The erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, the terrifying, the pathetic, the marvelous, and the peaceful—these nine aesthetic moods (rasas), consisting of various emotional states, appear in some [dramatic works]. (92)

Those made of cloth, those made of wood, and those that are red—by means of the correct ritual application of mantras—one may worship these according to one's own desire. Now, those made of clay are being described.
The rite is "unripe" when performed according to the primary or secondary arrangement;
it is "ripe" through the immediate mantra, or by the sequence beginning with the nine-fold [rite], and so forth. 94.
One should prepare a superior, cooked [mud-pitcher] three cubits in size, endowed with the formidable mantras;
it may be made from the earth of the twice-born castes and so forth, or according to one's desire, using unmanifested [ordinary] clay. || 95 ||
One should collect earth from lotus ponds, from riverbanks, and from the roots of trees; as well as from step-wells, wells, tanks, and long oblong ponds.
It should always be made from well-kneaded clay or baked clay;
for the sake of nourishment, it should have a core of the three metals, and for the increase of wealth and treasures.
Having gathered pure stones, the knower of mantras, having prepared the funeral pyre with the mantra called Vāma and having cremated it with Ghora, [should proceed]. (98)
Having cleansed the linga with the Śivāgni mantra and having looked at it with the Puruṣa mantra,
one should take hold of it with the Īśāna mantra, and then, having consecrated it, one should worship it.

The five barks, neem roots, water, the marrow of *bilva*, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), resin (*sarja*), asafoetida, *pura* (guggulu—so called because "pura" is explained as guggulu in the *Dharaṇī*; "bola" is *gandharasa*, as in Amara's lexicon: "bola, *gandharasa*, and *prāṇa*"), and linseed oil. (100)

Having cast the powder of śrī, bāla, godhūma, yava, māṣa, and atasī into clay—[“sana” refers to the *ghaṇṭāpāṭali* tree; according to the *Bṛhad-vācaspatya*, it is also called *haskirṇa*]—and having prepared it, one should knead it for a month. || 101 ||
First, having made the bone-binding firm with strong iron and wood, and having joined it with hemp fibers, one should fashion a beautiful vessel out of clay. (102)
Having cast in the minerals, medicinal herbs, gems, metals, and grains in their proper order;
and in the absence of these, mercury combined with diamond (vajra). 103.
For the enrichment of the colors, one should apply a coating made of well-nourished *karkara* seeds combined with milk, curd, young molasses, and both cow’s products and *sarja* resin. 104.

One should go to the forest or the woods for the purpose of gathering firewood when it is joined with a favorable lunar door, a lunar mansion, and a season, and endowed with an auspicious ascendant. 105.
Then, at the time of departure, one should likewise observe the omens—those celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial—in order to obtain the results of both auspicious and inauspicious [signs]. (106)

"Having the brilliance of the sun drinking from a perfectly clear path through the atmosphere," and so forth—such is the auspicious divine [dream]; whereas this [following] one produces inauspiciousness. (107)
The falling of meteors, thunderbolts, and stars, the appearance of comets, the burning of the quarters, violent winds, and the eclipsing of the moon and sun. (Mūla, A, Kha: *pasajjana*) 108.
(14) Suddenly there was a sound in the sky, the falling of fruits and flowers, and the sweet cries of crows perched upon the tops of the trees in Vāsava’s grove. || 109 ||
O circle of birds, this atmosphere was once auspicious;
now the atmosphere is inauspicious, with this terrible rain of dust and blood.
Now I shall describe the auspicious terrestrial omens:
curd, unbroken grains, barley, *dūrvā* grass, a lamp, yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), and a banner. (111)
A conch, an umbrella, fruit, a flower, gold, grain, a lotus, a crane, a cow, a bull, a donkey, a horse, ashes, a dice, a king, and an elephant. (112)
The sight of a prostitute, fish, meat, and the like is auspicious; likewise, Śiva, a jar filled with water, and an owl on the left side are auspicious. (113)
Know that on the left side (savyataḥ) there is inauspiciousness, such as the sight of an empty pitcher and the like;
likewise, loose hair, being struck by others, alkaline substances, charcoal, and wood. (114)
An anointed man, a serpent, a mendicant, a Śākya and a Daṇḍin, one with severed limbs, one without eyes, a diseased person, a skull-bearer, and one who causes the earth to tremble. || 115 ||
Chaff, cow-dung, cotton, oil, *taṛu*-grass, one who is hungry, one who is emaciated, a madman, a weaver, and a collection of medicinal herbs and seeds; these are the five. (116)
They desire movement during auspicious [periods] and cessation during inauspicious ones;
having abandoned half of a half-pakṣa (one-quarter of a lunar fortnight), the departure is made during the auspicious time.
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, there are seven constellations each in the directions starting from the east;
they belong to the Vedas and the worlds respectively, for the path traversed does not exceed the measure of the fire-sticks (the twelve zodiacal signs).

Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, musical instruments, auspicious songs, and Vedic chants, one should proceed first to the forest of Śaṅkara— praised for rites such as sacrifices— and then to the forest of the Moon and Indra.

And during the six months beginning with Māgha, one should not perform it on a *riktā* lunar day in the bright fortnight; nor when Mercury, the Sun, the Moon, Venus, or Jupiter are situated in a tree-sign (cardinal sign) or in the eastern or northern directions [or in a fixed sign]. (120)
In yogas designated as auspicious, in a karaṇa other than Viṣṭi, when the lunar mansions are at intervals of one, and in all other inauspicious activities. || 121 ||
Meru, Mandara, Śveta, Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Nīla, Gandhamādana, Śṛṅgin, and Ketur are the lords of mountains.
Mahendra, Pāriyātra, Hariścandra, Śuktimān, the one named Nanda, Malaya, Vindhya, Ujjayanta, and Ṛkṣaka. || 123 ||
Likewise, Śrīśaila and Sahya are renowned as principal mountain ranges;
ten yojanas from these mountains lies a forest.
On the bank of the river originating from that [source], there shall always be a grove;
and those auspicious stones and trees which have arisen from this sacred field [are likewise auspicious]. (125)
The performer himself, or another person seeking his welfare, should go forth, accompanied by the preceptor, the practitioner, and auspicious artisans. (126)

Having eaten the sacrificial oblation (caru) and consumed curd, and having likewise bowed to the full jar, one should meditate upon the primordial principle (tattva) below as the earth consisting of the Śiva-principle. (127)

Then, having cleared away the directions with the Astra-mantra for the destruction of obstacles, the preceptor should meditate upon the Vidyārājñī standing before him, holding an offering (argha) in her hand.
Having properly prepared the requisites, meditating upon the Three-eyed One,
and having performed the ritual for the protection of the mantra, he should recite the mantra while worshipping his chosen deity.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Entry into the Forest for Determining Gender and Substance," within the Compendium of Characteristics. || 1 ||

Now, the second [chapter] correctly describes the nature of the patron, the preceptor, and the artisans who assume the forms of the deities, regarding both desired and undesired results in their work.
One who is upright, wealthy, deeply devoted, peaceful in soul, fearful of what is unseen, steadfast, and a performer of the teachings of the scriptures—such a performer is the excellent sāttvika. (2)
One who is wretched, deceitful, unrighteous, and addicted to vices is considered to be of the *rājasa* nature;
one who is an atheist, a mere logician, cruel, and a doer of evil is the lowest type, belonging to the *tāmasa* nature. (3)
One's intellect, impelled by the Lord, should be directed toward the establishment of Śiva;
therefore, those gurus who are described in His scriptures should be sought out.
Those from Oujjanyā, the Madhyadeśas, the Kauruṣakas, and the Lāṭajas;
those from Antarvedī, Pratiṣṭhāna, and Śrāvastī—these are the excellent teachers. (5)
The Rāḍhas, Vārendras, Tairas, Gaujaras, Māgadhas, Āṅgas, and those born of the Jāṭas—these seven are remembered as the middle [castes]. || 6 ||
The Āndhras, Kāliṅgas, Kārṇāṭas, Māhārāṣṭras, Ḍhakkajas, Vīrajas, Drāviḍas, and Pauṇḍras—these eight are the lowest gurus. (7)
The Kāmarūpas, Campākas, those from Nepāla, the Saindhavas, the Vāṅgas, Gāndhāras, and Pauliṅgas—these seven are considered the lowest castes (antyajas). || 8 ||
The Kāñcikās, Kosalas, Kācchas, Kāveras, those born in Koṅkaṇa and Oḍra,
the Saurāṣṭras, and the Devarāṣṭras— these eight are severely censured.
The best [images] grant all desires without exception; the middling ones bestow prosperity;
and the lowest and so forth are not desired for auspicious purposes, yet they indeed cause no harm in Āryāvarta.
The region situated between the Sindhu and the Karatoyā rivers, as well as between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, is celebrated as Āryāvarta. || 11 ||
They consist of four feet and three awakenings, adorned with six paths;
they are joined with lineages and spheres of activity, and possess the characteristics prescribed by the samayas.
The four lineages (gotras) are Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, and Manonmanī.
The four spheres of activity (gocarās) are Śiva, Śikha, Vimalajyotis, and Sāvitra—this is the reading found in the written manuscripts.
Ṛcīka, Ātreya, Daurvāsas, and Gautama—these four are in the intermediate period.
Those who know the Saṃhitā, complete with the qualities of initiation (or endowed with the establishment of initiation), [13]
(19) Those teachers should be known as such; otherwise, they are worldly hypocrites.
The Śaivas born in Bhāryāvarta are endowed with all the [required] characteristics. (14)

They should be disciplined and endowed with devotion, knowledgeable of the *liṅgas* and conversant with the scriptures; they should know the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*), abodes, and sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), and be experts regarding the locations for consecration.

They know the times of the days, stars, and so forth; they are knowers of the presiding deities; they are entirely free from greed and delusion; they are peaceful, self-controlled, and devoid of envy. (16)
Endowed with the observances and vows, possessed of compassion and courtesy,
they were sattvic, skillful, dexterous, and knowers of the fivefold meaning of the Śruti.
Established in reality, with doubts severed, they observe the conduct of the sacred rules;
firm in their vows, free from malice toward living beings, truthful in speech, and compassionate toward all creatures. (18)
Endowed with the consecration of command (ājñābhiṣeka) and devoted to the six rites, these four—the Brāhmaṇas and the others—are initiated into this Śiva scripture. (19)
They were honored as teachers for the purpose of performing the act of universal grace;
he who was united with the Śiva-principle attained the very form of Śiva. (20)
For one who lives by the Śiva-dharma, there shall be the destruction of [lowly] birth;

just as earth, wood, stone, and gems may be transformed into their respective higher species, so too for Śūdras and others, through the application of mantras, there shall be the attainment of excellence [even for the lowly]. || 21 ||
Just as copper and other metals become gold through the application of mercury when perfected,
even so, through union with mantra, one of the four castes becomes Śiva.
Just as the waters of city streams and other sources attain oneness upon reaching the Gaṅgā, so too, through initiation by the Lord, even a Śūdra or others shall attain the state of Śiva. (23)
Through initiation, the embodied soul is liberated, even while remaining in the body;
just as a pot on a potter’s wheel continues to spin due to the momentum of its previous motion.

Bound by the fetters of its own karma, the individual soul (paśu) is dependent on impurity (mala). Just as one destroys a venomous snake by means of the power of a mantra, so too does one destroy that impurity through the splendor of the mantra.
Just as water turbid with mud becomes clear when placed in a jar through contact with the *kataka* fruit, so too does a human being become pure through mantras. || 26 ||
Just as a ploughman ploughs, or as a turner turns [the lathe], so too, having destroyed impurity through the power of mantra, one becomes Śiva. || 27 ||
Just as fire is produced from a gem through contact with the rays of the sun, so too does the state of Śiva arise for the bound soul (paśu) through contact with the mantra of the Lord. || 28 ||
Mantras consist of Śiva and Śakti and are endowed with the powers of Śiva and Śakti;
the Śaiva teachers bestow the state of Śiva upon all that is moving and unmoving.
Just as clay, gems, and metals attain divinity through mantras,
so too the preceptor who knows the mantras attains the state of Śiva in this very way.
The gods abide in the reality of mantra; mantra is Maheśvara himself in person.
Indeed, the gods, the teachers, and the ascetics are consecrated by means of mantras. (31)
Just as a linga made of wood, stone, metal, clay, or precious gems is established and worshipped by one who knows the Veda, so too is a Śūdra a spiritual guide (daiśika).
He who bestows the state of Śiva upon the various classes of substances such as clay and the like—he himself shall become Śiva, and never anything else. (33)

Just as those bitten by a snake— whether they be outcastes or the twice-born and others— awaken from their sleep through the application of mantras, so too, O Śivā, is that which was lost or undesirable restored.

Just as a helmsman leads the twice-born and others to the further shore in an instant by means of a boat, so too does the Śaiva teacher lead them to the supreme state by means of the boat of mantra. (35)
"Just as a helmsman reaches the opposite shore by boat in an instant,
so too does the Teacher proceed to the supreme state by means of the boat of mantra.
Just as a peace treaty made during the Kṛta age lasts for four thousand divine years, [so does this teaching endure]."
In the remainder, however, there is a decrease by one for each; and at a thousand, it proceeds by hundreds [or two hundred, according to the variant]. || 37 ||
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, there is one day of Prajāpati; the measure of Viṣṇu is ordained to last for as long as a hundred such [days] of Pitāmaha.
In half a *nimiṣa* of Rudra [or Candra], fourteen thousand Upendras perish, as do innumerable Pitāmahas. (39)
By a single day of Īśa, many Haras are destroyed;
by the blink of an eye of Sādākhya, Īśa goes to dissolution—of this there is no doubt. (40)
But through its own will or by the fault (or anger) of another, that which is called Sādākhya dissolves therein;
"There is nothing higher than Śiva"—this is the certainty established in the scriptures. (41)
Thus, according to the specific mental dispositions of individuals, the potency of the mantra is likewise;
therefore, the mantra originating from Śiva bestows the fruits of both accomplishment (siddhi) and liberation (mukti).
How could he, whose mother is Vāgīśī and whose father is Śiva, the pervader of the sky, who was born through mantras at the sacrifice of Śiva—how could such a person be a Śūdra again? (43)
Just as earthen objects such as jars do not become clay again through refinement (*saṃskāra*), [so it is with those who have fallen]. (Note: This following passage is interpolated in manuscript *ka*:
"Those Brahmins and others who wander about having been consecrated by an improper door, having violated the Veda, are clearly fallen from their initiation and [reborn] in the Raurava hell.")
In the same way, the initiation mantras are brought together by their very nature;
likewise, the destruction of sin arises as something natural. || 44 ||

Having killed [the officiants], and having performed the initiation, consecration, and so forth with Caṇḍa, those Brahmins and others have been cast down; they are destined for hell in this world, not saviors.
If, through the rite of purification by Śiva, the state of being Śiva were not attained by men, then surely the twice-born and the teachers of the gods and others would not exist. (46)
Therefore, with respect to restraint and favor, the mantra is primary;
for poisons, spirits, planetary influences, and the like are indeed restrained by means of the mantra.
When the moving and unmoving world has been consecrated by the Guru through mantras, purificatory rites, and initiation, it certainly attains the state of Śiva at that very moment.
The fourfold caste system is to be favored, and food is to be eaten from within the fourfold caste system;
this perfected state is eternally Śaiva, having the form of the Guru and being unborn.
Wearing loincloths and girdles, with matted hair and sacred threads,
all of them were celibate students (brahmacārins) whose names ended in "Śiva" and whose bodies were smeared with ashes.
By initiation, initiation is destroyed; indeed, a previous initiation perishes. A general [initiation] is superseded by a specific one, and the same applies to the guru as well.
Those ending with a *nagaṇa* are indeed the Vaiśeṣas, while those ending with a *śiva* (short syllable) are designated as Śaivas.
Just as the lotus is called both *ambhoja* and *paṅkaja*, so too are the Śaivas, and not others.

Just as one who possesses a hand is called "hastin" (an elephant) by conventional usage and not otherwise, so too are the Śaivas, Pāśupatas, and others designated by their respective Śiva-liṅgas. (53)
He who regards ascetics and the teacher-gods as being of the same nature as the [other] gods, being joined with the fruits of such a distinction of signs, goes certainly to the Raurava hell. (54)
(24) Because it would contradict what is seen and what is unseen, there is no such injunction for others;
otherwise, one would become a doer of evil—such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (55)

Therefore, one should determine the gurus; for the supreme Śaiva tradition is twofold, existing in two ways distinguished by the states of being a celibate student (brahmacārī) and a householder (gṛhastha). || 56 ||
I shall now describe, according to their various divisions, the rites for those seeking specific desires and for those free from desire, endowed with the qualities that will be explained hereafter.

The performance of rites such as installation (pratiṣṭhā) is prescribed specifically for those who desire ascetic practice (tapas). A seeker of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, being a man of desire, should perform initiation and other rites by the command [of the Guru].
The householder is said to be of two kinds: the one seeking progeny (sāntānika) and the one dedicated to vows (vratārpaka).
The performance of rites such as consecrations (pratiṣṭhā), when carried out by the latter, is highly praised. (59)
One who is joined with a wife, possesses hair, is devoid of matted locks and the like,
and whose conduct pertains to the office of Śiva— he is called a *sāntānika*.

He who, being unable to observe the vows himself, offers the vow according to the prescribed rite and subsequently performs his marriage, is known as a *vratārpaka* (one who has offered the vow) and is a householder.
He should constantly practice celibacy, endowed with matted hair and ashes;
subsisting on alms and self-restrained, he is proclaimed as a true observer of vows.
The Guru [should act] gradually through the lineages, spheres of activity, and conventions;
however, the designation "flower-fall" is intended for the *maṭhī* by means of the mudrās. (63)
Women, garlands, perfumes, wealth, beds, seats, betel, ornaments, fine garments, collyrium, and oil—indeed, he who delights in these leads himself [to ruin]. (64)

A wise man should always choose for the sake of enjoyment one who is intent on progeny, and for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation one who has undertaken the vows that remove obstacles; likewise, for the sake of final emancipation (*mākṣa*), he should choose one who is observant of the vows. || 65 ||
A householder has two kinds of sons: those concerned with the world beyond and those concerned with this world.
The son who shares in worldly wealth is the one for this world; the one who shares in sacred knowledge is the one for the world beyond.
Whatever scripture, debt, or wealth belongs to a disciple observing vows belongs to the guru.
In the absence of the guru, it belongs to the brothers; for householders, it shall go to their own sons.
If a son, a grandson, or those born of their lineage are unfit for the rites of Śiva, one who is related to the Ghaṇṭā (the bell) shall take [the property], just as iron is drawn by a magnet.
The son of one who observes vows shall be fit for all ritual acts;
he alone is praised as the sole [heir] in respect of debt, property, and the ancestral funeral cake (piṇḍa). || 69 ||
The teacher, arisen through the lineage of disciples, is the performer of auspicious peace;
and among the four spheres of activity, he who belongs to Śiva is supreme as the eldest.

Since the primordial Śiva is all-pervading and acts for the benefit of all, the Śaiva teacher is therefore supreme; he shall install all the deities. (Alternatively, the reading is "together with the deities. || 71 ||

The Lord Śiva is the supreme vessel worthy of sacrificial gifts, the most excellent among those to be seen, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; indeed, there is no other teacher who is the creator of the universe. (72)
A follower of Śiva is desired as the installer for all deities; however, in his absence, those who observe the vows of their own respective deities should be appointed.
By birth one is born a Śūdra; by ritual action one is called a twice-born (dvija);
by sacred learning one is a Śrotriya; and by the practice of celibate studentship (brahmacarya) one becomes a Brāhmaṇa.
A Brahmin is consecrated by his own mantras and is a protector of his own duties and vows;
since he shares the same human nature as others, what cause for hatred is there toward a Śiva-brahmin? (75)

Just as there are distinctions among women, men, and neuters according to their three genders, such is not the case for the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes; therefore, caste is not the cause [of distinction].
For the sake of purifying the five principles, this sacred thread fashioned from the five Brahmans should always be worn by Śaiva teachers, and not by others. (77)
The Brahmin is Śiva, the King is the tuft (śikhā), and the one of Śūdra birth is the knower of luminaries (jyotirvit);
thus are these various leaves described in the Śiva-āgama as Sāvitra. 78.
Guru is Śiva among the three beginning with Śikha; he is designated as Śikha. It is said that Jyotis belongs to two [of them], while Sāvitra is within his own domain.
Accompanied by the beautiful sounds of trumpets, musical instruments, drums, conchs, and shells, all the Śaiva teachers were adorned with banners and parasols like kings. (80)
In whatever kingdom the preeminent Guru should be established, there shall be prosperity, victory, peace, health, and the increase of Dharma. (81)
When the deity has been installed by these [means], the patron, endowed with people and wealth,
increases in longevity, fame, prosperity, and with sons and grandsons.
His ancestors rejoice as long as the deities remain;
for thousands of yugas, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
The long-term prosperity of both the site and the deity arises;
the practitioner does not die prematurely and thereafter attains the state of Śiva. (84)
As long as his fame and renown endure, so long does he enjoy great fruit;
having attained the state of Rudra, he experiences imperishable happiness.

Furthermore, those who originate from lowly regions and others who are highly censured elsewhere—one should always employ all of them in cruel rites. (Note: This reading, which appears in manuscript *gh*, is an addition and is irrelevant to the context.)
Those with missing limbs, those with extra limbs, the hunchbacked, the dwarfed, and the lame;
the deformed, the variegated, the fierce, the deceitful, the cruel, and those of wicked livelihood. (87)

Those who are sinful, diseased, or possess little knowledge, those who subsist on the shadow of a deity, those with speech or throat disorders, the deaf, the corpulent, those with deformed nails, and those with ill-formed hair; 88.
Astrologers, logicians, physicians, servants, as well as farmers, priests, those who live by trade, merchants, and alchemists; (89)
Those who wear the sectarian marks, those of evil conduct, gamblers, and libertines;
those with crooked noses and hanging lips, the foolish, and those with trembling limbs. (90)
Fools born of evil associations, with voices like crows and nasal tones;
elders who corrupt the scriptures, the profligate, and those who have fallen from their commitments. || 91 ||

Those who are protruding-toothed, suffering from elephantiasis, paralyzed, afflicted with tumors, or having goiters—by these, the gods are established as destroyers of wealth, longevity, and sons. (92)
Those born from women of other stages of life, *punarbhūs*, *kuṇḍas*, and *golakas*;
*katthakas* (or *kaṇṭhakas*), *kauśikas* (or *kaulikās*), those born of such unions, those with three earlobes (*trikarṇa*), and others are excluded. || 93 ||

The Cārvākas, the Ārhats, the Buddhists, the twice-born followers of the Sāṅkhya philosophy, and others who observe the vow of renunciation have no authority in the matter of establishing [the image]. (94)
Formerly, the Magas, who were eaters of cow-flesh, were brought from Śākadvīpa by Śambhu, the son of Acyuta, for the purpose of consuming the remains of offerings (nirmālya). 95.
He who, without having received Śaiva initiation, merely recites the scriptures and constantly installs [images of] Śiva and the other deities, is a self-willed man, the lowest of men. (96)
He who, having abandoned the *liṅga* he had obtained, practices the Śaiva vow—that person is to be known as a *punarbhū* (one who has been reborn/returned) and must be avoided in the Śiva-āgama. (97)
If a son is born from a paramour while the husband is still alive, he is a *kuṇḍa* and will be cruel by nature; but if the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*.
One who is born of the teacher’s lawful wives is the teacher’s son; he is ruined by renunciation, first through association with women and likewise afterwards. (99)
He who is lost to both [lineages] has as his offspring the Katthakas;
those born from the three ears are the Trikarṇas, and from the three mouths they are the Trikarnakas.
From the constant and occasional worship of guests, the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, there arose Bhasmāṅkura;
his sons were Kauśika and the others.
The Bhojakas, Vratiputras, Kauśikas, and others who are despicable—these, as well as those men who are heretics, are indeed the destroyers of the kingdom. (102)
But that fool who performs the installation without first observing the rules and so forth—O Caṇḍeśa, he is punished merely by the inspection of the scriptures. 103.
If one who is a devotee of Śiva, with a mind deluded by greed, should install Īśa [in another temple], that preceptor goes immediately to hell along with the officiating priests. (104)
Regarding those five commitments that have been proclaimed by Śambhu for the five currents, one is celebrated as an Ācārya through the constant practice of them. (105)
The teacher, in the form of Śiva, acts for the benefit of the world;
therefore, one should not entertain a human notion regarding the spiritual guide.
Īśa, Vaktra, Aghora, Guhya, and that which is named Ajāta—these are the five faces of the God for the expansion of the five Āgamas. (107)
*Kāmika*, *Yogaja*, *Māntrī* [or *Cintya*], *Kāraṇa*, and likewise *Ajita*; *Dīpta*, *Sūkṣma*, *Sāhasra*, *Aṃśumat*, and *Suprabha*—these are the ten. (108)
The divisions of Śiva have been fully described; hereafter follow the divisions of Rudra:
Vijaya, Pārameśvara, and that known as Niśvāsa-udgīta. (109)
Prodgīta, Mukhabimba, Siddha, Santāna,
Narasiṃha, Candrahāsa, Vīra, Svāyambhu, and Aurava.

Makuṭa, Kirāṇa, Lalita, Virasa, and Parama (Smara)—these are declared to be the divisions of Rudra, numbering eighteen, including those that ascend upwards. (This reading, contained within the bow-shaped mark, does not appear in manuscript Ka.)
Hara, Huṅkāraka, Bindusāra, Kalāmṛta,
Davatrāsa, Sutrāsa, Sāvara, and Kālasāvara;
Pakṣirāja, Śikhāyoga, Śikhāsāra, and Śikhāmṛta.
And the classification of the five elements (or five nectars), as well as the determination of the divisions of emptiness. || 113 ||
Kālakāṇṭha, Kālāṅga, Kālakūṭa, Paṭadruma, Kamboja, Kambala, Kaṅka, Kālakuṇḍa, and Kaṭāhaka. || 114 ||
Suvarṇarekhā, Sugrīva, Tottala, and Tottalottara—these are declared to be the twenty-eight divisions of the Gāruḍa. || 115 ||
Svacchandabhairava, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava, Asitāṅga, Ruru, Kapālīśa, and Samuccaya. (116)
The non-terrible, the roaring, the terrible, the one with a foul face wandering at night;
the one with fearsome limbs, the one with a tumultuous cry, the formidable crusher of Vetālas. || 117 ||
Ucchuṣma, Vāma, Kāpāla, Śekhara, Puṣpa, Advaya, Triśira, and Ekapāda—these constitute the Siddhayogeśvarīmata. (118)
The Five Nectars, the Manifestation, the Yoginījālasaṃvara, Viśvarikaṇṭhasaṅkoca, and Tilakodyānabhairava. || 119 ||
Thus, there are thirty-two tantras along with their superior counterparts; these two groups together comprise sixty-four in number, and they have originated from the southern face.
The *Nayottara*, the *Mūka*, the *Mohana*, and the *Mohāmṛta*;
then the *Karapūjāvidhāna* and the *Vīṇātantra*, which is superior to that. (121)
Jaya, Vijaya, Ajita, Aparājita, Siddhanityodaya, Jyeṣṭha, and Cintāmaṇimahodaya. || 122 ||
The Vāgbhava, the Kuhaka, the Citra, the Kāmadhenu-kadambaka, the one called Ānanda-rudra-bhadra, the Kiṅkara, and the follower of Kiṅkara. (123)
The Anantavijaya, the Śaukra, the Daurvāsa, the Bījabhedaka, the Vāmada, and that which was spoken by Vāmadeva—these comprise twenty-four varieties. (124)
Halāhala, Hayagrīva, Karakoṭa, Kaṭaṅkaṭa, Karoṭa, Muṇḍamāla, Kaṅkoṭa, and Khaḍgarāvaṇa. || 125 ||
The fierce edge of a sword, the sound *huṃ*, the cry *hā hā*, the howling of jackals, the terrible loud laughter, the impure, the gurgling, and that which terrifies the wicked. (126)
Vimala, Vikaṭa, Sudhāraṇa (or Svadhāvaṇa), Mahotkaṭa, Yamaghaṇṭa, Bhūtāhva (or Bhūtāṅga/Bhūtājya), Viṣabheda, and Ajātajam. 127.
Thus, there are one hundred and sixty-four Śaiva Tantras;
furthermore, this compendium of scriptures is divided into a further million distinct varieties.
From Śiva comes Rudra; from him the gods; likewise from the gods the sages (ṛṣis);
from the sages come human disciples, the bringers forth of all the scriptures. || 129 ||
The Siddhānta, Gāruḍa, Bhairava, Vāma, and Bhautika—thus has the pentad of scriptures (āgama-pañcaka) pertaining to the observance (sāmayika) been proclaimed by Śambhu. (130)
In the Siddhānta, it is the eating of food from the four castes; in the Gāruḍa, it is poison;
in the Ghora, it is eating together; and likewise, in the Vāma, it is the nectar of the left (vāmāmṛta). || 131 ||
In the *Bhūtatantre*, touching a corpse is itself the procedure for the five streams;
he who practices the five commitments is called an *ācārya*. || 132 ||
One should practice the conduct prescribed by Śiva, as declared in the scriptures and spoken by the Guru;
for that must certainly be performed, otherwise there will be a fall.
(33) Worship, fire-offerings, oblations, alms-giving, sacrificial porridge, and honoring guests—these six duties must be performed by the Śivācārya, and not by others. (134)
Exegesis, listening, giving, receiving, initiation, and consecration—these are the six duties of the Guru at all times. (135)
A disciple should not perform initiation or the installation of an image in the immediate presence of the preceptor;
rather, having departed for five *krośas*, he should perform it according to the preceptor’s instruction.
The initiate (samayin) should abide by the rules; the spiritual son (putraka) is one who has heard the tradition (āgama);
the practitioner (sādhaka) should accomplish the siddhis; and the teacher (ācārya) should initiate the bound souls (paśus). || 137 ||
He who has been consecrated according to the sequence beginning with the *samaya* is a *deśika*;
for him, the rites such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) do not depend on the priority of birth or the priority of recitation. (138)
Regarding the proper installation of Śiva and the other deities according to the path of logic for the wise,
a certain reasoning is indicated here, which was also taught in the *Pārameśvara*.
Where a twice-born man, out of greed, installs Śiva based on mere recitation alone—not upon stone or other materials—there is no state of Śiva there; indeed, for such a person, Śiva is far away.

If a twice-born man should ever, out of negligence, install deities, he becomes an outcaste whose food is not to be eaten; he is a sinner—of this there is no doubt. (In version kh, gh: "he would become a denizen of hell.")
By installing a Śiva-liṅga, a Brahmin is certainly born into the womb of a dog;
by casting a blade of Kuśa grass into another’s lineage (gotra), that lowest of twice-born men becomes a denizen of hell.

Those twice-born who recite the Vedas according to their own whim, those who perform sacrifices without instruction, and those who establish [idols] based on mere marks and the like, are equal to outcasts. (143)
Such conduct may exist even among Śūdras, yet it is not found in Brāhmaṇas;
a Śūdra should be regarded as equal to a Brāhmaṇa, for he is more sinful than a Śūdra.
Viśvāmitra became a twice-born through his conduct as a Kṣatriya; Vasiṣṭha and others attained perfection through their conduct. This was stated by Vyāsa in the Mahābhārata.
Having abandoned sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and instead established Śiva [as the object of worship],
the performer quickly falls into hell along with his ancestors.

Those who do not turn back toward the goal of spiritual establishment and who do not remain fixed in the state of the twice-born—their own status as Brahmins is lost, and the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā) remains established within them. 147.

Those [deities] such as Śiva and others who are established by Brahmins who have stolen the status of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as cruel and destructive, bringing about the ruin of the patron. || 148 ||
O Brahmin, by installing Śiva and other deities, one falls from both states in an instant;
he becomes unworthy of gifts, worship, and so forth, just as a Brāhmaṇa who has lost his status. (149)
Just as honey situated in a wicked vessel becomes sour and causes harm, so too the Vedas, when placed with a corrupt priest, bring about misfortune for the performer. (150)
Śiva, Śiras, Jyotis, and Sāvitra as the fourth—these are declared to be Śaivas, but they are never Brāhmaṇas. || 151 ||
In the sacrifice to Śiva, for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have been consecrated, their previous births are destroyed. || 152 ||
Those who are Brahmins are not Śaivas, and those who are Śaivas are not Brahmins; for their mantras and scriptures are distinct, and their vows and sacrifices are separate. (153)
In the Kali age, those base Brahmins who are greedy, foolish, destroyers of their own Vedic knowledge, engaged in improper acts, and deluded, perform the installation of Śiva and other deities. (154)
Just as the Śaiva and other mantras are not used in the sacrifices of the twice-born, Buddhists, and others, so too the Vedic and other mantras are not used in the sacrifices of Śiva. (155)
In the Veda there is no threefold linga, nor the characteristics of a temple,
nor gates, pavilions, and so forth, nor the installation of Śiva and the other deities.
The definition beginning with Śaṅkara and others has been stated precisely in the Śivasiddhānta; therefore, one should install Śiva and the other deities by means of a Śaiva mantra. (157)
The *liṅga* of Śiva is twofold, by way of the distinction between the moving and the unmoving (*carācara*).
Through the mantras of Śiva, the state of Śiva is properly attained for both of these, but not through other mantras. (158)
The installation of Śiva cannot be performed by means of the Vedas, nor by the Pañcarātras, nor even by the Agamas spoken by the sages, nor by the mantras of other philosophical systems. || 159 ||
The Śaiva consecration is not in the Veda, nor is the Śiva-vow in the Veda;
neither is the Śaiva ritual in the Veda, nor are the supernatural powers such as the sword and so forth.
The purificatory rites beginning with conception, the vows of the three castes,
and sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, which are declared in the Vedas, were indeed established by the Lord.
The Śaiva vow for the four castes, which accomplishes the four aims of life and establishes the Siddhānta, as well as initiation (dīkṣā), were not taught by Śambhu in the Vedas.

Just as a banyan tree (*vaṭa*) arises from a very small seed, so too does a disciple arise from his own seed; likewise, the gods are born from the seed-syllables of their own mantras, not from the ostentation of many syllables. (163)
The twice-born who offer salutations, the students, and those who live by recitation—these are not knowers of the reality of the path of Śiva; they are merely panegyrists who delight the common folk.
By which scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, is the Lord Śiva not praised?
By means of praise alone, the installation of the Śivaliṅga—whether mobile or immobile (or moving and unmoving)—is accomplished. (165)
The fivefold consecration which has been taught by Śiva in the Śiva-āgama should be performed by Śaiva preceptors for Rudra, Brahmā, Arka, and Cakrin.

All the planetary deities (grahas), as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with the nāgas, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, yoginīs, the Gaṇas, Gaurī, and other goddesses are to be established. || 167 ||
The cause of stability, arising, and destruction, as well as of pleasure and pain, is self-evident; yet the twice-born, blinded by passion, revile the Lord. 168.

Even those who follow the Pañcārtha system, such as the Kārakas and others, who are included within the fold of Śaivism, must be avoided in rites such as consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and the like; even more so, therefore, are Buddhists, Brahmins of other sects, and so forth, who should be shunned from afar.
Therefore, the installation of Śiva and the other deities must be performed by a wise Śivācārya who is himself of the nature of Śiva, and not by others such as Brāhmaṇas and the like.

The teachers of the sixfold systems, established eternally in their own respective doctrines, are Brahmins devoted to their own specific duties, beginning with the Śaivas and ending with the Kāpilas. (171)
A twice-born man who knows the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti, who observes the vows of his own scriptures, and who is constantly engaged in his six duties, should not perform any other work. 172.
Giving, receiving, reciting, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, and teaching—these are the six duties that always belong to a twice-born man. (173)
Through seasonal observances, austerity, charity, ancestral rites, and the worship of Vaiśvānara, a Brāhmaṇa who subsists on grass, roots, alms, or food is the most excellent. (174)
One who lives by the sword, one who lives by ink, a gatekeeper, a domestic priest, a messenger, and a seller of the Vedas—these six twice-born men are equal to Śūdras. (175)
The Śrutis are declared to be the Vedas, while the Smṛtis are nineteen in number:
Manu, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Kātyāyana, and Gautama; || 176 ||
Yājñavalkya, Savarta, Vyāsa, Viṣṇu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Hārīta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara; || 177 ||
The Smṛtis of Āpastamba and others, as well as their utterances, are the authoritative restrictors; these [other texts] such as the foremost Śaiva scriptures are not so. || 178 ||
The *Pratiṣṭhākalpa*, the *Kaumāra*, the *Kiraṇa*, the *Piṅgalāmata*, the *Devīmata*, the *Maya*, the *Nandi*, the *Pratiṣṭhā*, and the *Pārameśvara*. (179)
Bhāskara, Liṅgakalpa, Vidyāpurāṇavāṭhula, the one called Śaka, Vāmadeva, and likewise the two-fold Paitāmaha. || 180 ||
The Bāṇa, Garga, Yāmya, Haṃsa, and Vaiśvakarma—
these twenty-one Tantras of installation (pratiṣṭhā) were spoken by Śiva.
Having extracted the essence from these—the Nārada, the Pauṣkara, as well as the Padmottha, the Mārkaṇḍeya, and from Rambhā (or Gaurī), the Siddha, and so forth—[he composed this work]. (182)
And from the *Ratnaprayojana*, as well as from the *Ahitilaka* and others, and from the *Mārtaṇḍa*, one should observe all this collection of principles (*sarvatattva*). (183)
These many secret tantras are not for a Brāhmaṇa; the installation [of the deity] is to be performed by Śaivas established in the Śiva-āśrama, and not by those of other philosophical systems. 184.
Śaivas do not bow down to a linga installed by non-Śaiva twice-born men, nor to one established by those of other religious views. (185)
Remaining constantly established in the vow of Brahman, he should practice the vows of Śiva and others;
however, a twice-born man who is devoid of the Śaiva consecrations falls from both Umā and Śiva.

If [the bridegroom] falls away, whatever was performed for him, whatever sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) was received, and whatever rites such as the binding of the sacred thread were completed—all that shall become fruitless. || 187 ||
But when an action is performed by oneself in the form of another, that which is desired will not come to pass; there, this exertion is indeed in vain. (188)
Liberation in the grasping of all goals, as well as the supernatural powers (siddhis), are attained through the Śiva-āgamas;
how could these be obtained without the mantras spoken by Śiva? (189)

If there were a sign from the Vedas, how could there be worship by Śūdras and others? Or if it were by means of mixed [texts], then what of the fault and so forth, according to the scriptures associated with Kumāra and others? (190)
If one performs a different deity, a different mantra, and a different ritual procedure, his ritual action becomes fierce (caṇḍa), and he himself becomes a Caṇḍāla in his actions. (191)
It is not [attained] through one's own philosophical system because it has been so stated, nor from passion toward Brahmins and others, but rather from dispassion;
the beneficial means for achieving liberation in this world is established by logic, and that which was spoken by Skanda is now written here.
That ritual which was enjoined by sages such as Sanaka, Ātreya, Vyāsa,
and others would not be efficacious if it were corrupted by a confusion of mantras.

Just as the defects of sense objects and so forth are subject to decay, and the Vedic sciences—such as the Agniṣṭoma and other rites—are likewise impelled [by that nature], so too is their foundation desired [to be impermanent]. (194)

Vedic ritual action, which is performed for the sake of purity through wealth, lineage, mantras, and so forth, and which is virtuous and results in the world of heaven, should be understood as such. 195.
Falling away from the heavenly world and passing from the moon to the sun,
those performers of sacrifice reach the state of a tree and transmigrate here in this world.
Having performed a hundred sacrifices, Śakra attained the heavenly world;
yet, when his merit from those deeds was exhausted, he was born again among stationary beings and the like.
There is nothing superior to Satyaloka, nor is there any greater fruit of knowledge than that;
therefore, all those sages were not experts in the true meaning of Śiva. (198)
For all castes alike, the Śaiva rite is the bestower of fruit;
for the three beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, it is impelled by the knowledge of the Vedas. (199)

For one desiring the fruit known as heaven, [the deity is worshipped] always in sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, together with sacrificial porridge (caru), cake (puroḍāśa), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and so forth. || 200 ||
Śūdras and others have no entitlement here, and it is prohibited in the Veda. (Mū, A, K, Kh, G, Ṅ: "it is not prescribed").
And whoever should bestow upon Śūdras and others that which has been accomplished through Vedic knowledge... (201)
If that preceptor should partake of the sacrificial oblation along with them, he will certainly go to hell;
therefore, the ritual of Śiva has been perfected by the wise through Śaiva mantras.
In the ritual installation of Śiva and others, in sacrifice, and especially in initiation,
he is the supreme bestower of grace upon all castes.
Twenty thousand lakṣas, koṭis, and arbudas,
as well as a multitude of koṭis, kharvas, and abjas— these are the mantras that have issued forth from the Lord.
Seventy-two thousand, ten million, one hundred thousand,
and fifty thousand mantras have issued forth from the two mouths of Rudra.
Thirty thousand crores, seven hundred and eight, and thirty-six million mantras have emerged from Rudra. (206)
Nine thousand crores, eighty-five million, and five hundred crores of mantras have issued forth from the left. || 207 ||
Seven thousand million, thirty-seven hundred, one hundred, ten thousand, and one hundred thousand [mantras] have issued forth from Sadyojāta. (208)

The liṅga and other [images] should be installed with those mantras spoken by Śiva that arise from the five faces and bestow both supernatural powers (siddhi) and liberation (mukti); they should not be installed with others enjoined in the Vedas and such.
The letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa* have emerged from the body of Sadāśiva [emerged from Śiva].
By means of these, the fivefold scripture known as Śaiva was composed, which bestows both supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*).

For the sake of the great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhi) such as atomization (aṇimā), the Khecarīs and others are perfected; just as those previously mentioned by the Creator, such as Vyāḍi, Indradanta, Kambala, Bhāskara, and so forth, were perfected by relying upon the Liṅga. (p. 41)
Free from envy, the perfected ones (siddhas), who are auspicious, speak quickly when the mantra is recited over a corpse. || 212 ||
The word of the Lord is never false; who has not attained perfection age after age?
One who is initiated by those who know the reality of the correct ritual procedure is liberated from the state of a bound soul (paśu).
The Śaiva mantras possess seeds, radiate light, and extend from the heart up to the fire and Śiva; they are the bestowers of grace upon all and the accomplishers of the four aims of life. || 214 ||

The Śruti was composed in sequence by those whose faces were directed toward the east, south, north, and west, consisting of one hundred thousand verses each, as the Ṛg, Atharva, Sāma, and Yajur Vedas respectively. (215)
The gods described in the Vedas with preceding hymns of praise are not of a corporeal nature;
apart from spiritual perfection and liberation, they are considered by all to be nothing more than mere words. (216)

The Vedic revelation spoken by the Lord is intended as the basis for the three Vedas and for the vow of the three [fires] at the sacrifice; subsequently, it serves as the means for achieving the fruit known as heaven. (217)
In the Śaiva Āgamas and Purāṇas, as well as in other scriptures,
it is stated by Avadhūta that Brahmā and Viṣṇu are ignorant and subject to bowing down.
Let alone any other [quality] of yours; even that sovereignty which is the cause for the title "Lord," being of incomparable rank,
has reached its end here with you, O Blessed One.
Viṣṇu is united with Pitāmaha; what need is there for another? || 219 ||
If the Vedas were composed by non-Vedic Brahmins and others, they would be faulty;
[furthermore], for those who perform sacrifices, there would be hell after killing cows, humans, horses, and so forth. (220)
Having understood the suns of the Lord— his insatiability, primordial consciousness, sovereignty, eternally undiminished power,
and infinite potency— one who knows the ritual procedure [attains liberation].
They say these are the six limbs of Maheśvara. || 221 ||
The Vedas are declared by the authoritative sages to be the means of valid knowledge regarding heaven; [the Mīmāṃsakas hold that] heaven has the omniscient one as its cause.
Logicians, however, state on the basis of reasoning that God is the cause. || 222 ||
The division consists of the Sāṅkhya and the Yāna; the first is the Āślāyaka, and the second is the Dvitīyaka.
There are one thousand and ten mantras, and the Brāhmaṇa portion consists of two thousand [verses]. || 223 ||
For the Ṛgveda was indeed established as authoritative by Dvaipāyana and others;
likewise, there are one thousand nine hundred and two mantras of the Yajus.
There are one hundred and ten branches of the Brahmins, and eighty-six sub-branches;
namely, those known as the Kāṇvas and Mādhyandinas, as well as the Kaṭhas and the Prācyakaṭhas.
The Maitrāyaṇīya, the Taittirīya, the Vaijavāpī, the Nekā, and other such branches are established within the Yajurveda. (226)
One is known by the name Kauthuma (or Kaustuma), and the second is Carāyaṇī (or Dharāyaṇī);
there are also four Gānas, as well as the Veda and the Āraṇyaka. || 227 ||
The *ūha*, *ukha*, and the fourth, the *mantras*, are nine thousand; the *santus* and the *śatakas* are remembered as originating from Brahmā. (228)
In this regard, the measure of the Sāman is proclaimed to be exactly twenty-five.
Sumantu, Jājali, Ślokāyani, as well as another, Śaunaka, Pippalāda, Muñjakeśa, and others [are the authorities]. (229)
The Atharvasamuccaya was proclaimed by many sages who knew it;
it contains ten thousand eight hundred and six hundred mantras, along with a hundred Upaniṣads.
Therefore, the mantra and likewise the sacrificial rite for Śiva and the others should be performed with effort by one's own preceptor; otherwise, they yield defects. 231.
If Śiva is installed by means of mantras belonging to the Buddhists, the Arhats, the Vedists, or others,
there will be harm for the kingdom, the king, as well as for the one who performs the rite and the one who causes it to be performed.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are devoid of the Śaiva sacraments are declared to be inhabitants of hell; they cause ruin to the lineage of the performer [of the rite]. (233)
A twice-born man who establishes his status as a religious order (liṅga) merely through the study of books should be known as one of mixed livelihood; he is always unfit to be fed by the wise.
If one has eaten there due to compulsion or negligence, one should recite the Bahurūpa mantra one hundred times; thereby, one will indeed become free from fault.
This renowned twice-born man is indeed full of agitation; he is celebrated in the world as a teacher merely by name, for he is not one who possesses the ultimate truth. || 236 ||

When the initiation has been performed by the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) through the mantras for installation and so forth, the three kinds of teachers previously mentioned according to the lineage of gurus are to be accepted as the *deśikas*. (237) p. 44)
O Lord, that teacher who is established in either destruction or enjoyment—even if he is equal to Śiva—must be abandoned, for he is like one whose hand is burnt. (238)
Those who are perfected through the Śaiva sacraments, learned in the scriptures,
and excellent practitioners may install all the deities in the absence of a preceptor.
Disciplined, a speaker of Dharma, skillful, free from laziness, and devoid of envy;
upright, possessed of a sense of shame, virtuous, with anger conquered and senses subdued. || 240 ||
One who knows the object to be measured, the means of measurement, and the dimensions; who understands the site, the time, and so forth;
who possesses clear vision, is of noble birth, wise, free from agitation, and devoted to the well-spoken scriptures (sūtras). || 241 ||
He who knows the leaf-pattern, the four-legged base, the pillar, the pedestal,
the image, the temple, the pavilion, and the doorway— he indeed is a master craftsman.

Those who possess all limbs complete, who are endowed with the purificatory rites of Śiva, who know the rules for the performance of Śiva-dharma (or -karma), and who are image-protectors, preceptors, and so forth; || 243 ||
His companions should be of noble birth, steadfast, capable, and devoted;
they should be humble, skillful, dexterous, and obedient to the commands of their guru—or, according to some versions, to the king.
Thus ends the second procedure, titled "The Examination of the Author, Teacher, and Others," in the *Lakṣaṇasārasamuccaya*.
Now, the third [chapter]:
those auspicious trees or stones that are to be selected by the preceptors together with the artisans, according to their various species, are now being examined. (1)
The earth covered with forest flowers is that which is rich in water;
the *kāśmīrī* is in the east, while the *khadira* and *brahmavṛkṣaka* are in the south.
For one who feeds on amālaka fruits, pigeons, snakes, peacocks, vultures, and raw meat,
the earth appears as if filled with water within, yet in form it is like fire.
To the south there should be a field of rice, and to the west a milk-tree;
to the north there should be water, and in the northeast (Māhendrī) it should be provided with the Pīlu, Uddāla, and Snuhī plants.
That earth which is strewn with gravel and *arka* trees, filled with mirages,
devoid of grass and water, and abounding in jackals, is known as the airy (*vāyavī*) earth.
From these regions, stones and trees are produced in succession, consisting of the same nature as those regions;
those born from Māhendrī and Vāruṇī are weapons, while others are censured.
Spandana, madhuka, śipra, rudrākṣa, dhava, candana,
śamī, drākṣā, and surāhva— these nine grant peace to brahmins.
The *śrīvṛkṣa*, *āragvadha*, *ariṣṭa*, *śirīṣa*, red sandalwood (*aruṇacandana*), *kadara* (as defined by Vācaspati as *śvetakhadira*), *śoka*, *śāka*, and *śṛṅgī* bestow royal prosperity. (8)
Śyāmā, bakula, kāśmīrī, jambu, campaka, śiṃśapā,
sarala, panasa, and bīja— these indeed bestow prosperity upon Vaiśyas.
The *karṇikāra*, *arjuna*, *nimba*, *saptasāra*, *tinduka*, *kāñcanāsana*, *lodhra*, and *sāla* trees grant prosperity to the Śūdra. (10)
Those that are graspable, glossy, and large-bodied are to be accepted; those that are ungraspable and crowded with leaves are not.
Those standing in a favorable position are beautiful and pleasing to the heart; they bring health and signify the onset of youth.
There were also other beautiful, dense trees endowed with milky sap; they were solid in their core, exceedingly firm, and had not been employed for any other purposes.
One should avoid trees that are entwined, split, crooked, infested with worms and the like, hollow, possessed of knotted trunks, or those that are old, young, or diseased. (13)

One should avoid those that are withered, burnt by the fire of lightning, inhabited by birds, spirits, and the like, as well as those arising from anthills, those from cremation grounds, and those frequented by [the water of] fruit-infusions.

One should avoid dwelling places situated in the middle of rivers, those struck by the wind, those arising from the confluence of streams or from deities, and those located within the hermitages of ascetics. || 15 ||
He who would cause the weak, temples, Brahmins, or trees to tremble shall,
before long, no longer be a mover himself.

It is stated in the *Pārameśvara* that there is no fault in cutting, moving, or [according to manuscript *a*: piercing] them by means of ritual procedure, mantras, and offerings for the sake of a divine purpose. (17)
Having observed an auspicious sign, one should perform its consecration;
one should then purify the ground on all four sides in every direction. (18)
The preceptor is to be honored with sacrificial fees, garments, gold, and ornaments; thereafter, the chief artisans and assistants are to be honored with flowers and other offerings.
If, when addressed, a tree trembles, one should say it is a "mānavī";
in that case, the practitioner should avoid it from afar. || 20 ||
Then the Guru should wash a tree or a beautiful stone with water;
thereafter, he should smear the ground with cow dung.
Having performed his daily rites and become pure, the wise one there, having formed the limbs of Brahmā upon his body,
meditated upon the Lord, made his petition, and offered the respectful water (arghya).
Having first performed self-worship, the practitioner of mantra should survey the directions;
having meditated upon the weapon-mantra (astra), he should worship and encircle [the site] with the armor-mantra (varma). || 23 ||
Then, having performed the purification of the ground, one should worship on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south;
having fully worshipped Śiva, one should offer the flawless sacrificial porridge (caru) situated within the fire.
Having performed the satiation of the mantras, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra;
then, having informed [the deity], one should worship and also satisfy the ritual implements and weapons.

Taking recourse in either the northern or the northwestern direction, being composed, he should then inform the Lord of Gods and perform the ritual touching (ālabhana) once again. [Variant reading in gh: having first performed the ritual touching].
One should also bathe [the image] with four jars belonging to its own class;
then there is striking with ash using the Astra-mantra, and sprinkling with the water of Śiva. (27)
Writing with a blade of *darbha* grass, protection by means of armor (*varman*), a three-stranded cloth from a tree, and [an object] from stone accompanied by *kuśa* grass. (28)

Having recognized the auspicious signs, the Guru should then worship the tree with the mantra prescribed in the *Saṃhitā*; the bathing, clothing, and other requirements shall be performed accordingly.
One should worship the tree with perfumes, flowers, incense, and food offerings;
and one should present a bali-offering consisting of black-gram rice mixed with non-meat preparations and spirituous liquor.
Then, one hundred offerings should be made in the chamber of Indra, followed by one hundred for Rudra.
Having offered the respectful oblation (arghya) to the tree, one should recite the mantra of Rudra and speak the words to be proclaimed. || 31 ||
Oṃ! O abode of glory, salutations to you, O Lord of the Forest (vanaspati) cherished by the gods!
Move from this place to another location that is virtuous and beautiful. 32.
Oṃ śrī hrī vauṣaṭ. This is the mantra to be proclaimed.
Then, with the very mantra of Śiva, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the external bali-offering;
whichever mantra is prescribed for the rite of bali in the scripture, that one should be used in each respective case.
That very same mantra shall be the offering-mantra (balimantra)—the prescribed mantra—or else the syllable *praṇava* (OM) followed by one’s own name.
"Whatever beings are in this place, and whatever piśācas and rākṣasas there may be... (34)
The Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Nāgas, Devas, and even the Dānavas—having worshipped them according to the prescribed rites, one should satisfy them with pleasing words. (35)
"This journey of ours is for the sake of the Śiva-liṅga by the command of Śiva.
Whatever task may be for the sake of Śiva, that shall be yours as well. (36)
By this offering of the bali, may you always be pleased;
go elsewhere in comfort, leaving this place and this tree. (37)
Then, having sipped water according to the rules and having made his body complete [or:
fruitful], he should worship Śiva according to the rules and recite the *Māṇavaka* prayer after informing him of his dream.
