Having consumed the sacrificial pap (caru), the performer of the sacrifice should sleep there upon a bed of kuśa grass;
during the night, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over a young boy while sleeping.
Oṃ, salutation to the Victorious One, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
salutation to the Left-handed One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams. 40.
"O Maheśvara, tell me the truth in my dreams regarding all matters without exception; by your grace, I shall accomplish the success of my undertakings. (41)
Oṃ hili 2 Mātaṅgin Maheśvara [the reading "Maheśvara" does not appear in manuscripts K and G], O wielder of the trident, destroy 2 bad dreams! Show 2 what is auspicious! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

Thus ends the mantra regarding the boy in the dream. Having seen in a dream a chest blazing without smoke, flowering and fruiting with splendor, and accompanied by Rudra, one should always declare it to be auspicious.
One should abandon that [person] who is being drenched with blood, or likewise joined by demons and spirits, or being devoured by monkeys and camels, as he bestows inauspiciousness.
When it is not possible to abandon that which is well-adorned with auspicious marks and very beautiful, then, having bathed, one should offer oblations to Aghora for the removal of defects. (44)
Above the tree is the head, and below is the arrangement of the feet;
likewise, in the directions of Indra, Soma, and Īśāna, the faces of the Unmanifest and so forth are situated in sequence.

In the northern direction, one should strike down a tree with a weapon smeared with honey and clarified butter, having consecrated it with the *siddha* mantras and the like for the purpose of recitation (or victory). || 46 ||
Having meditated upon himself as Śiva and the weapon as being in the form of a missile (astra),
the preceptor should first strike [the obstacle], and then, while reciting the Śivāstra mantra, he should strike again.
Thereafter, a highly skilled artisan should perform the work exactly as prescribed;
he should respectfully fashion the liṅga from wood, according to the sequence of the mantras and the directions. 48.
The directions presided over by Indra, Īśāna, the Moon, and Agni bestow prosperity;
one who possesses devotion should cut down the fallen tree from the falling tree, even while it is not yet fully grown. (49)
One should take wood that is red-black, excellent, and substantial for the purpose of a liṅga; that which is yellowish-red is middling; one should avoid wood that is pale-white or light.
Just as the side of a tree is, so one should establish it;
however, if it is established inverted, it portends the ruin of the kingdom.
When the head is above the chest and the base is below, it brings happiness;
when the head is below the linga, then there will be the destruction of one's lineage.
A precipice on another side of the tree does not bring happiness;
therefore, one should perform a propitiation of the deities of the directions for the sake of liberation from faults. (53)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations according to the Pāśupata scripture,
one is released from other defects caused by the falling of stars and shall attain peace.
Having thus performed the purification of the directions and worshipped Śiva, one should offer libations;
one should also offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and thereafter one shall attain all desires.
If, through negligence, blood should flow from the cutting of the tree,
or if it should fall with its middle broken, then a fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed.
One should indeed offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the *bahurūpa* mantra,
and one should also present the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *śiva* mantra that removes all inauspiciousness.
In the event of an ill omen, one should perform an auspicious oblation a hundred times with the Ghoramantra;
likewise, the worship for the offering of stone is as prescribed for the offering of wood. 58.

Now I shall describe the stones, which exist in three ways—beginning with those for young couples and women—and according to the distinctions of the twice-born castes and so forth, as well as by differences in their form. (59)
That stone which possesses the thirty-two marks and is free from the eighty defects should be accepted as a young woman among the three types of lingas, and no other.
A young stone slab, endowed with auspicious marks, will surely bestow an increase of righteousness, longevity, wealth, the lord of the earth, subjects, the kingdom, and one’s own family. (61)
Two sources are to be known as being designated as forests (vana) and groves (upavana);
there are three sprouts, three directions, and fourfold are the scents and tastes.
(52) Nine lines, three [types], four sounds, likewise four classes, and one youth—thus there are thirty-two characteristics. (63)
A stone that is extensive, large, thick, uniform in its length,
smooth, and slightly concave is auspicious when sprinkled with the waters of a sacred river.
Born from the mountain of the family, protected by the earth, she produces a very deep sound;
she is fragrant, possesses dense limbs, and always remains in the shade of trees. 65.
Free from disease, devoid of a central core, and without pegs;
firm, beautiful, heavy, and adorned with a sweet resonance. (66)

Through their taste, which resembles molasses, honey, mango, and neem, and through the smell of cow dung, clarified butter, cow urine, and cow-dung respectively, stones originating from the twice-born (brahmins) and other castes are auspicious.
Bells with the sound of clouds or lutes, conch shells, and excellent stones bestow peace, victory, wealth, and long life upon the four castes. (68)
Resorting to sacred fords, virtuous, worthy of being well-served, and very cool;
possessed of great splendor and endowed with beauty, she is situated in the direction of the Lord of Wealth (the North). || 69 ||
O twice-born ones, the stone is white like a pale lotus, resembling a night-lotus;
its asterism is Mṛga, and its presiding deity is the moon, marked by the hare.
The Bhā-nakṣatra is indeed like the Kulattha pulse, reddish-brown and dark, resembling a blue lotus;
its presiding deity is Śatakratu (Indra). || 71 ||
Greenish-yellow, pigeon-colored, resembling molasses, and tawny—these are its colors.
Its lunar mansion is Phalgunī, and its deity is known as Bhaga. (72)
She who has the appearance of a black pigeon or is black is known as a Śūdrā;
her two presiding deities are considered to be the Aśvins and the constellation Aśvinī. || 73 ||
It is dense, melodious, smooth, expansive, and thick-skinned;
it is cool, pleasant to the touch, firm-limbed, and enchanting.
A woman who resembles a plantain leaf is a stone among women; she bestows happiness and wealth.
One who is of a single color, steady, and glossy, with a voice like that of an elephant's throat or a bell, [is likewise auspicious]. (75)
This stone, which is broad, long, and has a luster like a banyan leaf, is heavy; it is a man who bestows prosperity upon men. (76)
The neuter [image] should be of two forms and is the cause of the increase of neuter offspring.
A female image should be made by a woman; a eunuch by a eunuch; and a male by men. (77)
That which has a broken bell-metal sound, is rough, resembles red ochre or chalk,
is rich in veins, hard, and straight— this stone is neuter.
In rites dedicated to Śiva, a stone endowed with the characteristics of the masculine gender is prescribed;
for the remaining [deities], such as the wielder of the trident (Śūlin), feminine stones are declared for the pedestal and other components.
In black stone, white marks are givers of prosperity; in yellow stone, red ones;

and in stone possessing all colors, white ones are auspicious. All others are traditionally held to be inauspicious. (Note: Variant readings in manuscripts mū, a, k, kh, g, ṅ read "inauspicious" for "auspicious").
White lines resembling lotuses bring prosperity to the twice-born;
those that are red or yellow belong to a king, while those with the luster of dark lentils belong to the Vaiśyas. (81)
For Śūdras, those that are green, black, of their own color, or reddish-white,
and those with lines resembling a rainbow, all bestow prosperity and wealth.
That which has inferior lines at the top and is low is inferior; that which has inferior lines at the top and is auspicious is excellent.
That which is rich in characteristics and has few defects should be accepted, having been purified by fire-offerings (or beautified).
One should mark the directions with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and extract [the lines] with the *sadyojāta-mantra*.
Its head is intended to be in the directions of Indra, Īśāna, and the Moon (the north).
Above and below that, one should mark the back and the face respectively;
this is the rule for all three types of lingas made of stone, and no other method exists.

We shall describe the thirty-two types of stone, beginning with those originating from the directions and ending with those belonging to the castes, as well as their eighty-eight varieties of defects, such as being oversized and so forth. (86)
The images of the old and the young, joints with holes and pins, cavities, pustules, the void, soot, and layers of film; || 87 ||
These twelve great defects are to be avoided in all places;
I shall describe their characteristics briefly according to their distinctions. (88)
That which is variegated with the marks of snakes, frogs, and fish, exceedingly harsh, cruel, very rough, aged, and destructive of undertakings; || 89 ||
A girl who is slender and soft, resembling a slightly burnt brick,
and unable to endure the blow of a chisel— such a one should not be employed for the deity.
From the mandala the embryo is born; from the embryo, defect is perceived.
Therefore, one should cut the stone which is of the nature of the image, and likewise the wood. (91)
(55) The eighteen mandalas of all that is visible are dense, as are the seven other variegated ones, as well as the fourfold application of ointment. || 92 ||
White, resembling jaggery or sugar-candy; madder-red, red-yellow;
tawny like a Kapila cow, resembling yellow orpiment; pigeon-grey, and the color of a bee. || 93 ||
Black, blue, honey-colored, partridge-feather colored, ash-colored, resembling the *kiṃśuka* flower, resembling safflower, and resembling the *atasī* flower. || 94 ||
Now I shall describe the eighteen pure images and the seven variegated ones:
those with the luster of campaka flowers, blue luster, and a mixture of red and yellow. (95)
Black, various, variegated, or likewise spotted;
red and pale-white—these I shall now describe as defects of the embryo. (96)

If fish die in a pale-colored reflection, then goats and sheep will perish; if there is a stone-like appearance in a molasses-colored reflection, there will be a long period of drought because of that. (97)
If it has the luster of a sword or is like crystal, there will be a miscarriage;
if it is the color of madder, there will be a frog, the destruction of crops, and danger from water.
If it is red, it is a chameleon, which causes leprosy and loss of wealth;
if yellow, it is a monitor lizard, which kills the king and brings suffering to the subjects. (99)
If it is brownish-yellow (kapila), there will be swelling and fear of thieves and asthma;
if it is the color of a palmyra fruit (tālābha), it is a crab, which causes bilious diseases and brings about famine.
When it has the luster of a bumblebee, that poison does not cause rain even if it is a "poison-cloud" (viṣaka).
When Jyeṣṭhā has the hue of a pigeon's neck, it brings about disease, poverty, and fear. (101)
If it is black, that serpent kills the offspring and causes the destruction of the maker's family;
if it is blue, it is a fly, and it shall kill the wife along with her children.
A firefly appearing with the color of honey portends fear of poverty and fire;
a king-bird appearing with the color of a blue jay brings about the destruction of the progeny of the performer.
If the sand resembles ashes or the sky, there will be destitution and fear of thieves;
if it resembles the *kiṃśuka* flower or the *śakragopa* insect, there will be a loss of wealth for the king.
If it has a hundred feet and the luster of safflower, there will be a great disease;
if it resembles the flax flower, one should know that there is an ant within the womb.
From that [image], anxiety, fear, grief, and the increase of enemies arise;
thus, eighteen types of images have been described here by number. (106)

If the image has the color of jaggery and is painted with the hue of campaka flowers, worms will arise within its interior; consequently, there will be destruction of both the body and the purpose [of the rite]. (107)
If there appear a crow, a vulture, or a pigeon on a blue-and-variegated [cloth], then by that [omen], the king, the minister, and the perpetrator shall die in succession. (108)
If it has a variegated appearance like honey, there will be a loss of grain and wealth;
if it is red and variegated, it will have horns, and through that, there will be frequent sorrow and fear. (Variant: "it causes much sorrow.")
If there is a parrot on a yellow-and-variegated painting, it indeed causes the loss of one's entire dwelling; and if there is an ox on a black-and-variegated painting, it brings about many diseases.
The scorpion (*vṛścika*) is characterized by many spots and causes fear through its sting, pain, and venom.
These seven varieties are to be recognized by their external characteristics. (111)
If there is no perception of external objects and so forth, then one should smear [the area];
by means of the fourfold transformation, one should know the embryo through the application of the ointment. || 112 ||
One should grind *brahmāṇa*, *karavīra*—endowed with prosperity and growth—and *saurāṣṭrī* together with *tāla*, using *sauvīra*. || 113 ||
Coated with that [substance], they remain white at night, accompanied by vapors, sweat, and the like;
having recognized them as being like bees or black fish, one should abandon those which give rise to defects.
Having ground equal parts of triphalā, aśvaghna, māṃsī, and meghakuṣṭha [or murata], a woman should apply this paste with milk. (115)
Having recognized a stone that is crackling while being plastered, one should know that there is a great poison within it;
by that, death would come to the maker, therefore one should cast it into water. (116)

Having smeared it with milk-paste, stone, cow-dung, poison, and red ochre, one should let it sit for a day and night; then whatever is red and possessed of waves (or, according to another reading, "possessed of tortoises") should be discarded.
Having ground together the Piśāca, Aśvaghnī, and Vajrī, along with Abhayā marked by the Vaiṣṇava [seed], and the sharp Rudrajaṭā, with the milk of a ewe; 118.
Having smeared it with clay and allowed it to dry, one should subsequently display the white and other colors.
Having understood the two-fold form within the womb, one should first abandon those things that cause defects.

(58) A hole, one with holes on both sides, or one shaped like a cavity extending outward—such a [liṅga], if it belongs to the family of the maker, will surely bring about a wasting disease for the Guru. || 120 ||
A wedge shaped like a wedge causes the destruction of both the wood and the artisan;
a joint that splits from the blow of a chisel brings about the ruin of the craftsman.
One should know that a hollow or hollow-shaped [flute] brings about the destruction of the maker;
likewise, one should recognize a "sphoṭa" or "sphuṭitaka" [cracked] [flute] as bringing about death by the stroke of a weapon. || 122 ||
Completely surrounded on all sides by subtle embryos (or cavities) that are beyond numbering, it becomes like space; that space, in no long time, brings about the destruction of the agent.
[This reading is not present in the root manuscript. If the smoke has the luster of crystal, it causes the breaking of the *taṅka* [bellows];
by that, the destruction of the artisan and his subjects occurs very quickly, without a doubt. (124)
That stone which resembles birch bark is proclaimed as *paṭalī*; one should not fashion lingas from it, for if they are made, both [the maker and the recipient] perish. 125.
The web-like structure (jālaka) is of six kinds, resembling the cells of a honeycomb:
yellow, white, black, red, blue, and variegated.
Loss, imprisonment, and likewise the seizure of wife, sons, and wealth—in this sequence, these nine and a half great defects are known as being distinguished by their divisions. (127)

I shall now describe the intermediate defects, which exist in sixteen varieties by name; they are situated according to the divisions of Brahma and Upendra, and they do not cause defects in the three types of *liṅgas*. (p. 59) [Mū: they cause defects in the *liṅgas*]. || 128 ||
One should abandon those wicked ones who resort to the portion of Rudra, for they bestow inauspiciousness.
With the veins (the word *śirā* here is palatal and dental according to the classification of sibilants), with knots, with frost, and with pure drops, [one should purify]. 129.

One should avoid those marked with broken lines, curved lines, circles like flies, or diamond-shaped figures, as well as those marked with the footprints of a cat, a horse, a camel, a jackal, or a crow.
A stone that has the appearance of a discolored creeper bestows many defects;
one with a knotted form or a protruding knot brings about diseases of the stomach.
One should recognize that which is like a drop of water resting on a lotus leaf as being frost, which brings about the suffering of grief for one's son.

Indeed, impure copper is of four kinds, characterized by the smell of fish; it is [also] gold-colored, sounding like a bell, and free from disease. That which is otherwise is defective, according to the Piṅgalāmata. (133)

A meteor shower (haima) portends famine and drought, while a thunderclap (ghoṣa) brings about the destruction of artisans; a stone struck by iron kills the people, and one struck by copper kills the craftsman.
If it is soft, round, and smoke-colored, it is *dadru*, which causes excessive disease; if it is black, yellow, or reddish with spots, it brings grief, fear, and illness. (135)
If [the drop] at the crown is white, there is death; if red, sin will certainly occur;
if yellow, there is loss of wealth for the performer; if black, there is bondage in both ways for both.
A line that is thick, extremely thin, rough, or as crooked as a snake,
or a line intersected by another line, shall destroy one's royal power.

A line that is broken once brings death to one's wife; broken twice or thrice, it robs one of children and wealth; broken four times, it brings death to one's husband; and if broken many times, it causes the end of the entire lineage. (138)
A smoky, dark blue-black streak causes suffering, famine, and disease;
a mark shaped like a fly brings about most dreadful leprosy. (139)
If a whirlpool-like swirl (āvarta) is situated in the region of Rudra (or in the remaining portions), then it will undoubtedly bring about various calamities for the performer. || 140 ||
If a clockwise whorl is seen on the left side in various places,
then the linga must be abandoned in three ways by one who desires a king, a kingdom, or subjects.
But if a whirlpool is seen situated in the middle of the mark,
or if it rests slightly on the left side, it will destroy the kingdom along with its king.
She who has red limbs and lacks yellow is the bringer of famine and disease;
she who possesses all colors is indeed the destroyer of life, while she who lacks black is the remover of fear.
One whose paws possess four joints and five claws at the tips,
and which are seen to be elevated, such a cat-footed person is possessed of defects.
Just as one would abandon mud trodden upon by horses, camels, jackals, crows, and dogs, so too, having observed the form of a stone, one should discard that which portends misfortune. 145.
These twenty-three varieties of moderate faults have been described by me;
now I shall explain the minor faults as they are set forth in the scriptures. (146)

A stone that is not joined with other stones, one that is touched by the foot of a tree, one arising from an anthill, saline soil, or a funeral pyre, as well as one that is lukewarm or situated in the midst of alkaline water, should be rejected. (147)
Born in a field of demerit, frequented by people such as Bhillas and others, situated in an evil direction, scorched by the sun, arising from what is bitter, and defiled by what is impure. (148)

That which has a foul odor and a bad taste, as well as that which is defiled by lightning or fire, or that which possesses the sound of a wicked living being, should not be employed for any other ritual purpose. 149.
The Cāṇḍālī and the Antyajā—their characteristics are now stated: whichever woman clings to a stone causes the cessation of affection. (Mūla, Chapter A: The Cause) || 150 ||

One situated at the foot of a tree on the road bestows a journey; one situated on an anthill bestows victory in battle; one known to be situated on saline soil takes away wealth; and one situated on a funeral pyre causes suffering. (151)

A Liṅga that is lukewarm causes enmity; one situated in alkaline water causes leprosy; one located on Darbha grass causes misfortune; one situated in an unholy place inhabited by Pāśupatas causes slaughter; and one frequented by Bhillas [causes the same]. || 152 ||
The deities of fire, Yama, the Rakshasa, water, wind, and the one situated in the quarters (Indra) bring, respectively, burning, loss, grief, poverty, and likewise disease. (153)
The *tejohṛt* stone causes fever; the *sūyataptā* stone makes one perpetually childless and unrighteous;
the *surāpakṣi* stone smells of fat; and the *udvegajananī* stone produces agitation. (154)
That which is salty and pungent brings satisfaction to hunger;
yet, when scorched by lightning or burnt by fire, it brings fear of flames to the king. 155.
One who has broken vessels, one born of a camel, one with a voice like a crow, one with feet like a heron, and one who causes excessive disease;
one brought for another purpose, and one who causes madness and failure—[these are to be avoided]. || 156 ||
A stone that is lusterless, full of many cracks, light, and of indistinct color is known as an *antyajā* (outcaste) stone; it is censured by the twice-born and others. (157)
The one who is smoke-colored, blue, protective, thick-haired, and beautiful, as well as the Caṇḍālī of various colors—she destroys the lineage of the performer. 158.
One possessed of minor defects, consecrated by the refinement of mantra, should be accepted for the benefit of ordinary people and at will for men seeking liberation. 159.
The Antyajā is beneficial for the Antyajas, that is, the Cāṇḍālas;
these twenty varieties, distinguished by their hundreds of thousands of sub-divisions, are said to involve only minor faults. (160)

The color, caste, age, lines, marks, and circles—these are to be known [as the characteristics] of stones and trees that have become true earth. (161) [This portion enclosed in brackets is absent in manuscripts k, kh, and g.]
If a stone of one color should be treated as being of another color, the production of that [new] nature occurs through a mantra born of that [intended] nature. (162)
Having marked a stone or a tree for the purpose of a linga or other object according to the desired measurement,
one should have it carved and purified in accordance with the prescribed rules.
Whatever be the color and whatever be the material of the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is held to be of that same material;
together with its base (*piṇḍikā*), it should be elevated up to the portion of Viṣṇu.
It should be as wide as the length of the *liṅga*, adorned with circular lines (*vartanābhiḥ*),
and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) of Śiva must indeed be made in a single solid piece.
The Brahma-pīṭha should be made with many petals, or likewise with a single petal;
the water-channel should be in the northeast, and the water-reservoir likewise below.
Having first marked the stone, one should collect it for the sake of the pedestal (piṇḍikā). The pedestal may be taken even from another site, provided it possesses the same color as the liṅga;
however, the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) must not be so obtained—thus it is declared in the scriptures (or tantras) by the wise. (167)
The auspicious Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) should be taken as that which remains at the base of the linga;
it may be situated in the upper portion above the cut-off part of the linga, or likewise in the lower portion.
That [pedestal] should be one-third or one-fourth of the height of the liṅga;
however, for the liṅgas, a single block is prescribed for the height.
For a liṅga measuring one cubit (hastamātra), the [thickness of the] shaft (niḥsārā) is two fingers more;
for other liṅgas as well, it increases by one finger in successive order.
Alternatively, the cord extending to the ears should be greater than the width of the *liṅga* by one-fourth of the portion belonging to Brahmā;
or else, that [portion] belonging to Brahmā should be greater in width by one-sixteenth part.
[This passage within brackets is not present in manuscripts *k* and *g*: Her girdle should be equal to her own measurement, or the excavation should be of that same dimension. (171)
The portion for the feet is equal and its own surface is praised;
the excavation (khāta) is greater than the Brahmā-portion, with an extent of six barley-corns.
The eldest [pillar] is reduced by half of a half-yava, and the others are reduced sequentially in that same manner.
One should fashion nine circular *ratnādhāra* (jewel-support) bases in their center.
The tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) should also be fashioned, or else the pure Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā); it should be endowed with a thickness equal to half its own length and breadth. (175)
The measurement should be increased, but a fool should not decrease it from the measurement.
The Brahma-stone should be made of wood when the Linga is wooden, and the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should likewise be so.

Having fashioned a square stone slab and smeared it with sandalwood paste, the best of mantra-knowers should worship it with weapons, umbrellas, flowers, and other offerings in order to summon [the deity]. (177)
One should worship Śiva along with his limbs (attendants) and diligently offer libations;
having offered libations to the ascetics who are devotees of Śiva, one should cause him to mount the chariot.
Having yoked that chariot with the finest buffaloes, the guide, having placed the Lord of Gods upon the chariot and worshipped him, should bring him there. || 179 ||
Peace must be practiced day by day until one reaches home;
for when the wheels of the chariot should falter due to negligence, [the journey is in peril]. (180)
Having generated the Śiva-fire, one should satisfy the multiformed deity;
by offering one hundred and eight oblations, one is liberated from all evil deeds. || 181 ||
Having meditated upon Śiva, one should remember the Astra-mantra and cast half [of the linga] onto the pedestal;
then, having set the chariot on the path, one should slowly lead it back to one's own city.
The sacrificer, having gone out to meet him, should honor him with beauty, banners, flags, and the like, as well as with women singing auspicious songs. (183)
Having had it constructed and having caused the twice-born to recite auspicious benedictions, one should bring it there;
on the northern side of the temple, one should perform the work and offer it. (184)
In the northern part of the temple, according to the divisions of the smallest [size] and so forth, the workroom (karmakuṭī) is considered to be five, seven, or eleven cubits [in size]. (185)
A Bhadrā stone, obtained according to the prescribed rite from another direction,
should be placed in a pit to the north of the temple and the hole filled with earth.
Having worshipped Śiva above that, situated in the western direction,
he should offer libations to the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) and to the Great Pāśupata weapon.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should again offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
When the weapon-mantra has been thus propitiated, the stone is liberated from the defects of the directions.
Even when drawn out, if its head and mouth cannot be discerned, that *liṅga* is honored by a virtuous Brahmin, a maiden, and an artisan. (189)
"O dear one, even if only a single [drop] should enter a limb, having touched it, that [limb], including the head and face, must certainly be purified; so said the Blessed Lord Parameśvara. (190)
Furthermore, one should carefully avoid any stone that has been used for other purposes or consecrated by someone else; such a stone is not auspicious for the rite of the *liṅga*.
One should likewise procure all the components such as the pedestal and petals, as well as the bull, according to the prescribed rule;
and in this same manner, one should also bring materials for the linga and other items made of wood.
The procedure for the consecration of a stone that is rich in auspicious marks and has few defects is now described.
According to some opinions, one should place the stone in the previously mentioned directions and sub-directions.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *ghora* mantra, one should worship Hara up to the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Alternatively, one may worship the Conqueror of Death (*Mṛtyujetṛ*) accompanied by the six limbs of the Vidyā. (194)
In this way, these defects arising from the dullness of the head, face, and so forth are released;
having grasped either wood or stone according to this procedure. (195)
On an auspicious day, when all favorable omens have been duly performed,
one should fashion the linga according to the Guru’s command, characterized by three measurements.
Thus ends the third procedure, titled "The Taking of Wood and Stone," in the Compendium of Characteristics. || 3 ||
Now, the fourth:
I shall explain the measurement of the *liṅga*, which consists of four types.
It is established by means of the hands of the doorway and the interior, measured in four *aṅgulas*. (1)
An atom (aṇu) is formed by eight particles of dust from the sun's rays;
a barleycorn (yava) is formed successively by eight times each of the hair-tip, the nit (likṣā), and the louse (yūkā). || 2 ||

In the *Pārameśvara*, it is stated that for the purpose of measurement, one should use excellent barley grains free of husks, or those situated in clay or on a mound of rice-husks, which are horizontal and equal in circumference. (3)
With eight, seven, and six barley-corns respectively, the three parts beginning with the *jyeṣṭha* should be three finger-breadths;
that which is measured by one-sixteenth, a sphere, two eyes, and a digit is traditionally held to be two finger-breadths.
The Dharma [measure] is four finger-breadths; that called Śakti is six finger-breadths;
the Ardhahasta, the Vitasti, and the Tāla are twelve finger-breadths each. || 5 ||
One should know that the *kara* measure consists of two *tālakas*; by means of the *kara*, ritual actions are performed according to one's desire.
It is considered the standard for all ritual procedures, including the installation of the *liṅga*, the temple, the pedestal (*āsana*), and so forth.
The household liṅga may range from one finger-breadth up to fifteen finger-breadths;
it is threefold according to the measurement of the door and ninefold according to the measurement of the sanctum.
One should worship the liṅgas by means of ninefold measurement;
thus, thirty-six liṅgas are to be known according to the superior measurement.
By the middle measurement there are thirty-six, and by the lowest measurement also thirty-six;
by the sum of these lingas, there shall be one hundred and eight.
I shall now state individually those various names which belong to these [reasons], which generally possess the three characteristics according to their different types of proof. (10)
Earth, water, fire, air, and space; the directions, the sky, and one's own form; the lords of touch and sound; the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears—these are the lords.
One should know that there are exactly fifteen types of supreme limbs (liṅgas):
speech, grasping, excretion, pleasure, and movement, each presided over by its own lord.
The Lord of Nature (Prakṛti) and the Person (Puruṣa), along with speech, hands, anus, genitals, feet, mind, intellect, and ego—these fifteen constitute the intermediate [principles]. (13)
Īśvara, Ananta, Rudra, Śrīkaṇṭha, Triśikha, Tridṛk, Vidyeśvara, Pati, Sraṣṭṛ, Garutmān, Sakala, and Akala. (14)
The two Lords of Māyā are Śarva and Sarva; in the five lowest [levels], however, they are Śānta, Aja, and Mahātejas. Beyond the Ānanda [level], there is the triad of the highest.
Sudhāmā, Tryambaka, and Śuddha constitute the middle triad from the door; Skanda, Sūkṣma, and Ambikānātha likewise form the lowest triad from the door. || 16 ||
Caṇḍeśa, Kapālīśa, Khaḍgī, Pāśī, Dhvajī, Gadī, Bhujaṅgī, Vṛṣabhī, and Siṃhī—these nine born from the womb are the most excellent. (17)

[This verse is not present in the original manuscript; it was inserted from the *Cāpacintā*: Balī, Śaktī, Harī, Raṇī, Śmaśānī, Bhairavī, Piṅgī, Krodhī, and Māyī—these nine born from the womb are the central ones.
Agra, Agra, Pinākī, Cakrī, Nādī, and Mahāvratin.
Vyāpī, Śūlī, Viśālī, and Cetthadhamā—these nine are born from the womb. || 19 ||
The Unmanifest, the Lord of Procuresses, the Restrainer, and the Conqueror of Time;
the Omniscient, the Bull-bannered One, the Restrainer, the Destroyer of Sin, and the Eternal.
In the nine Liṅgas measured by the best of hands, the deities are:
Śambhu, Sthāṇu, Hara, Diṇḍī, Hartā, Kartā, Śiva, and Avyaya.
And the ninth is named Sureśa; from the middle [lineage] comes Haratamānata; then Bhadra, Vimala, Jyeṣṭha, Gāṇḍīva, and Puṣṭivardhana. || 22 ||
The Self-Existent (Svayambhū), the Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśa), and the Excellent Protector (Śreṣṭha-pālayitṛ)—these nine are proclaimed as the lowest according to the measurement of the hand. (23)
That which measures from one finger-breadth up to five is called the inferior mobile [liṅga];
that which measures from six up to ten is the medium mobile liṅga. (24)
The measurement of the best liṅga begins at eleven aṅgulas and extends in sequence up to fifteen; it is characterized by these aṅgulas starting from the largest.

A liṅga made of gold and silver should be six aṅgulas in height; one made of great gems or other precious stones should be nine aṅgulas; and those made of the remaining materials should be fifteen aṅgulas.
The fulfillment of desires, a son, righteousness, good fortune, and the destruction of enemies;
health, royal happiness, and the king’s glory that brings victory to the world—[these are attained]. (27)
Fortitude, the wealth of women, and longevity arise from a phallus of one finger-breadth and so forth;
according to some opinions, the desired result for practitioners may also arise from a movable phallus.
In the square and the four-angled [diagram], one should omit a yuga (four units) from the upper region along with a sixteenth part;
likewise, one should omit thirty-two parts and sixteen parts at the two corners.
The neck should be twenty-four finger-breadths;
likewise, with both sides slightly tapered, the excellent *calaliṅga* (movable liṅga) should be firm.
The door should be reduced by parts equal to the number of *yugas*, seasons, and serpents (*8, 6, and 5*) respectively, starting from the smallest;
the *liṅga* should be half the height of the door, or successively reduced by one-quarter. (31)
The lowest type of liṅga is half the height of the base (garbha), while the best is three parts of the elements (bhūta);
between these two, one should duly establish seven equal lines.
In this manner, there would be nine threads; with the elemental threads (bhūtasūtra), the middle [measurement] is formed.
With two intervals between them, the length of the lingas is nine times the number of Rāmas (three).
The hand measures two cubits, and there may be up to nine hands;
the female organ is considered middling, while the male organ is excellent—thus it is threefold, consisting of three types.
Within each individual linga, the wise one should join together three threads— one for each quarter—
at intervals of six or eight [units].
This [liṅga], which is stable and immeasurable in its length, consists of the nature of the gateway, the womb, and the maker;
one should install that single liṅga, whether it originates from the hand or from the foot.

Peace, longevity, and honor are the fruits obtained in succession from the two [Mānas]. From the [first] Māna, there is gain of the womb and so forth, fame, wealth, sons, women, land, victory, purpose, strength, and long life. (37)

Liberation, nourishment, destruction of enemies, longevity, knowledge, fame, wealth, supernatural powers, and sovereignty—these results are to be produced by the hands from the [positions of] the linga and the teeth. (38)

[This passage is not found in manuscript *kh*; it appears in the text from verse 39 to verse 50, marked by the symbol for a bow. Having determined the desired length of the *liṅgas* in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) by that [measurement], the skillful practitioner should subtract [the remainder] by means of the vowels, the elements, or the fires, starting with the banner (*dhvaja*). 39.
One should observe those remaining finger-breadths for their auspicious or inauspicious nature:
among the [eight] signs beginning with the banner (dhvaja), the banner, the lion, the bull, and the elephant are auspicious. (40)
The wise man should avoid inauspicious signs such as smoke, an elephant, a horse, a donkey, or a crow.
A banner portends sovereignty; a lion, victory; a bull, gain; and an elephant, prosperity.
In the case of smoke, there are faults; with a dog, death; with a donkey, constant expulsion;
and with a crow, total destruction. Therefore, one should always avoid them. (42)
Among the notes, Ṣaḍja, Gāndhāra, and Pañcama are the bestowers of auspiciousness;
Ṣaḍja bestows prosperity, while Gāndhāra increases one's following. (43)
The fifth [year] always bestows prosperity and brings the acquisition of land for men;
in the sixth year, there is an increase of enemies, while the middle [seventh] year causes the loss of sons (or, according to other readings, the destruction of auspiciousness).
Dhaivata brings ruin to the performer, and Niṣāda causes total destruction.
Among beings, those that move upon the earth and others such as those rich in water are exceedingly inauspicious.
The earth grants all things to men; water makes a wife inexhaustible; fire, when accompanied by fever, causes burning; but wind brings about the destruction of the family.
The fire that causes the destruction of brothers, sons, wife, debts, the sky, and the king is auspicious; however, the Āhavanīya fire and two other fires are considered inauspicious.
The first fire grants everything to men; the second causes the loss of sons;
the third fire indeed brings death to the performer and bestows fear upon the king. (48)
In hands that are empty of income, one should add one finger-breadth from the hand;
or else, having divided that income into six parts, one should preferably subtract one part. (49)
He says that with the middle [size] it is two parts, and three parts for the smallest.
Furthermore, the lord of the parts (bhāgeśa), the non-lord (anīśa), and the preceptor of the gods (devejya) are designated as equal. (50)
One should mark out four linga-forms by means of the width;
having made the length endowed with *māyā*, one should fashion the linga as threefold in form.
It is square, eight-cornered, and circular, consisting of the three principles and their qualities.
When its stated length is divided by half a part, then by eight parts, in succession: || 52 ||
The water-element rasa (six) becomes one hundred increased by a sixth part and a third part;
this constitutes the squareness of those [squares] equal to the numbers called the first, the non-first, and the preceptor of the gods (Jupiter). 53.
The three groups of five, known as the measures, increase by multiplying them by the spans (vyāsa);
due to their twofold division, many [varieties] will be described here according to Viśvakarman.
The first [measurement] and the others are threefold through the increase of thickness and so forth; thus it is eightfold.
And that which is called the *jīvā* from the hand is threefold, joined with the "all-equal" (*sarvasama*).
There are twenty-five varieties of these signs worshipped by the gods in the beginningless [tradition]; likewise, through their unification, they become seventy-five when honored by the Jinas. (56)
Fourteen thousand and four hundred; thus, by increasing the finger-breadths, starting from one cubit and nine fingers. (57)
One should divide their corners with cords placed at the half-angle of the ears;
having divided the width into seven parts, three should be established from the center. (58)

Above two parts, there shall be an eighth part; with sixteen parts (two eighths), there is the portion for Śiva. Each single part is divided into four, and the reduction at the corners is by two parts.
From the intersection of those diagonal lines, ten points will arise again;
having made each of those a pair, one should collect each individual part.
Then, by means of threads applied sequentially to those two ends, one should mark the ten-angled [die] in two ways;
having marked it by inserting a grain of rice at a certain point, it becomes a sword-sharpening [die].
In that same manner, there should be a sixteen-sided figure, and likewise one with twice sixteen [sides].
In the center of that, by the intersection of the threads, Rudra becomes circular.

Having withdrawn [the breath] by means of the auspicious objects and the goddesses [Ramā], which possess the portions of the arrows, fire, and mountains, one should cast it from the hand, increasing by one finger-breadth in sequence, to destroy the defects of emptiness. 63.
The sixfold [division] should be joined with Brahmā and the others, along with the qualities of the principles (tattva) in sequence.
One should add a sixteenth part to the first, and a quarter-part to that which is honored by the immortals.
What is to be given and what is to be abandoned in the first eight houses is declared according to the view of Piṅgalā, who was honored by the primordial gods, using entirely equal [weights]. (65)
From one's own forearm, from the tip of the leather-bound part [of the bow], from the finger-joints, and from the hollow of the hand [or, according to k and g:
from the mouth], there shall be increasing [measures] of eight hundred, two hundred, six hundred, and one hundred [finger-breadths]. (66)
Now, for the sake of removing defects related to shadows in the three genders beginning with the first (masculine),
one should describe the construction of the pedestal (pīṭha) after consulting the doctrine of Viśvakarman.
Divided into three parts— lower, middle,
and upper— that linga, being symmetrical, is beneficial whether installed in a temple or a house.
Thus, the entire work should be performed equally, bestowing the fruits of all desires.
The two feet up to the knees are the Grandfather (Brahmā) in a square shape. (69)
Above that, up to the navel, Viṣṇu resides within the eight-cornered [figure];
from the navel upwards to the top of the head, Hara himself occupies the circular portion.
Just as it is with the unmanifest (avyakta), so too it resides sequentially in the image (arcā) and the face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga).
These fivefold unmanifest liṅgas are all situated upon the same pedestal.
One should fashion the Īśāna face as having an equal width, or it may be "well-faced" (sumukha) if worshipped by the gods.
Liṅgas should be made in this manner; otherwise, they would lead to defects.
This is the arrangement for the five faces; now the procedure for the head (śirovartinī) is described.

One should declare the results according to the desired form, based on the fourfold divisions of each [mark]: resembling an umbrella, resembling a hen’s egg, having the shape of the young moon, or like a water-lily bud. (73)

With eight parts of the base and four parts of the top (or, according to another reading, eight parts of the base and nine parts of the top), one should fashion the *puṇḍarīka* (lotus) for the destruction of suffering;
through it, great fame accrues to the maker. For prosperity, it should be made with two parts less;
for the sake of affection, with three parts less; and for the subduing of the quarters, with four parts less.
(75) The fourfold varieties of the royal parasol are renowned as bestowing long-lasting sovereignty. (75)
In the final portion of the yuga, through the destruction of the eightfold reality (tattva), it becomes pure;
and through the abandonment of pride (māna) and the lotus-like attachment (pakṣa), it shall be vast and bestow renown. || 76 ||
The *Vardhamāna* bestows long life when made from three parts, and wealth when made from four parts;
it grants prosperity when made from five parts, and sons when made from six parts; thus the *Kūrtudakṣāṇḍa* is of four kinds.
From a third part, one attains the age-parts; with a single decrease, it is called "Immortal" (amṛta);
from a double decrease, it is "Nourishing" (puṣṭida); when full, it always produces great joy.
From the abandonment of three parts, it is known as *bala*; from the destruction of the pair (*yuga*), it bestows good fortune (*saubhāgya*).
*Āyudā* and *kumuda* are to be understood; *candra* is considered to be of four kinds.

The *Ṛtvaśaiścarame* [rite] is declared by the Vedas to grant victory, destroy worldly existence, and bestow all desires; it brings about destruction for the sake of prosperity through the decay of the two [opposing forces].
From the third abandonment, it is the terrifying *jayada* (victory-giving) marked with variegated signs (*citrāṅka*) due to the destruction of the Vedas;
and that which bestows belovedness is the fourfold *trapuṣa*. || 81 ||
One should fashion, in sequence, a gourd, a parasol, a moon-like object, and a hen’s egg—or even a single hen’s egg—for the purpose of rites for the Brahmins and other castes. (82)
From the *trapuṣa* and other [seeds], there is the attainment of desired success; from the *ātapatra*, sovereignty;
from the moon [or, according to mū, a, k, kh, g, ṅ: from the half-moon], long life; and from the egg of a cock, wisdom. (83)

Having first calculated the portion for the measurement of the linga and its modifications, one should then multiply it by twenty-one [the number of] tigers among Jinas; this constitutes the first enclosure, beginning with Brahmā. (84)
From the *nakhā* [digit], there are sixty parts of transformation (*vikāra*) in the beginningless state;
likewise, it occurs through transformation by means of *smara*, conjoined with one-third of a part. || 85 ||
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, it is joined with a portion consisting of half a division and a fraction,
and also with a third of a division increased by twenty-one.
The circumference shall consist of one-third part plus one-eighth part,
together with seventeen parts, when the whole is divided into equal shares.
Having encircled it with four arms made of red powder, one should form the arm as seven parts;
Viṣṇu is formed with two and a half, three, and two arms, while Hara is formed with one and a half, three, and two arms.
If the head is elevated, there will be great enjoyment; if the back has the luster of a cow's hide, likewise.
If the belly contains a barley grain, there will be nourishment; if the abdomen is prominent, there will be food and drink. (89)
If it is rounded in all its parts, there is happiness and an increase in progeny and fortune;
if the belly is level, it destroys fear; and if the base is thick, there is freedom from disease.
If the head appears as if pierced by a spear or is deformed, it destroys the subjects along with their leaders;
if it is sunken or bald, it causes the destruction of wealth and grain.
A linga that is wounded on the head shall kill both the maker and the king;
one that is perforated shall likewise kill the wife, and one that is depressed on the forehead shall kill the son.
A wheel that is thick at the top brings death to the maker; one with four spokes robs the artisan of his wealth.
(p. 77) One that is thin in the middle leads to grief, while one that is thin at the bottom bestows famine.
If [the moon] is in Hīnāṅga or Cipiṭāṅga, fear and suffering arise;
there is an increase in wounds and diseases, and famine occurs in Atikoṭara.
If it is long and thin, it destroys the kingdom; if short, diseases break out. A depression on the back brings loss of wealth, while a depression on the sides or the belly likewise causes disease.

When the emblem has been fully prepared, the wise man, having rubbed it with emery and other materials until it is perfectly smooth and free of blemishes, should then wash it and examine its characteristics.
The svastika, the lotus, the goad, the parasol, the wheel, the sword, the banner, and the conch;
the makara, the mirror, the bow, the garland, the tortoise, the archway, and the gateway. || 97 ||
The fish, tortoise, mountain, sun, drop, barley-corn, lion, rosary, śrīvatsa, nandikāvarta, chariot, necklace, elephant, and earth—these are the auspicious marks. || 98 ||
The eye, the jar-born (Agni), the matted locks, the linga, the weapon, the woman, the stars, the trident, and the chowrie;
the peacock, the horse, the garment, the tree, the thunderbolt, and the purifier (the sacred grass). || 99 ||
Wherever there are lines on the body of the linga that resemble a palace, the flame of a fire, or the female organ (bhaga), they bestow the increase of the king and the kingdom. (100)
[He was surrounded] by headless trunks, monkeys, cats, tigers, bears, and wolves;
by skeletons, herons, vultures, snakes, hawks, crows, donkeys, and mice. || 101 ||
With cranes, shackles, owls, nooses, pincers, and insects;

with the forms of moths, skulls, garlands, camels, wolves, and dogs—the sign of the sacrificer, the subjects, and the king brings fear and sorrow. (Or, according to the Mūla: it brings grief to women. 102.

(p. 78) [In this [text], there is a discrepancy in the sequence and the mention of phonemes (*varṇa*) during the classification of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with the earthly (*pārthiva*). Furthermore, the principle of space (*ākāśatattva*) is not described at all. However, in other texts, only five principles are found mentioned. This reading appears to be corrupt and incomplete. Those learned in the Śaiva Āgamas are the authority here. As for the sequence of the classification of the phonemes of the principles, it is presented in a different manner in the section on initiation (*dīkṣāprakaraṇa*) within the *Kulākula-cakra* of the first wave (*taraṅga*) of the *Puraścaryārṇava*. It is as follows: "Air, fire, earth, water, and space"—[the phonemes] *a, ā, e, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, ṣa, ha* are of air (*māruta*); *i, ī, ai, kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, ra, kṣa* are of fire (*āgneya*); *ṛ, ṝ, au, gha, jha, ḍha, dha, bha, va, sa* are of water (*jalīya*); *ḷ, ḹ, aṃ, ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma, śa, ha* are of space (*nābhasa*). *i, ī, cha, the two l-s (ḷ, ḷ), and likewise the five nasals.*
And these earthly colors are the signs and marks for prosperity on the earth.

The letters ū, aṃ, a, ca, ḍa, ṭā, [k, kh, gh: phaṭā], and those below kṣa, namely ka, sa, ha, ja, va, and sā [mū: kahājava ṛsā], are white; these are the Varuṇa letters, which bestow progeny, longevity, and the acquisition of wealth. || 104 ||
The vowels ṛ, ṝ, ā, ya, ra, the diphthongs e and o, and the visarga, as well as the retroflex consonants (ṭa-group), are individually fiery; they increase fire, fear, famine, and disease. (105)
The letters *e*, *o*, *e*, *u*, *pa*, *ga*, *bha*, *tha*, *ḍha*, and *kha* cause rain during the rainy season;
those belonging to Vāyu cause fear of wind, quarrels, and agitation. (106)
When these are mixed, they yield results that are inferior, superior, or equal;
therefore, the threefold gender in the means of accomplishment and the gender according to direction shall now be explained.
A single-pointed [yantra] is for the destruction of enemies; a two-pointed one bestows the increase of sons;
a three-pointed one is for the sake of attaining all perfections; and a four-pointed one grants whatever is desired.
A five-pointed [yantra] is for the destruction of enemies; a six-pointed one bestows enjoyment;
a seven-pointed one is known to produce hatred; and an eight-pointed one increases fame. (109)
For the purpose of eradication, there should be nine weapons; for the destruction of disease, ten weapons;
for the increase of disease, eleven weapons; and for the destruction of fear, twelve weapons. (110)
The five-pointed [linga] destroys enemies for one who desires sensual pleasures; the six-pointed [linga] is for paralyzing [enemies];
the seven-pointed [linga] is a meritorious linga; and the eight-pointed [linga] bestows happiness. || 111 ||
Their measurement is to be conceived as before, in the form of a pinnacle;
for one whose hand reaches nine [fathoms], there is no defect of emptiness for anyone. (112)
In the Vasukṛta (eight-fold) Diśāliṅga, the measurement may be one finger-breadth or according to the sequence of cubits;
by three measures or by a single measure, it is sixteen-sided and two hundred [units].
Its width should be made like that of the sun, divided into four parts;
it is four-cornered, eight-cornered, and six-cornered, marked by Indra and having the form of a thunderbolt.
An eight-sided figure should be constructed as before; from the southern side of the triangle, one should rotate it by means of horizontal lines through the junction of the points.
Half of that is not for the portion of Rudra; in the portion of Bāṇa, there is a square.
Above the eight sides, however, is a seven-sided [shape]; the Śakti and Āgneya [weapons] cause burning.
But without one's own portion, the southern part of the enemy is flattened;
then, having divided half the circumference into nine parts, one should mark them with arrows at the front, the back, and the extremities. || 117 ||
(80) From the side, by means of six two-sided planets, it causes the destruction of water in the corners;
thus, surrounded by eight sides, it becomes the "Staff of Yama" (yāmyadaṇḍa), which bestows disease. || 118 ||
Having made half the length equal to that of Rudra, one should fashion a square with parts of the elements;
the Rākṣasa [enclosure], which is terrifying, shall be octagonal, semi-decagonal, and sword-shaped.
One should not perform half of it like a sage; rather, the *viṣkaṃbha* should be derived from the portion of the *yuga*.
It may be four-sided, eight-sided, or circular; that which is shaped like a noose is auspicious for Varuṇa.
Half of the length, by the portion of twelve (the Sun), forms a four-cornered [or four-moon-cornered] figure;
by the portion of seven (the Sages), it is slender, possessing its former form, long, mobile, and a banner that effects eradication. 121.
One should fashion a Yakṣa-liṅga that is symmetrical throughout, fashioned with a thick belly, and topped with the head of a mace; it is auspicious and brings about an increase in strength.
The width is half of that, produced from six parts by means of the Rudra-division;
the four-sided, five-pointed, and three-pointed trident of Rudra bestows liberation.
The circumference is made with six parts; a square is formed with one-fifth part, and half of that is an octagon and a quadrangle. The Brahma-pada is like a lotus for the sake of attaining heaven.

Half a *vāha* by the mountain-portion (*nagabhāga*) for the width, and a fourth part for the height; it should be circular with four and eight corners, auspicious like the conch of Viṣṇu (or like the *śakti*). (125)
At the onset of the seasons, by discarding two parts and then half [of that], the Vajraśiras [arrangement] arises;
from Rudra [eleven] by a threefold reduction comes the Śukti, and from the directions [ten] by a threefold reduction comes the Daṇḍa.
Divided by three, the rays are from the mountain (seven); in the north-west is the crescent moon;
in the north-east is the hen’s egg; and from the five parts (five), the mace is obtained in the north.
From the third part of the planets, due to their destruction, there arises that which is known as the "three-fold elevation" (tryunnata) and the "spear" (śūla);
this applies to the right-egg-born Vaiṣṇu and likewise to the line of the jewel.

One should place in the office of the water-supervisor (ābhivārika) those who are short, tall, thin, stout, humpbacked, lame, or crooked, as well as those with cracked skin or those seen to be like a fetus.
Thus have been proclaimed the auspicious and inauspicious signs of the unmanifest;
now I shall describe the other manifest signs of various forms.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Unmanifest Linga" (or, according to the reading in the manuscript copies: "The Procedure for the Fashioning of the Linga"), in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya* from the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*. 4.
Now, fifthly,
the characteristics of the manifest image (vyaktārcā) of the Rudras shall be correctly explained,
[measured] from fifteen finger-breadths up to twenty-five finger-breadths according to the measure of a previous finger-breadth.
In the home, an image should be worshipped; indeed, one that is larger than that is not recommended.
In some cases it should be the measure of a cubit, and in others thirty finger-breadths.
One should establish the *adhikās* (superior elements) in the abode, measuring one cubit for the door;
having first divided the height of the door into eight parts and then performing the ritual (*vidhāya*). (3)
Then, having divided [the space] again into three parts, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be fashioned with one part,
and that smallest image (kanyasī pratimā) with two parts.
Having divided the length of the door into nine parts, one part is set aside; the remaining [length] is further divided into three.
The middle image (madhyamārcā) should be made with two parts, and the pedestal (pīṭhikā) with one part.
Having divided the door-jamb (dvāranāha) into three parts, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be made with one part;
the image (pratimā) should be made with two parts of that, which is considered the best.
In the case of *karamāna*, *karāda*, and so forth, for each successive one, there are nine [units] at the end of every three; these are proclaimed as the *kanyasa* (smallest) and the others.
Maya, in his own doctrine, has established that the height of the image and the liṅga should be equal to the width of the temple,
while the width of the pedestal should be equal to the width of the door.
Externally, however, a large image should be made measuring one cubit;
it is of three types—inferior, middling, and superior—being respectively diminished by one, two, or three digits (tithis), months, or navartas.

Adorned with ornaments, they become threefold; having become women, they are Vetālas, Stūlavāmanas, and those in the form of the lame—thus one should cause the Kūṣmāṇḍas to manifest in seven ways as images.
On an auspicious day, having divided with a power-line (śaktisūtra) a stone that is free from defects, elevated, and rectangular in shape, starting from the constellations and so forth; || 11 ||
Having first worshipped the Guru and performed the rites for well-being and so forth,
one should then fashion the pedestal, the substratum, the individual soul, and the [divine] splendors.

Having divided the ground, which is twice the width, into five parts, one should fashion the pedestal occupying the lower portion; the arrangement of the *jīva* (the central life-axis) occurs in the third part.

Then, one should fashion the image together with its own support, along with its attendants, its splendors consisting of elemental portions, and its limit extending to the Vidyādharas and others, as well as its true messenger (sadūtī).
There should be thirty-seven threads and one hundred and twenty-four horizontal lines;
having made each part one finger-breadth (aṅgula), the wise man should fashion the great image.
Having divided the length into nine parts, one part is equal to the sun (twelve units);
in that one part, there is one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and by means of that, one should determine the limbs.
Having laid a level thread upon the crown of the head, the forehead, the nose, the eyebrows, the navel, the genitals, and the feet, one should have a beautiful, straight-lined [image] fashioned.
From the big toe to the forehead, the length of the individual soul (jīva) measures one hundred and eight finger-breadths; now I shall describe its various limbs.
The height of the crown is one tāla, and its width is ten aṅgulas;
the encircling band of the crown should consist of fifteen mātrās.
The width at the top is one tāla, and the height is two golakas;
the curvature should be the measure of one tāla, and the neck four aṅgulas.
The hollow of the throat, the chest, the nipples, and the navel should be positioned with increasing intensity in their proper sequence;
each should measure one *tāla*, and the thighs should extend for two *tālas*.
Her two knees are two *kalās* each, and her two shanks are two *tālakas* each; the two ankles should be known as two *netras*, and the two heels are considered to be two *aṅgulas* each. (p. 84) 22.
When the height is three finger-breadths, the two feet are seven finger-breadths long;
in the middle, the height is two kalās, and at the tips, they are each one and a half [finger-breadths].
Their width is three and two eyes [six and four finger-breadths] respectively;
for those two, the circumference is five finger-breadths, and with the wrapping, it is two joints plus half a finger-breadth.
The ring finger (pradeśinī) is considered to be three finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length;
now the others will be described as being three finger-breadths in circumference. (25)
The toes are devoid of any other length or proportional variations, and they are encircled by eight [lines]; each toe has three joints, adorned with nails that occupy half of each joint.
The two big-toe nails should be made concave at the tips and raised by one barley-corn;
the surface of the feet should be red, and the nails should be elevated and ruddy. (27)
The chest has a width of two tālas; at the base of the arms it is six aṅgulas [wide].
The forearms are each eight-sixths [of a tāla], and the arms are sixteen aṅgulas long.
The forearm should be seven finger-breadths in length and five finger-breadths in width;
the middle finger should be five finger-breadths, while the ring finger should be half a finger-breadth less.

The index finger is equal to that; the ring finger, middle finger, thumb, and little finger [are likewise]; the first three fingers are considered to have three joints, while the thumb has two joints. (30)
The middle finger should be half a finger-width shorter than its full length at the tip;
the joints of the index and ring fingers should be reduced by one-quarter of a barleycorn (yava). || 31 ||

That [hand] should have two joints less [than normal], with the thumb reaching to the base of the index finger; the knuckle of the thumb measures two finger-breadths, and the nails extend to the middle of these joints. (32)

Then, the forehead, nose, and mouth are divided into three parts; the elevation of the nose, together with its width, is auspicious when it measures two finger-breadths and has two nostrils (or two cavities).
In the auspicious opening of the nose, which is circular and measures half a finger-breadth,
the width at the thick part of the nostril is two and a half barley-corns, while in the middle it is three barley-corns.
Half an *aṅgula* below the nose is the *gojī*; below that, one *aṅgula* is the lower lip (*adhara*).
Below that, another *aṅgula* is the chin-joint (*cibuka*), situated at two *aṅgulas*. (Note: This reading enclosed in brackets is not present in manuscript *kh*.)
The cavity of the mouth is known to be four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula), while the corners of the mouth (sṛkkaṇī) are one barley-corn (yava) in measure;
the two eyes, located at the sides of the base of the nose, are two finger-breadths in length.

A woman whose belly is like a fish, whose eyebrows are curved like a bow, whose eyes are like those of a man, whose form is like a water-lily, and whose complexion resembles the petals of a blue lotus or the fruit of the *paṭola*—such a woman is auspicious. (37)
Its width shall be one *aṅgula*, and the star (*tārā*) shall be one-third of that;
the light (*jyotis*) shall be one-fifth [of the width], measured from the line of the corners of the mouth (*sṛkkaṇī*). || 38 ||
The two nostrils are beautiful and barley-shaped, situated on the same horizontal line;
the nasal cavity is half a finger-breadth wide and one and a half finger-breadths long.
The two eyebrows, measuring one and a half finger-breadths in length, are two barley-corns wide;
the distance between them is half of that measure, while for a woman, they are half a barley-corn wide. (p. 86) 40.
When the two kārmakas are equal and auspicious, the position of the ears is seven units from the ground;
the length of the ears is two units, and their width is half of that. (41)
A *śaṣkulī* measuring two barley-corns should be made equal to that; one should fashion the two loops and the two cords as desired, with half a *kalā* [or *tuṭuka*] for each. 42.
Above the two ears, at the top of the head, there should be one and a half talas;
they know the distance between the two ears to be five aṅgulas.
The ear should be made one and a half barley-corns in width, and it must not be greater than that.
The forehead is said to be eight finger-breadths in length, and the temple (śaṅkha) is three finger-breadths.
Two finger-breadths above that, there are two shells (śukti), the head (śiras) is three tālas in circumference,
and the two cheeks are seven finger-breadths long, one finger-breadth wide, and one yava in height.

The two corners of the eyes and the two outer corners [of the eyes] are two and a half kalās; the two cheeks are five finger-breadths long; the two jaws are three kalās long; and the protrusion of the chin is two kalās.
The neck has a width of eight aṅgulas and a circumference of two tālakas;
the shoulder has a width of eight aṅgulas and a length of four kalās.
The two upper arms are known as the *trigolāvaśaka*, each six finger-breadths wide;
the width of the elbow from that point is five finger-breadths and likewise [measured] in barley-corns.
The upper arms and forearms are five finger-breadths each, and their middle portion is two kalās;
the wrist is proclaimed to have an extent of four finger-breadths. (49)
The circumference of these two arms is three times that [of the forearm];
the distance between their breasts is one *tāla*, and the ends of those two [breasts] are two *netras* apart.
The nipples are the size of a barley grain, while the circle of the breasts is two barley grains in diameter;
the navel spirals to the right and is half a finger-breadth deep.
One should know that its width is one finger-breadth; below the navel, the belly is two fingers wide.
The heart is said to be twenty finger-breadths [in height], and the region of the navel is fourteen.
The line is prescribed to be eighteen finger-breadths in width;
the chest is fifteen finger-breadths, while the region of the heart is five less than that.
Then, by means of wrapping, the navel is forty-two finger-breadths;
the waist is said to be one hundred and two finger-breadths by means of the full circumference.
The buttocks are plump, well-rounded, symmetrical, elevated by two finger-breadths, four eye-breadths in width, auspicious, and resemble the frontal globes of an elephant. (55)
The two testicles are two finger-breadths in length; between them is situated the penis.
The penis is three finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths in circumference.
That tip of the sheath is said to have two eyes in its circumference,
and at the width between the anus and the testicles, it measures two golakas.
At the root of the thighs, in their middle, the two knees from the region of the knees, below that on the calf, and above the ankle-bone (ghaṇṭikā). || 58 ||
Each *tāla* is reduced by one until the state of five *aṅgulas* remains;
such is their width, while the circumference is three times greater. (59)
On a slender penis shaped like a barley grain, as well as on the tips of the fingers and toes,
and likewise on the ends of the arms and shanks, the circumference is three times its own width.
And this general characteristic of both woman and man has been stated:
a woman with eight parts diminished is slender-limbed, yet her eyes, hips, and breasts are increased.
With the thread of the cheek-bone [gaṇḍāsthi-sūtra], the vulva (bhaga) should be triangular and elevated like the shell of a tortoise;
in its center, at the lower part, there should be an opening like the lip of an elephant.

One should fashion the faces of the God and Goddess as resembling a well-formed egg and shaped like a sesame seed; for the spirits, such as pretas and rākṣasas, one should make their faces circular or triangular.
The others are known to have nine parts, while the principal ones consist of ten parts; the characteristics of those belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the rest are now stated in brief.
One should add one finger-breadth each, starting from the crown of the head down to the feet;
this sequence applies to the chest, arms, thighs, shanks, hands, and so forth. (65)
One should fashion [the faces] of bhūtas, vetālas, and rākṣasas with eleven tālas;
two finger-breadths each should be assigned to the mouth and other features in their proper sequence.
The servants (kiṅkaras) are considered to have gross forms and a height of seven tālas;
Vāmana is five tālas, while the lame and the hunchbacked are composed of portions of the bhūtas.
The wise one, having understood this with effort through subtle vision, should fashion the *kūṣmāṇḍaka* with a height of four *tāla*s. (68)
One should perform the nourishing and the taking away in every single image;
they should be fashioned according to the measure of the unconscious [subject], adorned with all their limbs. (69)
Bringing all peace, auspicious, neither deficient nor possessing extra limbs,
and endowed with the proper postures and gestures— this image bestows its fruit.

The distracted, the downward-facing, the stiff, the inferior, the withered, the squint-eyed, the crooked-limbed, the flat-nosed, the miserable, and the one with emaciated limbs is the Fierce (raudrikā). || 71 ||
With her limbs scattered, she causes destruction; when facing downwards, she is considered to bestow evil.
When she is contracted, rigid, and with a lowered face, she bestows disease. (72)

One who destroys her vehicle [or gift], who is deficient in the hips, or lacks hands and feet, will bring grief to people; one with short shanks brings misfortune, while one who is emaciated brings about the destruction of the king. (73)
One whose hands, feet, and so forth are withered, and who has withered calves, is an Ācāryā;
she indeed always causes agitation and acts as a deluder. (74)
One with all eyes visible is known as "eye-stealing"; one with crooked nostrils causes suffering.
One with crooked limbs leads to the destruction of wealth and wife; one with flat [nostrils] bestows misery. (75)

An image with a dejected appearance destroys the artisan; one that is fierce brings about the destruction of the maker. One with emaciated limbs destroys wealth, while one with a thin waist destroys the grain.
If the cheeks, head, heart, and chest are sunken at the outset, one will certainly lose friends, wealth, and children; therefore, these [parts] should always possess auspicious characteristics.
The straight gaze, the sidelong glance, the one that causes fear with the cheeks, the one reflected in a shadow, the one directed toward all limbs, and likewise the one cast upon a wall. (78)
In dramatic performance, there are nine states characterized by the presence of fear and its reversal;
the *karaṇas* (bodily movements) number one hundred and eight, while the *vyantaras* (intermediate gestures) are exceedingly numerous.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Manifest Signs," in the Compendium of Characteristics.
Now, the sixth [section]:

The Nine Śaktis. [The names and sequential numbers of the illustrations printed in the first part of this work, *Devatācitrasaṃgraha*, are stated in their respective places; examples of the characteristics described here should be seen therein. For example, for the illustration of "The Nine Śaktis," illustration number 1 should be consulted. This should be understood for all cases.]—Seated in a circle, with matted hair, three-eyed, and possessing a radiance equal to a blazing fire.
The nine powers, beginning with Vāmā, are fierce, holding a skull and the gesture of fearlessness in their hands. || 1 ||
Śiva—[as described in the *Saṃkṣiptacintāmaṇi*]:
Four-armed, seated upon a lotus, Śiva is as pure as a jasmine flower or the moon;
he wears a tiger skin and a serpent, is peaceful, three-eyed, and adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon. || 2 ||
Holding a skull and a trident in his hands, with both palms turned upward before him,
and endowed with the six limbs, he shall swiftly become a bestower of siddhi.

p. 91) A division of Śiva [see Saṃhitā 3, Ciñciṇīmata]: That very same Lord, seated upon a lotus, with arms reaching to the directions and five eyes, possesses the forms of youth, maturity, old age, womanhood, and childhood, and bears five faces. [Regarding this, there is a marginal note in manuscript *ka*: "yuvan" = Īśa; "yauvana" = Puruṣa; "vṛddha" = Aghora; "strī" = Vāmadeva; "bāla" = Sadyojāta. || 4 ||

In his right hands he holds a curved knife, a mirror, a water-pot, the gesture of granting boons, and a trident; in his left hands he holds a noose, a staff marked with a mantra, a skull-cup, and a blue lotus filled with seeds.
Kapila has a heart, Muṇḍa is yellow, Pīta has a crest, and Sitacchada has white wings;
their eyes are red, they have the luster of fire and ghee, and all possess three eyes and matted hair.
Having two arms and faces like wheels, with skull-bowls and tridents in their hands,
possessing tawny eyebrows and beards, they bore terrifying weapons and carried excellent yellow-colored armaments.
The Śivabheda [of this, see 4th chapter of the Saṃhitā; cf. Ci.]:

in the left hands are the water-pot (kuṇḍī), the noose, the goad, and the trident; in the right hands, in some cases, are the spear (śakti), the thunderbolt (vajra), the rosary (akṣamālā), the sword, and the discus (cakra). || 8 ||
Śiva is seated upon a lotus, clad in an excellent leopard skin, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread;
he may have one face or five faces, possess three eyes, and bear matted hair and the moon.
In the four cardinal directions are Ananta and the others, red, blue, white, and crimson;
and in the corners are Rudra and the others, white, smoke-colored, blue, and blood-red. (10)
All of them have eight arms, are gentle, possess four faces, and are endowed with matted locks;
they bear the weapons of Śiva and have three eyes, though in some cases they are without the goad and the sword.
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) have the colors of the directions, wear matted hair, possess three eyes, and carry thick tridents;
all of them have their hands joined in the *puṭāñjali* gesture and have a single face. || 12 ||
Someśvara [see his *Saṃkṣiptacintāmaṇi*, chapter 5]—(first): White, four-armed, three-eyed, seated upon a lotus, adorned with ornaments;
he holds the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, a skull, and a lotus, and bears matted hair, the crescent moon, a Jina, and a serpent. 13.
Someśvara—the second [form]—should be made: Someśvara is red, four-faced, and eight-armed;
in his right hands he holds a trident, a sword, an axe, and displays the gesture of fearlessness. 14.

In his left hands, he holds a bell, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a noose; adorned with a garland of severed heads and mounted upon a corpse, he is considered to represent duality and non-duality respectively. 15.
Nāṭyeśvara—[see Aśvaghosa’s Saundarananda 7.3 and Saṃvarodayatantra Ci. dra0]:
With full limbs, bursting with youth, ten-armed (or ten-fold-bodied) and three-eyed;
gentle, with a smiling face, moon-crested, and wearing matted locks. (16)
Clad in a tiger-skin garment, peaceful, with a serpent as his sacred thread,
girded by a great serpent as a belt, and adorned with all ornaments.
With his penis erect and greatly radiant, standing in the Vaiśākha posture, he dances with great joy, his hands filled with blazing weapons. (18)
Holding a staff, a sword, a spear, and a trident in his right hands, he makes one arm in the form of a plow and places it upon his chest. (19)
Having properly extended his left arm, he holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a shield, and the lord of serpents, making him truly beautiful. (20)
One should visualize him as wearing a garland of skulls, divine, exceedingly gracious, the bestower of prosperity, the performer of all pacifying rites, and possessing a gentle form. (21)
One should depict Hara seated upon a bull, surrounded by gods and asuras,
and accompanied by Skanda, Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and the hosts of attendants.
Maheśvara was surrounded by the Apsarases, such as Kūṣmāṇḍā and others, and by the Vidyādharas and other beings; he was being gazed upon with joy by those endowed with beauty. (23)
And before him, those clothed in divine garments and adorned with all ornaments were dancing, while Bhṛṅgī remained extremely emaciated, performing his duty.
In front, in the east, in the middle, and at the end, there are those with blazing and fierce forms who can assume any shape at will;
they are deformed with sharp noses, and they sequentially bestow thieves, fire, and so forth. (25)
Just as the form of the sun exists throughout its beginning, middle, and end,
so too shall the image of Hara bestow fruits in every location where it is established.
Caṇḍabhairava—[see his 8th *Saṃkṣiptacitta*]:
His eyes are covered, his body is yellow, and his eyebrows, beard, and hair are tawny;
he is terrifying with a frown, black in color, licking [his lips], and fanged. (27)
The divine [form] was filled with garlands of severed heads, radiant with ornaments of skull-bowls, wearing a sacred thread of serpents, blazing, and adorned with serpent-ornaments. || 28 ||
He sits in the heroic posture upon a corpse, with an elephant hide as his upper garment;
he has fourteen arms and one face, is gentle in appearance, and is clothed in a tiger skin. (29)
In his right hands, he holds a trident, a sword, a spear, and arrows for the rite of pacification (śāntika);
[in his left hands, he holds] a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a shield, a noose, a bow, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and a skull-cup (kapāla).
One should visualize Bhairava, who brings about peace, as being accompanied by the Mothers, holding an elephant hide in his two left hands.
Aghoraghaṇṭeśa Bhairava—[refer to his 9th chapter in the Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]:
