One should fashion Aghoraghaṇṭeśa, endowed with all these [attributes] and additionally possessing a vajra and a mallet, adorned with sixteen arms. (32)
[This reading enclosed in brackets exists in manuscript G, but not in others: The great form with eight faces, colored like the directions, with eyes like a Jina;
seated, eternally black, the bestower of all desires. (33)
[Regarding the *Andhakāntakabhairava* (cf. its 10th chapter, Samputa-tantra):

One should visualize him standing in the *ūrdhvālīḍha* posture, wrathful, possessing his original form with five faces and eighteen arms, and devoid of the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*). (34)
With his two hands he pierces the Dānava Andhaka, who holds a trident;
likewise, [he holds] a bell, a hand-drum, an axe, and a mallet.
One who bears [the form of] Bhairava, the destroyer of Andhaka, with quivering fangs, the eternal slayer of all enemies, surrounded by the Mothers. || 36 ||
Vaidyanātha [see his *Saṃkṣipta-cintāmaṇi*, 11]: Six-armed, with matted hair, white, three-eyed, and adorned by the moon [variant:
moon-crested], clad in a gentle tiger-skin garment, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread. || 37 ||
Holding, respectively, a trident, a rosary, a skull-cup,
and a water-pot in his right and left hands, he likewise displays the gesture of exposition with two hands.

One should visualize the Lord Hara, the Master of Physicians, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), fair-complexioned, clad in white garments, peaceful, and endowed with a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). || 39 ||
One should always place Dhanvantari and Suṣeṇa at his two sides; the former has the face of a monkey and the body of a man, while the latter holds the vessel of nectar in his hand.

Sadāśiva—[see 12th chapter of the Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]—is of that same form [kh: as well as Time], devoid of the water-pot and other attributes, seated upon the seat of the half-moon, and situated in the center of a white lotus. || 41 ||

On the eight petals, he is surrounded by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) beginning with Ananta in the cardinal directions, and by the Rudras and others, as well as by the Gaṇas beginning with Gaurī, in the intermediate directions;
he is seated upon a divine lion-throne, encircled by Brahmā and the other deities. (42)

Mṛtyuñjaya—[see 13th chapter of the Saṃvitcintāmaṇi]—is three-eyed and six-armed [kh, gh: six-handed], peaceful, adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon, wearing a garland of skulls, white in color, seated in the yogic posture upon a lotus. || 43 ||
Rudra, whose garment is a tiger skin, adorned with a great serpent upon his chest,
and holding a trident and a rosary in his right hands.
One should depict the god Mṛtyuñjaya, the destroyer of death and disease, holding a skull-cup and a water-pot in his left hands and the yoga-mudrā with both hands. || 45 ||
Ardhanārīśvara:
Hara, as Ardhanārīśvara, should be depicted standing upright with two arms;
on his left side, a woman should be fashioned, adorned with female ornaments. (46)
To the south is the three-eyed Puruṣa, joined with matted hair and the lord of serpents;
in the northeast (Īśa), there is a trident and a skull-cup, while on the left are a rosary and a blue lotus.
Umeśvara (as described in his 15th Saṃkṣiptacāmuṇḍāvidhi):
Seated upon a lotus on a crescent-moon throne, adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon, decorated with earrings, gentle, two-armed, and wearing an elephant hide. (48)
With a beautiful Umā resting on his left thigh, his left hand concealed, his faces gazing at one another, and a blue lotus held in his right hand; || 49 ||
Embraced by the hand of the Goddess, with the sun upon his shoulder, and with another mirror [held], Umeśvara, whose liṅga is upright, should be fashioned by those learned in the scriptures. (50)
The Rudras— Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, Virocana, Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Sureśvara. (51)
Jayanta is the tenth Rudra, white-complexioned and unconquered;
likewise, there are two born from each starting with Sadyojāta, joined with walls and lotuses.
[This reading enclosed within brackets does not appear in manuscript K. In some places, there are eleven Rudras, resembling snow, jasmine, and the moon;
they are gentle, adorned with matted hair and the crescent moon, three-eyed, and wear serpents as sacred threads.
Seated upon bulls, they grant boons, holding water-pots, tridents, and lotuses in their hands. (53)

One may fashion the beautiful form of Viṣṇu with four, two, or eight arms— [according to the Saṃkṣipta-cintāmaṇi-draṣṭānta, these correspond respectively to the forms of Caturbhuja, Dvibhuja, and Aṣṭabhuja Nārāyaṇa]. Alternatively,
he may hold the conch and discus in his left hands, while holding the Śānti-goad in the remaining hands.
Richly adorned with yellow silk garments, possessing a luster like that of a blue lotus,
with the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha on his chest, he has full limbs and a broad breast.
Adorned with a crown and earrings, graced by a forest garland, with a serene countenance and gentle appearance, he was decorated with all manner of ornaments. (56)
Alternatively, he may be depicted with one face, standing upon a lotus or seated upon Garuḍa, possessing four arms;
the two hands holding the conch and the discus should be placed at his left and right sides respectively.
Likewise, Sarasvatī and Śrī have a lute and a lotus in their hands respectively;
the remaining two-armed one grants protection with the left hand and holds a conch in the right. (58)
One should place an image of gentle form with hanging hands in the house; it bestows auspiciousness.
However, when situated in a temple, it is traditionally held that he should always be depicted as wrathful with his hand raised.
Blue in color, four-faced, and with intensely reddish eyes,
his lips bitten in rage, Viṣṇu is considered to have eight arms.
Holding a mace, a sword, and an arrow in his right hands,
and likewise a discus, a bow, a shield, and a conch in his left hands.
Viṣṇu has four arms, wears a garland, and holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
according to my view, he may have one face, four faces, or three faces. (62)
Having divided the length of the fish [as seen in Asya 21, Saṃvarta-cintāmaṇi] into eight parts, the substance has its tail facing upwards and downwards;
its width is one-third of that, and the lower half of the tail is seven parts.
From the rotation of the thread, the back is formed; likewise occurs the turning of the belly.
The two hands are positioned near the chest, and the two feet are at the sides of the belly. (64)
The hands and feet [are formed] by two and three parts respectively; the formation of the mouth is by half a part.
Its eye, however, is half a finger-breadth, [measured] from two, one and a half, one, and half parts.
Having divided the head of that [fish] into two halves in sequence,
one should fashion the remainder like a rohita fish for the Lord who has assumed the form of a fish.
The tortoise [cf. *Saṃkṣiptacintāmaṇi* 22]:

Having determined half of the diagonal line from the corner of the square by means of its fourth parts, one should draw a circle from the center of two of those parts, reduced by one sixteenth on both sides. (67)
The head and neck are at the top and bottom [of the body], the tail is in the remainder, and the hands and feet are likewise;
the neck together with the head is twice the length of the foot.

Having examined the back, which should be well-raised and beautiful, and the belly, which should be broad like a lotus petal (or according to some versions, "broad with four divisions"), as well as the nose, eyes, nails, ears, and so forth, one should turn the tortoise over.
The boar [as described in his 23rd Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]:
the neck is eight finger-breadths in length, and the face is eight *golaka*s;
the two jaws at the front part of that face are considered to be seven finger-breadths in length. (70)
The nostril-opening extends seven finger-breadths from the mouth;
the two fangs are three finger-breadths long in the mouth, resembling white jasmine buds.
The two ears should be raised, and between them the two eyes should be sixteen finger-breadths apart;
however, they should be reduced by one *yava* from the previously mentioned measurement, and their eyes should be like those of a red discus-bearer (*cakragāruṇa*).
From the feet up to the neck, he has the form of a man with four arms, enriched with a mace, a discus, a lotus, and a conch, and stands in the *ālīḍha* posture. || 73 ||
Śrī is on the left [neck], while Kṣiti and Ananta are situated at the elbows and follow the feet;
thus is the form of Varāha, adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
The preliminary form of Nṛsiṃha (as seen in the 24th chapter of the Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata) has a dense, white body with high shoulders and a mane;
it has a human torso and a lion's face, with round eyes and joined eyebrows. (75)
(100) With mouth wide open and fierce fangs, having made the gift with his left thigh,
he was rending that chest while wielding a shimmering discus and mace.

One should visualize Narasiṃha, the Lord of the universe, who is difficult to withstand, blazing with radiant splendor, wearing a garland of forest flowers, and appearing as if he were devouring the three worlds. (77)
Vāmana [see his 25th Saṃhitā, Ciṭi]:
One should fashion Vāmana facing east, with two arms and holding a parasol;
he has matted hair, is equipped with a water-pot (kuṇḍikā), is fair-complexioned, and has dark-red eyes. (78)
Trivikrama—[see his 26th form in the Saṃkṣipta-cintāmaṇi]:
"The Lord has four arms, holds a mace in His hand, and bears the conch and the discus;
He stands with His left foot treading upon the universe. That particular variety is Trivikrama. (79)

Paraśurāma—[see his 27th form in the *Saṃkṣipta-cintāmaṇi*; here the reading "Vāmana-Trivikrama" occurs in manuscript G]—is two-armed, has matted hair, and is equipped with a quiver, an axe, and a bow;
he is dark-complexioned, broad-chested, and is Rāma, the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas. (80)
Rāmabhadra—[see 28, Saṃvarta-cintāmaṇi]:
Rāma, the destroyer of the ten-faced one, should be depicted with a gentle form, large eyes, slightly stout, and two arms; he should have matted hair and hold a bow and arrows in his hands. (81)
Valabhadra—[see his 29th Saṃskāra and Ciṭṛka]:
Rāma, the slayer of Kaṃsa, is dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus, has two arms, wears yellow garments, and holds a mace and a plough. || 82 ||
The Buddha—[refer to his 30th form in the *Saṃcayagāthā*]—is peaceful in nature, with long ears, a fair-complexioned body, and is clothed in monastic robes.
Seated upon an upward-facing lotus, the Buddha displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 83 ||
Kalkī—[see his 31st form in the *Ciñciṇīmata*]—is a twice-born man equipped with a bow and quiver (or, according to manuscript *kh*: equipped with a palm-tree; *gh*: equipped with a *skola*);
he is the destroyer of the Mlecchas, fair-complexioned, mounted upon a horse, bearing a sword, and sometimes having tawny eyes. (84)
Hari is tenfold:
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Rāma, Rāma, Buddha, and Kalki—these are the ten. (85)
Keśava—[see 32 of the Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]—is said to have a differentiation of forms through the method of weaving warp and woof [meaning in direct and reverse order].
The conch and lotus are considered to be in the upper and lower hands on the right side [k, kh: from the right portion]. || 86 ||
Below and above the mace and discus, one should fashion the form of Keśava in the left hands respectively,
having a form like blazing fire.
Nārāyaṇa—[see his 33rd Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]:
"In his hands, there is a lotus and a conch above and below respectively;
likewise, a mace and a discus in the left ones; such is the dark-blue body of Nārāyaṇa. (88)

Mādhava [cf. his *Saṃkṣiptacintāmaṇi* 3.4]: "In the case of Mādhava, who resembles gold, the Sudarśana discus and the mace are in the upper and lower right hands respectively, while the conch and the lotus are in the left hands. (89)

In Govinda, who is of a tawny (piṅgala) nature, there is a discus and a mace respectively in his left hands, positioned above and below; and in the case of Govinda, there is an upward-facing lotus and a conch in his right hands, positioned above and below. (90)
Viṣṇu [see 36th chapter of the Saṃvit-cintāmaṇi]:
One should place the conch above and the discus below, and the mace above and the lotus below, on the left and right sides respectively, for Viṣṇu who is white, according to some opinions. (91)

Madhusūdana [see 37, Saṃkṣipta-citra]: In Madhusūdana, who has the luster of the moon, there are a discus and a conch in his two right hands respectively, and a mace and a lotus in his two left hands. 92.
Regarding Trivikrama (see his 38th form in the *Saṃkṣiptacintāmaṇi*): a mace should be placed in the upper right hand and a lotus in the lower one;
a discus above and a conch below, on a white bull, in the first Trivikrama.

Vāmana [refer to his 39th Saṃskāra-cintāmaṇi]: In the Vāmana form, which is his previous manifestation, there is a discus and a conch in the two right hands, while a mace and a lotus are in the remaining two; he is yellow in color. (94)
Śrīdhara [see his *Saṃkṣiptacintāmaṇi* 40]:
One should depict a discus in the upper right hand and a lotus in the lower right hand;
likewise, a mace and a conch in the two left hands for Śrīdhara, who resembles coral in color. (95)
Hṛṣīkeśa (as described in the Saṃhitā-cintāmaṇi, verse 41):
In Hṛṣīkeśa, who has a golden luster, there is a conch and a lotus in the right and left hands respectively, and a mace and a discus below and above them in due order. (96)
Padmanābha (see his 42nd form in the Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata)—in the upper right hand he holds a lotus, and likewise a conch in the one below;
the mace is in the lower left and the discus in the upper left, in this Padmanābha of white luster. (97)
Dāmodara [see his *Saṃkṣipta-cintāmaṇi* 43]:
"In the god Dāmodara, who is reddish-brown, there is a conch above and a lotus below in the right hand, while a discus is below and a mace above in the left hand. (98)
Hari is twelvefold:
from Vāsudeva three are born, and from Saṃkarṣaṇa likewise three;
from Pradyumna and from Aniruddha, three each are to be known. (99)
All of them wear yellow garments and are adorned with forest garlands;
these are declared to be the twelve forms [of the Lord] from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa until the end of Kārttika.
Vāsudeva [see his entry at 44, Saṃhitā-cintāmaṇi]:
"The tranquil, white Vāsudeva, mounted upon a lotus, four-armed, holding the yoga-mudrā, a conch, and both the mace and the discus. (101)
One should form the mudrā at the heart, which destroys all sins without exception: the left fist is half-closed, while the right thumb encircles the left thumb. 102.
(104) One should fashion the all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa, who has four arms and a beautiful golden luster;
he holds a vessel and a *śānti* [staff] in the south, while in the left [hands] he holds a lotus and a plow. (103)
And he saw Smara, bearing bow and arrows, red-hued and resembling a cloud, as well as Aniruddha, with the Kaumodakī mace— the king of weapons— and the Pāñcajanya conch, which is like a lotus.
One should arrange four root-mantras on the left and right;
another five, beginning with Nārāyaṇa, hold the hand-attributes as previously described.
In the same way, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, and Sūkara—this Navavyūha (ninefold manifestation) joined with these [deities] should be known by the best of teachers. || 106 ||
Dattātreya [see 48 of this work, Saṃkṣipta-cintāmaṇi]:
One should depict the all-pervading Dattātreya as having two arms and endowed with youth, holding Śrī on his left lap and seated upon a half-moon throne. (107)
Holding a lotus in her left hand, she is beautiful with lovely eyebrows and long, alluring eyes;
her right hand rests upon the shoulder of the God of Gods to his right.
He should be depicted with his beloved embraced by his left arm, while a wine-cup rests in his right;
his eyes are rolling, and he is surrounded by singers and dancers. 109.
This hero Dattātreya is the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
he should be worshipped by the wise according to the non-dual (advaita) rite. 110.
Reclining upon the waters—[see his 49th verse in the Saṃskṛta-cintāmaṇi]—wearing yellow garments, four-armed, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
he lies asleep upon the body of Ananta, absorbed in the supreme state of yogic sleep. (111)
Ananta, endowed with seven hoods, should be depicted above the head of the Lord;
the goddess Earth is clinging to his feet, and he lies upon the waters, surrounded by the planets.

Padmanābha [see his 50th form in the *Saṃvit-cintāmaṇi*]: Padmanābha, endowed with Śrī, even when reclining upon a bed of serpent-bodies, is seated upon a lotus that has risen up, accompanied by Pitāmaha (Brahmā). || 113 ||
Kāma—[refer to 51, Saṃvaracintāmaṇi]:
Kāma is fair-complexioned, youthful, and lovely; he stands between Rati and Prīti.
He is embraced by her, full of passion, always bearing a bow and arrows, and auspicious. (114)
Garuḍa [see 52 of this work, Saṃkṣiptacāritra]:
Before Upendra, the bird Guḍākeśa stands with palms joined in reverence;
he has a prominent nose (or, according to manuscripts k and kh, a prominent snout), human feet, bird-like shanks, and a human body. || 115 ||
Resembling a black bee, gold, and the moon, adorned with serpents on his head and other parts, Tārkṣya, endowed with wings, stands upon the earth with his left knee touching the ground. || 116 ||
Viṣvaksena—[see his 53rd form in the Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]:
Resembling a blue lotus, bearing a discus, clad in yellow garments, and equipped with a mace;
holding a plow and the excellent conch, and wearing a garland—Viṣvaksena is an attendant of Hari. (117)
Baladeva—[see 54, Saṃkṣipta-citrāvalī]:
White, four-armed, with a full body, holding a plow;
he carries a lotus and a sickle in his left hands, and in the remaining two, he holds a mace and a cow (or, according to k, kh: a pair of weapons). || 118 ||
Hara-Harī (or Harihara, according to another reading; see Aśvalāyanasmṛti 5.5 and Saṃkṣiptacāritra):
with half of his matted locks and half of his crown, he is not joined with the upright liṅga;
in each half he is endowed with his own respective ornaments, and the upper portion stands upon a lotus. (119)
The great-souled one has four arms and is adorned with matted hair and a half-moon;
he holds, in sequence, a rosary, a trident, a conch, and the Kaumudī [mace].
Holding [the two hands] with the right and left hands, one below and the other above,
one should fashion the form of both male and female, consisting of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa.
The Brahmā Section [Note: This refers to the 56th chapter of the Saṃhitā; however, here it is not a group of Brahmās, but rather a single Brahmā who appears in various forms].
One should depict Brahmā as having four faces and four arms, with a long beard and a large belly; he is observing vows and is adorned with a crown of matted locks. (122)
He had tawny eyes and a gentle appearance, wearing an upper garment and a sacred thread; a black antelope skin was upon his shoulder, and he was clothed in garments of deerskin.
In his right hand, he holds a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, or a staff;
in his left, a spoon, a water-pot, as well as kuśa grass and a vessel of clarified butter.
[He should be visualized] mounted on a swan or seated upon a lotus, endowed with the yogapaṭṭa and the yogāsana;
likewise, Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī, as well as the Ṛṣis, are at his sides. 125.
They had matted hair and long beards, possessed the appearance of the elderly, and were hairy;
their chests, eyes, and bellies were sunken, yet they carried rosaries and water-pots.

p. 107) One should fashion Caṇḍī—[see 57, *Saṃkṣiptacintāmaṇi*]—as golden-hued and beautiful, with three eyes and established in youth; one should fashion her as wrathful, standing upright, lovely, and possessing twenty arms. (127)
She always holds in her right hands the trident, sword, spear, discus, arrow, conch, bow of Indra, the gesture of fearlessness, the hand-drum (ḍamaru), and the small knife.
And in his left hands, he holds a serpent-noose, a shield, an axe, a goad, a bow, a bell, a banner, a mace, and a mirror, as well as a mallet.
Having abandoned the five beginning with the conch and likewise the five beginning with the bell, that same goddess may also be made ten-armed according to some traditions. (130)
Below that was a buffalo with its head severed and its skull fallen;
it was a man born from the marrow of that [buffalo], enraged, with a weapon raised in his hand. 131.
Pierced by a spear, vomiting blood, with his eyebrows, hair, and eyes red as blood,
he was being devoured by a lion while his neck was tightly bound with a noose.
With her left foot treading upon a lion and her right leg in the ālīḍha posture pressing against an asura, this Caṇḍikā, with weapons raised, is the destroyer of all enemies. 133.
Regarding the Nine Durgās (navadurgāḥ)—in this collection of illustrated manuscripts, there are two paintings titled both *Durgā* and *Navadurgā* (see 59 and 60, S.C.I.
Dra.)—Durgā is to be worshipped in her own form in a place consisting of nine lotuses:
first in the center, and likewise in the directions beginning with Indra, in sequence according to the syllables of the nine principles.
With eighteen arms, she possesses a lovely, full chest, breasts, and hips;
[she holds] hair, a shield, a bell, a mirror, the threatening gesture, and a bow. (135)
She holds a banner, a hand-drum, and a noose in her left hands, and in the others, a spear, a mallet, a trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, and a goad. (136)
She is endowed with these very weapons—the arrow, the discus, and the dart;
the remaining sixteen hands, excluding the ink-pot (añjanī) and the hand-drum (ḍamaru), are likewise present.
Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Aticaṇḍikā. || 138 ||
And the ninth is Caṇḍikā, the Fierce One; she resides in the center and is delighted by fire.
She is yellow like gorocana, reddish, black, blue, white, and smoke-colored.
She should be known as yellowish-white, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture upon Hari;
the man, born from the buffalo, holds a weapon and has his hair seized by her fist. 140.
"They should be established either in a square or in a row," so it is stated in the Skandayāmala;
by installing the nine Durgās, one obtains sons and long life. (141)

Umā—[In the *Citrasaṃgraha* manuscript, there is a painting of Umā under the name Gaurī. Since Lalitā, Sarvamaṅgalā, Kaiṭabhī, and others are also included therein, they are referred to by their respective names; see *Saṃ.

Ci.* 61, 62, 63, 64.]—She is joined with the five fires and the planets, stands in the posture of asceticism (*tapaḥ-sthita*), and holds, in sequence, a staff, a water-pot (*kuṇḍī*), a rosary (*akṣasūtra*), and the gesture of granting boons (*vara*). (142)
In her left and right hands is Taporūpā Gaurī of great soul;
she herself is Siddhā in the Rambhāvana forest, while in another form she is Agnihīnā Lalitā.
With her upper hands raised toward the shoulder, she holds a mirror in the second left hand;
in the right, she holds a fruit and a collyrium box, and there, the Saubhāgyā is positioned above.
Seated upon a half-moon and a lotus, endowed with breasts, possessing six or four arms, three-eyed, with matted hair, gentle, and adorned with various ornaments. (145)
She always holds a rosary for peace and a lotus in her right hand, while in her left hand she holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a water-pot (kuṇḍikā), and a trident (śūla). 146.

According to some opinions, she should be depicted standing on the back of a lion with her left foot, possessing four arms; however, in the case of Savamaṅgalā, she should be made without the lower [left] hand and the [upper right] hand of protection. 147.
The body of Kaiṭabhī has two arms, is fair-complexioned, and beautiful;
she is reclining on a bed, fast asleep, and absorbed in yogic slumber.
Kālarātrī has a single braid, her ear-ornament is a hibiscus flower, she stands upon various donkeys,
her ears are adorned with lotuses made of bamboo, and her body is smeared with oil. (149)
Her left foot is adorned with a sword made of iron;
she has ninety upward-pointing vajras, is black in color, and is the terrifying Kālarātrī. 150.
Mahāśrī—[see 66, Saṃvarodaya-tantra, Ciñciṇī-mata]:
She has a round face, large eyes, a slender waist, and is in the prime of youth; she is golden-colored, seated upon a lotus, and possesses full, elevated breasts. || 151 ||
Beautiful, with all her limbs perfectly formed and adorned with every ornament,
she always holds a lotus in her right hand, while in her left, Śrī holds a śrīphala fruit.
Two women should be depicted at his sides holding yak-tail whisks;
and two elephants, with water-pots in their trunks, should be shown bathing him from the sides.

(110) Sarasvatī—[see 67, Saṃkṣipta-cintāmaṇi]: Sarasvatī is fair-complexioned, seated upon a white lotus, and adorned with white ornaments; she holds a book and a rosary in her hands, or alternatively, she bears a lute. || 154 ||

Gangā is white, seated upon a crocodile [or a lotus], with her upper body raised and very beautiful; holding a water-pot and a blue lotus in her hands, this daughter of Jahnu stands at the gateway. (155)
And Yamunā, mounted upon a tortoise, holding a lotus in her hand, standing at the gateway and endowed with a water-pot;
likewise, Yamunā is beautiful in form and dark as the petal of a blue lotus. (156)
Tumburu [see his 70th form in the Saṃkṣiptacāmuṇḍācakra]:

One should depict Tumburu as white and gentle, mounted upon a bull, endowed with matted hair, a serpent, the crescent moon, and the third eye; he wears a leopard skin and holds a lute in his hand. 157.
First, one should always worship the Mothers, or else Śūlahasta;
immediately after that, the seven Mothers beginning with Brahmāṇī.
Brahmāṇī—[see 71, Saṃkṣepa-cintāmaṇi]:

One should meditate on Brahmāṇī seated upon a swan, four-faced and full-bodied, holding a rosary and a *sruva* ladle in her right hands, and a sacrificial pit and a vessel of clarified butter in her left. || 159 ||
Rudrāṇī—[see 72, Saṃvarodaya-tantra and Cakrasaṃvara-tantra]—is three-eyed, holds a trident in her hand, and is adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon;
she wears a garland of skulls, is white in color, and is seated upon a bull (or, according to manuscripts k, kh, g, a bull). || 160 ||
Kaumārī— [see 73, Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]—
is the goddess who is red, bearing the moon, adorned with red garlands and garments,
mounted upon the back of a peacock, and possessing the form of Skanda. || 161 ||

One should fashion Vaiṣṇavī as dark-complexioned and beautiful, wearing a garland of forest flowers, with four hands holding a discus, conch, mace, and lotus [according to Mū., A., G., and Gh., a discus and sword], and riding upon Tārkṣya. (162)
Vārāhī is black, pot-bellied, fierce, with the face of a boar and the body of a crocodile;
she is well-clothed, blooming with youth, and adorned with the ornaments of women. (163)
One should visualize Vārāhī as standing upon a buffalo, holding a staff of liquor, and equipped with a sword and a shield, or alternatively, as having four arms. (164)
Indrāṇī—[see 76, Saṃkṣipta-cīna-darśana]—who has a thousand eyes, is mounted upon an elephant, is golden-hued, and holds a thunderbolt;
one should worship Indrāṇī, adorned with garments and ornaments, for the sake of all accomplishments. (165)

Cāmuṇḍā—[see 77, Saṃkṣiptacāmuṇḍā]—is she who has deep-set eyes, an emaciated body, and a thin belly; she is terrifying, with a wide-open mouth and fierce fangs, and she stands upon a corpse or a jackal. || 166 ||

(Not present in the root text; included within the bracketed section) [One should meditate upon Cāmuṇḍā, who is licking [her tongue], whose limbs (or eyes, according to *kh* and *g*) are deeply red, who is adorned by the blazing Lord (Śiva), who wears an armor of islands, who is wrathful, and who wears a garland of severed heads.
(pp. 112) The forms of the Mothers—[illustrations for these are to be seen in the paintings from numbers 78 to 86].
She bears matted locks, is round-faced with three eyes, and possesses four arms;
she holds a skull and a katarī-knife in her right hands, and a noose and a trident in her left.
Or she may have two arms, holding a skull and a sword, and be tawny-colored;
she may be alone in the place of the Mothers, or Gaṇeśvara is at her side.

Holding a skull, a curved knife, a trident, and a noose in her southern and northern hands, and holding an elephant hide with her two upper hands, Rudracarcikā has six arms. [Note: In the illustrated manuscript, Mahālakṣmī appears; however, "Rudracarcikā" seems to be the more appropriate reading. See illustration 78. || 170 ||
That very goddess has eight arms and is endowed with a skull-topped drum upon her head;
therefore, as Rudracāmuṇḍā, she dances in the dance of Nāṭyeśvarī. (171)
This very Mahālakṣmī, having assumed a form with four faces, is present; she devours kings, goats, buffaloes, and elephants held in her hands. (172)
In this [direction], there are hands holding human skulls, and the remaining arms are as before.
She has one face, is white in color, and is adorned with white ornaments. (173)
Endowed with her previous form, she dances, yet is not excessively fierce;
she has ten arms [or a hundred arms], three eyes, and holds a weapon, a sword, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a human corpse.
Holding in her right hand [the skull-cup], and in her left a bell, a shield, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a trident—she is known by the name Siddhacāmuṇḍikā. (175)
The goddess Siddhayogeśvarī is the bestower of all accomplishments;
another [form] of her may be of this same appearance, reddish in color, and joined with a noose and a goad. (176)
Seated upon Bhairavī—[as described in her 83rd chapter in the Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]—she is adorned with twelve arms and surrounded by vetālas, śākinīs, vultures, crows, owls, and jackals. 177.
All these dwell in the cremation grounds and subsist on the finest human flesh;
this is known as the primary group of eight, while the remaining divisions are extensive.

Emaciated, covered with lice, aged, two-armed, with an open mouth, and having protruding teeth, she who causes misfortune should be depicted standing on the ground with her knees and hands resting there. (179)
The yakṣiṇīs have very long eyes; the śākinīs have wheel-like gazes; the eṅgās (? are laughing;
the mahodarīs are always beautiful in form like apsarases. (In some manuscripts of this very work, there is also a reading "caṇḍaḥ" here. 180.
Now, regarding the hosts of Rudras, first among them is Yogeśvara [the variegated images of Yogeśvara, Vīreśvara, and Caṇḍeśvara appear in succession; see Saṃ0 Ci0, pp.
87, 88, 89]: he has a nose, eyes, and a shaven beard, is tranquil, and wears a yogic band (yogapaṭṭa).
Furthermore, Yogeśvara is a hero seated upon the half-moon posture (ardhacandrāsana). || 181 ||

Having formed [the mudrā] with the thumb covered by the fingers of the right hand and the fingers of the left hand contracted, one should place it upon the heart; or else, one may hold both hands with palms facing upward.
White, three-eyed, and two-armed, with matted hair, holding an axe and a rosary, fierce and bearing a staff—thus should the great Caṇḍeśvara be fashioned. (183)
Among the Gaṇas—[see 90, Saṃskṛta-cintāmaṇi]: Gaṇeśa has the form of a man, with elephant ears and an elephantine face;
he has a large belly, a massive body, a single tusk, and three eyes. || 184 ||
He should be depicted with a solid body, a large trunk, and firm calves, thighs, and knees;
he wears divine garments and has a serpent as his sacred thread.
His auspicious face is fourteen finger-breadths in width,
sixteen finger-breadths in length, and his trunk is thirty-six finger-breadths long.
The neck should be one *arka* (twelve) or half an *aṅgula* in width, and three *aṅgulas* in height;
the leader of the Gaṇas should be made with a thick and well-elevated chest. 187.
The wise should fashion the navel with a depression two finger-breadths deep and wide;
the distance between the throat and the cavity should be made equal to thirty-two finger-breadths. (188)
The thighs and shanks should be fashioned, and the feet twelve finger-breadths long;
the head should be firm, either turned aside or elevated like a water-pot.
The ears are considered to be two finger-breadths in width at the outer corners of the eyes and two finger-breadths in thickness;
the cavities are one finger-breadth wide, and the temples (kumbhas) between them are measured by the length of a thread.
At the base of his trunk within the enclosure of the tusks, it should be ten finger-breadths;
by decreasing it one by one, it remains at four finger-breadths. || 191 ||
The opening at the tip should be one and a half finger-breadths wide, and the mouth [of the nozzle] should be equal to one finger-breadth.
Its length should be five tālas, and its entrance four tālas. (192)
At each beat of the rhythm, having cast the "eye-marked" [instrument], one should roll it with thickness;
the "own-tooth" [staff] is held in the right hand, and the "sweet-ball" in the left hand. 193.
One should place a battle-axe in the right hand and likewise a blue lotus in the other [in the left].
This form, when joined with the mental visualization, brings welfare to all the worlds. Thus has been declared the characteristic of Gaṇeśa as having four hands, and not otherwise.
One should represent Heramba holding a noose of serpents in his left hand and a rosary in his right;
with two additional arms, he should be made six-armed as before. (195)
Endowed with these, [the image] has two additional hands:
one right hand extended and the left hand granting fearlessness; thus it is auspiciously possessed of eight arms.
Adorned with various ornaments and joined with the Vaiśākha hand gestures, a beautiful great bull (mahokṣa) should be depicted beneath the lotus. 197.
Seated upon a white lotus, he possesses his former form with four arms;
alternatively, he may have six or eight arms, joyful and absorbed in the *tāṇḍava* dance. (198)
The form of Gaṇeśa is threefold, destroying obstacles and bestowing all accomplishments.
The first is white; it is desired in the home, while all three types are suitable for a temple of the gods.
(See *Saṃskṛta Citra* 92; two separate illustrations of Ekavaktra-kumāra also exist here, see *Saṃskṛta Citra* 93 and 94.
In a village, a city, a town, or a capital, one should worship Skanda, the six-faced one, who is endowed with twelve arms, the foremost, and of beautiful form. (200)
Holding a spear, an arrow, a noose, a sword, and a trident, with the index finger raised;
likewise, he holds a bell in his right hand, and with six [attributes] in his left hand. (201)

The secondary [form] is praised when it has a peacock-feather bow, a shield, a banner, the gesture of fearlessness, and a cock in its field; or else, it is praised when it has six cords and one face. (202)
He always holds in his six right and left hands, respectively, a trident, a sword, and a vajra; and in the [right] hands, a bell and a shield. (203)
Whether in a village or in a forest, he is two-armed and wears a single garment;
he holds a spear in his right hand and likewise a cock in the other.
With red limbs and a red face, youthful in form and well-proportioned, this son of Śarva is mounted upon a peacock and adorned with all ornaments. (205)

The bull, known as Piṅgala [the root text, commentary, and Kha manuscript read *piṅgalākṣa*], is said to be of the same length as the liṅga [the Gh manuscript reads *liṅgadairghyāt*; here, a marginal note in the Ka manuscript states: "The length of the liṅga; it is of that nature, meaning one should make the bull consist of the same material as the liṅga"].
One should make the bull out of stone, gold, or other metals according to one's desire. (206)
Furthermore, in the worship of Śaṅkara, the bull has not been prescribed here as previously mentioned in the Purāṇas and other texts; rather, the bull is ordained by context only for common lingas.
In that case as well, this very [suffix] is the *karma* (object), and the action (*kriyā*) is connected with the future time (*prāntādhvan*).
It should be formed by excluding the three genders (*liṅga*), and its compound should consist of two syllables followed by the suffix *āyi*. (208)
His eyes were slightly lowered, like the back of a seat;
his auspicious eye-mark was slightly opened, reaching as far as the top of the linga. || 209 ||
Although its form is well known as being subtle, it is nevertheless described for the sake of instruction:
the measurement of a finger-breadth (aṅgula) is calculated from eighty-four parts of its length. 210.
The spherical globes of the eyes and so forth, along with their major and minor limbs, constitute the aggregate;
there should be a width of eight eyes, as well as height and the length of the face. (211)
The two eyes should be equal in length; their width, however, should be half of that. The pupil should be one-third of the eye, and its light [the iris] should be one-fifth of that.

The thickness of the eyebrows is half an eye (one digit), and their length is twice that (two digits). The nose is curved with a measurement of one digit, and the distance between the nostrils is two eyes (two digits). || 213 ||
There, at its base, the width is six eyes; above that, it is five eyes in width, and from there it increases further upward. (214)
The interval between the eyes should be two eye-units; the two temples should be three eye-units each.
On both sides, the measurement of the face from the joint should be four eye-units.
From the root of the ear to the edge of the mouth, it is proclaimed as five units;
at its base, it is seven units in width, including the root of the ear.
The root of the ear is four *netra*s in length;
from the tip, which is thin, it measures half a finger up to the base, which is five-finger-widths in circumference.
In the middle of that, there is a cavity; likewise, the earring (śaṣkulī) is a straight line.
From the root of the ear, one should lead [the line] evenly to the midpoint of the nose by means of a measuring cord. || 218 ||
The upper part of the body should be slightly elevated; it should likewise be beautiful between the two eyebrows.
There should be two eyes at the base of the temples, just as there is a quarter-eye at the front.
The distance between those two [pillars] is equal to the fire-altar (twelve units), while the interval between them is two eyes (two units).
The side-piṇḍī is half of two eyes (one unit), and the depression at the front of the six eyes (six units) is prescribed.
The neck is said to have eight eyes, and the hump has three eyes;
above the height of two eyes, it should be rounded so that it becomes elevated.
Below the *kakuda*, five *kalās* are considered for the shanks;
the joint is said to be two and a half *netras*, and the lower shank (*upajaṅghikā*) is four *netras*.
Below that, there are two and a half eyes for the two ankles; two eyes for the hooves;
half an ankle for the hoof-socket; and one eye for the length of the foot. (223)

If it is deficient by ten, seven, or other such numbers, it is called *sthūla-jaṅghā* (thick-shanked), but not struck by the *nāha* (circumference). Likewise, if it is deficient by fourteen and so on, up to three, it is called *upajaṅghrikā*.
The back has eighteen eyes, and furthermore, it has three eyes and three humps; likewise, the end of the tail should be known to have six eyes, and from that, the continuity of the tail proceeds.
She has two eyes; the tail should be one finger-breadth at its base and equal in length at its tip.
It should be three *tāla*s in total length, while the mass of hair is half a *tāla*.
The back should be as broad as ten eyes; at the middle joint it should be reduced by two, and likewise at the front it should be reduced by three;
below that, there should be two eyes for the kambala.
In the region of the belly, the navel is said to be fourfold;
elsewhere it is remembered as threefold, and the two eyes should be [two] units.
The two eyes and the testicles likewise [make five]; from their width, there are five eyes.
The shank is known as one eye, and the joint is six eyes; the lower leg (upajaṅghikā) is also [six]. || 229 ||

Know that the two ankles are two fingers long, and the [two] feet are one and a half fingers longer than that; the two [knees] are five fingers in measure, excluding the three [fingers] for the [two] shanks.
One should fashion the *tāla* from three parts with a slight smile;
it should be understood as being on the back [of the hand], measuring either two finger-breadths or one and a half finger-breadths.
In width it is one-quarter of a finger, while its depth at the tip is three times that;
it has three openings, a triple-folded smile, and a small ankle-bone on the back.
Whatever beauty one obtains according to how one fashions the limbs, that is the result;
however, I shall now describe another bull more briefly than the one fashioned by Viśvakarman. (233)
Having made a square field with a length equal to the desired life-span and a width equal to half of that, one should divide it into nine parts.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be made with nine parts, while the shaft (jaṅghikā) consists of three or four parts.
The upper shaft (jaṅghā) at the front should be three parts, and one part should be deducted from the top.
Then, having taken one half-quarter (one-eighth) from below, the nose is formed with that one-and-a-half-quarter.
Having taken two parts above, the nose and forehead should be fashioned. (236)
One should indicate the horn in the remaining half, having taken one-half of a quarter from the corner and the base;
likewise, having removed a portion from below that and having made it lean like a horn.
One should sequentially remove three and a half parts from each of the six seasons;
one must certainly draw the diagonal line below the ear and remove half of the portion above the teeth.
The wise one should fashion the crest with two and a half parts;
the back should be fashioned with exactly two and a half parts.
The hip, situated above the tail, is formed by half the portion of the ear-line;
having taken one part from below and discarded half a part from the diagonal line, [the hip is established]. || 240 ||
In the same manner, having fashioned the chisel with a portion equal to half the diagonal cord, the wise man should fashion the buttocks, the tail, and the hair.
The wise one should know that the chest is one and a half parts; the belly and the space between the two hooves are each one part;
likewise, the knee-joint, the thigh-joint, the shank, and the hoof are each one part. (242)
Having understood that it has three eyes, is covered with a blanket, adorned with bells and chowries, and possesses the marks of a bull, one should fashion the bull-bearer.

Nandin—[see his description at 96, Saṃvarodaya-tantra]: a youth with three eyes, wearing matted hair and bark garments, red-bodied, with two arms, holding a rosary and a trident; Nandīśa is the guardian of the gate. || 244 ||
Mahākāla—[see his *Saṃkṣiptacaryā*, verse 97]—has four arms and a broad face; he is full-bodied and charming.
He has a beard, tawny hair, wears a garland of severed heads, and possesses three eyes. (245)
In his right hands he holds a sword and a human skull, and in his left hands a trident and a shield;
Mahākāla, whose body is black, stands indeed at the gate on the left side. (246)
Bhṛṅgin—[see his 98th and 50th forms]:
He is emaciated, with limbs covered by veins and enveloped in skin and bone;
he has the appearance of an elder, wears a topknot, is joyful, has a thin belly, and is very pale. (247)
Three-eyed and holding a trident, wearing only a loincloth with a shaven beard, Bhṛṅgirīṭi and the hosts likewise dance eternally before Śiva.
Kūṣmāṇḍa (see his 99th Saṃhitā and Cakra)—three-eyed, white, and very short, with a thick head, limbs, and belly;
holding a staff and provided with a basket, Kūṣmāṇḍa is bowed toward the east. || 249 ||

The form of the Gaṇas—[there is no single fixed image for the Gaṇa]—and other Gaṇas such as Vīrabhadra and the rest, who assume various forms, should be depicted; they have ears like those of elephants and cows, diverse faces, and large bellies. || 250 ||
Ghaṇṭeśa (see his 100 names and characteristics)—He possesses fierce splendor, is white, terrible, formidable, and has three blood-red eyes;
he is licking [his lips], highly enraged, and adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon. || 251 ||
With fangs formidable and limbs robust, he stands tall upon a great mountain;
possessing eighteen arms, he is terrifying, with blazing weapons held in his hands. (252)
With right hands brandishing a vajra, sword, staff, wheel, mace, goad, and mudrā, [he] tramples upon sin and disease situated below. (253)
With her left hands she holds the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), a shield, a spear, a skull-cup, a noose, a bow, a bell, and an axe; with two [hands] she holds a trident.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa should be fashioned, adorned with ornaments of bells;
the god is covered with garlands of bells and clothed in a lotus and an antelope skin.
The Sun’s divine chariot has a single wheel; its foremost charioteer is Tārkṣya’s elder brother (Garuda);
it is yoked with seven horses, and the Sun stands upon it above. (256)
Lampāka, Vipāka, Śveta, Śaṅkhanandana, Kapila, Hemabhadra, and Bhavasena were, in some accounts, the horses. (257)
Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇih, Jagatī, Triṣṭubh,
Anuṣṭubh, and Paṅkti— these are said to be the meters that serve as the bay horses of the Sun.
He has a broad chest and is deep red in color; he is playful or wears a crown;
he possesses a thousand rays and great splendor, adorned with jeweled earrings.

With his feet like the quarters of the horizon, with a sword at his side, and his body covered in armor, he bore a lotus with its stalk and petals respectively upon his shoulder and in his hand. (1) 260.
To his right is Daṇḍī, fair-complexioned, with a large belly and a beard,
holding an ink-pot and a pen in his two hands.
Piṅgala and Daṇḍa are on the left side as the Pratihāra; the two bearers of the yak-tail fans are Rājñī and Chāyā (the reading *saṃjñāchāye* would be better) on both sides. (262)
Standing in the ālīḍha posture at twilight, she holds a bow;
with her arrow drawn back, she stands on her right side.
Likewise, the Vidyā should be on the left, and Sarvatomukhī in the center;
or else, Bhāskara alone should be depicted as mounted upon a horse.
The twelve Ādityas [have no variegated ornaments; they possess only the twelve names of the Ādityas inscribed upon twelve squares].
In front is Dhyānaraskandha, holding a half-lotus, bestowing peace and fearlessness;
in the middle is Kuṇḍa, possessing a rosary; and in the eastern half is Vedikākara. || 265 ||
Āditya, possessing great luster, should have his hand placed at his side with the index finger extended;
the others, from Yama to Anyahya (or according to variants k, kh, g, gh: up to Rakṣas), have four hands on the sixteen-petaled lotus.

The lotus-seated lords, beginning with Varada, all have the weapons of the world-protectors (*dikpāla*) in their hands in sequence; those situated in the intermediate directions, starting from the southeast, hold a mallet, a goad, a discus, and a sacrificial ladle.
Varuṇa, Sūryanāman, and another, Sahasrāṃśu. || 268 ||
Ravi, Parjanya, Sraṣṭṛ, Mitra, and Jiṣṇuka—these twelve should be known as the deities presiding over the zodiac signs beginning with Aries. || 269 ||
Black, red, slightly red, yellow, pale-white, white, tawny, yellowish, pigeon-colored, and likewise brilliant white. (270)
Their colors should be known as smoky and blue respectively;
they are named Iḍā, Suṣumnā, Viśvārcis, Bindu, and Pramardinī. (271)
Praharṣiṇī, Mahākālī, Kalpikā, Prabodhinī, Nīlāmbarā, Dhanāntasthā, and Amṛtāhvā are the Śaktis. || 272 ||
The Śaktis, beginning with Varuṇā, should be known as being in pairs;
one should place them, possessing the forms and colors of their respective deities, upon the tips of the filaments.
Mārtaṇḍa is of two kinds [see 103, 104 of the Saṃhitā and Ciñciṇīmata]: Mārtaṇḍa should be understood as previously described, specifically with four arms;
he holds a trident in his right hand and carries a skull-cup in his left hand. || 274 ||
Holding a trident, a sword, and a plough in his left hands, and a plough, a noose, and a skull-cup in his other [right] hands, he holds two lotuses with his [remaining] hands. || 275 ||
One should fashion the *vyoma* (vaulted roof) in front of the sun, provided with twenty-two pinnacles (*śṛṅga*),
or with four or eight; in its center, upon a lotus, it should be endowed with eight spokes.

Having made the height equal to the width of the living being (jīva), one should fashion the sixteen parts with the weapons applied. Then, by dropping off a quarter-part, the corner is formed; thereafter, the neck (or *kambala*) is made with eighteen parts.
With sixteen units of height, the hooves should be formed by divisions of two, two, one, one, two, one, two, one, and one-eighth of a *pakṣa* (half-verse),
with each successive part receding by one-third from the neck and projecting outward by one unit.

One should fashion the pitcher (kumbha), the cloth-band (paṭī), the neck (galaka), the neck-band (kaṇṭhapaṭṭikā), the bell (ghaṇṭā), and the girdle (mekhalā) in due order; and one should form the spires (śṛṅga) from the corners.

Revanta— [see Asyatantra 106, Saṃkṣiptacintāmaṇi, and others]— should be depicted as a youth mounted on a horse, having two arms and beautiful limbs; he is covered with a turban and a *golaka* (head-ornament), has a reddish body, and is adorned with ornaments.
His left hand should be in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and his right holds a vessel of wine;
he is accompanied by Revanta, who leans upon him, and by attendants such as the umbrella-bearer. || 280 ||
The retinue of the Sun—[there is no illustrative example for this]—has red bodies and great brilliance, possesses two arms, and holds a sword and a lotus;
they are richly adorned with various jewels and fine garments, possessing fierce brilliance, and are born of their own nature. (281)
The offerings for the nine planets [for their various illustrative examples, see Citra Saṃkhyā 107 onwards]:
One should first fashion the original form of the planets, with the Sun at the front. (p.
126) [One should depict] Soma as gentle, white, holding a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), and wearing a garland. || 282 ||
[He saw] Mars, tawny-eyed, radiant, red, holding a spear and a rosary;
and Mercury, dark-complexioned, youthful, handsome, and with a bow in his hand. || 283 ||
The elder [Brahmā] is fair, venerable, and stout, holding a rosary and a water-pot;
Yama is one-eyed and white, holding a water-pot and a rosary. || 284 ||
He is black, lame, with eyes cast downward, wearing a garland of khiṅkhirī seeds; his face is turned away yet smiling, and he has tawny eyebrows, beard, and eyes. (285)
Rāhu has the form of a half-moon, his body is half-formed and deep red;
he has three hoods, appears smoky in color, and possesses the nature of being half-human and half-nāga. || 286 ||
One should visualize them all as having two arms, adorned with ornaments and garments, and holding either a blazing sword as their banner or joined palms in reverence. (287)
A horse, a crocodile, a peacock, a dog, two swans, a frog, a donkey, a cart, and a cloud—these are always their vehicles, proceeding in order beneath them. (288)
The forms of the eight Nāgas—[the illustrations for these are to be found in sequence in Citra-saṃkhyā 116 through 123]—are as follows:
Ananta has a red body and his head is adorned with a lotus crown; Śeṣa (Hīśvara) is white, possesses a thousand hoods, and is endowed with blue water-lilies. (289)
The great Takṣaka has a red body, is adorned with a svastika, and possesses great splendor;
Karkoṭaka is black, and his neck is marked with three white lines.
The one resembling a red lotus has a white head marked with a beautiful dot;
Mahāpadma is the color of a conch shell, bearing a black trident upon his head. (291)
Śaṅkhāpāla shall be golden-hued with a white streak on his neck;
Kulika, however, has a red body and a head fashioned from the half-moon and the sun.
The *eṅgas* [Brahmās] have two arms and seven hoods adorned with jewels;
they all hold rosaries and are joined by water-pots and tails. || 293 ||
The five enjoyments or the three enjoyments—namely their wives, sons, and so forth—and the servants should be made as single-hooded snakes, having the same form but devoid of jewels. || 294 ||
With a mind [focused on him], she is dark-green like the seven types of grain, gentle, two-armed, and holding a serpent;
she is adorned with necklaces, earrings, and armlets, and is always decorated with all ornaments. || 295 ||
Alternatively, she who was born from the mind of Śrīkaṇṭha should be visualized in the mind as seated upon a lotus in a jar, granting boons and intent on meditation.
Jaratkāru has two arms and long ears; Jaratkāru has a lean belly.
He is covered by a yogic cloth (yogapaṭṭa), stands upon a lotus, and holds a water-pot (kuṇḍikā) and a rosary of beads (akṣasūtra). (297)
[As described in the *Aparivāra* (see Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, p.

126; Saṃpuṭa; Ciñcinīmata): Their retinue consists of those with beautiful red bodies and a single hood, two-armed, having the form of infants, adorned with various ornaments, and holding blue lotuses and jewels in their hands. (298)
Svaṅgadevī (see Asya 127, Saṃ. Ci.
has a dark-blue body, a broad chest, seven ornaments, and four arms;
she is beautiful to behold, speaking, and holding her son upon her own lap. (299)
Holding a leafy creeper in her hand and adorned with various ornaments, she is celebrated as Padmā, the goddess Svāṅgā, seated upon a lotus in the Nandana grove. (300)

The constellations—[their vivid illustrations, numbered from 128 to 154, are to be seen in sequence for the constellations beginning with Aśvinī; these are generally not included in the [standard] definitions]:
They have faces resembling a horse, an elephant, a crow, a goat, a horse, a dog, and a pig;
a lotus, a crane, a monkey, two eyes, a tiger, and a tiger’s face, in order. (301)
The Bhadra [seat] has the faces of a pair of buffaloes, a lion, a tiger, and a cat;

and it has the mouths of two Rākṣasas and a crocodile (the crocodile being a specific aquatic creature known as a *nakra*; however, in the illustrative examples of this [text], there exists a bird named Śuka; according to the verse, it ought to be a specific aquatic animal indeed). And the Bha [seat] has the mouths of a serpent and a wheel. 302.
The deities of Aśvinī and the other [nakṣatras] have the faces of a deer, a bear, a donkey, a camel, a horse, and so forth; two of them are not upright.
These are the two Aśvins, Yama, Vahni (Agni), Prajāpati, Indra, Indu (Soma), Hara (Śiva), and Aditi. (303)
The Guru, Sarpa, Pitṛ, Yoni, Aryaman, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Surendra, Agni, Mitra, Indra, and finally Pāmpati (or Yātudhāmpati). (305)
Viṣṇu, Vasu, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, and others. || 306 ||

The zodiac signs (*rāśayaḥ*)—for their various illustrations, see Citra-saṃkhyā 155 through 166—are as follows: the two fishes constitute Pisces; the empty pitcher is Aquarius; the man with a staff is Sagittarius; and the woman with a lute is Gemini. (307)
A man with horse-like calves, a man with a deer’s face, and a sage;
(1) a woman, a boat, a firebrand, a girl holding a sword, a man holding a balance, and a scale. 308.
And the other five, beginning with Aries, have forms identical to their own names. || 309 ||
Indra—[as seen in Āsya 167, Saṃkṣepa Ciṃtāmaṇi, and others]—is thousand-eyed, mounted upon an elephant, with a thunderbolt in his hand and arms raised high;
he has a golden luster, wears a crown, is the king of the gods, and is surrounded by deities. || 310 ||
Agni has tawny eyebrows, beard, hair, and eyes; his limbs and belly are stout, and he is ruddy.
Seated upon a goat (though in the illustrated manuscript a deer appears in its place), he is fierce, holds a rosary, possesses seven flames, and wields a spear. || 311 ||
Yama—[see Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 169; Saṃvarodaya-tantra; Cidgaganacandrikā]:
Yama should be depicted as slightly yellowish-white (or six-fold diminished), holding a staff in his hand and inspiring fear;
he is black with red eyes, carries a noose, and is mounted upon a buffalo accompanied by fierce messengers. (312)
Niṛti—[see Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.52; Saṃgītaratnākara, Ci.
170]—has fangs, bloodshot eyes, and is enraged; Niṛti has a deformed face, stands upon a man, holds a sword in his hand, is blue in luster, and is surrounded by Rākṣasas. || 313 ||
Varuṇa [see Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 171; Saṃvarodaya-tantra; Ciñciṇī-mata], seated upon a makara, white in color, gentle, holding a noose in his hand, and large-bellied;
Varuṇa is adorned with all ornaments and wears yellow garments. (314)
Vāyu is plump, fair or dark-complexioned, with arched eyebrows and a restless nature;
he has a red face, wears red garments, stands upon a deer, and holds a goad and a banner. (315)
Kubera [Liṅgapurāṇa: Vaiśravaṇa], seated upon a ram, is gentle, yellow in color, surrounded by Yakṣas, and holds a mace;
the Lord of Wealth, the bestower of boons, should be depicted adorned with various ornaments. || 316 ||
Īśāna is three-eyed, white, with matted hair, holding a trident, seated upon a bull, and adorned with bones;
Īśāna also bears a serpent and the moon—these are the world-protectors (lokapālas), each having two arms. (317)
Viśvakarman has two arms and a yellow body; he wears matted hair and sits upon a lotus. Viśvakarman is always fair-complexioned and holds the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and a rosary. (318)
Hanumān—[see *Asyām* 176, *Saṃgītaratnākara*, *Citraratnākara*]—has his mouth wide open and reddish, with his tail raised and hair standing erect;
he is intent on the *ālīḍha* stance, possesses a massive body, and is most terrifying. (319)

Endowed with long fangs and claws, tawny-eyed (or tawny-limbed), and adorned with ornaments, he holds a yellow banner in his left hand, or displays the threatening gesture (tarjanī) before his heart. || 320 ||
One should form the mountain-hand (adrihasta) with the right arm extended,
pressing down the Rākṣasas with the feet while letting out a roar like that of the Son of the Wind (Hanumān).
Regarding the *kinnaras* (this word appears in the plural in the written manuscripts; see Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, p. 177, Saṃyutta Nikāya, etc.):
Yakṣas with feet like those of an elephant should be depicted, and the *kinnaras* should hold lutes in their hands.
They must always be shown accompanied by yakṣas on their shoulders and attended by women. || 322 ||
The Vidyādharas— residing in the intermediate space together with Yakṣas, holding swords in their hands and possessing beautiful forms,
or else wearing garlands and joyful— are always situated in the sky. (323)

The *pretas* and *vetālas*—[the *Liṅgapurāṇa* lists them as *pretavetālau*; see *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* 179, *Saṃvarodaya-tantra*, and *Cintāmaṇi*: cf.]—are tall, sword-bearing, black, and have weak limbs;
the *piśācas* have tawny, matted hair, while the *vetālas* have distorted faces. (324)
The Kṣetrapālas—[Liṅgapurāṇa: Kṣetrapālās; cf. AS 180, Saṃhitācintāmaṇi]—are brown-haired, with fierce fangs and mouths, black in color, and terrifying.
Wearing garlands of skulls and bearing tridents, they are the guardians of the fields (Kṣetrapālakas). (325)
The examples for these [hosts of *kinnaras* and others] should generally be seen in Citrasaṃkhyā 181 through 189. Furthermore:

the *godhas*, those with jackal faces, and those with crow faces; likewise the *śivās*, the needle-faced ones, the emaciated, those with large bellies, the *pretas*, those with protruding jaws, and the hairy ones. (326)

[The reading "yoginyaḥ" does not appear in the manuscript copies. Among the sixty-four Yoginīs mentioned here, the illustrations for Ilā, Līlā, Layā, Lolā, Laṅkā, Laṅkeśī, Lālasā, and Vimalā are not seen; furthermore, even in the enumeration, the number exceeds sixty-four.]—I shall describe the group of eight Yoginīs from Indra to Īśāna, arranged in a circle (*cakravṛt*);
all of them bear the colors of their respective limbs, as stated in the *Brahmayāmala*. (327)
Akṣobhyā, Ṛkṣakarṇī, Rākṣasī, Kṣaṇapā, Kṣayā, Piṅgākṣī, Akṣayākṣapā, Ilā, Līlā, and likewise Layā. || 328 ||
Lolā, Laṅkā, then Laṅkeśī, Lālasā, and again Vimalā; Hutāśā, Viśālākṣī, Huṅkārā, and Vaḍavāmukhī. || 329 ||
Hāhāravā, Mahākrūrā, Krodhanā, Bhayānanā, Sarvajñā, Taralā, Tārā, and Ṛgvedā Hayānanā. (330)
Sārā is known as Rasasaṅgrāhī; Saravā (variant: Sabarā) is Tālajaṅghikā;
Raktākṣī is well-known as Vidmujjihvā; and Karaṅkiṇī is [well-known]. || 331 ||
Meghanādā, Pracaṇḍogrā, Kālakarṇī, Varapradā, Candrā, Candravalī, Prapañcā, and Pralayāntikā. (332)
Vicuvaktrā, Piśācī, and the flesh-eating Lolupā; Yamanī, Tapanī, Vāmanī, and Vikṛtānanā.
Vāyuvegā, Bṛhatkukṣī, Vikṛtā, Viśvarūpikā, Yamajihvā, Jayantī, Durjayā, and Yamāntikā. || 334 ||
Viḍālī, Revatī, Pretanā, and Vijayāntikā—
these sixty-four are declared to be the various manifestations of the Goddess.

The first Aṣṭakā [to be seen in sequence from Saṃvarodaya-tantra 190 to 197]: She who holds a vajra and the gesture of fearlessness in her mouth, and thereafter holds a heron, a shield, and a fruit; she is golden-hued, richly adorned with ornaments, and Akṣobhya is seated upon her elephant. (336)
The syllable *ṛ* is very white, located in the left ear, holding a conch, an arrow, and the gesture of granting fearlessness;
in the north, it is situated on a bear, holding a bow and a skull-cup, and joined with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).
With her two hands above the head, she holds a corpse at her hands and feet;
Gaurī, the abode of the deceased, is accompanied by a small knife.
Kṣapaṇā, who has the luster of a campaka flower, stands in a crouching posture facing a man; she holds a mallet and a goad in her right hands, and a skull-cup and a fruit in her left.
Kṣayā is established upon a tortoise; she is Gaurī, endowed with a rosary and a water-pot, holding a skull-cup and a peacock-feather brush in her left hands, and adorned with all ornaments.
She has tawny eyes and tawny hair, is brownish in color, and is mounted upon a horse;
in her right hand she holds a silken noose, and in her left she carries a goad and a shield. (341)
Mounted upon a wolf, she is of the letter *la* (meaning the letter *ra*, i.e., red in color), with beautiful limbs that are inexhaustible;
holding an axe and a thunderbolt in her southern hands, she is endowed with a noose and a goad in her northern hands. 342.
Śavasthā is yellow, dancing, and holds a spear, a skull-bowl, and a bow;
in the southern [direction], she is considered to have a hand-drum, a trident, an arrow, and a severed head in her hands, with eyes on her feet.

Āgneyāṣṭakā [see examples of these in Saṃskṛta-cintāmaṇi, pp. 198–205]: Holding a spear and a sword, three-eyed, with a shield and a skull-bowl in her left hands; she is red in color, standing outside, and sporting with fires as Īlā. || 344 ||
And Līlāvatī is situated on a bear (dakṣasthā—*ṛkṣasthā* is the correct reading); she stands upon a painted seat of a bear (*bhalluka*). Līlā is endowed with red matted hair;
she holds a *paṭṭiśa* and a noose in her left hands, as well as a skull-cup and a lotus. (345)
Mounted upon a mouse, she is red in color;
in her right hands she holds a staff and a sword, while in her left she carries a pair of scissors and half a skull-cup, her face drawn by her raised index finger.
In her left hand she holds a broom, and in her right hand, O gentle one, a peacock feather and a human skull;
with two [other hands] she wields a trident joined with a deer skin, while she gazes at the lake of Sūsa.
On her left is the head of a buffalo, which she gazes upon as it drips with blood;
seated upon the thigh of the Lord of Laṅkā, Laṅkā devours and drenches herself in thick flesh.
In the south, she holds Triphalā, Saka, Kheṭendra, and Modakas;
and Śoṇā, the mistress of Laṅkā, holding a sacrificial pit and Ūrdhvabālā (or Ūrvālācaraṇā). || 349 ||
In her right hand she holds the gesture of granting boons and a discus, and in her left hand a conch;
dwelling in a *kola* tree, she is red in color and is considered to be dripping with saliva, blood, and mucus.
Seated upon a lotus, she is stainless and red, possessing three eyes and adorned with ornaments;
in the eastern direction she holds a knife and a jar, and in the northern direction she holds a noose and a skull-cup.
Yāmyāṣṭakā [see Āsāṃ0 206–213, Saṃ0 Ci0]:

Kṛṣṇā, Hutāśanā, and Jvālinī are stationed in the south; she holds a *sruva* ladle in her right hand and a gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in her left, and is accompanied by a seat, a vessel of clarified butter, and a water-pot. || 352 ||

Śūkarāsyā is white, large-eyed, and rests upon the shoulder of a woman; she holds a knife and the gesture of fearlessness in her right hands, while in her left hands she holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff. (353)
Mīnāsyā is seated upon a fish and holds a *huṃ* syllable and a rosary;
she carries a pestle in her southern hand and fruit and sprouts in her northern hand.
The Paryaṅkā is the Vaḍavāsyā (Mare-headed), holding an infant with both arms;
she holds a fish in her left hand along with half a conch-shell, while the other [hand] is marked by a fish.
In the north, she is gentle, holding the gesture of threat and the gesture of fearlessness; in the south, she holds a staff and a skull-cup.
She utters cries of "hā hā," is white in color, cruel, has the face of a donkey, and sits upon a donkey.
Lulāyāsyā, who stands upon a buffalo, is extremely fierce and white in complexion;
she holds an ink-pot, a noose, and a writing-stick in her left hands. || 357 ||
White and wrathful, she stands upon a jackal, eating a piece of flesh with her right hand and holding a vessel containing liquor in her left.

Kṛṣṇā has a terrifying face; she is adorned with fierce fangs and bones, and on her southern side she holds a *khiṅkhiri* (?), a trident, and a skull-bowl, while licking [something] from another [hand]. (359)
Naṛtyāṣṭakā (see Āsāṃ 214–221, Saṃci):

She holds a skull-topped staff, a book, and a skull in her left hands, and carries a *ḍamaru* drum and a *śava* (corpse) with two right hands; she rides upon a corpse and is praised by all the wise. (360)
Placing her hands with palms turned upward, rising, tremulous, and long;
holding a *śala* drum and a *ḍamaru* in her hands, she is a restless goddess of dark hue.

Tārā, surrounded by hosts of stars, is seated upon a black owl and a human corpse; she holds a half-decadent corpse in her gentle [left] hand, while in the other [right] hands she bears a trident and a mallet.
Seated upon a lotus of the Ṛgveda, Kṛṣṇā bears the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā);
in her right hands she holds a rosary for recitation, and in her left hands a book and a water-pot.
The fierce horse-faced goddesses, seated upon headless trunks and dark in hue, hold winnowing baskets and skulls in their hands in the southern direction;
elsewhere, they bear *śephālikā* flowers.
Then Kṛṣṇā, holding a corpse with severed hands, possessing a sturdy body and thick matted hair, and bearing a sword, a deer-skin, a trident, and a torch in the north; 365.
Residing in a corpse, she gathers the essence; dancing, she has matted hair and is black.
Carrying a trident, darkness, and a skeleton, she dwells in the non-dual state.
Upon the back of such a corpse-like Brahmin, she holds a small bow (kaniṣṭhā) and an arrow;
in her left hand, she holds a noose, a bell, and a trident below. || 367 ||
The Vāruṇāṣṭakā [see Āsāṃ 222–229, Saṃci]:
Tārkṣyasthā, known as Tālajaṅghā, is beautiful and has the luster of crystal;
holding a conch and a shield in her fierce hands, she carries a svastika and a sword in the southern direction. (368)
Gaṇḍāruḍhā, Raktākṣī, Raktāpānā, and Śaśiprabhā, bearing a mace and a banner on the right and holding a noose and a skull-cup on the left, [are situated] in the southern direction. (369)
Vidyujjihvā is white and fierce; she holds a plow and a skull-cup in her left hand, while in her right hand she holds a discus and a chopper (kaṭṭārī). || 370 ||
Grāhasthā holds a chowrie and an umbrella and is joined by a pair of female messengers;
Karaṅkiṇī is white, holds a jar and a noose, and has a boar as her son.
Candrābhā, who possesses the sound of thunderclouds, holds a sword and a shield;
she is surrounded by waters, mounted upon a cloud, and adorned with a circle of lightning.
If it stands in the north, it is fierce and terrible; if in the south, it yields the fruit of the *kartarī*.
Elsewhere, it is a skull or a severed head; those that destroy enemies possess the luster of crystal. (373)
White, seated upon a fish, and fierce, she holds a lotus and a rosary;
known in the world as Kālakarṇī, she has Time (Kāla) as her ornament on her ear.
Seated upon a cat, white in color, bestowing boons and destroying great sins;
she holds a pair of scissors and the gesture of fearlessness in her southern hands, while holding a trident and a noose in the other two.
Vāyavyāṣṭakā [see Saṃhitā-cintāmaṇi, Āsāṃ 230–237]:
Gaurī is seated upon a swan with the moon; she has four faces and, in order, holds a water-pot, a *kuśa* grass, a sacred thread, and a *sruva* ladle, along with the sun. || 376 ||

To the south is Candrāvalī, who has a radiant golden luster and sits upon a black antelope; she holds a lotus and a banner in her remaining hands, while holding the gestures of fearlessness and a rosary.
Adorned with a garland of fruits, holding a conch and a water-pot in her other hands, riding upon an elephant, she is known as Prapañcā; she is Gaurī, the manifestor of the universe. (378)

Residing on a tree with thick branches, possessing the sky as her garment, and appearing at the end of the dissolution, she who has the face of a monkey and a fair complexion constantly eats mango fruit. (379)
Picuvaktrā, who is tawny like a deer or a beast of prey, stands between the southern and northern directions,
equipped in battle with a bhindipāla and a shield, as well as a spear and a sword.
Kākāsyā, who rides upon a hawk and is fair-complexioned, is a Piśācī adorned with red; she holds a skull, a fruit, a knife, and a sword in the northern and southern directions. (381)
Holding a fruit and cotton in her left [hands], and bearing weapons and a sword in her right, she is mounted on a donkey, brown in color, a consumer of flesh, and exceedingly emaciated. (382)
Dancing, greedy, and intoxicated, she stands upon a chariot between the southern and northern directions;
she bears a drum, a banner, a small hand-drum, a knife, a noose, and a peacock-feather fan.
In the north, [the goddesses of] the Aṣṭakās (from Āsāṃ 238 to 245, see Saṃhitā-cintāmaṇi) are as follows: the gentle one holding a mace and a spear, then the one with a trident and a javelin;
then Vamanī (G: Ramaṇī), who resides upon a flower, and Gaurī accompanied by hosts of Yakṣas. 384.
Sarpāsyā, Sarpagā, Svaṅgī, Gautyugrā, Tapanī, and Varā—this [deity] should have her hands placed upon the portion of the body where the excellent hood is situated. || 385 ||
Vāmanī, who is yellow in color, should be visualized as holding an axe and a sweetmeat (laḍḍuka) in her left hands, and a rosary and a jackfruit (panasa) in her right hands. || 386 ||
She who has swallowed the tongue of a boar pierced by a spear and whose body was dragged away by a lion;
she who bears a thunderbolt on her tongue, is yellow in color, possesses four arms, and has a distorted face. (387)
Śaṅkhapūraṇikā holds two conch shells and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her two hands;
she stands upon a chariot drawn by two swans. Vāyuvegikā is as tall as a palm tree.
In the north, she should have a radiant appearance, a large belly, and carry a skull-cup and a shaven head;
she has a massive body, is white in color, holds a sickle, and devours human flesh. (389)
Mounted upon a camel, Gaurī is deformed and creates terror with her distorted face;
to her right she holds a tūrya drum and a ḍamaru hand-drum, while at the end [of the staff] is the head of a khaṭvāṅga.
Holding a shield, a conch, and a lotus in her left hands, and holding a mace, a discus, and a sword thereafter;
she is Viśvarūpā, seated upon the king of birds (Garuḍa), possessing a golden luster and wearing a garland of forest flowers.

The eight [deities] of the northeast (as described from Āsāṃ 243 to 253 in the Saṃskṛta-cintāmaṇi): In the south, [the goddess] named Yamajihvā holds a pestle, a mallet, an axe, and a noose; she is terrifying and seated upon a buffalo. (392)
Dancing, white-complexioned, and mounted upon a bull, she stands in the southern direction holding a hand-drum and a tuft of cotton;
fierce with a trident and the severed heads of Daityas, she is Jayantī, bearing these in her two left hands.
Bearing swords and spears, fierce and mounted upon [beasts], she is considered invincible;
white and surrounded by various spirits, she dwells in difficult forests and strongholds. (294)
To the south are those holding spears and arrows, and then those holding bows and javelins;
Yamāntikā is situated on a cart, with an extremely terrifying face and a milk-white complexion. (395)
Viḍālī, who stands upon a cat, is white in color and has large eyes;
she holds in her left hand a drum, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, and a chisel (or bell). || 296 ||
Kṛśā, Piśācavaktrā, Ugrā, Pretasthā, and Revatī are considered [to be there].
She who holds a trident and staff is in the south; she holds a bhindipāla, mace, and sword.
The *pretas* are like jasmine flowers, three-eyed, with deformed bones, and standing upright;
they hold a knife and a trident in their right hands, and a severed head and a skull-cup in their left hands, [whether facing] the sun or the moon. (398)
White-complexioned and seated upon a bull, Vijayā bestows victory;
thereafter, she holds a trident and a ḍamaru in her right hands, and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) in her left. || 399 ||
All the Yoginīs, who bestow all perfections without exception, should always be fashioned by artisans wearing celestial garments and adorned with every ornament. (400)
Bhairava—[see Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 254, Saṃvarodaya-tantra, and Ciñciṇīmatasārasamuccaya]—shall have twelve arms, four faces, and wear matted hair and the moon;
from his right side, he holds a sword, a goad, and an axe, while bestowing universal fearlessness with the remaining hands. (401)
On one side, he holds a bow, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a noose, and a half-moon;
with two [other hands] he wears an elephant hide, is clothed in a skin, and is adorned with serpents. || 402 ||

Three-eyed, fierce with formidable fangs, possessing a violent and loud "aṭṭāṭṭa" laugh, resembling the color of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution, and wearing a garland of severed heads and skulls. (403)
Seated upon a tortoise, a water-jar, a lotus, a vessel, and a lotus, and resting on the heart of a corpse,
he who is named Caṇḍa stands in the midst of the Mothers, bearing a yellow beard.

From *kha* up to *vilomāgni* (the letter *ra*) in length, according to the divisions of each vowel (*khekaikabhedataḥ*), one should worship its six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgāni*) in sequence, accompanied by the respective seed-syllables (*jātyanataiḥ*) and joined with *kha* (the letter *ha*). || 405 ||
Mounted upon the power of the limbs of the temple, endowed with the grace of its own phonemes, joined with the Nāda, Bindu, and Indu, and illuminated by the end of Mātṛnātha. || 406 ||
In brief, I have described the procedure for the form of the deity;
as for the secret deities and other forms, their definitive characteristics are established in their respective scriptures. (407)

Those standing upright, those seated, those on vehicles, those sleeping, and those moving through the air—these are known as the fivefold images; likewise, they are sevenfold according to their measurement.
Just as the various limbs exist separately within a single body,
so do all the gods exist separately from the Lord, due to the distinction between cause and effect.
Thus ends the sixth procedure in the Compendium of Characteristics, titled "The Application of Manifest Liṅgas such as those of Rudra."
Now, the seventh [chapter]: I shall proclaim the Manifest and the Unmanifest, established in ten divisions;
beginning with the five faces and according to their characteristics, there is the well-manifested pentad. (1)
It should have five faces, four faces, or three, two, or one face respectively;
a five-faced [image] is for undesirable purposes, while a four-faced one brings happiness. (2)
The three-faced [liṅga] is eternally bestowing peace; the two-faced is for malevolent rites (abhicāra);
the single-faced destroys disease; and that which has more than one face is not desirable, being unstable.
In a temple, it may have one, two, or three faces, with the front face facing east;
however, in a pavilion (or at the base of the sky), it may have four faces or five faces.
White and reclining on his back, with three eyes and adorned with a crown and earrings,
his face is situated upon the top of the *liṅga*, as he gazes toward the northeast as the Lord.
Red in color and possessing great splendor, he has three eyes and is adorned with a crown;
he has the face of a lion, is richly endowed with beard and hair, and that face of Indra is the Puruṣa-face.
[The face] called Aghora is black, with a tawny beard, and most radiant;
it is formidable with fangs, has round eyes, and is adorned with flaming hair and other features. (7)
The left face should be yellow and gentle, situated in the direction of the Giver of Wealth (the North);
it is adorned with beautiful ornaments, hair, and the like, and embellished with a *tilaka* mark and a *kolaka*.
He has a face like Varuṇa, white in complexion, with a moon upon his matted locks;
he is three-eyed, full-bodied, youthful in appearance, exceedingly gracious, and most beautiful.
The face of the Lord of the Vineśa [mantra] has four mouths; that of the Aja-mantra has three mouths.
With the Sadyojāta-mantra, it should have two mouths, and with the Puruṣa-mantra, it should have one mouth.
When the measurement of the diameter is established as equal, the worship is performed on the portion extending half the width.
Having divided the liṅga by the principles (tattvas) and the planets (grahas), one should remove the water-portion (ambhaṃśa) in the intermediate directions.
The linga, arising from the central thread, is encircled by five palm trees; its faces, according to the division of the directions, always possess four or five faces.
One should cast the three spheres of the unproduced [or well-produced] facial substance into the three [openings];
likewise, one should place those called "two measures" on the two faces and three fingers' breadth each on the single face.
The liṅga should be made with eighteen parts of the face; by dividing it into twelve parts, the liṅga is encircled by six tālas at the corners, having been reduced by nine parts.
