With a portion of *dhṛti*, there should be a two-faced [liṅga]; then, in the middle, the *aindra* liṅga.
With two and two [units] there, its face is a liṅga encircled by seven faces. (Note: This reading enclosed within brackets does not appear in manuscript G.)
The width of the face is thirty finger-breadths, and its protrusion is one palm-measure;
it is ninety finger-breadths from the circumference, having one face which is the eastern face.
When the portion for the *pūjā* is divided into nine parts, the *liṅga* is at the upper third;
below that, one should fashion the faces of Śiva according to a sixfold division. (17)

The face and the base of the shoulders [should be made] with one part each; likewise the neck, the chin and the lips with one part each, and the nose, forehead, and crown of the head [with one part each]. 18.
Gradually, by means of the portion of the quality (guṇa), one should fashion the beautiful crown above that;
on the sides of the liṅga, having set aside one part consisting of two divisions, [one should proceed] above that.

And the hair-tufts and so forth should be fashioned with effort according to the previously mentioned procedure for the images; furthermore, this same rule applies to those ranging from five faces down to one face.
Then, the remainder, such as the head, the two eyes, and so forth, is circular in shape;
the five faces and other features are said to be clearly manifest, as described hereafter. (21)
The previously mentioned five faces are endowed with all their limbs;
they have two arms, upward-turned bodies, and feet like those of Viṣṇu.
And one should fashion the Lord of one's own direction, holding a rosary and a trident;
on the eastern body, however, there is a male figure holding a citron and a rosary.
In the south is Aghora, whose eyes do not wane, who always holds a bell and a trident;
in the north is Guhya, in female form, joined with a mirror and a lotus.
In the west is Ajātaka, whose form bestows boons and fearlessness with his hands;
he is clearly manifest in five ways, thus situated according to the rule of the faces [or joined with them]. (25)

The limbs are complete by means of five, two, three, one, and one [respectively], not according to that sequence. Having thus produced the lingas, one should then fashion the pedestal (piṇḍikā). || 26 ||
Thus ends the seventh rule, titled "The Tenfold Manifestation of Those with Manifest, Unmanifest, and Subtle Signs," within the Compendium of Characteristics; now follows the eighth. 7.
Now, I shall describe the eighth section; furthermore, the eighth is auspicious in three ways:
for the great [consecration], for the first [foundation], and for the accomplishment of the directions, signs, and locations.
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be the goddess Umā, and the liṅga is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
Therefore, one should never cause the measurement of both to be less than nine [units]. (2)
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) is declared to be as wide as the circumference of the linga and equal to Viṣṇu in height; it is auspicious when neither deficient nor excessive.
The girdle (mekhalā) is endowed with a thickness equal to one-sixth of its own width; the excavation (khāta) is one-third of that, diminished by one-thirtieth.
Or it is declared to be threefold, each being one-quarter less than its own measure.
Having drawn a circle in the center, one should carefully fashion the excavation.
(The following passage is not present in manuscript *ga*: "The outer portion and the middle portion should be equal in thickness (*bāhulya*);
starting from the line of the circumference, one should gradually decrease the excavation until it reaches the excavation for the girdle (*mekhalā*) at the base.
One should thus gradually diminish [the width] until the excavation for the girdle is reached.
The winding of the girdle (mekhalā) outside [the altar] is by one-third of the length from the front.
The water-channel, situated in the middle of the pedestal, should be one-third the length of its base;
at its opening, its width should be half of that, and the exit of the water should be one-third of that [width].
Moreover, the thickness of the channel is always maintained by the leaf-like membrane that holds the water;
for above the throat it is thus, otherwise it would cause disorder.
The watercourse situated at the secret opening is always [present], as is the northern float;
it is formed by the entry of a sixth part, or the throat by a fifth part of the movable [elements].
The entire eightfold group of Vedāsras is not a sacred seat (pīṭha), for it is like a chasm; likewise, the Catra and the Putra are not [seats], being equal to the Sūtras.
In the unmanifest (avyakta) and the mixed (miśraka), within their own portions, they exist in the form of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
In the third part of the extensive pedestal, there should be a cavity in its center;
it should be equal in measure to the thickness of the *liṅga*, symmetrical, and situated toward the cardinal and intermediate directions. (12)
It may be quadrangular or octagonal according to the division of Brahma and Viṣṇu;
it is increased by six barley-corns on all sides from the Jyeṣṭha-liṅga.
For others, it is always reduced by half of that half; for the youngest (the smallest), it is two *yavas*.
The pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) should be made spotless and pure like a *liṅga* by the wise. 14.
The eight-sided [pedestal] of the Jyeṣṭha-liṅga should be visible and exceed [the base] by five barley-corns;
for the remaining liṅgas, one should decrease it by half a barley-corn at each step.
The entry into the terrestrial portion of Brahma is said to be sixfold;
we shall now briefly state its divisions according to their desires. (16)

When [the area] is divided into eight parts for the Brahma [portion], it is praised whether it be three-quarters, half, a fourth part, or the whole as fivefold. (17a) Having understood the entry into the Brahma portion, one should fashion the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
One should divide the height of the pedestal (pīṭhikā) into eight parts.
One part is for the base (aṅghri) seated upon the ground; the shank (jaṅghā) should be in the fourth part;
likewise, the pitcher (kumbha) is in three parts, and the pitcher-band (kumbhapaṭṭi) is one part.
The neck is one part of Rāma (three parts), and the neck-band is made of thin parts (one part).
On the side-parts is the water-reservoir (one part), and on one remaining part is the final band.
According to the system of Bāṇa, the entry and exit from the neck are each by one part; thus is the smallest (kanīyasī) breast described. 21.
In brief, another [form] is described: the Pūrṇakumbhā, beloved of Hara. (p.

146) [From here onwards, this additional reading appears in manuscripts *k* and *kh*: "The abundance of the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) in the Āgama is indeed for the eight-cornered [mandala]. The portion within brackets is not found in manuscript *gh*. One should place two parts on the ground; with three parts, the *padapaṭṭikā* [should be made]. With two [parts], there should be a *paṭṭa*; the *paṭṭī* is considered to be three [parts] in height.
The *paṭṭopapaṭṭikā* is the small band around the neck, the *galapaṭṭa* and its accompanying band. || 23 ||
Each pitcher (kumbha) and each jar (ghaṭa) should be one and a half parts;
however, the belt (mekhalā) and the fillet (paṭṭikā) above that should be one part each.
The pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) arising from the middle [of the plinth], known as the *pūrṇakumbha*, is constructed with thirty-two or thirty parts;
the height of the pedestal (*pīṭhī*) should be half of that, when the [plinth] is divided into eleven parts. || 25 ||
The *khurapaṭṭī* consists of six parts; the *paṭṭopapaṭṭikā* consists of two;
the *arja* consists of three; the *dvipaṭṭa* likewise consists of two; and the lotus consists of two.
The *hīnopahīnika* neck-band, the *paṭṭa*, and the *upapaṭṭikā* are produced respectively by two, two, and [one] and a half parts; the emergence from the throat is thus formed. (27)
In this very manner, above the neck, there is an upper fillet by one part,
joined with two necks (or two parts) and adorned with six lotuses.
In this supreme realm named Padmākula,
there is always a water-bearing ocean called Saṃvarta, which rises as far as the portion of Viṣṇu.
The circular base (piṇḍikā) of the unmanifest (avyakta-liṅga) is proclaimed to be provided with the previously mentioned nāla, khāta, and other features,
and is encircled three times by the liṅga.
For the manifest [mandala], however, there may be a pond whose length and width are equal;
its breadth is half its length, and the height of the nāla is half of that. (31)
The water-channel should be as bright as a measure of grain; the three enclosures (paridhis) should be one-third of that in the middle.
When the height is divided into ten parts, one part is for the base (pada), likewise for the pitcher (kumbha), and for the neck (gala).
One should fashion the circular water-reservoir from the *laghnī* [base], dividing it into two parts;
then one should fashion the hoof, the shank, the knee, the neck, and the collar-bone.
It is surrounded by its fillet (paṭṭikā) and likewise by the water-holder (jalādhara);
[it is formed] by one pair, one wing, one pair, and one neck-section. || 34 ||
For the middle-sized seats, the pedestal should always be divided into twelve parts by those who are well-versed in devotion;
for the largest seats, the height is always made with sixteen parts.
The base-moulding (caraṇa), the fillet (paṭṭikā),
the pitcher (kumbha), the fillet, and the neck-fillet (galapaṭṭikā) are measured by fifteen, one, two, three, six, and one [units] respectively.
That circular base for the band shall be the girdle-band (mekhalāpaṭṭikā);
it should be made with eight, ten, or twelve cubits for the three types—inferior, middling, and superior. || 37 ||
The pedestal for the great images may consist of two sections, like a water-bearing cloud;
the entry, the base, and the abundance of the shaft and so forth are as previously described.
The image, standing on half [of its total height], is without ornaments and devoid of radiance;
the width of the pedestal is one-third of that [height], and its height is three-quarters of that [width]. (39)
The two broad bases are each one-sixteenth of the sun's portion, while from the single reality of the moon [the neck arises];
together with the pitcher, the neck is circular, and the fillet is quadrangular in sequence.
The lotus [pedestal] consists of three parts: the entrance, the remainder of the moulding (vṛtta), and the top (śeṣa), each being half, one [unit], and half [respectively].
[This reading within brackets is not found in manuscript Kh; elsewhere, however, it would be as follows: from the *saṃvṛtta* moulding, the *karṇa* and the pedestal (*pīṭaka*) are likewise formed.
On the face-liṅga, an additional part should be made quadrangular and divided into two sections;
it should be very smooth with well-joined seams, and in appearance like a water-bearing cloud.
It should be constructed with copper, silver, or gold, with each successive part being one-quarter the size of the preceding;
it may have a thousand, a hundred, or eight spokes, and consist of a single section.
However, according to the opinion of some, there should be a parasol atop the clearly defined liṅga.
If the pedestal is deficient in its characteristic marks, there will be death from service; if it is excessive, there will be severe disease.
Therefore, for the longevity of the patron, the pedestal must be made in accordance with the characteristic marks of the linga.
If the pedestal is higher than the *liṅga*, or if the *liṅga* exceeds the pedestal, the maker, the kingdom, and likewise the preceptor will be afflicted by diseases. (45)
Therefore, both the portions of Hari and Brahmā should be made either smaller or larger;
however, among the three lingas, that of Hari must not be smaller nor larger [than the others].
Having made the antelope skin equal to one's own height, one should fashion the lotus seat with eight and a half parts;
Śambhu with seven and a half parts; and Hari, the destroyer of wealth, with six parts.
The three-eyed [Śiva] should be made from one-eighth plus a quarter [of the unit], and the wielder of the discus [Viṣṇu] from one-eighth plus a sixteenth;
Brahmā should be made from one-eighth minus a quarter, and in some cases, he may be fashioned without any [additional] wealth.
Then, one should fix Viṣṇu at one-eighth of the height of Hara;
in a Liṅga worshipped by the gods, Brahmā is certainly fixed at one-seventh.
Furthermore, another source well-known for this is the *varṇasamāśilā* (stone of uniform color), which is to be grasped;
the colors such as white and so forth are not produced from seats (*pīṭha*) and the like that are devoid of color.

A Linga situated within one's own portion or body, auspiciously made of stone, minerals, and so forth, or born of gems, or even of metals—now I shall specifically describe it for the sake of fame. (51)
For pearls and crystal, the pedestal should be made of silver; for topaz, it should be made of copper;
but for the finest gems such as lapis lazuli, a pedestal made of gold is always the most excellent.
One should further divide that which is produced from the jewels either fivefold or threefold;
then, one may place two additional portions in the cavity for the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
One should determine the portion for worship by means of three parts or two;
the division of its girdle and other features has been described as before.

The cavity for the entry of the *liṅga* should be sloped toward the *liṅga*, its dimensions matching the configuration of the *liṅga* itself; neither less nor more than the prescribed measurement, such a pit is considered auspicious. (55)
If there is a wound or another defect, death occurs; if it is on the face, there is loss of wealth.
Due to defects in the pedestal (pīṭha), there is always ruin for the woman and the maker. 56.
Furthermore, the square, the circular, and the lotus-shaped [seats] arise in sequence from the unmanifest and so forth;
they are for the attainment of both enjoyment and liberation, while others are for the sake of specific desires.
Dharā, Bhadrā, Yakṣī, Vajrī, Tryasrā, Maṇḍalā, Padmā, Ardhendugaṇā, and Kāmadā are located at the auspicious summit. (58)
A square plot of land with four corners, having equal divisions, bestows the earth;
likewise, a plot with four corners and two boundary lines is called Bhadrā, which grants the perfection of yoga.
The Yakṣī Trimekhalā is circular, a queen who bestows cows;
she is six-cornered, bestows long life, wields a thunderbolt, and is endowed with three girdles.
The triangular [vagina], endowed with three (or two) girdles, causes the contraction of enemies;
the circular one, possessing the luster of the full moon, bestows wealth when it has five girdles.

(150) By means of the lotus-petals resting upon the pericarp of the hand-lotus, the throat-pericarp, and the ear-lotus—[or, according to some, the reservoirs of water]—divided by the lunar digits (tithis), with the portions of earth, fire, and sky on the left, [the result is obtained]. || 62 ||
The pericarp, measuring half of the entry [of the petals] and half of the sixteen [petals], is circular, shaped like a lotus bud, and kissed by both [sides]. 63.
The eight-cornered lotus, known as Gaṇa, bestows sons, longevity, and prosperity; it grants peace and, with two girdles, it shall grant liberation (or worldly enjoyment).
The length, width, and height of the liṅga should extend as far as Viṣṇu;
it should be provided with the previously mentioned girdles, cavities, stalks, and so forth.
The three corners of his pedestal are considered to be the enumeration of the female lingas;
all details regarding its width, height, stalk, and so forth, have been stated in sequence as previously described.
Having encircled the liṅgas of the lords of the ten directions with threads of one's own [color] and those of Yama, one should fashion a piṇḍī that accomplishes the desires of the practitioner.
One should always [worship] the goddesses of Indra, Vaiśvānara, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, as well as those of Vāyu, Dhana, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
Having given the thread (sūtra) from Ainghrāṃ to Pūra, [he should draw] a pair of fish at the two sides;
with half the thread in the middle of the thread, he should draw fish in all the corners.
Having further drawn four lines, one should accomplish a square;
for all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the area of the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is always a quadrangle.
Having taken half of the diagonal line at the fourth part, one should carefully rotate it;
then, from the center, having drawn another thread reaching to the center, one should enclose the other corner.
Having made the field and having made a portion toward the north, one should establish the *triparṇikā* (or *bodhiparṇikā*) from the junction of those two lines. (72)
Having divided the field into four parts, one should rotate the thread from the center through two portions on each side to establish the half-moon shape.
Having divided the site into five parts and assigned one share to each,
one should draw three lines toward the directions of the Rakshasas (south-west), Agni (south-east), and Soma (north) to form a triangle.

When the field has been divided into seven parts, one part from that is placed outside; by means of the intersections of the central vertical and horizontal lines, the circular pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is formed. (75)
Having removed the portion of modification from the center toward the corner, once the circle has been drawn,
one should drop the thread between the square and the circle at the points of Yama and Indra.
That thread, from the middle of the threads, should be drawn toward the diagonal corners;
by the removal of the remaining lines, there shall be a hexagonal cluster.
When the field has been divided into nine parts, one part should be set aside;
from the center of the cord, a circle should be drawn, and the lotus [to be placed] therein is as previously described.
When the field has been divided into nine parts, one should project a portion outward;
then, by means of half a portion of the central line—or two portions—one should diminish the corners.
Having removed one part from the outside of the Jina-parts,
one should always fashion an octagon by means of the corners marked with half-marks and defined by threads.
p. 152) Having set aside one part outside of the eight parts, and having cut off the corners with lines drawn from below the corners, one should then divide it into ten parts.
Having removed two parts from both ends of the corner, one should drop a cord from the corner;
then, by means of sixteen parts, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) for the abode of Keśava should be constructed.
Having divided the field into six parts and set aside one part on the exterior, one should,
as before, construct a thirty-two-sided figure using sixteen parts.
The Aindrī [mudrā] is four-cornered; it is considered effective for paralyzing an army.
The Āgneyī [mudrā], resembling a Bodhi leaf, causes the burning of diseases and fire. (84)
The southern region, shaped like a half-moon, causes the destruction of enemies;
the triangular region of the Rākṣasas always brings about the concealment of faults.
The western [vārūṇī] mandala is circular and it causes nourishment;
the northwestern [vāyavyā] is said to be hexagonal and it effects the eradication of enemies. || 86 ||
The supreme [wheel], lotus-shaped and gentle, always bestows wealth and nourishment;
the fierce one, known as eight-cornered, grants liberation and destroys the flow [of rebirth].
The Vaiṣṇavī [yantra] has sixteen sides and brings about the crushing of enemies;
the Vāhnī [yantra] has thirty-two sides and bestows the fruit known as heaven.
The Rakṣas is situated within the lord of the three worlds; in the villages of Keśava and Aja, it is like a half-moon, blue in color, and the remainder (the Śeṣa) should be like a bow.
All [the goddesses], marked with their own weapons and possessing lotus-stalks, stationed in their respective directions, produce such results for Piṇḍī, Māma, Staka, Ādi, and the others. (90)

The *liṅga* is situated in the middle of the *bhaga*, and the *bhaga* is established beneath the *liṅga*. The entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is marked by the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*. (91)
Śakti, then, is the power that supports; Umā is she who takes the form of the sacred seat (pīṭha).
That supreme Śivaliṅga is the ultimate reality; from the union of these two, there arises great fruit.

Extending as far as the portion of Viṣṇu, it is fashioned with half of that, and then with half of that again; the hollow at the foot of the petal is shaped like a tortoise, and the line at the corner of the square is shaped like a liṅga.

The Brahma-area, four-cornered and three times the height of the Veda-portion, should have its width increased by one part; it should be dug out as a square pit, and the Brahma-portion should be duly prepared. 94.

In some cases, the stone for the planetary pit (grahagartā) should have a width equal to half the length of the linga, with its corners extending half of that [in height], and its hollows being one-fourth of that, provided with lotuses. || 95 ||
Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus with a hollow in the center and on the petals,
the *brahmaśilā* should be made circular for other purposes, but triangular in the case of a ritual accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Likewise, the Devapīṭha, Īśāna, Vṛṣa, and the Brahmaśilā—whether they are of a single origin or a single color—this is auspicious; anything other than this is inauspicious.
Once the characteristics have been fully ascertained and the measurements and qualities have been examined, the best of guides should first determine the price for the merchant. (98)
For the sake of increasing his own subjects and the king’s prosperity, he should first observe the teacher;
afterwards, having [observed] the twice-born, the outcastes, and the heretics, he should then disclose the price.
When that which was acquired through heroic effort (or purchase) has been kept for six years,
then, having performed half of the sacrificial rite, the Liṅga should be installed on an auspicious day.
Thus ends the eighth procedure, titled "The Formation of the Pīṭha," in the Compendium of Characteristics.
Now, for the ninth [chapter], I shall describe the trident and other weapons, such as the tridents and so forth, belonging to the lords of the directions beginning with Hara.
In a four-cornered [figure], divided by nine, there should be a trident in the center, starting from the ninth [square]. || 1 ||

With half and half again of those parts, the two petals are formed in the shape of a bud; leaving aside one and a half units each, the two widths are considered to be six and a half units due to the curvature.
The two shoulder-blades and the two sides of the spine should be like the joints of skin and bone;
their two sockets should be made very beautiful, measuring one and a half times as long.
In the center, with a length equal to half that of the base (mūla), the altar below is adorned with a lotus;
beneath the altar, a shaft (daṇḍa) should be made three times as long and threefold in width.
Having erased the line with white [pigments], one should draw a trident in red; on a staff, a lotus;
and on a white [background], there should be a line and a staff, while in the northeast (aiśyām) alone, a trident.
Having fashioned a staff with a vajra at its base, there is a yellow vajra upon a white lotus;
the central prong is yellow, while the two side-prongs are green.
When the horn of its wing is yellow, then its interior becomes green;
thus, in brief, the vajra of Indra is described as being in the east.
When the staff and so forth, as well as the trident, are placed on the wings and the horns,
and the middle horn of the fire-diagram is red, then that is the direction of Śakti.
Regarding the staff:
having divided its length into eight parts as for the Jina-image,
the width at both the base and the tip of the staff should be made from the second part, and it should be circular from the base to the tip.
In the middle of the staff, within the white portion of the fist-sized grip, there is a white lotus;
outside the four [squares], there is a white line, while to the south is the black line of Yama.
The Sword: It should be seven-limbed and quadrangular, with a hilt at the bottom consisting of one part from the middle;
its tip should be rounded, and the base of the corners should be beautifully shaped for the insertion of the foot. (11)

Above that, by means of a rotation with one and a half parts, from a length of three parts, there is always a bark-like border resembling a crescent moon; in its middle, it extends upwards by two and a half parts.
From one-sixteenth of the inner staff, the middle part should be thick and the two lower parts thin;
even when they are equal, the face should be raised in the middle, with its base at the two sides.
The two clusters (gucchau) should be half a part wide and one-third as long, resembling the digit of the moon;
one should thus form a fist, which is yellow or white in appearance. 14.
One should fashion its face on both sides, with a width of half a part [on each side].
From the height of the hilt (*muṣṭi*), it should be four times as long, with a rounded tip like a sword-blade.
The stream should be smoke-colored and white; the water extends half a part in width.
Having abandoned three parts, the sword [of the weapon] is like the color of a bhr̥ṅga bee in the southwest, the direction of the Rākṣasa.
The *paṭṭiśa*:
the *paṭṭiśa* resembles a sword and is endowed with four edges;
this weapon has been mentioned incidentally, for it is dear to the Yoginīs and [the Buddha] Akṣobhya. (17)
Regarding the cord (pāśa):
on the auspicious part of the nāha, its width is one-third [of the nāha];
at the beginning and end, it is half the length of the mouth and tail; and in the middle of the yoke, it is determined by the directions and regions. || 18 ||
At the end of the division by two lines in the middle,
the wise man should rotate [the cord] like a circle on the left and right sides by means of two parts each, within the two central squares.
There, between the central line and the end of the cord, one should eliminate that [corner-line] in such a way that it forms a proper knot. (20)
At the front, in the middle portion, the face is fashioned resembling the *bakula* flower;
below that by one part, there should be the face endowed with the nose, eyes, and tongue. 21.
One should rotate [the cord] like a half-moon from the middle of the lower part of that;
then, on both sides below that, at the two parts, the ear-line (karṇasūtra) is equal for both. (22)
The *phaṇasa* is like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, marked with a lotus in the center;
one should shorten the tail by one-third from below, or by its own part (one-fifth) from the tip.
By the removal of the remaining lines, it is beautified in the center by the [remaining] lines;
the white serpent has a black tongue and mouth, red eyes, and is most beautiful. (24)
In front, there is a white time (or form), and in some places a dark, terrifying one;
in the western direction, the western noose should be made by the guide. || 25 ||
The Banner:
Having removed one-sixteenth part as the width from the corner, and having removed one-third from the water-side in the wind-corner, the Mirror is said to be [placed] there. (26)
From the middle of that form, one should erase two parts by rotating from the half-moon [candrārdha] to the arrow [bāṇa];
then, from the half-moon to the corner [koṇa], one should erase two parts, starting from the water-line [jala].
Having left the corners which occupy nine parts below the *randhra*,
[one should proceed] downwards by the height and twice upwards from the horizontal line of the width.
In some cases, it may have the luster of a plantain leaf and be spread out like a *kadalī* leaf;
one should make that [flagstaff] straight with half of its length, or curved like a serpent.
Having always laid out the thread from the southwest corner with a fivefold placement, it should have the luster of the tail of a rohita fish due to its constant contraction by two parts.
One should rotate it by half of a six-part [unit], and again below that by two parts;
from Īśāna to the east for seven [units], and again from the eastern direction for seven through rotation. (31)
Then, from that point, one should rotate the cord by two parts toward the side—
from the mirror, toward the east, and from the portion below the Brahma-sūtra.
The staff (daṇḍa) should be made equal to the field, and its width (vistara) should be one-third of it.
By the destruction of the remaining lines [the letters mū, a, k, kh, g, ṅ: the remaining lords], there is the banner of Vāyu in the wind. || 33 ||
The banner has a lotus, a mirror, and a crescent moon at its top; it is yellow or green.
The mallets (gadās):
"I am not one," having divided that [syllable] into two parts, it becomes extensive through its elemental portions;
at the beginning and end is the goddess Saṃvikā, with two [syllables] for the circle and one on each side. || 35 ||
Having omitted one part on both sides, the middle is yellow; it is a white lotus with waters (lines).
The mace is yellow, the lines are reddish, and the central line has the luster of a parrot.
At the beginning and the end, a chain should be made hanging from the middle line;
likewise, four circular lines should be equal in height to the hips and the feet.
They should be made yellow in color, or green, or sometimes white;
thus the weapon of Kuvera is always situated in the direction of the Moon (the north).
One should fashion the lotus—the Brahmā-weapon—as a lotus with filaments, pericarp, and stamens;
it is brilliantly white, endowed with a red rim, and situated between Īśāna and Indra. (39)
The Sudarśana-cakra has eight corners;
when divided by twelve, from the middle portion through rotation, the nave is formed.
From the center of the nave, by means of a portion, the rim (mekhalā) is formed through rotation.
Having revolved again from the center of the navel, [the line] goes outside the girdle (mekhalā) from the fire-line;
likewise, by revolving with a further portion beyond that, the circle (cakra) is formed.
Having erased the line within the center of the navel, one should rotate it;
there should be eight spokes in the eight directions, or in some cases sixteen spokes. (42)

And the two wheels have a luster like the petals of a blue lotus; like a flower, they possess three parts at their lower edge, extending from the center with a width of six parts, while the *masūrī* (the raised rim) is slightly elevated. (43)

Below that, the width is equal to the extent of the Veda (four units), and it is called circular in shape; likewise, its height is one unit. The square-shaped *paṭṭikā* has a height and width of one unit each.
That [lotus] should be made with a portion of one-sixteenth (or, according to manuscript *g*, one-eighth) on each side, straight or following the sequence of the seasons (*ṛtu*).
Thus is the seat of the wheel, and from there, the rays extend all around.
Its height at the summit is three parts, and on the two sides it is half a part;
by revolving, it resembles the bud of a lotus and is situated in the center of the wheel.

p. 160) Or, from the remainder, the long lines for the attainment of success are to be drawn according to the proportion of the width; thus, eight numbers should be established on one side and likewise on the other. (47)
One should draw rays, a red and white pedestal, and with the remaining [colors], a destructive line;
within the sword and the noose, one should depict the Sudarśana of Hari.
Tridents and other weapons are auspicious when placed on the head of Soma;
the mace and staff have their heads pointing eastward, and the calculation of the portions is according to their respective parts.

From Īśa (Śiva) up to Viṣṇu, the weapons of the world-protectors should be known as beginning with the trident and ending with the discus; they consist of the splendor and power of their respective directions.
In another manner, the one called *trika* is again otherwise;
the weapons beginning with the arrow (*bāṇa*) have been described, and now those beginning with the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) and the elephant (*ibha*) will be explained. (51)

When the field of the bell has been divided into eight parts, one should form a petal from half a part in the middle, on both sides, and above; it should be circular and angular, with circular bands (or wing-bands).
The head is thick by half a part; its projection on the two sides is half a part.
From the neck, or from the width, the shoulders project out by half a part. (Or: the projections from the shoulders are by two parts.)
In a circular form, with two wings, there is a descent of four and a half [parts];
the two wings have an extension of four parts and are joined by a half-part.
That work should be done by means of the ear-line (*karṇasūtra*), emerging half-and-half below that;
the height is half [the width], and it is provided with three bands (*paṭṭikā*) in width. (55)
Indeed, by destroying the remaining portion [specifically], the bell is thus dear to the gods;
it should be fashioned with two parts from the stem of the lotus, endowed with the proper characteristics.

Adorned with a series of pearl necklaces and decorated with nooses and *lālū* [or *lolūka*] ornaments, the excellent bell made of bronze possesses a beautiful sound; it bears the weapons of its own deity and is held amidst the musical instruments. 57.
The carriers:

having divided the Vedas and the Āśramas into eight parts, one should arrange them in sequence; likewise, elephants, horses, mules, and camels, along with their riders, should be assigned from three parts.
Above that, by one-quarter less, there are cows, gavayas, and buffaloes;
other animals such as deer, donkeys, and gaṇḍakas may also exist there. || 59 ||
Vyulaghya, gavyaja, śvānastena, akṣa, lakṣamāhika;
jalonā, vyāghra, kapi, uṣṭra, lakṣādārjanaka—and likewise [others]. || 60 ||
Likewise, for the killing of a brown mongoose, a hare, or a rat [or a mosquito], fifty less [than one hundred] should be performed;
for a crocodile, a monitor lizard, a crab, or a fish, it should always be six less [than one hundred].
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Maneuvering of Vehicles and Weapons," in the Compendium of Characteristics.
Now begins the tenth [chapter].
Hereafter, I shall explain the determination of the time-lagna and other factors.
Two truṭis are said to constitute one lava; a niṣeṣa consists of two lavas.
Those who know time have declared that fifteen *nimeṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*;
a wise man should know that thirty *kāṣṭhās* make a *kṣaṇa*, and thirty *kalās* [make a *kṣaṇa*]. (2)
A muhūrta should be known by those who know the truth as consisting of twelve kṣaṇas;
and from two such [muhūrtas], a nāḍī is formed when sixteen parts have been subtracted from the two nāḍīs.
A *prahara* is proclaimed to consist of four *ghaṭīs*;
eight of those constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*), and fifteen of those constitute a *pakṣa*.
From two of those [fortnights] comes a month; from two months, a season (ṛtu); from three of those, a solstice (ayana);
from two of those, a year is said to be formed; and by hundreds of those years, the lifespan of a person is measured.

At whatever constellation it may be, at all times during both fortnights, the installation of a seeker of liberation is recommended; however, for an ascetic who desires worldly gain, I shall speak [of the fixed constellations].
Installation during the rainy season leads to success; in autumn, it bestows yoga;
in winter, the Liṅga grants knowledge; and in the cool season, it grants all prosperity.
The installation of a Liṅga is considered to bestow prosperity during the spring, to grant victory and peace during the summer, and for ascetics, it is deemed auspicious at all times.
When the sun has reached the northern quarter, the installation of a *liṅga* is most excellent;
however, during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), it is unworthy of worship, and after three years, it brings about fear.

The placement of the syllables beginning with *kṣmā* (earth) and ending with *dhvaja* (flag)—that is, the six syllables—leads respectively to loss and increase when the sun is in the south, north, or west. (10)

The results for the agent, the king, the subjects, the kingdom, the location, and the deity are given in sequence according to the system of Maya, over three years plus six months and six days respectively.
Establishing [the deity] during the period of gathering (saṅgraha) is not desired; likewise, it is forbidden during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana).
If one establishes [the deity] during the southern solstice, there will be malevolent magic (abhicāra).
When a Liṅga is established in a place of gathering, the people are afflicted by diseases;
the youths are severely tormented, and the destruction of maidens occurs. || 13 ||
Then a very great outbreak of weapons arises among kings;
there is always destruction for the perpetrator, and terrible grief occurs in his home. (14)

Therefore, one who seeks auspiciousness should not install a deity during the period of gathering or during the southern solstice; nor should one engage in the mantras and other teachings of the Goddess according to the scriptures.
A king, desiring the welfare of his own kingdom, should protect the Dharma;
therefore, having obtained a preceptor of his station, he should perform protective rites against malevolent magic.
For half a fortnight, the installation of the planets should be performed in their respective houses as long as the sun remains in the northern course;
specifically, it should be carried out during the three seasons beginning with winter (śiśira).
On that day, during the bright fortnight, adorned by the [auspicious] lunar mansion and the day of the week,
at a conjunction with the moon and stars, and endowed with an excellent *lagna* and *karana*, (18).
Establishment occurs in the dualistic deity and in Mitra during the bright fortnight,
and likewise in the non-dualistic deity even during the dark fortnight, according to the distinction of the mantra-form.
The Raudrī of the Dvaita school remains for one hundred years;
the Miśrā of Pāñcarātra and Arha remains for fifty years. || 20 ||
That non-dual power born of the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa mantras remains for a hundred years;
it should abide as a self-manifested (svayambhu) Liṅga, like the Bāṇaliṅga. || 21 ||
The word *pratiṣṭhā* is established from the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *prati*;
because particles have multiple meanings, it signifies "establishment" (*saṃskāra*) and so forth. (22)
Therefore, this very meaning is proclaimed by those learned in grammar:
that which is the refinement of a substance through mantras, and likewise that of a deity. (23)
Whether seated, sleeping, standing in a vehicle, or positioned upright in the air—
the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is declared to be fivefold, according to these five types of images.
These, however, should be performed during the bright fortnight;
then, on the lunar days beginning with the second, one should give: on the second day, long life; on the third, the wealth of sons.
The fifth always brings prosperity, the seventh destroys disease,
the tenth brings the gain of land, and the thirteenth brings good fortune.

Various kinds of wealth and grain [are obtained]; the full moon day (pūrṇamāsī) is always auspicious. A single season is joined with Śaṅkara (eleven); Nandā is joined with the Bhadra days, the number of the sages (seven), and the suns (twelve). (27)
When the [lunar] day is empty (riktā) due to the Rāma (3), Ahika (8), and Kāma (3) [factors], it is beneficial for Veda (4), Graha (9), and Indra (14);
when it is full (pūrṇā) due to Bāṇa (5), Diś (10), and Tithi (15), they are respectively harmful, equal, and beneficial. (28)
These [periods] are favorable during the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa) and unfavorable during the dark fortnight (bahula-pakṣa).
Jupiter bestows a lifespan of ten years, while Mercury grants victory and wealth. (29)

Venus is the bestower of prosperity during auspicious times, while the Moon is so for the growth of peace; [this applies when they are] in Cancer, Taurus, Libra, Sagittarius, Virgo, Leo, Capricorn, and Gemini. (30)

The predominance of the lords of the days occurs in Pisces, Aquarius, Scorpio, and Aries, according to the sequence of the four signs starting from the sixth, eighth, fourth, and tenth houses respectively. (31)
O twice-born one, Puṣya, Rohiṇī, Hastā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Citrā, and Jyeṣṭhā belong to the king. (32)
Dhaniṣṭhā and Śravaṇā belong to the Vaiśya; likewise, the two Bhādrapadas belong to the Vaiśya.
Aśvinī and Revatī belong to the Śūdra, as do Svātī and the two Phalgunīs.

In the four castes, Maghā bestows prosperity; Mūla, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, and Mṛgaśiras—these [four] belong to those who are proficient in the world; likewise, these same four belong to the lowest caste (antyaja).
Tiṣya brings victory and health; Rohiṇī bestows the increase of wealth;
Hasta grants success; and the pair of Āṣāḍhās grant long life at the Liṅga.
Punarvasu bestows happiness, while Anurādhā grants prosperity; Citrā provides constant wealth and happiness, and Jyeṣṭhā brings about the destruction of disease.
Dhaniṣṭhā bestows the destruction of enemies; Śravaṇa always grants wisdom and supernatural powers;
Bhādrapadā bestows prosperity; and Aśvinī grants many friends. (37)
Revatī always bestows nourishment; Svātī shall bring much wealth;
the two Phalgunīs grant prosperity; and Bharaṇī causes the destruction of enemies.
Ārdrā bestows the attainment of good fortune, Mūla royal honor,
Mṛgaśīrṣa is eternally a giver of peace, and Śatabhiṣaj is auspicious for one who renounces at the end.
Aśleṣā, Kṛttikā, and Viśākhā bestow auspiciousness; Jupiter is always praised in all nine types of increases and in the seven positions. (40)
Mercury is strong when situated in the sixth, second, eighth, fourth, tenth, seventh, or first houses from the Moon;
likewise, the Moon bestows strength when stationed in the seventh, third, or tenth house from the Ascendant.

The Sun is auspicious when situated in the third, tenth, or sixth house; Rāhu is auspicious when situated in the third, tenth, or sixth house; and Saturn, Mars, and Ketu are excellent when situated in the sixth or third house. (42)
Whether they are auspicious, cruel, or malefic, all [planets] situated in the eleventh house grant their full aspect to a sage (the Moon), whereas for the other planets, it is only half. (43)
In the northeast direction, the first is *pādikī*, which is devoid of a quarter when the number eight is halved;
the second is named *saṃpadā*, while the fourth is designated as *kṣema*. (44)
The sixth is Sādhikā Tārā, the eighth is named Mitrā, and the ninth shall be Atimitrā; these five bestow strength. (45)
Prīti, Saubhāgya, Āyuṣmān, Sukarman, Śobhana, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Siddhi, Dhruva, Sādhya, Varīyān, Śiva, Śubha, Śukla, and Kaula. (46)
Brahma, Indra, and Śubha—these are the yogas known as "Satsaṃjñaka" (the Auspicious Ones).
Furthermore, Bālava, Kaulava, and likewise Taitila; || 47 ||
Gara, Vaṇija, Śakuni, Catuṣpada, Nāga, and Kiṃstughna are for the sake of wealth, provided they are free from Viṣṭi during both fortnights.
In Pisces and Aries, the duration of the transit shall be three and three-quarter nāḍīs;
however, Taurus and Aquarius enjoy four nāḍīs minus a quarter. (49)
Capricorn, Gemini, Sagittarius, Virgo, and Cancer each have five [ghaṭikās];
Libra and Virgo have six minus a quarter; while Aquarius has five and a half. (50)
Leo, Taurus, and Aquarius are fixed signs that bestow success; Sagittarius, Libra, Aries, Gemini, Pisces, and Virgo are movable signs. (51)
Cancer, Capricorn, and Scorpio cause the destruction of the undertaking of renunciation;
a fixed sign aspected by benefic planets, occupied by benefics, is auspicious as the ascendant. 52.
The ascendant joined by Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury bestows wealth, long life, sovereignty,
happiness, riches, sons, fame, and much merit and other virtues.
The first, seventh, fourth, and tenth houses are called the Kendras;
Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury situated therein bestow all accomplishments. || 54 ||
Malefic planets situated in the third, eleventh, and fourth houses from the ascendant are auspicious;
for other purposes, the wise should employ the lunar days and so forth for inauspicious rites. (55)
In a good conjunction, there is eternal dharma; under Tārā, nourishment and life; in a favorable ascendant, great enjoyment; and at the equinoxes, the desired fruit. (56)
On the meritorious occasion of the Ṣaḍaśītimukha, during the winter solstice (uttarāyaṇa), and on a great lunar day,
prosperity, health, and sovereignty shall result from the consecration of a deity.

When the auspicious moment has arrived at the junction of the watches (saṃdhyā), when the planets have set, under an unfavorable asterism, with malefic planets, during the Viṣṭi yoga, and likewise when the asterism is in conjunction (saṅgraha). || 58 ||
When ill omens, portents, or the eclipsing of the sun and moon occur,
deities installed during these times bring about destruction, famine, and disease.

Therefore, having first examined the day, one should procure the ritual implements for the sacrifice. Among the three [types], that which remains as a single perfected Linga standing firm—whatever it may be—is free from defect; therefore, when established facing eastward, it bestows boons.
Thus ends the tenth procedure, titled "The Examination of the Seasons and Other Days," in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*.
Now, the eleventh [chapter]:
one should have the pavilion constructed in three ways according to the sequence of the *jyeṣṭha-liṅga*;
it may be thirty cubits and so forth, or according to another opinion, with a reduction of ten [cubits] at each stage.
Another [type of stūpa] is considered middling with twelve cubits, while the largest is held to be three times that; one should have it constructed in this manner, or otherwise as well.
Starting from twelve cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time up to twenty-eight, one should construct nine pavilions.
Ghana, Ghoṣa, Virāja, Kāñcana, Kāmarāmaka, Suveśa, Ghargharā, Dakṣa, and Maṇḍapa—these are the nine (ten) by name. || 4 ||

Having established another thread from the [previous] location— meaning, having moved the measuring line to another spot— one should construct the pavilion for the sacrifice in the area in front of the temple,
neither too close nor too far.
Having worshipped the presiding deity of the site (Vāstvadhidevatā), one should construct the pavilions (maṇḍapas) starting from the smallest;
once the debris has been excavated to the depth of a knee, and the ground has been leveled toward the east, the northeast, and the north.
Having divided the field into three parts for both [the mandala and the altar], one should fix pillars in the corners—
square or circular, straight, made of sacrificial wood, and firm.
Then, twelve [units] outside and four pillars in the middle;
one should join the two door-frames by means of the binding of their crest-pinnacles (cūḍāśalya).
(170) The *śikhāṅghrika* [maṇḍapa] consists of three wooden beams and a *valikā* above them;
covered with six layers of cloth, it is the first of the three types of *maṇḍapas*, beginning with the *ghanādi*.
The triad beginning with gold is likewise [to be offered], but it is provided with a neck,
joined by eight monkeys, and endowed with three door-keepers.
The upper portion, bound with fastenings made of fine metals and excellent timber,
and covered with eight layers of roofing, shall constitute the three parts beginning with the beautiful exterior.
The elevation of the wing (pakṣa) is one-third [of the width]; the elevation of its crest (śikhā) is double that.
This same [proportion] applies to the eight upajaṅghās; what then is their width and how is their height? 12.
One should fix the pillars on the ground at a measurement of one-twelfth of the width;
by that same measurement, the neck [of the pillar] should be formed, which is said to be the interior of the pavilion.
Leaving aside the space for the height of the door, a Linga of the householder type should be fashioned in front of the house;
it is known as Jaya, ten cubits in length, and solid in form.
In the arrangement of the Mahārcā, there should be three pavilions resembling well-constructed dwellings, each consisting of twenty pillars. || 15 ||
They are provided with two necks, joined by five holders,
and equipped with iron spikes and monkeys, together with the Jina.
Well-increased and firm, provided with twelve coverings— or, according to another reading, provided with twelve lotus petals—
the width shall be fifty cubits, and the circumference shall be four hundred and fifty.
When the site has been established upon the plane of reality, the fortyfold prosperity [of the pillars] should be joined to the pillars reaching the ears; thus is the three-fold pavilion. 18.
All the maṇḍalas should be made square, with four gates, adorned with four archways, and provided with a pedestal in the center. || 19 ||
Starting from one cubit up to eight cubits in sequence,
all seats (pīṭhas) are generally [of these sizes], though in some other opinions they are otherwise.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be one-third of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) and square in shape;
in its center, there should be a tortoise with a raised back, twelve parts in height.
Alternatively, for the sake of attaining all perfections, it is stated in another tradition that the brick-altar may consist of three, four, or even seven layers.
Trihāra, Durjaya, Caturhāra, Subhīṣaṇa, Viśālākṣa, Pañcahāra, Saptahāra, and Sutāraka. (23)
It should be straight, free of thorns, pleasing to the mind, and endowed with auspicious marks;
according to the Siddhānta, it should be filled with sand, provided with a seat and a bed, and beautiful.
The pavilion was provided with eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), adorned with Tantric mandalas,
covered with various kinds of cloths, and furnished with pillars.
Above the pedestal, one should fashion a canopy adorned with clusters of plantain trees,
featuring hanging flower garlands and provided with bells, chowries, and cloths.
Endowed with excellent banners, beautiful, and possessing the directions as its flags, it is crowded with jars;
it is yellow, red, black, smoky-grey, white, and the color of a parrot.
One should employ nine banners for Indra and the other deities—golden-hued, crystal, and yellow for nourishment;
white for pacification, and black for the fierce rite.
The banners should be made five cubits in height and two cubits in width;
the flags, however, should be seven cubits long and twenty finger-breadths wide. (29)
Those that enter into the hand of the staff are five cubits for the banners;
those of the flags are ten cubits, with a fifth part inserted [i.e., five cubits]. || 30 ||
In some other methods, the measurement of the banners is determined differently:
the banners should be made with twenty spokes, [measuring] seven or ten [units].
In the smallest, medium, and largest [mandalas], they are two cubits [in height] due to their expansion;
they are eight cubits in length and two cubits in width.
The middle ones are half that size, and the banners are half the size of those;
they are always worshipped with firm, new cloths in rites for the gods.

One should decorate the pavilions on the outside with banners, chariot-flags, and pennants; the archways (toraṇas) in the east and other directions should be made of copper, iron, silver, and gold. [According to Mū, A, Kh, G: the archways of the palaces.]
Having placed, in order for the sake of prosperity, kucandana, laghu, śveta, candana, and amaradāru in the directions starting from the east, there are archways (toraṇas).
Madhuka, cūta, kāśmīrī, and palāśa grant wealth and peace;
vaikaṅkata, śamī, bilva, and khādira destroy enemies. (36)
The nyagrodha, the palāśa, the udumbara, and the sidhraka;
the aśvattha, the mādhūka, and the plakṣa—with the bilva as the eighth in some accounts. (37)
For these [mandapas], there are eight archways (toraṇas) in the eastern and other directions within the eight-faced pavilion;
three of them should face east in the directions of Indra, Agni, and the intermediate corner.
In the pavilion, if it is in the northwest or the southwest, the face should be toward the west;
if in the north, the face should be made to face north; and if in the south, it is considered that the face should face south. (39)
Those originating from the Śālaka, Koṭaja, and Śāka trees, as well as the Sāralas, bestow nourishment and prosperity;
those arising from the Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Vṛkṣa trees are auspicious. (40)
If these are not obtained as desired, the archways (toraṇas) should first be constructed;
they may be square, octagonal, or circular, provided they are free from flaws like those on a wheel.
The shanks are five cubits, and the forehead is half of that;
the circumference of both the shank and the forehead is one cubit.
Above that, there is a trident thirty finger-breadths in height,
adorned with bells, chowries, fine cloths, flower garlands, and incense.
Having worshipped the archways with the Vaktra-mantra in their respective directions,
and having assigned the deities to the pillars and other parts, one should plant the two hands in the ground.
Indeed, the Vasus are to be placed on her shanks, and the Lords of the Yugas on her forehead;
on the horns are those situated in the twelve zodiac signs, along with the Rudras, the Suns, and the Wheel-bearers, each in their respective places.
Āpa, Dhara, and Dhruva, as well as Soma, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are remembered as the eight Vasus. (46)
In the Kṛta age, the Lord is named Śrīkaṇṭha; in the Dvāpara age, the Lord is Śaṅkara; in the Tretā age, he is called Ananta; and in the Kali age, he is Svāmī Sadāśiva.
One should place Indra, Antaka, Jala, and Indu in their respective directions; and for the zodiac signs beginning with Pisces, one should assign three signs to each direction in sequence.
Sthāṇu, Śiva, Paśunātha, Ugra, Śarva, the three-eyed one, Īśvara, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and the one known as Śambhu. (49)

One should install Maheśvara and Mahādeva in the triad beginning with the Fish (Mīna) in due order; and for Viṣṇu and the Sun, one should arrange Viṣṇu, Indra, and the others in their respective foundations.
Viśvāyana, Mahāmūrti, Vikāśa, and Mahābala—these four are proclaimed as the guardians of the archways starting from the east. || 51 ||
Having thus decorated the exterior with seed-vessels containing growing mustard plants, one should then decorate the interior once again.
There are eight jars and door-panels situated at the doors, adorned with sprouts;
they contain precious gems within their bellies and are filled with fragrant water.
Anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with garments, and placed upon the necks [of the images],
they should be provided with lamps, unbroken rice grains, and fruits, and consecrated with the eight door-guarding mantras.
Śānta, Śiśira, Parjanya, Viśoka, Āpyāyaka, Amṛta, Raudra, and Vīra—these should be known as the eight deities of the jars (kalaśa). || 55 ||
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, the fifth named Śaṅkukarṇa, and another, Sarvanetra. || 56 ||
Sumukhāhva (or Sumukhāṅka according to k and g), the renowned Supratiṣṭhita (or Vaidyapratiṣṭhita according to mū),
and the deities of the banners are each surrounded by ten million bhūtas.
Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Dakṣa, Bhṛṅgī, Caturmukha, and Dāra—known as Sitāsita—should be understood as the door-keepers. (58)

Outside the pavilion, it is considered appropriate that it be surrounded by a row of mango trees, provided with eight plantain trees, and accompanied by the eight guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas). || 59 ||
Hetuka, Tripuraghna, Agnyākhya, Agnijihvaka,
Kāla, Karālīka, Ekāṅghri, and Bhīma— these eight are the Kṣetrapālakas.
In that [structure], which has three doors secured with mats made of cloth and wood covered by variegated stories such as those of the Kirātas, one should cause [the image] to face westward.
One should cause the outcastes, the Capacas, and others initiated into other stages of life to enter right there, and one should perform the protection of the sacrifice [or the pavilion].
For the purpose of the bathing ceremony and other rites, a pure pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed to the north,
according to the proportions of the temple, provided with a pedestal and two roofs.
To the north or in the northern direction of the palace, one should [construct] a beautiful structure,
four-peaked and four-cornered, for the hero Vimala with due reverence.
The beautiful pavilion called Snāna-maṇḍapa was adorned with the requisites for bathing;
it was graced with banners and canopies in its corners and decorated with plantain and mango trees.
It has a single archway and a single entrance; in its center is an auspicious altar-platform, elevated by one-fourth of the width of the pavilion's extension.
One should construct two altars in the pavilion, either according to the *iṣṭi* rite, provided with sand, having gentle stalks, and two girdles, or else in a general manner. (67)
One should perform the extraction of the marks on one side and the act of cleansing on the other;
from that, one should prepare a pedestal known as the Bhadra, made from a milk-tree.
It should be sixteen finger-breadths in height and twice that in width, and it must be firm;
for the smallest [images], the length is always twice the width. (69)

The increase for the others shall be by four finger-breadths each in successive order; this is declared to be the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha). Now I shall describe the measurement of the hut (kuṭī).
On the other half of the pavilion, there should be constructed a well-guarded hut, facing east,
equipped with utensils, covered, and provided with a double roof.
Thus ends the eleventh procedure, titled "The Construction of the Maṇḍapa," in the Compendium of Characteristics. || 11 ||
One of the manuscripts held in the National Archives is the Vairocanīya.
This *Pratiṣṭhālakṣaṇasārasamuccaya* consists of chapters twelve through thirty-two.
The second volume,
under the supervision of Paṇḍita Buddhisāgara Śarmā,
was edited by Vedācārya Paṇḍita Dāmodara Śarmā.
Edited by Paṇḍit Bābū Kṛṣṇa Śarmā, Vedānta-Śāstrī;
published by the National Archives.
First Section:
Now, for a [pile] of fifty or a hundred [oblations], the measure is one *muṣṭi*; for a hundred, it is the measure of a *vāratni*.
Now, when a thousand oblations are to be offered, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit.
That pit should be two cubits for ten thousand oblations, four cubits for a hundred thousand oblations, and eight cubits in size for oblations numbering ten million; it should not exceed this.
One should fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) like a pedestal, with a cavity of its own measurement,
provided with corners and a girdle, and likewise adorned with a womb-shape (yoni).
The lip of that [pit] should be one-twelfth of its [diameter];
the width and height of the girdle should be one-sixteenth part [of the pit], and the girdle should have the shape of the pit.
The *yoni* should have a width equal to one-third of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) and likewise its height;
it should be as long as half the pit, and its neck and lip should be like a bodhi-leaf.
From one fistful up to the limit of the hands, the yoni and the girdle of the fire-pits have been described;
thereafter, for the others, the dimensions increase by a sequence of two finger-breadths each.
However, for all [the classes], only a single girdle should be made for the sake of simplicity;
alternatively, three girdles may be fashioned, measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths [respectively].
Increasing further and further in width by one finger-breadth (or three finger-breadths) and rising by one finger-breadth,
they have widths of six, five, four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively.
(2) With two *rāma*s (three) and six [units], there are generally five girdles;
this is the rule for a [mandala] of one cubit, while for the remainder, it is by increasing by two fingers and then by one finger.
Having rotated a circle twice at two finger-breadths from the central line,
one should then place four finger-breadths forward there and draw two wing-lines.
The lip and the navel are one finger-breadth [in measure], and the neck is sometimes equal to the lip [or has a uniform elevation];
for the establishment of the unmanifest, the pit (kuṇḍa) is circular in all directions. || 11 ||
It is likewise used for eating, liberation, nourishment, and especially for the restoration of the worn-out;
it is always employed in fire-offerings (homa) and for pacification, situated in the direction of Indra or Varuṇa.
But for the planting of manifest [seeds], one should perform the rite of Indra in the eight directions with a noose of yokes;
likewise, in one's own direction during initiation, this is for the accomplishment of the goals of enjoyment and liberation.

When established upon both the manifest and the unmanifest, the quadrangular sacrificial pit (vedāsrakuṇḍa) should be employed in the cardinal and intermediate directions for the attainment of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. 14.
The fire-pit (kuṇḍa) that causes the burning of enemies is like a bodhi leaf in the southeast;
for pacification or for hatred [or agitation], it is considered to be like a crescent moon in the south in some cases. 15.
A triangular diagram is for the destruction of Rākṣasas; a hexagonal one is for Vāyu;
a lotus-like one brings nourishment; and an eight-petaled one is used for the accomplishment of certain goals.
An eight-sided [kuṇḍa] causes fear and is fierce, yet in some cases it bestows knowledge and liberation;
thus, according to one's desire and one's own wealth, one may construct eight such kuṇḍas.
(3) There are five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to the faces [of the deity] in the four directions beginning with the northeast (aiśāna).
Three are in the east, west, and northeast; one pit is situated in the direction of the wind (vāyu). (18)
Leaving a space of thirty finger-breadths from the altar,
this [distance] for the middle and the superior [altars] is increased by seven and seven finger-breadths respectively.
One should place a fence of *pālāśa* wood around the directions, with its tips pointing toward the northeast;
likewise, one should place thirty-six seats made of *darbha* grass at the sides of the sacrificial pit.
Or, for the increase of the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*), one should fashion a girdle (*mekhalā*) resembling a braided braid (*veṇī*), with five knots and three loops;
it should be sixteen finger-breadths in length and made from nine stalks of *darbha* grass.
The fire produced from sacrificial wood and that which comes from a sun-crystal gem—
both of these are for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, whether taken from the house of a Brahmin or otherwise.
Having cut [the material], one should perform the pounding, as well as the vajra-line and the preparation of the seat;
one should perform the worship of Vāgīśvarī, the casting of the seed-syllables, and so forth.
The consecration by fire as stated in the *Saṃhitā*, as well as the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*,
the sprinkling, worship, and oblation, along with the purification of the clarified butter and so forth, are to be performed as previously described. (24)
Having worshipped the Exalted One with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, starting from the heart in due order,
one should dismiss the Goddess and offer oblations into the fire for the faces in the cardinal directions and the limbs in the intermediate directions.
In the case of a fire-oblation (homa), one should indeed use *svāhā* for the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), while *vauṣaṭ* is used for the final offering;
one should employ *su-vauṣaṭ* for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), and *vaṣaṭ* is beneficial for rites of nourishment (*āpyāyana*).
One should use *svadhā* in rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkriyā*), *phaṭ* in rites of destruction (*kṣayakarma*),
*hūṃ* in incantations for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), *hrīṃ* for subjugation (*vaśa*), and likewise *namaḥ* at the beginning of recitation and worship (*japārcā*).
The phonemes beginning with their names are divided into twelve measures (mātrās).
Indeed, a single phoneme, divided by these measures, exists in twelve ways. || 28 ||

The short vowels are the designators of the Brahmās, while the long vowels are the designators of their limbs. The eye-mantra (netra) should possess an anusvāra, and the weapon-mantra (astra) should be distinguished by a visarga.
All [the syllables] should be pierced by the *bindu* and endowed with the *dīpaka*;
joined at the end with another *jāti*, they should be employed by the practitioner of mantra (*mantrin*).
Having understood this, one should perform the ritual action, which consists of the nature of the [five] colors:
ghee, sesame seeds, barley, milk, rice, edible foods, and even curd. (31)
In the daily ritual, one should offer fuel-sticks, milk-rice, flowers, bulbous roots, roots, fruits, honey, parched grain flour, cakes, and buttermilk mixed with rice.
The oblation of clarified butter, milk, and honey should be one karṣa each;
the offering of curd should be the measure of a śukti, and that of milk-rice should be one prasṛti.
Of edible foods there should be an amount equal to an akṣa, and of parched grains (lāja) a measure equal to a handful;
for the destruction of disease one should offer a mālūra fruit, and for the sake of prosperity a white lotus (kuśeśaya).
There should be three pieces of roots and fruits according to their own size, five small pieces of fruit, and morsels of food according to the size of a mouthful. || 35 ||
All the fuel-sticks should be one span (prādeśa) in length, cut evenly, and possessed of bark; they should be produced from the Plakṣa tree, free from knots, uncracked, and straight. (36)
The Śrīvṛkṣa, Khadira, Parṇī, Palāśa, Śamī, Udumbara, Vaikaṅkata, Apāmārga, and Pippala trees bestow peace and prosperity. (37)
For attraction, the khadira tree is recommended; for good fortune, the one called madana (or damana);
for causing harm, the hair of a living creature; and for inciting hatred, the śleṣmātaka and the śigru trees.
For the rite of expulsion (proccāṭana), one should offer into the fire the letter *ya* (or *pa*) accompanied by the visarga;
for the rite of destruction (nidhana), one should use the ashes of that [offering], a crow’s wing, and the blood of a neem tree.
Arka, Palāśa, Gāyatrī, Mārga, Aśvattha, Udumbara,
Śamī, Dūrvā, and Kuśa— these sacrificial materials are for the propitiation of the planets beginning with Arka.
One should discern the auspicious or inauspicious nature of the fire by its color, fragrance, and inherent character—[whether it resembles] a ruby, sapphire, the sun, pure crystal, or gold. (41)
A fire that is greenish-yellow is auspicious, whereas one that is black is to be avoided; a fire that is glossy,
turning to the right, well-satiated, and compact is auspicious.
One that smells like honey, ghee, milk, bilva, arka, or puraga is auspicious;
whereas one that is odorless, pale, rough, or resembles black charcoal is inauspicious.
Likewise, a fire that has strayed onto a wrong path, accompanied by smoke, is inauspicious;
knowing this, one should not perform the *homa* sacrifice with it, or else not at all.
The procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya), which accomplishes all desires and aims, has been proclaimed;
it applies likewise to the preparatory consecration (adhivāsana-dīkṣā) and to the initiation by sprinkling (abhiṣeka). (45)

One should make the *sruva* ladle from *khadira* wood, thick by the measure of one finger-breadth, resembling a cow's tail, beautiful, reaching to the height of the hand, free of blemishes, and firm. || 46 ||
At the top, it is three finger-breadths in diameter, with its opening filled with a karṣa of ghee and flowers;
its excavation is three finger-breadths deep in the middle, and there is a bridge two barley-corns wide.
[The ladles] are made from the two types of sandalwood, saffron wood, udumbara, and bodhi;
likewise from āmrī, vaikaṅkata, bijā, palāśa, and śiṃśapā wood. 48.
The handle of that [staff] is thirty-six finger-breadths in length, twenty-four finger-breadths in diameter,
six finger-breadths in circumference, and eight finger-breadths in both height and width. (49)
In the middle of that, there should be a circular or quadrangular pit three finger-breadths deep,
adorned with a girdle and eight lotus petals, containing a kuḍava measure of clarified butter.
Having first established a space of four finger-breadths, one should remove two finger-breadths from the two corners at the front of the altar;
then, the neck of those two [corners] shall be one finger-breadth.
At its base, it should be equal to the altar; in length, it should have a face of seven finger-breadths;
and at its tip, measuring two finger-breadths, it should resemble the lip of an elephant.
One should lead the aperture located in the middle of the mouth of the altar evenly toward the mouth of the lotus;
it should be as thick as the little finger and serve for the exit of the serpent.
The jar should be made with two finger-breadths (yuga-aṅgula), beautifully adorned at the base of the staff;
and at the tip of the staff, there should be a small pedestal (upavedikā) measuring four finger-breadths. (54)
Then, having thoroughly washed those two with warm water and heated them,
one should touch them with *kuśa* grass in sequence at the base, the middle, and the tip.
Then, having worshipped with the heart-mantra using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one of uplifted body should indeed offer the *pūrṇāhuti* into the jar reaching the navel.
At the conclusion of each individual *tattva*-oblation, the final *pūrṇāhuti* must be performed.
At that time, a gift should also be respectfully offered to the preceptor.
Thus ends the twelfth rule, titled "The Characteristics of the Fire-pit, the *Sruk*, and the *Sruva*," within the compendium of characteristics [the procedure for drawing lines, Viṣṇupurāṇa]. || 2 ||
Then, on the thirteenth day, on a date favorable to the sacrificer, when all the ritual materials had been prepared,
and when the auspicious signs such as full water-jars and other omens previously mentioned had appeared.
Bards, singers, Brahmins, and players of conch shells and musical instruments should be employed for the sake of auspiciousness, as well as women for the sake of beauty. || 2 ||
When there is abundance [of wealth], those known as Śaivas are proclaimed to be Brāhmaṇas;
for there is no such restrictive rule here regarding the acceptance of Brāhmaṇas.
Nothing at all is accomplished here by the mere recitation of the Vedas;
rather, the sound of the Veda is prescribed for the festival for the sake of auspiciousness. (4)
In the Śiva-āgama, the knowledge of astrology (jyotirjñāna) is the primary authority for consecration;
it is to be honored in all undertakings, and the Veda is not the cause in that regard.
Whether he be a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa, or even a Kṣatriya, he becomes an astrologer (daivajña) because he knows the true principles of the science of luminaries (jyotirjñāna). || 6 ||
For in this Śaiva knowledge, birth is not honored as the Guru is;
knowledge is eternally worshipped, and there birth is not the cause.
Endowed with the characteristics of his own treatise, expert in the knowledge of astrology, skillful, well-guided, and a demonstrator of many proofs. (8)

One should thoroughly honor the astrologer—who knows the instruction regarding what is beneficial and harmful, who is single-minded, and who has conquered his senses—with offerings of fine garments, perfumes, incense, and so forth. (9)
Then, having been duly honored, the learned astrologer, intent upon the auspicious moment,
should determine the time for the consecration by means of the water-clock and the gnomon.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a knowledge superior to the knowledge of Śiva;
it is endowed with all means, meritorious, and bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
Whatever is not achievable through the knowledge of Śiva is not achieved in the Vedas;
however, whatever is not achievable in the Vedas is easily achieved in the Śiva-āgamas.
Whatever is not seen in the knowledge of Śiva is not found in the Vedas;
it would be merely a worldly convention, like a festival held when there is wealth.
This is not the cause for the establishment of the Śiva-āgamas by means of the Vedas.
For the awakening of the ignorant, for their ultimate welfare, and for the sake of auspiciousness, I have extracted this from the Mother of the Goddess and written it down in brief. 14.
Having purified the liṅga in sequence with clay, cow dung, ashes, and water consecrated with mantras, he should then carefully place it upon a chariot.
One should slowly lead the beautiful Liṅga, which is the abode of a hundred thousand streams,
and one should draw the chariot by means of elephants, horses, buffaloes, or bulls.
In the event of an undesirable omen such as the breaking of the chariot, one hundred oblations of clarified butter should be offered for the sake of auspiciousness;
then, having carefully lowered the Liṅga which was situated upon the vehicle, it should be brought forward.

When the deity remains in the remaining place, one should cause the Liṅga to enter [the sanctum] after offering the eight-limbed *argha* accompanied by the sounds of conchs and musical instruments. || 18 ||
One should offer the *arghya*—which destroys demons—with these eight items: sesame seeds, darbha grass, water, curd, unbroken rice, milk, and barley, using vessels such as those made of gold.
Then the performer should offer the arghya water to the preceptor and the others;
having then performed the washing of their feet, he should again place the sandals [in their positions].
One should offer him a four-legged seat, and upon it, one should smear the Guru— who is like Śiva— with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood paste.
Excellent garlands and fine incense, two beautiful white garments, a crown, earrings, a necklace, armlets, and bracelets. (22)
One should give a ring set with jewels and a jeweled girdle;
having worshipped the Guru, one should give five cows according to one's wealth.
For ascetics at the sacrifice, one should adorn them with *darbha* grass or garlands of flowers.
In the ritual for householders, one should not practice deceit regarding wealth.
Thereafter, he honored those bearing physical forms with garments and ornaments like a cloud with rain;
he honored the chief artisan with fresh flowers and the others likewise.
Having offered betel-leaf with camphor, one should make this request:
"By the grace of your feet, may the entire fruit of my sacrifice be attained. (26)
The increase of the Dharma in the world shall be certain as long as the moon, sun, and earth endure; the performer, touching his feet, shall say: "May they perform the ritual at your command. (27)
Having sipped water again, the knower of mantras, having washed his hands and feet with water purified by a cloth, should drink the water that has been strained three times. (28)
Having gathered [the water] with the base of the thumb, one should wipe the mouth three times;
first, one should thus rinse the mouth with the three *saṃhitās*. (29)
Next, immediately thereafter, one should touch the nose with the thumb and the index finger;
then, repeatedly, the eyes and ears with the thumb and the ring finger.
One should touch the navel with the little finger and the thumb, the heart with the palm, the head with all the fingers, and afterwards the two arms with the tips [of the hands]. (31)
First, with the Astra-mantra and a triple measure (tritāla), the Guru should cast a flower;
then, having entered the sacrificial hall, he should do so with the well-visualized sword-seeds (khaḍgabīja).
One should quickly perform the purification of the directions; thereafter, the Guhyakas release [the bonds].
Then one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), followed by the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkṛta) with the forms (mūrti) and so forth.
At the end of the ritual placement (nyāsa), the performance of the rites and worship is as stated in another Saṃhitā:
"He should wear a white turban that rises twelve finger-breadths high. || 34 ||
Adorned with matted locks and smeared with white ashes through meditative practices,
the true preceptor at the sacrifice should always assume the form of Śrīkaṇṭha.
"I am Śiva myself, the pervasive Lord, whose very nature is the Śiva-mantra"—thus one should always contemplate with a mind free from conceptual construction. (36)
For when Śiva is thus established in the Bhairava [rite], the teacher should become identical in form with Bhairava;
whatever form the Lord may have, in that very form should the teacher be.
Then, the knower of mantras should worship the Lord residing within himself during the offerings of water (argha).
Having sprinkled all the flowers, fruits, and other offerings with that water half-filled [with the mantra], || 38 ||
One should scatter grains with the Astra-mantra upon the ground and so forth for the pacification of obstacles;
thereafter, one should collect them with the Varma-mantra using chowries or tufts of peacock feathers.
Then, having placed the Śiva-pitcher, which is joined with the limbs of the Śiva-mantra, enriched with fragrant water, fruits, and jewels, and provided with medicinal herbs and cloth; || 40 ||

And one should place [the image] upon a cloth in the northeastern direction, its face adorned with mango leaves and unbroken grains (akṣata), worshipped with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and joined with the weapon-mantra (astra).
One should offer an uninterrupted stream [of water] encircling from Īśa to Īśa;
having placed the jars there, one should worship them to the south.

The pitchers for Śiva and the others should be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, according to the king’s means; they should be placed at the entrance and likewise used for the ritual bathing. One should now set down those aforementioned karīra shoots.
One should provide a canopy for the couch with a portion of the materials previously mentioned, as well as banners and archways.
Having done this and protected the site of the *liṅga*,
one should then depart from the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). There, one should first scatter flowers with a sword upon that reality (*tattva*).
It is firmly established. || 45 ||
One should perform the scattering with the Astra-mantra and erect the archway facing west;
one should spread pure, unbroken grains along with Darbha grasses whose tips are as sharp as Indra’s thunderbolt.
One should offer a cloth with a cotton wick using the Sadyojāta mantra;
having offered the arghya with the [Aghora] face, one should indeed offer incense with the central [Vāmadeva] face.
One should cause the God to rise with the *hṛdaya* [mantra] and establish Śiva with the *guhya* [mantra].
