The unmanifest and other *liṅgas*, as well as the eastern, lunar, and lordly heads, [should be established]. (48)
The Guru should always cause those [liṅgas] to be placed one by one upon a cotton mattress;
he should then perform the general mantra-installation (mantranyāsa) common to all tantras.
"Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Rudra, the golden-eyed [or: the seed], the Great Self, Śiva;

to him whose form is auspicious, hā/ hau/ [mū: hā/ hā/]—thus one should recite 'salutation, salutation' as the mantra for the establishment of the liṅgas by means of the Hiraṇyaretas mantra [or: the triad of mantras]."
Then, one should carve lines on the thousand-spoked and hundred-spoked [mandalas];
I shall now describe, in due order, which specific gem-line belongs to each of them.
A liṅga with one thousand facets is formed by lines that are unequal,
using ninety-one parts for the height and ninety for the width, after omitting one part.
In the *vṛtta* (square), there are fifty parts; in some cases, twenty-two parts are placed transversely.
By omitting the parts above and below, one again divides the *vṛtti* into two parts.
One should join them at the crown with two lines and a line for the parasol;
by erasing the interior thousands, it is always [rendered] with intervals.
The sun-god Īśa is eternally present as the *liṅga* upon the *umendupiṇḍikā*;
the radiant Sun is surrounded by a thousand rays, and therefore he is encircled by ten hundred [rays].
In this manner, a thousand repetitions constitute the *saura* (solar) rite,
while a hundred repetitions of the *liṅga* constitute the *brāhma* (brahmic).
When performed with the *kapāla* and other mantras, it destroys great sins and brings merit to the performer.

Having divided [the height] into five parts and omitting one part from the top, the portion representing the *tattvas*—due to being half-sunken—becomes the *liṅga*, exceeding one hundred [units]. || 56 ||
Likewise, hundreds and thousands of supports were established;
even in the house, there may be a movable liṅga, or again, various types of liṅgas that remove sin.
For the purpose of measurement, [the lines] are drawn with threads smeared with saffron and the moon (or great Indra).
One should carve a line on the linga that is eight yavas in height for the best type.
One should divide the others by their ninth parts until reaching the end of the hands;
within those intervals, that which is stated as "inner" (antara) brings misfortune, while that which is deficient by one hand (or garment) brings calamity.
The laying out of the lines has been fully described; from half of that, one should make an auspicious depression (avaṭa) that is level,
even-surfaced, pleasing, and endowed with the proper characteristics.
Having thus carved out that line which brings ease,
one should make the central thread level and bring it down from the forehead. (61)
The characteristic mark should be at one-third, one-half, or one-quarter of the way down from the neck;
it should not be above the throat, the tip of the neck, or the forehead, for such upward placement is not auspicious.
That which is characterized by light is intended for the purpose of making the unperceivable perceivable;
it is said that the characteristic of the lines is for the destruction of all non-characteristics.
One should create an interval between the two threads using the *graha*-finger-breadths for the eldest;
for the others, having subtracted one finger-breadth each, one should place them in sequence.
Cetā, Dīptā, Pramopā, Dhātrī, Māyā, Matī, Śivā, Caṇḍā, Lakṣmī, and Sumedhā—these ten Maṇirekhās are proclaimed. (65)
When Rudra has been divided into eight parts,
one should know that the characteristic of the *latraṇa* consists of five parts after discarding three parts from above; its interval is one part.
Having omitted two threads upwards, one should measure the eastward extent of the two wing-threads;
then, from the thread situated in the middle, the descent of the wing-threads is performed.
Having abandoned the junction with the lower portion up to the end of the two parts,
one should fashion its interval at the edge as being equal to half the distance between the two [upper] parts.
Just as the head of the inferential mark (liṅga) is, so too is that of its definition;
and for other inferential marks belonging to the same class, this [definition] would be the first to be stated.
Alternatively, on a surface measuring one cubit, a bright line should be drawn.
When this is divided into three parts, one part is set aside, and the remaining two parts form the openings of a six-cornered [hexagonal] shape. (70)

With two *rāmis*, it has the appearance of barley; on the third [measurement], the wing-line (*pakṣasūtra*) is called *Dīpā*, and the target-mark line (*lakṣmarekhā*) is said to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In a span of two cubits, when the rising [of the shadow] is divided by the lunar days (tithis), there is that called "delight" (pramoda);
when the ninth part is set aside and the sixth part is divided threefold, [the result is as follows].

By rotating both [lines] from the center of the middle line, the wing-line (pakṣasūtra) will emerge in the shape of a barley grain or an elephant's eye, even without [the explicit drawing of] the wing-line itself. || 73 ||

In the case of a three-cubit *dhātrī* liṅga divided into eleven parts known as the *rudra*-division, one should set aside two parts at the bottom and one part above that; then, the remaining eight parts below should again be divided into eight.
Above that, having omitted one [mark] at the end of the qualities (guṇa), there should be a head;
having omitted one [mark], one should rotate the thread until it rests at the end of the back.
In a four-cubit [square], Māyā occurs when divided by the remover of modifications;
likewise, the characteristic of the directional portions arises from the abandonment of the upper six.
Having abandoned the fourth part above, there should then be a short plumb-line;
having left two parts below, the junction of those two occurs at the back.
When the fivefold mark (*pañcakara*) is present in the *liṅga* which is a portion of Śiva and divided by the lunar days (*tithi*),
and when it stands at the front, abandoned by the sages (*muni*), it shall be characterized as being situated in the hood (*phaṇi*).
(p. 17) When one-third of that is set aside above, the suspension (lambana) occurs by that one-third;
and when two-thirds are set aside below, there is the meeting of the thread from behind.
In the *eḍḍhastaka* measurement, Śivā is there, and Hara shall be a sixteenth part.
Having left a space above the sixth part, there is a mark on the portion of the hump.
One should rotate the wing-line from one-third to five parts;
leaving two parts at the bottom, there shall always be a junction between those two.
In a liṅga measuring seven cubits, the characteristic known as Caṇḍa occurs;
it is located below the lines, at the seventh part excluded from the portion for worship and the portion of modification.
One should discard a fourth part as the downward depression, or two parts below;
for that [line] which has the form of a lotus-stalk in the northern direction, its junction occurs from the middle of the back.
In a *liṅga* measuring eight cubits, when divided into parts as previously described,
the line known as Lakṣmī is considered to be the vertical drop from the third part.
This very same characteristic is called Sumedhā in a nine-cubit [liṅga].

In two parts, the *lambana* (the characteristic mark) belongs to it; however, due to the exclusion of one part, the *lambana*-line is not to be joined in the half-measure of Viṣṇu (fourteen units), according to the opinion of some.
On the other hand, it should be applied to the *pakṣasūtra*; below that, one should remove the *lambana*.
In some cases, the powers of knowledge and action are all-pervasive in both the Sakala and Akala [states];
therefore, there may be contact with Viṣṇu, as in the case of the support on the thread of the wings.
Among these, the crown [of the head] is desired to have the appearance of a parasol, an elephant's eye, or a parasol;
it is like a hen’s egg, or like a young crescent moon, or comparable to a barley grain. (88)
The egg of Dakṣa resembles a cucumber, while the cucumber is at the tip of the moon;
[these yield] fame, sovereignty, wealth, a son, good fortune, and long life, respectively. (89)
Then, one should provide these six heads, beginning with Gajekṣaṇa;
this is declared to be the Bāṇa doctrine, characterized by universal applicability.
In some cases, having broken the solar lineage, there may be the characteristic of being fond of Rudra;
or it may be nine, or one by one.
The suspension [of the body] is half, a quarter, or more than half of the height of the torso. || 91 ||
One should fashion the form characterized by a hollow, like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree;
it may be half the width of the conduit, or shaped like a pedestal, a pit, or a crescent moon.
Two *yūkās* and five *likṣās* shall be the distance between two lines;
the width of a line is one and a quarter *likṣās*, and likewise, the hair on the head is two *likṣās*.
According to some opinions, for lingas made of metal measuring one finger-breadth and so forth,
there should be an increase in the lines, as well as the placement of the vital points (marmans), excluding the first [finger].
Their characteristic arises through the increase of their positions, just as previously described;
this is the characteristic formed by the three groups, even for the subtle signs. (95)
By abandoning the vital points (marmans) of the Śubhakṛt [Liṅga], it yields the opposite of the merit performed;
however, for the Liṅgas of the world-regents (digīśas), they accomplish the fruits desired by oneself. (96)
One should draw a jeweled line having the form of one's own weapon:
a trident, a thunderbolt, a spear with a sharp point, and likewise a conch-shell.
Immediately thereafter, one should draw the lines resembling a staff, a lotus, a sword, a noose, a banner, and a mace, using a golden needle, following the same procedure as for the *liṅga*. (98)
Facing north, he should offer three māṣas for the eldest son alone,
two māṣas for another, and one māṣa for the youngest.
The artisans, by the command of their preceptor, should carve it out with the Astra-mantra;
it should be smooth, level, deep, and straight, for such a one bestows all desired objects. (100)
A line that is thick, crooked, thin, broken, or rough brings about the destruction of life and wealth;
having consecrated the blade, one should scratch [the forehead] with the blade using the right hand.
The wise one should fill [the cavity] with honey and clarified butter using his own finger.
This is the procedure for the Brahma-line in the case of unmanifest, stable [liṅgas],
as well as for those made of precious stones, mobile ones, and Bāṇaliṅgas located in the northeast.
For being situated upon the head is indeed the defining characteristic of Īśāna.
The characteristics of the arrow-liṅga (bāṇaliṅga) are fully accomplished through the preceding mantra;
it may bear marks produced from its own radiant jewel-gems, or it may be made of metal, or sometimes of clay.
The refinement of the eyes for both moving and stationary objects, as well as for manifest forms, occurs through the application of mantras;
the measurement begins with a single finger-breadth and increases by one finger-breadth for each increment up to a cubit.
In the hollow at the midpoint of the back of the line, there are two images; in some cases, the opening of the eyes is performed.
[The goddesses are] Saumyā, Abhayapradātrī, Vīrā, Hṛṣṭā, and Prabodhikā. (106) p. 20)
Laughing, compassionate, established in the yoga of desire, and possessing divine vision;
cruel, wrathful, formidable, terrifying, deformed, and wonderful. || 107 ||
The glances of the Ghoras and others are fearful, swallowing upwards and downwards; that which is called the "pupil" is proclaimed to be in the middle of the third part of the eye. 108.
One should fashion their luminosity as one-third of the height of Tārā;
it should not be above, below, or horizontal, nor should it have the error of being too small or too large.
The drops, fragments, and jars (kalaśa) are not rough; their gaze bestows auspiciousness.
The twelve gentle ones are for the sake of increase, possessing smooth lines and beautiful gazes.
The Rākṣasas and others have round eyes, and their gazes are cruel and so forth.
Upon the extraction of the marks, one should always give a cow to the preceptor;
having thus understood the procedure correctly, one should then perform their consecration through bathing.
When the suffix *lyuṭ* (or *ghañ*) is applied to the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *adhi* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), the usage *adhivāsana* is established. || 112 ||
Dwelling together with one's guru and others at night, according to the prescribed rules—the meaning of this is considered to be manifold due to the polysemous nature of particles (nipāta). || 113 ||
Having performed the sprinkling with the Astra-mantra, one should consecrate it with the third mantra;
then one should offer the Arghya with the Nara-mantra and the Pādya with the Ajātaka-mantra.
One should give clothing with the secret [mudrā], unguent with the unborn [mudrā], a garland with the fifth, and indeed incense with the southern [mudrā]. (115)
One should fumigate with *purū*, *kunduru*, and metals, as well as with *sarja*, sandalwood, and *vānara*, along with *śrīvāsa*, *sarala*, and incense made from sugar-candy (*khaṇḍadhūpa*).
The purifying water (pavitra) should be offered with the heart-mantra, the lamp with the middle mantra,
the food offerings (naivedya) with the third mantra, and whatever is not specifically mentioned should be offered with the heart-mantra.
The instructor should cover [the disciple] with a pair of garments while reciting the secret mantra;
a jar of sleep, consecrated by the Rudra-mantra and well-worshipped, should be placed upon the head.
One should bind five healthy, well-lactating tawny cows at the four gates and in the northeast; with their milk, one should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru). || 119 ||

Having consumed the sacrificial oblation (caru) there, after the prescribed cleansing of the teeth has been performed, he should sleep upon a bed of kuśa grass together with those who embody the forms of his gurus.
If success is indicated in a good dream, otherwise the Guru should perform the oblation in the middle [of the rite].
On the second day, having performed his ablutions, the observer of the vow, accompanied by his wife, should carry out the ritual.
The Guru, having bathed along with the presiding deities of the icons and being adorned with garments and ornaments,
should perform the bathing of the deity and other rites accompanied by the sounds of auspicious proclamations.
Thus ends the thirteenth procedure, titled "The Exposition of the Method for Extracting the Characteristics," within the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*.
Now begins the fourteenth:
Śiva, who is omnipresent and subtle, elevates everything by himself.
Clearly, by means of the power of the mantra [or: the mantra], through the form of the Teacher, he pervades the moving and the unmoving. || 1 ||
Having descended from Kāleśvara among all the castes,
he shall assume the status of a Guru by the will of Śiva for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
With ten thousand twice-born ones who know the Vedas, one becomes equal to that [Samayin];
with ten times that many, one is called a Putraka; and with as many again, one is a Sādhaka. || 3 ||

But by means of ten thousand of those [sacrifices], performed with devotion through gifts and worship for the Teacher of the Śiva-teaching, the fruit shall be equal to that of Vāsuki’s [work on] architecture (or ritual service).

Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa rite upon the deity [or: the body], one should offer the arghya and other offerings; thereafter, one should perform the sprinkling (abhyukṣaṇa) upon the liṅga with arghya, flowers, incense, and perfumes.
The preceptor himself should anoint the liṅga with oil and with a hundred stalks of dūrvā grass; afterwards, the performer, along with his kinsmen, should do so in secret.
At that time, auspicious, non-widowed women sing auspicious songs;
one should give them jaggery, grain, and sometimes salt as they wander about.
Then eight non-widowed women, endowed with all auspicious marks,
should touch [the body] with a blade of kusha grass along a thread drawn from left to right or from right to left.
They bathe them again, and they will rinse them again and again;
thereafter, the preceptor himself should perform the ritual bathing according to the prescribed rule. (9)
With clay, cow dung, cow urine, ashes, and milk, respectively;
or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or with curd, or with honey, or with the five barks.
The bathing [of the image] should be performed with seventy-eight, twelve, seven, eighteen, twenty,
and five *palas* of *palāśa* wood when the image is one cubit in height.
Then, one should bathe [the deity] with eight kinds of various fruits and a hundred flowers, using either the Guhya-mantra, the Rudra-hymns, or the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having rubbed [the image] with powders made from barley and wheat, as well as other powders such as those of bilva,
one should then bathe it with pure, fragrant water.
One should likewise [bathe] with the powder of all medicinal herbs, with water containing jewels according to one's ability,
as well as with golden water and water from a cow's horn.
If one desires, one should wipe the Lord of Gods with rice-water and then with fragrant scented water, using a white cloth.

In this regard, according to the opinion of Bhāskara, bathing in the case of other liṅgas as well as in images (arcās) should always be performed with their respective mantras, whether for Hara and the others or for those who are mixed [deities]. 16.
With water, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), with the five sweets, as well as with earth, decoctions, medicinal herbs, and excellent waters from sacred fords and rivers.

Having bathed [the deity] in due order with the sixteen great baths and directional baths—consisting of ocean water, jewel-water, fragrant water, flower-water, and fruit-water—[one should proceed]. (18)
First, one should bathe Śiva with water from the Astra-mantra for purification;
then, five parts of milk from a copper-colored cow [should be offered] by means of the Īśa-mantra.
A man should take curd from a white cow, consisting of four parts,
and ghee from a tawny cow, consisting of one part of fire, using the Aghora mantra.
Cow’s urine, with a blue-colored [cow], is two parts by way of the secret [mantra];
cow dung, with a black [cow], is always pure when situated in the sky [the mouth] by means of Aja. 21.
Having placed it in a vessel made of copper or other materials located in the intermediate directions— Indra, Yama, Yakṣa, and Ambu—
one should stir it into oneness with Śiva, or else with the five [deities] according to the Kāpila method.
With half a portion of *kuśa* water consecrated by the *sādākhya* mantra—when joined with these five, bathing, worship, and so forth are purified. (23)
Milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar constitute the "five sweets" (pañcamādhura),
which should be consecrated with the mantras of the faces of Īśāna, Aghora, Guhya, and Ajāta.
Those [clay] extracted from anthills, mountains, the banks of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, from elephant-lakes, dug up by the horns of bulls, or produced from the vicinity of sacred fires; || 25 ||
It is purified by the clay from the four roads at the king’s gate;
and by the earth from a goat, washed in sequence by one who possesses the [proper] digits.
A bath with lukewarm water infused with the bark of *bakula*, *udumbara*, *aśoka*, *vaṭa*, and *bodhi*— this third [method] removes the affliction caused by the *ṭaṅka* [demon].
(25) Together with *ṛddhivṛddhi*, *sahā*, *siṃhī*, *kanyā*, and *chinna*—and with *bahuprajā*, *nidigdhikā*, and the roots of *balā*—a bath taken in secret removes defects. (28)

By bathing with cinnamon, cardamom, nāgakeśara, tagara, granthiparṇa, and so forth—along with [the faculties of] wisdom and the rest—and with dhātrī, when the "earth" has been cast off, one becomes pure through the Sadyojāta mantra. (29)
Having rubbed Mahādeva with fragrant rice-flour consecrated by the Gāyatrī mantra, one should bathe him with waters drawn from sacred fords (tīrtha).
Aja-gandhi-prayāga, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava; Puṣkara, Naimiṣāraṇya, and the sacred ford Varūṇa as well. || 31 ||
By bathing in the waters of these sacred fords, the skin of a person is purified;
namely, the Jāhnavī, Yamunā, Kauśikī, Sarayū, Śoṇa, and Narmadā.
The Kāverī, Gaṇḍakī, Sindhu, Trisrotā, Candrabhāgikā, and Saptagodāvarī—these are the meritorious rivers with their great waters. (33)
Through bathing with the secret mantra, they purify Viśveśa (the Lord of All)— who is the lineage of Viṣṇu—
by means of the waters of salt, milk, curd, oil, sugarcane juice, and wine.
And the eight oceans should be known as having sweet waters within;
a man should bathe in their waters for the sake of purification through touch. (35)
Topaz, lapis lazuli, diamond, pearl, crystal, ruby, emerald, and fine coral; || 36 ||
Sapphire, emerald, karketana, and suṭiṭṭibha—bathing with water containing these gems is supremely conducive to great prosperity. (37)
Purified by the Aghora mantra, one should perform the purification of the form of the Liṅga with camphor,
agallochum, musk, kāśmarī, sandalwood, and other such substances.
One should bathe [the deity] with fragrant water scented with nutmeg, cloves, cardamom, and the four aromatic spices (*caturjāta*), consecrated with the *ajāta* mantra.
For the destruction of defects in the scent and for the purification of the earth and Brahman,
[one should use] the lotus, the water-lily, the *mālūra*, and the blue, red, and white lotuses produced from the sun.
Mālatī, tagara, aśoka, hemacampaka, mallikā, sahakāra, aśvamāra, punnāga, and bakula [trees]. || 41 ||
Karṇikāra, uddraka, kahlāra, kunda, kumuda, yūthikā, pāṭalā, droṇa, nepālī, kuśa, kiṃśuka, and siṃhikā. || 42 ||
The kadamba, the atimukta, the kuṭaja, the nāgapuṣpaka, the mṛdukunda, the abjapatrī, and the flowers of the vṛṣa, ṛṣi, and buka; || 43 ||
A bath with these and other purifying substances brings about purity of speech: the wood-apple (bilva), mango (āmra), mocanā, āraṅga, breadfruit (panasa), and coconut (nālikera). (44)

The *kakka* (or *ṅko*), *lāmalaka*, grape, *jātīphala*, *parūṣaka*, pomegranate, *udumbara*, rose-apple (*jambū*), date-palm (*kharjūra*), sugarcane (*ikṣu*), palmyra palm (*tāla*), and *bimba* (or *bilva*). || 45 ||
Prācīnāmalaka, pīlu, kapittha, and likewise bakula; badarī, bījapūra, karamarda, and tinduka. (46)
Betel nuts and other items, as available, consecrated with the Īśāna and Aghora mantras—this is the "Fruit-Bath," which is meritorious and bestows upon the performer the fruit of his desires. (47)
Or with the juices of toyika and mango, together with the five grains beginning with rice;
and with sesame, wheat, sugarcane and the like, barley, dhānya, and priyaṅgu.

The aforementioned clay, mixed with the fragrance of flowers and medicinal herbs, constitutes the auspicious Great Bath (mahāsnāna) when performed with the mantras originating from the five Brahmans. 49.
With a water-pot having a mouth of *kadamba* shoots, one should bathe Indra together with his retinue;
with one having a *śālmali* branch, the deity of the southeast; this supreme bath is performed with the heart-mantras.
The *vaṭa* tree of Jambūpatra is for the southern direction; bathing is performed with the *aghora* mantra.
That which pertains to the *rakṣasas* is with the *aśoka* tree, while the excellent *śikhā* mantra is combined [with it]. (51)
The water-element bath is performed with the mantra of the *Ajāta* [A] while it rests upon the petal of awakening;
the wind-element bath is performed with the *Cūta* [U] syllable, accompanied by the *varman* [Hūṃ] mantra. (52)
The Saumya bath is performed with water consecrated by the left [hand] using the mouth of the *vaṭa* leaf;
the Aiśa bath is performed with ashes and *bilva* leaves, accompanied by the head [mantra].
The bathing of the face with *nāgapatra* is infinite; it is adorned with *netra*.
That which is like the leaf of Brahmā is *brāhma*, accompanied by *kuśa* grass. (54)
One should bathe the Bull-bannered Lord with the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, and musical instruments, with the melodious tones of trumpets, and with the auspicious songs sung by excellent women.
Then, having become free from pride, one should worship Śiva with the weapon-mantra or the heart-mantra.
Having offered the *argha* with the face-mantra, one should draw up the water with the cloth-mantra. (56)
Just as one should perform [the rites] for Śiva, so too for Arka (the Sun), Viṣṇu, and the others;
one should perform the bathing and other rites with their respective mantras, and in this regard, the four types of clay are superior.
These clods of earth from the cow-pen of Krodapa, originating from the roots of Kuśa grass,
as well as the previously mentioned clay, are praised by the twelve Viṣṇus for the purpose of purification.

One should perform the bath with thirty-two, sixteen, eight, and nine [or more] *kṛmbhas* respectively; in the case of mobile images, this should be done with great care, while for stationary images, the number should be doubled in sequence.
Having given the food offering, the vessel of oil, the bathing cloth,
and the probe to the artisans, one should consecrate the image with mantras and then worship it.
Thus, for signs made of baked clay and the like, the five substances are required;
for paintings, modeled figures, and manuscripts, bathing with a mirror is prescribed.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Threefold Enumeration of Signs," in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter:
the signs of metals and other minerals; however, those pertaining to the elements are each distinct.
From sound, from touch, from form, from taste, and from smell, indeed, in due order. || 1 ||
Having purified the elements beginning with space through the manifestation and removal of their respective seeds by means of the five sequences starting from one, one should then fashion the form.
One should assign the mudrās consisting of the phonemes to the three forms beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta);
then the five Brahmans, the limbs, and all the kalās of Śiva.
Then one should offer clothing, fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp,
and food offerings as before, and [offer] yellow pigment (rocanā) over which the root-mantra has been recited.
The collyrium is consecrated with the Netra-mantra, the mirror with the Puruṣa-mantra,
the parasol with the Īśāna-mantra, and the fly-whisk with the Nara-mantra.
Having thus worshipped Mahādeva and entered the pavilion,
one should scatter sand, free from grass, hair, and other such things, upon the pedestal.
One should worship Ananta upon the pedestal with the heart-mantra preceded by meditation;
one should spread darbha grass with their tips pointing eastward, and with uncut (ajāta) blades pointing northward.
Above that, one should place the gateway adorned with gold and jewels;
likewise, the feet of Śambhu beginning with Dharma, and his limbs beginning with Adharma.
In its covering, however, one should contemplate a lotus made of cotton with filaments starting from the left;
there, the Vidyeśvara-petals [form] the mandala with three pericarp-sections.
When the water has been established in the *iḍā* vessel, one should raise the Lord and lead him to the chariot,
accompanied by auspicious omens, musical instruments, and those reciting hymns of praise.
With beautiful canopies, chowries, and umbrellas held aloft, as well as with splendid banners, and with heavy streams from golden water-pots being poured forth in front; ||| 11 ||

One should perform the entry through the water-gate to the sacrificial site of Maheśvara; on the couch, one should place the sleep-vessel with its head toward the east, positioned at the head of that [bed].
Then, having recited the *madhura* mantra one hundred times, one should worship the deity:
Thāṇu, Nīlakaṇṭha, Mahādeva, and likewise Śiva. (13)
Rudra, Śaṅkara, and he known as Nīlalohita;
Īśāna, Dhanada, Bhīma, Tryambaka, and the Lord of Pārvatī. (14)
Having worshipped these twelve leaders of yoga here at the beginning of the path and so forth, with lamps, perfumes, flowers, and incense, according to the proper sequence. || 15 ||
With various meritorious food offerings, such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and other delicacies, along with *lopikās*,
*pūrikās*, cakes (*pūpas*), *maṇḍalakas*, sweetmeats (*modakas*), and curd; 16.
Laddukas, baṭakas, and phenas; milk with jaggery, rice with jaggery, parpaṭa, ghṛtapūra, and sugar-candy with white rice.
Various divine foods and diverse celestial fruits, as well as an excellent sword, a mantra-master, a spear, and auspicious arrows and equipment. (18)
Betel-leaf with camphor and mango,
along with a betel-nut, a vessel for the ritual sustenance (sthitipātra), a vessel for honey (madhupātra), and a water-receptacle (patadgraha).
Likewise, the conch-shell, the skull,
and the oyster-shell situated upon the stool,
as well as whatever other substances such as the grinding stone have not been mentioned here.
In whose house [it is]. || 20 ||
One should bestow that with effort by means of the terrible mantra, provided one is free from deceit;
then, upon the auspicious and beautiful *geḍḍuka* (or *gaṇḍuka*) where the head is elevated.
One should cause the Lord Liṅga, together with its pedestal, to rest,
and having anointed it with honey and ghee, one should offer many white mustard seeds.
Having taken recourse to the southern form, one should install the Lord of Mantras;
having covered the deity with fine silk or red garments, one should protect it.
Then, with the Mahāpāśupatāstra, one should worship the personified [deities] of the kings and others, numbering thirty-two, sixteen, and eight, respectively.
The *sādhakas*, however, [may act] without the *ācāryas*; the *putrakas* without the *sādhakas*;
the *samayins* in the absence of *putrakas*; and when all are absent, the teacher himself [acts]. (25)
[He should worship] the lords of the Vidyās, the Ganeśas, the Carlakeśas, and the Bhairaveśvaras;
the Vidyeśas for those desiring liberation, and the Gaṇeśvaras for the sake of worldly enjoyment.
For the purpose of accomplishment, however, one should worship these presiding deities of the forms—Lokeśāna, Advaita, Bhairava, and Īśvara—along with their respective forms and powers. (27)
Earth, fire, the sacrificer, the sun, the moon, and ether—these are declared to be the forms (mūrtis).
Now I shall speak concerning the lords of these forms (mūrtīśas). 28.
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, as well as Īśāna, Devadeva, [Mṛḍa], and Bhīma are the presiding deities of the forms (mūrtis). || 29 ||
Dhārīkā, Dīpti, Atyugrā, Jyotsnā, Cetā,
Balotkaṭā, Dhātrī, and Vibhvī are renowned as the personified powers (mūrti-śaktis) in brief.
Anantīśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekalocana,
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍaka. || 31 ||
Umā, Caṇḍī, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Mahākāla, Nandika,
Bhṛṅgīśa, and Vṛṣa— these are the lords of the Gaṇas, ending with Ṣaṇmukha.
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattaka,
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra are the lords of the Bhairavas.
In some scriptures, for the others, they are considered to follow the sequence of four, two, and one;
[the first four] are named Ajātaka and so forth, and likewise Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara. (34)
Vimala, Viśāla, Sārasvata, Mahāmukha,
Lelevāsurak, Śāstṛ, Phaṇyāśī, and Kuṇḍadevatā. || 35 ||
The Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, and the World-Protectors, beginning with Indra, are well-known in all scriptures; they have been previously mentioned in this scripture as well.
Having honored the astrologer and the Brāhmaṇa,
the Preceptor, who is the embodiment of the mantra, should gather all the necessary materials and enter the sacrificial pavilion.

Having prostrated before Śiva and made his request, he whose body was composed of the limbs of Brahmā established those who had conquered their senses as embodied forms in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, facing east and north respectively in the proper locations of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
one should indeed recite these mantras in the sequence beginning with the east.
In the sixty-first Liṅga, by omitting half and then half again starting from the middle [of the measures],
the vessel for the oblation (homa-pātra) and likewise the respectful offering (argha) are each reduced by ten according to the sequence of the kings.
One should cause a vessel filled with clarified butter to be given for each individual, whether it be made of gold, silver, or copper, or even of other materials if these are unavailable.

Seating mats, vessels for the arghya offering, fuel-sticks, darbha grass, and firewood; as well as fragrances, flowers, and offerings, along with the sruk and sruva ladles endowed with the proper characteristics.
The wise one should offer oblations to those guardians of the images individually;
all of them should be clad in white garments and anointed with white sandalwood paste.
Adorned with white garlands, joyful, and with their minds fixed upon their own forms,
having honored them with gold, garments, and other offerings, he should then give instructions to them.
One should first recite the Pāśupata mantra in the east, and the Aghorāstra in the south;
likewise, the Khādaka in the west and the Khurikāstra in the north.
Seated upon their own seats, having conquered the pairs of opposites, and endowed with all necessary requisites, they—
being experts in the true essence of the scriptures and in ritual action— should first perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
With mantras originating from a single tantra, they should generate the Śiva-fire;
thus all the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), having performed the libation upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), [should proceed].
Then they should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) together with the consecrator;
and the consecrator, having gathered the previously prepared materials, should stand at the head of the deity.

Wearing a white turban, observing silence, clad in white garments and anointed with white unguents, he should be single-minded, having conquered anger, full of faith, and having subdued his senses. || 49 ||
Having first performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the wise one should generate the Śiva-fire;
once the fire has been generated and propitiated, he should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Having fully satisfied the seat, the face, and the limbs by means of the entire collection of mantras, or else by the previously mentioned ritual mantras arising from the horizontal and upward movements; || 51 ||
Mantras that bestow accomplishment and liberation are prescribed to be kept secret in all ritual actions;
the prefix *su-* (or *su-*) serves to negate the literal meaning of the root, as in the case of the secret speech of a minister (*mantri-gupta-bhāṣaṇa*).
Endowed with silence, the preceptor should always mutter the mantra while joined with its meditation;
however, during the rite of placement (nyāsa) and the fire-oblation (homa), he should perform it in a whisper and so forth.

If Hari is installed without the presence of the image-bearers (mūrtipas) and without the recitation of weapon-mantras (astrajāpa), the sacrifice becomes beset with obstacles; therefore, one should worship the image-bearers.
For the purpose of protecting the three, for the sake of pleasing the wise, for the purpose of prohibiting harsh words, and always for the sake of auspiciousness; (55)

[He should invite] Brāhmaṇas who know the true meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras, who recite softly, whose senses are conquered, who possess the characteristics prescribed by their own scriptures, and who are well-composed.
Having honored those reciters of auspicious benedictions with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
the preceptor should afterwards seat them outside in the four directions.
Having stationed the Bahvṛcas in the eastern direction, the Atharvaṇas in the south, the Vājasaneyins in the west, and the Chandogas in the north; 58.
Having established them in their respective directions according to the opinion of the Goddess,
he then instructed the Brahmins who were well-versed in the Vedas by pointing out the gates.
The reciter of the Rigveda (Bahvṛca) should mutter the Śrīsūkta, the Pāvamānī hymns, the Nāsadāsīt hymn,
the Vājika, the Vṛṣākapi, and the Maitra hymns in the western direction.
The Devavrata, the Rathantara—the foremost Sāman for men—as well as the Bhāruṇḍa Sāmans and likewise the Vāmadevya; || 61 ||
Facing the northern direction, the singer of the Sāman hymns (Chandoga) should always recite the Rudra, the Puruṣasūkta, the Ślokādhyāya, and the Śukriya.
The Brahmins, with friendliness toward their friend, should recite from the beginning the *Adhyaryu* [hymns],
as well as the *Atharvāṅgirasa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, and likewise the *Skandasūkta*. (63)
One should recite the *Kṣurika*, the *Nīlarudra*, the *Garbhopaniṣad* and others, as well as the *Kālī*, the *Karālika*, and the *Rudra* from the *Atharvaveda* in the southern direction. (p.
36) This is the sequence for the placement of the door-keepers and the sequence for the recitation of the hymns.
[This refers to] that which concerns another philosophical system. || 64 ||
Those who know the *Liṅgodbhava*, its constituent parts, the *Pavitra*, the *Gaṇapāṭhaka*,
and other hymns and mantras, should always recite them on the right side.
Then, having indeed offered the *argha* water, the Guru should worship Śiva,
who is designated as "the Foot," with the *brahman* [Om], accompanied by the syllables of his own *kalās*, or with the *piṇḍas* accompanied by his own *kalās*. (66)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the practitioner of mantra should then meditate upon the ninefold self (navātman) as the living essence,
having a form like a blazing fire, radiating light in every direction. (67)
The leader of mantras, ever joined with the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka), purifies everything—the entire world, both stationary and moving—by that very [mantra]. 68.
Below is the power called Ananta, then the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), and from that, the hells: Avīci, Raurava, and Mahāraurava—these are the nine groups. (69)
Rasātala, Pātāla, Mahātala, Gabhastika,
that called Nitala, Varāha, and the seventh, named Ābhāsa.
Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka— these, in ascending order, belong to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara respectively.

The cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which consists of fourteen worlds (dvisaptabhuvana), the intermediate directions, and one hundred Rudras, is of a fierce form (caṇḍarūpa); its presiding deity is the four-faced Brahmā. It is one billion (śatakoṭi) yojanas in height and equal in width.
The nature of earth has been fully described; it possesses two qualities more than water and the others, respectively.
Earth, water, fire, air, and ether, as well as odor, taste, form, touch, and sound—these five are the subtle elements (tanmātras) in their respective order. (74)
The nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and the organs of hearing and intellect; the anus, the genitals, the hands and feet, along with speech—all these are the organs of action.
The intellect of the mind (manobuddhi), the ego (ahaṅkāra), and the three qualities beginning with sattva;
the person (puruṣa), attachment (rāga), knowledge (vidyā), necessity (niyati), and the ender of the lineage (kulāntaka) [in the Mūla-kośa: the ender of the limited power (kalāntaka)]. || 76 ||
Māyā, as well as Sadāśiva—who is called the Lord of Ignorance (avidyā)—and Śakti;
beyond these is the supreme, imperishable one known as Śiva.
Established in the *śikhi* (the fire-element), the friend of all (or: bound to all), purified by mantras, one shall go to Śiva.
[The elements consist of] the five gross elements (*pañcabhūta*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the organs of action (*karmendriyāṇi*). || 78 ||
The mind, the intellect, the ego, and primordial nature (prakṛti) endowed with its qualities—these twenty-four principles, which constitute primordial nature, reside in the left ear. (79)
The Puruṣa residing in the skin is said to be named Rāga within the network of sinews;
Ignorance (avidyā) is declared to reside in the flesh, and Necessity (niyati) is situated in the heart. (80)
In the *kalākoṣa* (the sheath of the digits), Kāla and Māyā reside within the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Vidyā is eternally situated in the lips, and Īśvara is established in the *bindu*.
Sadāśiva is to be known as residing in the *nāda*, while Indhikā and the others are stationed in Śakti.
Furthermore, the twenty-five principles are contained within the Piṇḍī.
They are purified by the King of Knowledge (vidyārāja); above that is Śiva, partless (niṣkala).
One should place there Śiva, who has become mantra, for the sake of perfection and liberation. (83)

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the three principles beginning with the *ātmatattva*, and of the four Vedas beginning with the letter 'A' upon the unborn [deities] and so forth, one should meditate upon their pervasive presence and that which is the supreme form of Śiva.

In some cases, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the triad consisting of the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Puruṣa, those beginning with Earth and ending with Vidyā [or Rāga, or Dhana], and those beginning with Īśvara and ending with Śiva. || 85 ||
When a thousand *aghora* oblations have been offered, the Guru should worship the portion of Brahmā;
likewise, he should worship the form of Hari above that with the water from the Śiva-pitcher.
Above that, one should offer oblations to Rudra; having sprinkled [the area] with water, one should touch it in sequence with *darbha* grass.
One should offer the five Brahmans and the ten directions [with] one hundred and five [oblations] each.
One should perform the oblation for the limbs with a tenth part [of the total], and for their digits (*kalā*) in sequence.
[He worshipped] Varṇa, Rudra, and the other Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśas), the World-Protectors (Lokēśas), and the Leaders of the Gaṇas (Gaṇanāyakas). || 88 ||

Having performed the consecration (*āpyāyana*) immediately, one should cook the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) as before—well-steamed and not burnt, and consecrated with the mantras dedicated to Śiva. (Note: This reading enclosed within brackets is absent in the manuscripts *mū*, *g*, and *gh*).
Having likewise offered [the oblation] into the auspicious pitcher and to the deity, one should then offer the caru-oblation;
thereafter, with the mantra of Śiva, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for the completion of the sacrifice.
The teacher should bestow the full initiation upon the practitioner who has completed the recitation;
at that time, he should give a gift to the guru according to his wealth. (91)
One hundred cows with horns like the tips of a plowshare, or half that number, or even half of that;
with the right foreleg [as the sacrificial fee], one should cause the homa to be performed again.
Then, when hundreds of various forms have been offered, the rite reaches completion;
likewise, when the expiation for obstacles has been performed, one should subsequently offer the great weapon (mahāstra) into the fire.
Having thus properly performed the ritual, one should then awaken the deity;
a great festival should be held at night with the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments.
He should spend that entire night with singers, dancers, learned men, those who chant auspicious praises, and the resonant sounds of beautiful hymns uttered by the ascetics.
Having prepared a beautifully adorned chariot with cloths, banners, and canopies, one should perform the consecration for one, three, five nights, or even for seven days. || 96 ||
One should place Śiva upon a chariot filled with all kinds of food and other offerings, along with yak-tail whisks with golden handles and umbrellas with stalks of gold lotuses.
One should perform sacrifice with the sound of musical instruments accompanied by lamps and mirrors; with white pitchers marked by lotuses, and with songs and recitations many times over,
one should slowly encircle either the city, the town, or the temple.
Having halted the chariot, one should repeatedly offer oblations to the Guhyakas.
The officiant, belonging to the same lineage, should go before the *liṅga* in front of the preceptor;
having placed it before the *prasāda*, he should cause the offering for the *liṅga* to be presented. (100)
With his mind fixed on the reality (tattva), he should offer oblations to the lords of the site;
thereafter, he should place the tortoise-stone there according to the characteristics previously described.
Thus ends the fifteenth procedure, named "Consecration," in the Compendium of Characteristics. || 15 ||
Then, for the sixteenth [chapter], one should sprinkle the entire temple with water consecrated by the recitation of the *astra* mantra;
thereafter, one should lay out the lines for its interior so as to reach the central location.
Having made a cord extending from the corner of the womb (the southeast) into four parts,
the tortoise-stone is to be situated in the center with the measurement of one of those parts.
One should not place the liṅga in the center, nor should one abandon the center;
for Brahmavedha situated in the center kills the maker—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, relying on that measurement, its establishment is according to the sūtra;
having divided the door into seven parts, one should again place the chariot (or essence) in the middle part.
Having abandoned two parts on the north and two parts on the south according to the measurement of that thread,
one should worship it directly for as long as the moon and sun endure, through the presence of the mantra. || 5 ||

Established in the northeastern direction, Śiva shall bring about abundance of food, security, health, victory, and the prosperity of the kingdom; may he create auspiciousness for all sentient beings.
The [auspicious] direction for kings is the East; for those who live by fire, it is the Southeast;
for those with banners, it is the Southwest; and for those engaged in dance and song, it is the Northwest.
In the north, [the placement] of cows, Brahmins, and so forth, as well as artisans in the intermediate directions,
brings happiness to the patron together with his family when it is situated in the northeast.
If the maker dies in the middle, one must not move it from the center;
for a linga moved from the center would bring about faults. (9)
If the *liṅga* is situated in the north (Kauveryā), there is suffering for the agent and distress for the twice-born (*dvija*).
But if it is in the east (Aindryā), the king dies and there shall be distress among the Kṣatriyas. (10)
In the south there is suffering for the Vaiśyas, in the west for those born as Śūdras;
in the northeast there is distress for ascetics, and in the southwest there is turmoil within the kingdom. (11)
If the Liṅga is installed toward the southeast, there is suffering from fire; if toward the northwest, there is fear of thieves.
Whatever fruit results from the manner in which one installs the Liṅga, that is now described.
And when the eighth part of the ground belonging to the Brahma-portion has been entered, there is a Liṅga that brings peace and prosperity to the builder, the installer, and the artisans. (13)
The worship of the *liṅga* is certain, as is its entry into the feet;
when one-third has entered, all embodied beings rejoice. (14)

If one-fifth [of the measurement] is entered for the builder, the supervisor, and the artisans, then the subjects, along with their four-footed animals, will prosper even when half [of the measurement] is entered. || 15 ||
Upon the entry of the entire portion of Brahmā, the Sthāpaka and the others, as well as the performer together with his kinsmen, attain great happiness. || 16 ||
Then one should install the *liṅga* so that it remains perfectly stable and free from obstacles;
for if it is moved, there will be great suffering, and if it cracks, there will be a loss of wealth. (17)

If [the bell] is crooked, worship is diminished; if it is bent, there is quarrel and disease. If it makes a sound, there will be the ruin of the kingdom; if it is tilted, the occurrence of illness follows. (18)
If it is shattered, there will be total destruction; if it trembles, there will be upheaval in the kingdom.
Having recognized the occurrence of these defects, together with the image-keepers (mūrtipas), [one should act]. (p. 43) 19.
Having informed the Lord and fully satisfied him, the best of instructors should offer one hundred and eight oblations upon the sacrificial mound for each individual, as the case may arise.
Having offered a full oblation with the Aghora-mantra of Śiva at the end, then, when the auspicious liṅga is being installed or is already situated in the center, it is auspicious. (21)
The door should be equal [in height], or reduced by one-third; the height of the central linga should be aligned with the threshold-line of the houses of the largest and other sizes. || 22 ||
Having understood this, the stone named Kūrma, fashioned previously by the primordial power, should be joined;
it is endowed with the Rasa-Kūrma, and above that, another stone is to be placed.
Having first cleared the excavation according to the dimensions of the *brahmaśilā*,
one should worship the *rājaśilā* there and install it with the *śakti-mantra*.
O Goddess, you who are the supreme power named Anantā and who uphold the path of pure consciousness,
you must remain here at all times by the command of Śiva.
Having made pervasion the support for meditation, one should contemplate and install the sign (liṅga) which is supreme, all-pervading equality, firm in its path, and firmly established. 26.
Oṃ! Salutation to you, O Pervasive One, infinite, eternal, very firm, and constant;
O stainless one, support of all, hrīṃ laḥ hrīṃ! Abide here, O Mother!
Thus [this reading does not appear in the manuscript copies] is the mantra for the installation of the Brahma-stone. (p.
44) Facing north, one should sprinkle it with the water of Śiva using the Astra-mantra.
Having covered the pit with a cloth, one should purify the pit.
Having scratched [the surface] with *darbha* grass and sprinkled it with auspicious water consecrated by Śiva,
one should first smear the stone surface with sandalwood paste and fumigate it.
One should place the jewels as desired with the hand holding gold,
using the mantra of the presiding deity of one's own direction, or the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), or the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with either Pañcavaktra or Vidyeśvara in some instances,
they are smeared with liquid guggulu resin mixed with cow-products and milk-rice (pāyasa).

First, the supports for the jewels should be prepared, and thereafter the placement of the jewels and so forth; having understood otherwise for each respective system, the Guru may install them according to his own discretion.
One should place diamond, pearl, lapis lazuli, conch-shell, crystal, puṣpaka, sapphire, and deep-blue gem in order starting from the east.
In the absence of coral, one should place rājāvarta;
and in the absence of lapis lazuli, one should place either sapphire or ruby.
A blue vajra marked with the sun, a great sapphire, fine pearl, topaz, ruby, and lapis lazuli, starting from the eastern direction [and proceeding clockwise]. (35)
When a *sūnīla* gem is unavailable, one should place a *marakata*;
if a *padmarāga* is not obtained, according to other traditions, a *saugandhika* may be used.
Having melted together copper, brass, tin, silver, bell-metal,
and lead, one should deposit these [metals] starting from the direction of Indra (the east) and ending with Īśāna (the northeast).
One should place yellow orpiment, realgar, collyrium, mica, as well as orpiment from Kāśī, vermilion, honey-gold, and red ochre. (38)

In the absence of añjana, one should use sulphur; likewise, in the absence of sindūra, mercury. In the absence of saurāṣṭrī, one should use māthikā; and in the absence of gairika, one should use rocanā.
One should place tāla, śilā, kāsīsa, mākṣika, and sūtraka;
and in some places, sauvarṇa, gairika, gandha, and bhṛṅga, starting from the east.
One should also place rice, wheat, oblation-grains, as well as mung beans, green gram, barley, wild rice (nīvāra), śyāmāka, and pūrṇa-dyā grains.
One should then place, in sequence: wheat, barley, sesame, mung beans, and *aulika*; then *syāmāka* millet, mustard seeds, black gram (*māṣa*), and likewise rice.
One should substitute mung beans for black gram (māṣa) due to its absence, and chickpeas for mung beans;
likewise, one may substitute kangu and śyāmāka grains for sidhārtha (white mustard), and the *kapi* grass-corn for black gram. (43)
One should place sandalwood, red sandalwood, *laghūka* (i.e., *aguru*), and *añjana*;
as well as *uśīra*, that which is called *viṣṇu*, *sahā*, and in some places *lakṣaṇa*.
One should obtain *sahā*, *viṣṇu*, red sandalwood, *candana*, *sāri*,
*vākuṇṭha* (or *kumbha*), *muśīra*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpikā*.
With the mantras beginning with *sadyojāta* and others, one should [consecrate] gems, metals, and minerals.
Having placed the seeds and the eight medicinal herbs inside the jars, one should install them in sequence.
The lord of essences (rasendra) should be administered from the middle [of the dose], combined with all of these [ingredients].
If the quantity of the substance is excessive, there is great harm; [the dosage] should proceed by degrees starting from half a guñjā.

One should place the five initial items, beginning with the jewel (ratna) and so forth, complete with their names and accompanied by their respective mantras; likewise, one should place the vajra, gold, tin, lead, and iron in sequence. 48.
In the absence of mercury, one should use cinnabar; in the absence of diamond, gold; in the absence of gold, silver; and in the absence of realgar, yellow orpiment. (49)
In the absence of barley, one should give sesame seeds—excluding *lājaka* and *sahā*;
or one may deposit everything in the guru; or, if even that is unavailable, in mercury alone. (50)

One should place in the center, within the cavity of the Brahma-stone, either a tortoise, the earth, a bull with Meru, or a lotus endowed with the proper characteristics— whichever one of these [is chosen].

The stone slabs should be sixty-four parts of the width of the eaves; the ear-projections (karṇāvaṭa) should be as wide as half the depth and breadth of that [slab], and from the center of its eight petals, there should be an encircling band.
Gold, copper, silver, and a tortoise possessing the previously mentioned characteristics;
or a golden or silver image of the Earth, and Meru always made of gold. (53)
One should place a bull made of silver, gold, or copper, endowed with the proper characteristics, and having set down a lotus made of eight metals, or indeed of gold or silver; (54)
For a *liṅga* measuring one cubit (*hasta*), the measurement for the tortoise-base and other components is one *māṣa*;
for the remaining parts that increase in sequence, it extends up to nine *bāṇas*.
(55) One should take clay originating from a mountain peak or produced from the banks of a river.
And one should place silver and barley together with a tortoise.
An equal gaze at the door is praised; it brings fearlessness to the kingdom and leads to victory in the realm.
When a *liṅga* is installed there, the patron prospers. (57)
One should place gold, all kinds of seeds, and earth together;
when Rudra is established therein, the subjects rejoice eternally.
One who desires prosperity, or for the sake of increase, should place madhuka, akṣata, añjana, and meru in the center of the deity. || 59 ||
One should place wheat, chickpeas, ghee, dūrvā grass,
and gorocanā,
as well as earth from a cow's horn, together with a bull.
One should place a great bull in the center, facing evenly toward the directions of the doors;
when the deity has been awakened therein, the four castes flourish.
One should place gold and kṛśara along with a lotus;
when that Lord is thus established, there shall be an increase of fortune and prosperity.
Alternatively, one may place a ruby, gold, or mercury;
even if these materials are unavailable, one should deposit at least one of them.
I have explained the deposition of the jewels (ratnanyāsa) and how it is to be attained through attainment; likewise, one should arrange all the ritual substances in various ways.
Afterwards, one should dissolve [the substances] with guggulu resin that has been processed;
having made apertures as large as a stone, one should likewise place the *netra* on top. (65)
Having protected [the area] with the armor-weapon mantra, one should offer oblations to the lords of the directions;
then, having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should offer a hundred oblations with the sword-mantra.
The removal of the stone from the hole may be performed by Śiva or for the sake of prohibition;
then, having offered oblations to Vāstoṣpati, one should inspect the pedestal and the cavity.
One should install a linga made of kṣīradāru wood into the cavity of the pedestal;
one should ensure that it is seamless and very firm, doing so with great care.
Thereafter, being purified in mind, one should offer the water of honor (argha) and incense to the liṅgas;
then, one should bind it firmly to a staff with a hair-thread.
One should diligently awaken Śiva with the auspicious sounds of musical instruments,
with the cries of throngs of bards, with beautiful hymns of praise, and with most auspicious omens.
Then, O Śivā, the patron (yajamāna), surrounded by all his own people, together with the image-makers (mūrtipas) and artisans, should proceed there, closely following behind.
The Guru should go in front of that, holding the vessel for the *argha* offering;
when the *liṅga* has reached the doorway, he should offer the *argha* and cause it to enter.
Without closing the door, one should cause him to enter without touching the doorway; in a dwelling where the door is closed, one should enter from above as if through the sky.
One should carefully insert the *garbha* [or *liṅga*] so that it does not touch the wall;
by touching the directions and the sky, one should perform the prescribed *dakṣiṇā* for those directions.
One should give gold, copper, a buffalo, a rhinoceros, pearls, fine garments, a conch, and a cow to the Guru; this removes the defects resulting from contact with Indra and the other [planets]. (75)
Then, having offered the arghya water and established the Lord within the interior of the doorway upon the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha),
the Guru should install him during a moment endowed with excellent qualities, while reciting the heart-mantra.
One should install the liṅga, the pedestal, the neck, and the water-receptacle in their proper order with the sound of a drum, when the equinox has occurred as the auspicious occasion.
Having raised the thumb and formed a fist with the right hand,
the Guru should place it upon the pedestal and touch the liṅga with his thumb.
For those desiring liberation, there is union through the mantras of Umā and Maheśa; for those desiring prosperity, there is union through the yoga of the mantras of Śiva and Umā. (79)
Furthermore, a seat should be offered as a means for establishing a connection;
then, one should again perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) starting from the form (mūrti) and ending with the limbs (aṅga). || 80 ||
One should arrange the seat there with mantras prescribed for independent use;
likewise, one should install the form of Śambhu, the limbs, and then perform the act of supreme unification (paramīkaraṇa).

Having performed the sealing (mudrā) according to the procedure taught in the Saṃhitā for the one known as Nirodhana-jñā, the installation of Rudra and all the others should then be carried out in due order according to reality. || 82 ||
One should meditate in successive order upon the seat, the form, and Śambhu, along with the three sides according to the three principles (tattvas), as well as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
Those who are remembered as being situated on the seat, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin,
are established in the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self), conjoined with the limbs of the Vidyā. (84)
And the three Śaktis are traditionally held to be endowed with the five Brahmans;
for the wise know that these reside within the principle of Vidyā as long as they possess authority.
The two powers, Śiva’s limbs, and the Śiva-principle—these are based upon it. Thus, the pervasion of the three principles is declared; here, indeed, the paths are sixfold.

The earthly element (pārthiva-tattva) extends for one hundred and ten million yojanas and has a height equal to its width; the elements beginning with water increase in size by double in successive order up to the limit of the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa).
From Śakti up to Śaktiparyanta, there are the five deities and their presiding divinities;
the thirty-five principles constitute the true path, the Īśvara-pīṭha. 88.
Having meditated upon Śambhu, the supreme [bearer of the linga], who possesses five faces and three eyes,
is endowed with ten arms, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair; || 89 ||
His head was adorned with the crescent moon, he wore a serpent as a sacred thread,
and he was surrounded by hosts of Gaṇas, gods, and Siddhas who were offering him praise.
Then, having meditated upon Īśāna as the supreme reality in the form of a *bindu*,
one should install him with the *vāmadeva* mantra using the "instantaneous whirling" (*sadyolāta*) visualization.

Just as an enjoyer [is connected] to the body through the union of the embodied one with the substances joined [to it], so too one should contemplate the object of knowledge as being established in cognition and action, resting upon consciousness. 92.
The bindu resides in the midst of the nāda; the dhvani resides in the midst of the bindu; the tārā is situated within the dhvani; and the moon is situated within the tārā. (93)
The subtle is situated within the moon; the sun is situated within the subtle. The Tranquil is situated within the sun; Śiva is situated within the Tranquil.
Just as the digit of nectar (amṛtakalā) arises from the union of the orbs of the sun and moon,
so too here, having recollected it in that manner, one should deposit the portion of vision and action.
If, however, while the work is being performed correctly, there is movement at the edge of the direction (or confusion regarding the directions),
then an oblation to the deities of the directions must be performed, as well as a pacifying rite that removes the defect.
In whichever direction the liṅga moves, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) in that direction;
otherwise, there will be terrible misfortune for the performer and the kingdom.
Therefore, one should not offer those vehicles to Indra and the other gods as they are;
namely, the elephant, the goat, the buffalo, the female servant, the fish, and the deer and sheep. (98)
Having correctly placed that thread or cord for the sake of tranquility directly in front [of the object],
one should then apply the side-thread and the vertical plumb-line for the purpose of straightness.
One should not move the liṅga again if one desires one's own welfare;
[the results are] respectively: when it is moved, when it makes a sound, when it wavers, when it bows down, and when it remains stable.
It seizes the village, the heart, and the kingdom; it causes disease and brings about decline or prosperity.
Having filled the chasms and fissures with auspicious substances such as milk, iron dross, and so forth, one should worship. (101)
Then, with sand, mud, and hair, combined with conch powder,
the bearers of the forms [of the deity] perform their own ablution with the waters from the peace-vessel (śāntighaṭa). (102)
After that, they perform the rites, and then the preceptor should bathe Śiva with water,
milk, curd, honey, ghee, and pure water.
A golden or similar vessel filled with four *pala* of water— known as a *gaḍḍūka* (a water-vessel or a specific type of jar, according to the *Śabdaratnāvalī*)—
is suitable for placing a small, moving object measuring only a few finger-breadths. 104.
For the remaining [liṅgas], there is an increase of one aṅgula per size; the increase in weight is three palas for every cubit [of height].
For a stable liṅga measuring exactly one hasta, the pedestal (gaḍḍūka) should be one prastha in measure.
For others, the increase should be by eight palas in succession;
there should also be anointing, bathing, and the great ceremonial bath for Śaṅkara.
And with twenty-five, five hundred, and two thousand *pala*s respectively, there are the various types of *liṅgas*, namely the movable, the fixed, and those of dual form. (107)
Those who abide in the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Śakti, as well as the gods and others who likewise occupy the same locations within those very principles; || 108 ||
In the section on authority (adhikārapāda), there is purification, supreme transformation, and dissolution;
their locations, portions, and states are situated below, above, and in the middle. (109)
Having performed the ritual bath (*snāna*), one should install the mantras within oneself according to one's intention; likewise,
the seat and so forth should be arranged according to the scriptures, as well as the faces and limbs encircled by the digits (*kalā*).
One should place the Power of Will (icchā-śakti) within the course [of the breath], and the Form (mūrti) together with the limbs of Knowledge (vidyā),
situated in the middle of the seat; then again, the one called Action (kriyā) and the one called Knowledge (jñāna) below that.
The ritual bathing of the deities according to the prescribed rules is the cause for their presence;
it is performed, joined with all mantras and the like, out of a desire to bestow grace upon the world.
O Mahādeva, remain ever present here at this Liṅga for as long as the sun and moon exist and as long as the earth endures. (113)
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, you should remain here at your own will for that long.
Having spoken thus, [she gave] the command of Śiva to Maheśvara, whose form is the mantra.

One should install Śiva, who is the life-force, consisting of earth, water, and the moving element (air), which effects the withdrawal of the fire of the pride of vital breath, and is known as the Rudra, Moon, Bindu, and Nāda.

Placing his hand upon the head of the limbs, he should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times; by that, the faces and limbs come into proximity. He should then perform the placement once more. (Note: This reading enclosed within brackets is found in manuscript *kha*.)
One should then assign the faces directed toward the cardinal directions, upward, and so forth, as well as the Śaktis upon the pedestal;
having meditated upon Aghora as the heart, one should then assign the Heart-mantra.
One should contemplate the Person Śiva in the position of his head;
one should contemplate the crest-lock as having become the deity Īśāna. || 118 ||
([This reading within brackets is not present in manuscript G: One should meditate upon the armor-mantra as Vāmadeva on all sides, beginning with the secret parts;
then one should assign the Sadyojāta-mantra and the weapon-mantra to the hand, and furthermore [the trident and so forth]. 119.
One should restrain those mantras associated with speech that belong to the dualistic and non-dualistic categories;
as for the Mudrā who is the Mistress of Power (Śaktīśvarī), she has come down through the lineage of succession. (120)
Having manifested that through his own physical form, the practitioner remains established in the Guru;
by means of those two, the mantras remain established in their own state for as long as the moon and sun endure,
by the command of Śiva.
In the case of duality, one should perform the suppression with the armor-mantra *mṛtyañjaya*;
in the case of non-duality, it should be done with the *aghora* mantra or with one's own heart-mantra. || 122 ||
The Guru should touch the liṅga together with its pedestal using those very five mudrās that stand in their proper sequence, beginning with the Ajātā.

O Śambhu, the five mudrās of these [faces], beginning with the fifth, are respectively: invocation (āhvāna), installation (sthāpanā), confinement (nirodha), piercing (niṣkura), and salutation (praṇāma); thus they are the five-faced [mudrās]. (124)
The pedestal (piṇḍikā) is the Mother of the World, and the linga is the Father, both mobile and immobile;
that which is the union of Śiva and Gaurī is designated as installation (pratiṣṭhā). || 125 ||
Through the four human goals—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—one always obtains them from Śiva alone by means of establishing [the image], worship, recitation, and meditation. (126)
The Linga, extending from the Prākartas to Īśvara, or its image, is likewise established;
Durgā is in Īśvarī, Āditya in Bhanu, and Mādhava in Hari.
When the *liṅga* has been installed by the teachers of Śiva while standing in the direction of Īśāna,
the Guru should mutter the divine Pāśupata [mantra], which effects the fulfillment of everything. (128)

The performer should perform the bath with the water of the Guru’s weapon-mantra and with the water from the auspicious jar; having offered ornaments and other gifts to the Guru, the performer should then receive the sacrificial rice (caru).
A Liṅga established in this manner brings wealth, land, and other riches;
it ensures abundance of food and health within the kingdom, and effects the destruction of thieves and the like.
Having attained victory, the king [and his] good minister [possess] the strength of their own subjects; there is always prosperity for the founder and for those who depend upon him. 131.
Herbs, milch-cows, trees, those joined with them, buffaloes, bulls, artisans, and all performers of labor go to the abode of Śiva. (132)
A linga established by Śiva-teachers that consists of the essence of Śiva-mantras should be known as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation; otherwise, however, the opposite result occurs.
One should offer clothing, garlands, scents, incense, food offerings, and lamps to the deity; likewise, anointing, ornaments, food, and gifts are highly commended.
On the fourth day, the preceptor should diligently offer [oblations] to the Śiva-yogins and the twice-born,
and thereafter install the deity Caṇḍeśvara according to the prescribed rite.

An ointment of *madhu* destroys sins; an ointment of *rajanī* cures diseases of the bile (*pitta*); an ointment with *rocanā* cures eye diseases; and an ointment with *phalinī* brings about what is dear. (136)

Sesame seeds bring satisfaction to the ancestors; the *padmakesara* flower destroys enemies; the *nāgapuṣpa* brings abundance of food; and the fruit [of these] brings success in sequence over seven days. (137)
On the eighth day, for Śaṅkara, there is the offering of water (argha), bathing, and likewise worship;
and anointing with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and other substances. (138)
One should offer clothing, incense, flowers, and the sacred thread with the Bahurūpa mantra;
likewise, collyrium and yellow pigment (rocanā) with the Aja mantra, and the mirror with the Puruṣa mantra.
With the Īśāna mantra, however, one should offer flowers, as well as a crown, earrings, bracelets, a waist-thread, and whatever head-band there may be. (140)
One should cause all these— parasols, banners, canopies, yak-tail whisks, and garlands of flowers (or mirrors and so forth)— to be given by him alone, or else by secret agents. 141.
Having thus performed the worship of that Lord, the God of gods,
one should prostrate oneself like a staff upon the ground and slowly perform a circumambulation.
Having returned once more, one should inform the Blessed Lord Hara of whatever has been done,
whether good or evil, performed either through ignorance or with full knowledge.
All of that, together with myself, has been offered by me to you;
at that time, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Śiva-yogin. 144.
The best [portion] should be given to the Ācārya; that minus one foot [of the portion] to the Sādhaka;
half of that should be given to the Putraka, and a quarter to the Samayins. (145)
p. 57) Furthermore, for those who observe other vows, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) shall indeed be one-quarter;
one should give gifts to the twice-born according to their ability and in accordance with the prescribed rule. (146)
One should satisfy the master builder, the craftsmen, the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others, as well as musicians, singers, and dancers, with food.
At night, one should perform a great festival with the sounding of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, for one night, three nights, or even seven nights. (148)
One should observe the ten-day period of impurity and provide a grand retinue;
one should give the edicts and other items to the two lords of ascetics according to one's wealth.
Having divided the thousand-fold [number] equally into two parts, one should place them in their respective rows along the path.
From the male [deities] and so forth, there is purification by day; from the Vidyā [deities] and so forth, it is surrounded by a hundredfold [repetition].
In the case of a *liṅga* known as the Thousand-fold or the Hundred-fold, which previously had its paths divided,
one should perform the stabilization of the mind; the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) shall then be as stable as before.
[Root: Steadfast] || 151 ||
When the field has been divided into ten parts, one should remove four of those parts from the center—
one from each of the four directions and one from each corner.
In this manner, one should construct one thousand and one compartments; within them, lingas should be installed according to the prescribed rite, in a number corresponding to those compartments.
As before, the sacrifice should be performed with respect to those threefold signs;
however, this injunction applies to the inferior ones, while for the superior ones it is preceded by their established state.
Having performed the extraction of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇoddharaṇa*), one should then place jewels and so forth;
there, the wise man should bring the great *liṅga* by means of the application of the *yantra*. (155)
Having made it octagonal in the middle and circular at both ends,
and having joined an octagon in the center, it is adorned with sturdy wood.
Having fixed the two ends of the pestle into two holes situated in the pillar,
one should fasten the linga and other parts with firm leather straps and strong threads.
Then, one should quickly pull him out with many people from the makara-shaped opening;
this is declared to be the "donkey" (khara) machine for the purpose of raising [the victim]. || 158 ||
Alternatively, two pestles made of thick, well-rounded wooden pieces may be employed for piercing wood in front of the pestle-end. || 159 ||
One should attach a wooden plank to the back as a yoke using iron spikes;
such a cart with a wooden frame is used for pulling large liṅgas and the like. (160)
One should tether the bull by means of leather thongs to the two nostrils of its nose,
using dhava, ālūra, bilva, or other such hard woods.
One should firmly join two strong mechanical frames called *śivikā*, each consisting of four wooden beams;
in the place of Brahmā [or Viṣṇu], the Liṅga should be quickly fixed with firm pegs.
Having raised it with those two mantras, one should then place it beside the stone;
having fixed a firm wooden plank levelly above the base of the jewels (or at half the height of the base), || 163 ||
There, one should allow the *liṅga* to rest, and then gradually cast it into the pit.
Then, having divided the eight gentle [deities] with *argha* offerings joined to the cardinal and intermediate directions, [one proceeds]. (164)
Having wrapped it with smooth cloths and encased it on the outside with bricks, and having filled it with sand, one should then place the water-vessel. || 165 ||
Having made a brick from its sands and bathed it, one should then install the mantras;
one should perform worship, fire-offerings, and recitation, as well as the offering of oblations and so forth, as before. || 166 ||
The mobile liṅga should be made in two ways: with separate pedestals or with a single pedestal.
That with separate pedestals belongs to the Moon (Cāndra), while that with a single pedestal belongs to the Sun (Saurya). || 167 ||
One should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the two lingas according to their respective domains of earth and air;
furthermore, one should separately join the pedestal with mercury, diamonds, and medicinal herbs.
Having meditated upon the power of knowledge and action within the liṅgas and seats in their proper order,
one should thus install the stationary or mobile liṅga preceded by a sacrifice.
I shall now describe the fivefold establishment of the manifest [deity] according to other traditions:
[the deity] standing upright, seated, sleeping, mounted on a vehicle, and moving through the air. (170)

For these [deities], preceded by the ritual of opening the eyes, there follows the bathing and perfuming, as well as the fire-oblation (homa) and the chariot procession, performed with their own mantras, beginning with the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha). || 171 ||

When the womb is divided into seven parts, the abode of Brahmā is in the center; the regions for the Rākṣasas, gods, [Rākṣasas, asuras (Liṅga Purāṇa, Liṅga-pu., pāda)], and humans are in the middle, each occupying three parts respectively.
One should always install the image of the deity between the human and asura portions;
installation in the rākṣasa portion is not desired, as it leads to the destruction of wealth, longevity, and grain. (173)
It should not be made touching the wall; rather, it should be at its own proper place, for that bestows prosperity.
If it is joined with the wall, it will bring destruction to the patron. (174)
There, having placed the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), which has a width equal to half the back of the pedestal (pīṭha) and a height equal to half of that,
one should fashion it so as to be joined with a nine-celled lotus.
The arrangement of jewels is as before; however, with the other directional mantra, the upper image should be joined with Tejas, while the seated one is joined with Varuṇa.

Whether lying down with the king, seated in a vehicle, or traveling through the air, one should first stabilize [the breath] with the wind; then, in the state of duality or non-duality, there is cessation.
The gods, accompanied by their retinues, abide pervading [the elements] beginning with the earth;
