Brahmā exists up to the limit of the individual soul (puruṣa), and Acyuta up to the end of Māyā, beginning with the letter 'Ka'.
Rudra is at the end of Vidyā and in Agni and so forth; Īśa is in the Bindu of Calā (Balā) and so forth;
Sādākhya is from Kha up to Nāda; and Śakti is the rule for the supreme [levels] beginning with Vyāpti (Gh). || 179 ||
Apsaras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, vidyādharas, serpents, and kinnaras;
bhūtas, vetālas, śākinīs, and the planets, lunar mansions, and zodiac signs. || 180 ||

The oceans, the guardians of the fields, the rivers, the seer Brahmā, the directions and so forth, as well as those born from a womb, from a sprout, and from an egg—all these, residing within the principle of the earth (urvī-tattva), are to be purified. || 181 ||
Kṣoṇī (the Earth) and Kāla (Time) are always to be known as [the presiding deities of] water; Vārī is the most excellent among those who have conquered [their senses].
Pradyumna resides in the element of fire, while Aniruddha resides in the wind.
Brahmā is designated as Vyoman; the mind is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
the intellect is Viṣṇu; and the Puruṣa is considered to be Kasarī, Garṣa, and Vāsudeva. (183)
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasimha, Vamana, Rama, Rama, Rama, Buddha, and Kalki—these are the incarnations beginning with the Supporter of the Earth (Dhara). (184)
In some places Bhū is said to be Keśava, and Nārāyaṇa is the lord of the waters;
Mādhava resides in the fire-element, while Govinda is of the nature of the wind. (185)
Viṣṇu is designated as the ether (viyat), and Madhusūdana is indeed the mind (manas); Trivikrama is to be known as the intellect (buddhi), and Vāmana is always the ego (garva). || 186 ||
The Unmanifest is known as Śrīdhara; Hṛṣīkeśa is considered the Supreme Person (Puruṣa).
Padmanābha possesses eternal power (Śakti), and Dāmodara is the eternal Lord (Īśvara). || 187 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, ego, the unmanifest, the Puruṣa, Śakti, and the Supreme—these are the twelve [deities] in sequence. (188)
Mitra, as well as Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, and Sūrya himself; Sahasrāṃśu, Dhātṛ, Tapana, and likewise Savitṛ. || 189 ||
Gabhasti, Arka, Parjanya, Sraṣṭṛ, and Anta are the leaders of the principles (tattvas). The Rudras situated within these principles extend from Mārga to Kārtika.
Tryakṣa, Umāpati, Sthāṇu, Nīlakaṇṭha as the fourth, Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita. (191)
Īśāna, Dhanada, and Bhīma—these twelve are the protectors of the universe (viśvapāḥ). Likewise mentioned are the nine Durgās and those who are the hosts beginning with Ambikā. (192)
Hari, Hara, Ardhanārīśa, and whatever other forms of Rudra there are, as well as the Yoginīs of various forms and others previously mentioned. || 193 ||

All those gods who travel the path of reality (tattva) stand one above the other; accompanied by their retinues, they are to be purified by me until the limit of the principle of Māyā is reached. 194.
The thirty-two [deities] beginning with the Earth-principle (dharātattva) and ending with Vidyā, as well as those born from the Self-principle (ātmatattva),
the limbs of Vidyā, and the Lords of Vidyā (vidyeśas), are to be established starting from the Self-principle.

One should establish the three powers and the Lord, as well as the five Brahmans, within the principles of knowledge (jñānatattva); and those whose nature is Śiva should be established in the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).

In the Śiva-tattva, one should perceive the limbs of Śiva; that which is called Sadāśiva resides within the Śiva-tattva. For each individual tattva, however, one should observe the limbs for the installation of the deities. || 197 ||
The form, the name, the mantra, the ritual service (upacāra), purification,
the purification of the principles (tattva-saṃśodhana), installation (sthāpana), and restraint (rodhana) follow in sequence. (198)

Enjoyment, external authority, absorption, and the process of supreme transformation—these, along with [the others], are the twelve limbs for the implantation [of mantras] in the Daityas and other beings. (199)

A teacher who knows the true meaning of the authentic scriptures, who is peaceful, and who has received the oral instructions, is a liberating guru even if he lacks all the [physical] characteristics, provided he possesses wisdom. (200)
Having ferried them across the terrible ocean of saṃsāra by means of the ship that is the path of establishment— the ship of Dharma—
he should lead the practitioners to the city of their chosen deity. (201)
He who does not know the path does not know how to undergo initiation, nor does he know the installation of the deities; therefore, one should have a guru who is a knower of the path.

Having observed the doctrine of Vīrabhadra, this has been written out of a desire for the welfare [of others], for the sake of the complete installation of the Guru who dwells within the womb of the two powers (Śaktis). 203.
Due to the difference in forms, a difference in ritual action, mantra, and fruit is maintained;
likewise, there is duality, non-duality, and their mixture, while from ignorance arises the opposite.

In the case of one who is unestablished in the manifest [state], that [practice] should be performed in its entirety as before, preceded by the opening of the eye of insight; this same procedure applies even in the case of the unmanifest.
Or it may be divided by Brahma, Vasu, and the seasons (sixteen), or consist of one and a half parts of thirty-two;
the entrance is one face, while in the three-faced [mandala], it is half of everything.
In the case of a four-faced [linga], all [the measures] are double; in a three-faced one, they are six or five;
or it is held by some that in a five-faced one, the whole is four times [the measure].
Beside that, one should construct a square altar (piṇḍī) with two edges;
likewise, in the case of that which is called the Unmanifest (avyakta), it should be made such that the flow of water exceeds three parts.
One should cause the *liṅga* to be sprinkled on the pedestal, or the pedestal on the two sides of the *liṅga*.
Having placed, established, and firmly settled it, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is said to be threefold according to the sequence.
When properly accomplished according to the rules, it bestows happiness like a true friend;
but when wrongly applied, it produces fear like an enemy. (210)
Therefore, it is considered that establishing [the image] after having correctly understood [the procedure] brings about happiness;
otherwise, due to defects in the ritual action, it yields inauspicious results for both [the patron and the artisan].
A linga installed by Brahmins, Buddhists, hunters, naked ascetics, Kaulas, or followers of the Lākula tradition,
or one installed by artisans, deserves to undergo consecration once again.
The ritual arrangement for Caṇḍa will now be described for the thousand-faced Mukhaliṅga, the hundred-faced one, the one known as Vyakta, the one known as Avyakta, and the Sthirārcā.
Thus ends the sixteenth procedure in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*, titled "The Threefold Installation of the Liṅga" (this title does not appear in the written manuscripts). 16.
Now begins the seventeenth [chapter]:
on the fourth day, having performed his ablutions, the sacrificer should always worship all the gurus who have assumed embodied forms with perfumes, gold, garments, and other offerings.
Then, having become the body of Śiva and having performed the protection of the half-pitcher and the weapon as before, the Guru should deposit the entire city upon the smeared pedestal.
Having first fashioned it like a half-moon, adorned with a single stream of water at the gate, provided with eight white petals, and endowed with a pericarp in the center. || 3 ||
In the smallest [size] linga, which measures two cubits and has a water-depth of one cubit,
one should [arrange] the pericarp, the filaments, the joint, and the tips of the petals in sequence from the center toward the outside.
The pericarp should be made yellow, and the five-petaled lotus green;
the filaments are white, red, and yellow, respectively, according to the Jinas.
The petals are white, and the lines are red and black in their intervals;

however, for others, the girdle and the door are white, with an increase in the number of fingers [for the others]. (Regarding this half-verse, there is a different reading in manuscript *kha*: "In the white [area], the petals are white, and those following are red and black.")
Then, having removed the floral remains (nirmālya) that were offered on the fourth day and having placed them in the northeast, one should dismiss the food offering (naivedya).
Having bathed Śiva with the five sweet substances, one should worship him with perfumes and other offerings;
he is gratified by the auspicious songs of chaste women and the sounds of musical instruments.
They should perform the sacrifice with red threads wound around [the vessels], using the *sammatā* and other [specified materials].
Then, at that time, the gurus should inform the Lord Caṇḍeśa of their desire to worship.

There, having meditated upon Caṇḍeśvara as illuminated by his own face and limbs, one should worship him with perfumes and other offerings; the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed one hundred times each in his sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
For the goddess indeed [bestows] the absence of malformation and masculinity, as well as the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*),

the naming ceremony (*jātanāma*), the birth, the exit from the womb, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*śikhākarma*), the vows (*vrata*), the marriage, and the auspicious signs of the limbs.
[In the] portions of pleasure. || 11 ||
Having offered oblations to Vāgīśvarī and Vidyeśa, one should mix the sacrificial porridge (caru);
then, one should offer oblations to Caṇḍa and the others with the five Brahmans along with their ancillaries.
Having first constructed the Caṇḍaveśma with a measurement containing the Prasāda,
one should establish Caṇḍeśvara in the northeast, outside the Jagatī.

One should worship Caṇḍa according to the prescribed rite— he who is born from the splendor of Śiva, fierce, cruel, and terrifying, whose body consists of the limbs and faces of the [Śiva] icon, and who is the personification of the command.

One should worship Caṇḍeśvara as before with mantras consisting of the words for the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), accompanied by the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, and joined with the prefix *caṇḍa*.
Or one should meditate on him who has the luster of a cloud, four faces, and four arms;
who has three eyes, a mass of matted hair with the moon, a radiant face, and is adorned with serpents as bracelets.

With a hand raised holding a trident and an axe, and bearing a water-pot and a rosary of beads, he has a great serpent as his sacred thread; he is the destroyer of the suffering of those who have sought refuge.

Having performed this with his vital breaths, he should cause Caṇḍa, who resides within himself, to enter there—specifically into the lotus of the Ādhāra-śakti, which is governed by the rules of the *samaya* and so forth. (18)

The consumption of the caru offering and the naivedya from the worship of Śiva, as well as the wearing of garlands and the giving [of these items], are forbidden even for one who has been initiated, by the command of Śiva. (19)
"O Caṇḍa, from this day forward you must remain here as long as Śiva remains;
whether intentionally or unintentionally, forgive me for any deficiency or excess. (20)
"Stay right here in his presence for the sake of protecting Śiva's interests;
indeed, by the command of Śiva, this offering of remains (nirmālya) is granted to you. (21)

Having abandoned food to be licked, sucked, or drunk, as well as water for drinking, betel, garlands, ointments, incense, lamps, discarded flower offerings (nirmālya), clothing, wealth, and ornaments; || 22 ||
Then one should offer the bali-oblation to the directions and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor;
[one should also give] a single cow and a single bull,
complete with hooves and horns.
Even a person endowed with spiritual perfection may quickly fall from it by giving away, stepping over, or consuming the remains of an offering (nirmālya) at a dualistic shrine; such is the rule.
On the fourth day of the sun’s course, there shall be bathing, worship, and fire-oblation;
the sacrifice to Tejaścaṇḍa and all other rites shall follow the previously prescribed procedure.
In the case of the mobile *liṅga* which consists of duality, however, one should worship without Caṇḍa as before;
its *nirmālya* should be cast into water, and its dismissal (*visarjana*) takes place in the fire within the womb-altar.
That which has two faces, five faces, or likewise is very clearly manifest—this should be installed in a secret place for the purpose of accomplishing the affliction of a kingdom. (27)
In a cremation ground, at the foot of a tree, in a forest, near a lake,
in the open air, or on a mountain peak— in one's own direction, it yields fruit. || 28 ||
The linga of the quarters (digliṅga), one that has not been consecrated with weapons (ahitāsra), and one made of copper (tāmra) located in a cave, serve only for worldly purposes;
because of this, Caṇḍeśa does not abide even in those [lingas] that are fixed (sthira).

On the fourth lunar day, there is a special bath and worship for Viṣṇu; one should worship Viṣvaksena in a lotus, preceded by fire-offerings, gifts, and so forth, as before. (Note: This reading enclosed within brackets is not present in manuscript Kha.)

Just as there is no discarded flower offering (nirmālya) for Śiva, so it is not [forbidden] for cloth, books, fire, the lords of the Nāgas and Yakṣas, the hosts of Yoginīs, and the Mothers (Ambikās). || 31 ||

The remains of offerings (nirmālya) from the Linga at Vidyāntamaikahika—provided it is not for Caṇḍa—and the cities, oceans, Daityas, and so forth, as well as the sages, directional deities, and planets; || 32 ||
Even these who abide in dualistic doctrines are not impure; they bestow auspiciousness.
That which arises from initiation (*dīkṣā*), consecration (*sthāpana*), and sacrifice (*yāga*)—such "remains of the offering" (*nirmālya*)—is by no means a cause of fault.
The self-manifested Bāṇaliṅga, that which was established by the great ones,
those belonging to Dvaita and Advaita, and the common [liṅgas] here are for the sake of spiritual attainment.
Kṣetrapāla, Aṣṭaliṅga, Dattātreya, Bhairava, and Mārtaṇḍa— these are the [deities] in Advaita, as well as the Nirmālya (remnants of offerings), excluding Caṇḍa.

Indeed, that which resides in one's own chosen *liṅga* is pure and bestows the attainment of flowers and other offerings; however, in the world of non-duality (*advaita*), one should not display one's chosen deity as something fashioned by ritual rules.
(69) Those [mantras] born of the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa [systems] should be known as *ahaita*.
For their bathing, *argha*, and libation (*tarpaṇa*), divine water and the like are beneficial. || 37 ||
Whatever is given to that one who is dear to oneself, like the sacrificial porridge (caru), is undoubtedly [efficacious];
one should cause that food offering (naivedya) to be given to brothers, sons, and sisters. || 38 ||

By consuming that [remnant], there shall be the destruction of sin; one obtains the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and others—this is not surprising when it is always in the presence of the Liṅga. (39)
"By this method, the gods beginning with Brahmā and Upendra attained perfection, as did others such as Jayadratha," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva. (40)
Thus ends the seventeenth ritual procedure in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*, titled "The Installation of Caṇḍeśvara. || 17 ||
Then, on the eighteenth day, one should establish those born from eggs, from sprouts, and from the womb by means of their respective mantras;
for them, everything beginning with the opening of the eyes shall be performed as previously described.
Mantras abandon an unhonored image made of gemstone, metal, stone, wood,
or clay, respectively, after one month; the fifth [type] after five months.
Because of the avoidance of desire. || 2 ||
The purification of plastered images, paintings, and scriptures is performed through their retention [in memory];
likewise, bathing and other rites, as well as the mental visualization of gems, stones, and so forth, should be performed mentally.
The opening of the eyes and so forth, as well as the seating and other rites, are to be performed as before;
the worship is performed with *nimba* flowers, by which the painting does not perish.
Having first constructed the gateway, the decorative eyes, the site, the sacrificial oblation,
and the offering to the spirits, and having worshipped the deities of the site (vāstu), one should then deposit the jewels.
And having placed the jewels and so forth [therein], || 5 ||
Having erected an archway five *gavyūtis* behind the village merely as a general indication,
and having placed the *vasus* upon the two pillars, one should likewise place the twelve suns (*dineśas*) upon the *udumbara* tree.
This is the procedure for pillars and other such structures belonging to the Śailālins and others;
likewise, they worship the limb upon the sacrificial post (śūla), and when joined with the staff (daṇḍa), it is the illuminating [rite].
On a white eight-petalled lotus, radiant with its pericarp and filaments, the Lord Guru is to be worshipped like Śiva, possessing one, two, or three hands. (8)
Then, joined with the [deity's] form, faces, and limbs, one should mutter the Śiva-hundred;
or else, the Aghora mantra facing west should be offered as an oblation according to the number of recitations.
One should place it toward the northern direction for liberation, or toward the east for the sake of enjoyment;
it should be wrapped in a pair of cloths, firm, excellent, and pleasing to the yogin.
There, having first worshipped Anantamatha, or else having installed another teacher of one's own,
one should invoke the reality of his mantra and worship that teacher who is no other than the Lord.
One should place the feet upon the seat with the *ajāta* mantra, along with the secret part (*guhyaka*) using the *piṭhaṃ* mantra;
one should grant presence (*sānnidhya*) with the *aghora* mantra, and the water offering (*argha*) should be given with the *nara* mantra. || 12 ||
Having worshipped the heart-liṅga with a garland using the Īśāna mantra, and being endowed with the [appropriate] mudrā, that Guru himself should stand like Śiva, his hands covered by a cloth. 13.
The practitioner should worship that Guru with various ornaments, garments, and the like—
namely, crowns, earrings, necklaces, armlets, and bracelets.
Having worshipped with girdles, sacred threads, anklets, rings, and garments of various kinds, one should also give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 15 ||
Kings [rule] the best of circles, the lord of the circle [rules] the district;
the lord of the district [rules] the village, and likewise the lord of the village [rules] the field. (16)
To him he gave a pair of intoxicated elephants adorned with excellent ornaments,
as well as eight horses of great speed decorated with golden trappings.
A thousand milk-yielding cows, a beautiful load of gold,
male and female servants, excellent food, a bed, and choice garments.
One should offer with devotion the parasol, the fly-whisk, the water-pot, the fan, the sandals, as well as all household utensils. (19)
This gift for kings and others is [one part]; for others, it is half of that, and so on in sequence according to their wealth; for the Guru, however, it is one-eighth [of the total].
Together with brothers, sons, wives, kinsmen, and servants... [20]
Having thus presented himself, he should then make a formal request to the guru.
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, supreme refuge of all dharmas!
Today my birth has become fruitful, since [I have been delivered] from the great ocean of saṃsāra.
"O Lord, I have been uplifted by you; you have been troubled, so please forgive me.
Then the Sthāpaka, being delighted, was honored by the patron (yajamāna). || 23 ||
Therefore, at the conclusion of the initiation, installation, and sacrifice, as well as when a festival day has arrived, he bestows the entire fruit of the consecration upon the performer.
Upon obtaining the mantra and upon its accomplishment, she should remain pure during an auspicious moment;
yet, out of delusion, she fails to worship the Guru, the guardians of the images, or the reciters of the mantra. (25)
One certainly does not obtain that fruit; for it would belong to the one who deposited it.
Every difficult task should be performed with the desire to win great merit;
otherwise, there would be no merit, but rather only fault would arise.
If devoid of ritual materials, it destroys the performer; if lacking the mantra, however, it destroys the preceptor.
If it is devoid of charity, that dharma perishes; if it is devoid of food, that kingdom perishes;
likewise, if it is devoid of cows, life-span perishes; and if it is devoid of flowers, the subjects indeed perish. (28)

If there is a lack of rice, there will be a failure of crops; if there is a lack of oblations, there will be a lack of rain; if there is no sacrificial fee at the rite, there will be a son; and if there is no incense, there will be a woman. (29)
If it lacks fragrance, there will be disease; if it lacks a lamp, it robs one of luster;
if it lacks a banner, it destroys the subjects; and likewise, if it lacks an offering, it destroys the family.

Poverty would result from a rite performed without gold; therefore, for the sake of a successful consecration, one should first provide pure and eternal materials according to the complete ritual procedure.
Then, having divided that portion into six parts and made half of it the abode of the Liṅga (the *dharmaliṅgasadmāna*),
the installation therein is performed with one-third of that; furthermore, the fourth part is again divided into three.
The builder should designate one [share] there for the presiding priest, a second for the purpose of giving gifts,
and a third for food and other necessities, dedicating it for the sake of Dharma.
One may cause [the work] to be performed even by deceiving them with unjust wealth or by force;
however, at the time of sacrifice, once the wealth has been given, there must be no failure to provide it.
Indeed, the perpetrator shall remain in the Sūcyāsya hell as long as the moon and stars exist;
that sacrificial pavilion, purified by the implements of the sacrifice, is to be accepted from the Guru.
Likewise, the artisan known as Snāna, together with his implements, [should be provided].

Whatever substance is fit for the *liṅga* and whatever is intended for enjoyment should be placed within the interior of the temple; that must be given to Caṇḍeśa, and he shall protect the treasury of wealth.
The ritual procedure for the Guru-yāga has been proclaimed, and the ritual procedure for the Siddha-liṅga is established. || 37 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth procedure in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*, titled "The Worship of the Arches, Pillars, and the House; the Installation of Beings such as those Born from the Womb and so forth."
Now the nineteenth [chapter]:
Those Rudras who exist in the form of the *liṅga* bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*),
for the sake of showing favor to the worlds, by their own nature as the Self-born One.
Like a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga, a Bāṇaliṅga leads to both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
through its installation and worship, it bestows a thousandfold fruit compared to other [liṅgas].
At Śrīśaila, at Kālikāgarta, at Liṅgādri, at Kanyakāśrama, at Kanyātīrtha, in Nepāla, at Mahendra, and at Amarēśvara; || 3 ||
The Bāṇa-liṅgas established by Śiva-tattva remain;
the configuration of the river's flow has the very form of a Bāṇa-liṅga.
Whatever other signs are to be understood as bringing all happiness— those which possess movement, those which are objects of enjoyment, those endowed with mantras, and those that manifest— [5]
By the power of mantras, Lakṣmī herself enjoys those [images] which have been installed here by others—
by sages, gods, deities, and serpents.
The independent [mantras] that bestow accomplishment grant enjoyments and other benefits;
even those with cracked or similar defects are not faulty for the attainment of one's purpose.
Now, the seizing of the Bāṇaliṅga and its installation are described;
this should be done by devotees who have bathed, fasted, and performed the Śiva-sacrifice with great devotion.
Then, for the sake of showing me favor, he should inform the Lord:
"O Bāṇeśa, come of your own accord to that place which I desire. (9)
There, having brought [the deity], one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) and the bathing and other rites as before;
one should then offer oblations into the southern face, or indeed into the *vyāhṛtis* of Śiva.
Whether by one's own will or for the sake of prosperity, or for the sake of liberation,
the measurement of the characteristics of the forms and the lines, beginning with the east and so forth, as well as the process of circumambulation and the rest, must be purified.
Even though it has been stated according to the ritual injunctions, there is indeed constant presence here;
for the lingas are eternally manifest, whether they arise from the pure or the impure.

Whether established on a seat or not, whether situated in a physical form or not, whether mobile or immobile, it should be installed for the sake of prosperity through the presence of consciousness. || 13 ||
In the fourth oblation, Caṇḍeśa is the specific deity; no other path exists for practitioners well-established in the yogas of mantra-sādhana. (14)
The ritual procedure should be as it was for the elder [predecessor], whether it occurs elsewhere or here;
or else, in the case of an arrow previously consecrated, the same procedure applies again.
Whether the mantra has been projected [into the object], or in a state of duality or non-duality, there shall be no confusion.
In that regard, since the placement [of the deity] is indeed within the *liṅga*, by that [placement], it is as if the deity is present there.

When the mounting of the *liṅga* has been performed in this manner, and another [deity] is joined [therein] as before, nevertheless the preceptors must always effect the presence [of the deity] therein. (17)
Having offered a thousand *aghora* oblations with *udumbara* fruits smeared with honey, one should then feed five preceptors out of a desire for spiritual accomplishment. (18)
Having performed the striking, the drawing of the sword, the piercing with the fist,
and the seizing according to the ritual procedure within this duality, one should plant the mantra in non-duality.
In the integration of non-duality and duality, one should not abandon one's own mantra;
likewise, a guest who has arrived should be honored, for as one who resides within his own portion, he becomes the bestower of success.
Having first abandoned the *dhāmagarbha* sūtra at the front of the ground,
the pavilion for the bull (*vṛṣamaṇḍapī*) should be constructed according to the measurement of the interior of the temple. (21)
Having carefully placed the bull there and completed all the preparatory rites (*sambhāra*),
one should carve it out, perform the consecration with clarified butter (*ājyādhivāsana*), and then conduct the bathing and worship as before.
One should then offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) of sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) produced from the Brahma-tree, in accordance with the sequence of the three principles (*tritattva*).
It should be sprinkled with water mixed with *sampāta* (the residue of oblations), and then one should deposit the jewels and other items. || 23 ||
Then one should place the Bull upon the pedestal situated within the principle (tattva) of the stable and the moving;
[one should worship] the limbs of the form and likewise the supreme [deity] with the mantra of the Bull-bannered One.
There is no untimely death, nor disease, nor fear of calamities among the people;
and the king there is victorious wherever the Bull is properly situated. (25)
The bull is indeed the Dharma of the Lord, whose quality consists of the enjoyment of knowledge and action;
because it supports consciousness (saṃvit), it is called Dharma by the wise. || 26 ||
Having performed the consecration (*adhivāsana*), covered with cloth, and adorned with garlands, one who places [the image] during an auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) enjoys double the fruit. (27)
Joined with Śṛṅgārka as before, it should be placed in front of Vyomāditya; likewise, Tārkṣya and the other mounts [should be placed] with their own respective mantras. (28)
Thus,
on a day favorable to the sacrificer, when all the ritual materials have been prepared,
the performer should worship the preceptor and others; thereafter, the preceptor should worship the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should perform the rites of gazing and acting beginning with the *nandī*, as well as the bath, worship, and fire-oblation as before;
one should then carry out the touching of the portions and purification in their entirety, following the proper sequence. (30)
Then, having worshipped the Vāstunara below the region of the door,
the wise one should place the jewels and so forth as before, and offer oblations to Rudra for the sake of pacification.

The door should be wrapped with fine cloth and surrounded by jars smeared with the Śiva-weapon (the *śivāstra*). Having loosened the central thread from the middle of that [enclosure], one should place it slightly toward the north.
Barley, bilva that destroys demons, phalinī, gadatantrikā, sesame, rice, and likewise rocanā, sahā, and [the plant] called cihnāṅkā destroy disease when used for oblation. || 33 ||
Having tied earth dug up by the tips of a cow's horns, dūrvā grass, and curds, along with an excellent cloth, to the belly of a Udumbara tree for the sake of protection; 34.
On the threshold, on the two door-posts, and in the space above, one should place Śiva as the knowledge of the Self;
there, for each respective principle (tattva), one should perform seven sets of seven oblations. || 35 ||
One should offer oblations in sequence to that which is called awakening—steadfast, immeasurable, designated as eternal, pervasive, indestructible, and named satisfaction. (36)
Having installed Nandi, the Pratīhāra, and others fashioned here by their respective names, and having offered the full oblation (bali) to the quarters, [he should proceed].
One should worship the preceptor who has assumed a physical form and the artisans according to one's own capacity;
the architect, however, should be at the entrance and on the face, and there will be auspiciousness in the directions and the sky.

Thus ends the installation of the door. Now, having first performed the sacrifice and recited the mantra [or: having worshipped at the beginning], one should offer oblations to Rudra one hundred and eight times.
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others, as well as the offering (bali) to Indra and the other deities. || 39 ||
Having combined the previously mentioned elements, gems, medicinal herbs, seeds, and all types of metals,
bound together with cloth, one established in the reality (tattva) should perform this on an auspicious day.
Having filled it with curd, ghee, milk, honey, and milk-rice (pāyasa),
one should place the jar— scented with fine cloth within its interior— like the heart-lotus.
One should place the vessel—which is the embodiment of the lotus of the Power that is the support of the Praṇava—made of gold, silver, or copper, according to one's means. (42)
Smeared with fragrance, his neck adorned with fragrant flower garlands,
and his face decorated with petals of mango, *aśoka*, banyan, and holy fig trees.
Having performed the protection (*rakṣā*) and having extracted the subtle atom (*aṇu*),
one should join it with the *tattva*.
This is the procedure for its acquisition, its manifestation, its location, and its higher and lower nature.
[They] attained their respective positions. || 44 ||

Having realized that the individual soul (aṇu) is non-different from the Self of all (or the Self of the Guru), one should seize it by means of the power of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti) from the "biter" (the object of consumption) and fully awaken the command of Śiva.
Having withdrawn [the breath], performed the retention (kumbhaka), and remained for a moment without thought,
one should tear open [the path] with the state of *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, which is like a shimmering thunderbolt.
Having drawn [the breath] from the *dvādaśānta* by means of exhalation (*recaka*), one should deposit it into the *ghaṭa* [vessel];
there, one should deposit the body which is the speaker of the [inner] sound and the awakener of its true qualities.
Having offered salutations with his own seed-syllables to his own Lord, from *kalā* down to the end of *dhāraṇī*, and likewise to *kalā* and to the bearer of *kalā*:
"Oṃ, salutation to *kalā*; likewise to the bearer of *kalā*. (48)

The application for the remaining path and its purpose should not be applied by the seer of reality in the same manner as the directions. There are ten channels, ten vital breaths, the instruments, and their respective lords. (49)
One should specifically assign their names in this sequence:
they are Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and likewise Suṣumnā. (50)
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśas,
as well as Alambuṣā, Kuhu, and Śaṅkhinī is recorded as the tenth. || 51 ||
These ten channels are indeed proclaimed as the carriers of the vital breaths (prāṇas):
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna; || 52 ||
Nāga, Kūrma, the one called Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya; speech, hands, feet, the genitals, and the anus constitute the group of organs of action. (53)
The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, and mind are born from the intense [rajas];
their lords, in order, are Agni, Indra, Upendra, Turya, Asya, and Vibhrānta. (54)
Likewise, Khadga, Vāyu, Arka, Varuṇa, Indra, Aśvinī,
and Niśākara are the lords of the organs of intellect; they should be especially worshipped as the fulfillers of modifications within Māyā and Kāla, who are the regulators.
[The relationship] between the two mantras is by virtue of being the self, the object to be accomplished, the means of accomplishment, and the impeller. || 56 ||
The wise one should join the deity together with the atoms through its pervasiveness;
then, by means of the *rodhamudrā*, he should restrain everything, including its limbs.
Having offered oblations, one should effect their presence and remedy any deficiency in the ritual procedure;
thereafter follows the construction of the altar-base, with a neck made of *āmalasāraka* wood.
On the square of the altar, one should place the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas); Īśvara is at the top.
Having placed Sadāśiva in the water-pot (kumbha) and Śakti in the cup for the planets (grahacūlaka), [one should proceed].
The abode consisting of all principles is called each respective principle in succession;
the earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the sequential positions of the elements.

p. 82) Through the *dhāraṇīs*, in the gathering, cooking, arraying, and in the abode of well-being [or: in laughter], the fragrance resides in the incense and flowers, and likewise the flavor in the food offering. || 61 ||

The form situated in the function of the chariot (or protection) is touch, consisting of the smooth and the rough; sound therein consists of music and the like, and the nose is always characterized by the scent of parrots.
The *piṇḍikā* (pedestal) is his tongue, and his two eyes are the *mañjarī-vedikā* (flower-vaulted altar). His two ears are the lattice-work of *sudhā* (mortar/nectar), and his nose is the fire.
His hands are situated at the base, and his foot is the anus; there, the ten-faced one (*rasānana*) resides.
The anus is like fierce substances, and the generative organ is the stalk of the pedestal. || 64 ||

The mind (manas) flows over the water of the established [elements], while the intellect (buddhi) is the determination in the formation of the thread [of thought]; ego (ahaṃkāra) is the certainty, and it is the intellect that effects its resolution.

[This reading enclosed within brackets is not present in the *mūla* and *ga* manuscripts: And the qualities (*guṇas*) are to be known as the coloring, while Nature (*prakṛti*) has the form of those qualities [kh, gh: has that form].
The Puruṣa residing in the heart is the cause; therein, passion (*rāga*) is situated in the primordial power (*ādi-śakti*). || 66 ||
For here, Vidyā is traditionally held to reside in discernment, Niyati in restriction, and Kalā in impulsion; therein, Kāla is established as the enumeration of age.
When the self is one with the principle of Māyā, Vidyā pertains to the domain of the palace;
the discernment of the consciousness of the abode of Śiva is Vidyā, and its Lord is Īśvara. (68)
(83) Sadāśiva presides over the *adhiṣṭhāna*, the *adhidaivatyam*, and the *samāpti*;
he possesses the power of *dhāraṇā* (retention) regarding capacity within the external and internal paths. 69.
Because he is all-pervasive, Śiva is thus declared to be the form of the temple;
the pedestal is known as the *jagatī*, and the *liṅga* is considered the temple itself.
"In some places, it has been stated by Śambhu that their foundation should be established;
having installed the three deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—in their respective sequences. (71)
One should offer as oblation the thighs, the shoulders, and finally the head; above that, one should again offer the wood known as Sthira and that called Bhava.
Thus ends the nineteenth procedure in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*, titled "The Installation of the Bāṇaliṅga and Others at the Heart of the Vehicle-Door. || 19 ||

Now, one should properly install twenty [images] of Īśāna, or a *grahacūla*, or a water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon the head according to the rite; thereafter, I shall describe the construction of the banner (*dhvaja*).
One should describe the various forms of Īśāna according to each respective tradition, as follows:
the crest-lock, the water-pot, and the banner; such are the characteristics to be stated here.
One should fashion Īśāna as identical in form to the primary Liṅga, making it composed of that very substance;
or, in the case of a temple made of stone, it may be made of stone according to some authorities. (Note: This reading is not present in manuscript *ka*.)
From the width of the Amalāsāra, by means of a thirty-sixth part of a lunar day (tithi),
each successive third part less one-third constitutes the length and width of Īśāna.
The Īśāna [face], worshipped by the gods, may be three parts less than the liṅga;
this applies to the principal ones such as Meru and others, or otherwise for other [liṅgas], according to the measure of the liṅga itself. || 5 ||
Know that when it arises from wood, it is born of wood; likewise, when it arises from bricks, it is so.
But the Graha-cūla is made of stone, or it may be encircled by a water-pot.
That thickness [of the pedestal] shall be one-tenth of the width of the top of the base;
it may be square, octagonal, or circular, and its height shall be equal to three parts, like the length of the liṅga.
Or its length may be half the width of the neck, and its thickness one-fourth of its circumference;
one should fashion it entirely like a *liṅga*, or else encircle it externally with a jar-shaped base.
(Aligned with the opinion of the Goddess, then, in the case of Bhāskara, the neck is half the width of the vyāsa;
in the abodes [of the deities], it is one-eighth from the portion; in that called Bāṇa, it is two-sevenths from the egg.)
From the side, one-sixth of the height is the width; from the width, the height is twofold.
Having divided this by twelve, the wise man should fashion the pinnacle (kalaśa).
The fillet (paṭṭī) below the three-quarter portion shall have a width of six parts, and its pitcher (kumbha) shall be one part;
the fillet of the pitcher, however, shall be one-quarter [of that].
The *sacūlā* (pedestal) has a width of three parts and a height of half a part;
its corners extend from the middle two parts, standing at a height of eight parts.
From the southern corner, at a distance of two parts toward the south, Skanda should be placed in due order.
When [the planet] is situated in the eighth part from any corner and so forth, one should draw a circle below the south according to the measurement of the cloud.
In the same manner, one should rotate the cord from the northern part of the jar;
then, with one part above, the neck [is formed], having a width of two parts.
The two cheeks shall have a width equal to two parts, and their height shall be half a part;
above that, the *kāla* (the dark mark) shall be half a part, and the lotus shall have a width and height of two parts each.
Beside the jar are vessels for liquor, made of iron, deep, elongated, and movable;
above them, on a tripod, is a lotus with a mouth like that of a jar, adorned with mango sprouts.

The teacher’s fee (gurudakṣiṇā) for the bathing with the ritual materials of the sacrificial hall and so forth, as well as the gem-depositing (ratnanyāsa), the fire-oblation (homa), the mantra-depositing (mantranyāsa), and other rites, are to be performed as previously described. || 17 ||
(86) Having established the Brahma-line starting from Īśa upon the foundation stone (ādhāraśilā),
one should install [the deities] above Viṣṇu, up to the end of the half-measure of Brahmā, according to the distinction of mantras. || 18 ||
Īśāna and Saṃpraveśa are portions of Brahmā, established like the Vedas;
in some cases, they are assigned two parts, three parts, or the whole, according to the sequence beginning with Jyeṣṭhā.
Alternatively, having inserted a subtle liṅga made of jewels or arising from [sacred] minerals according to one's desire,
the pitchers should be prepared with effort, placed in some location starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and so forth.
He was protected by the trident of the two abodes of the three-eyed Caṇḍikā,
by the discus in the abode of Viṣṇu, and likewise by the respective weapons of the others.
Then one should place the Liṅga, Unmanā, Śūla, and Ghaṭābja (or Śvetābja) around it;
these are fashioned from her own triad of powers known as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī.
In the best case it should be thirty-two finger-breadths; in the medium and inferior cases, it is reduced by eight [each].
Made of gold, silver, or iron, one should install it with mantras as before.
In some cases, it is fashioned by the powers known as Jñāna, Icchā, and Kriyā;
the wheel should be circular and consist of six parts, like a *karīra* fruit.
The staff should be equal in length to the height of the living being (the image), and its thickness should be one-twentieth of that;
for deities other than the Jinas, they should be installed according to their respective proportions.
Its length shall be twelve digits, and its thickness one-eighth of that;
it has the luster of a blue lotus petal, and its crest is always formed from its own seed-syllables.
Thus concludes the installation of the Īśāna-vessel, the Graha-cūḍī, and the sacrificial post (yūpa).

In this world, whatever fame exists without a banner is constantly seized in its entirety by Rākṣasas, Grahas, and other such beings, along with one's gifts, fire-offerings, and other meritorious acts. || 27 ||
Just as a tree that has borne good fruit is protected by those who desire its fruit, so too is this one protected by the bannered Lord of the Abode for the sake of the fruit of the Dharma. (28)
Therefore, a banner should be installed there according to the prescribed rite with a focused mind; following the various scriptures, I shall now describe it briefly.
The width of the base of the palace may be half or a quarter of that [measurement] in some cases;
its length should be twice that of the temple, while the flagstaff should be equal to half plus a quarter of it.

Alternatively, it may be two cubits wide, or else the width of the heel; according to some views, it is half of that, or as previously mentioned, it should be obtained by taking a sixteenth part of its own length, and in some cases it is said to be so from the width.
White for the pacification of all goals, and possessing the luster of the Lord of the Quarters for the sake of desire. || 32 ||
Marked with its own vehicle above, joined with small bells and chowries, variegated with the forms of its own deities, and in some places adorned by its own powers; || 33 ||
The staff is three-quarters of the *mañjarī*; in some cases, it is half of that minus one-quarter.
Thus, the handspan (*hasta*) for seizing the planets—in the case of seizing Indra, however—shall be of the size of Jyeṣṭha and so forth in sequence.
The lineage that increases the family line consists of the *dharmārtha* trees, the *śāla* and *sindūra*.
Five [trees] have been mentioned as its limbs; however, the *śelu* and *śigru* are inauspicious for that purpose.
Śirbhkau || 35 ||
But if it is placed on the side of fracture, the death of the performer will certainly occur;
when the propitiatory oblation is performed, there is happiness through the southern face, and not otherwise.
And on the roof-terrace of the palace, some said that it should be based on a flagstaff,
while others said it should be in the northeast or the northwest region, or otherwise.

The support for the primary banner (ādidhvajādhāra) is said to be one-fifth, one-fourth, or three times the height of the spire (śikhara); in some cases, it is also stated to be half the height of the top (mastaka).
As before, there should be the pavilion and so forth; by means of bathing, [the consecration] is performed upon the flagstaffs.
Then follows the placement of gold and other materials, as well as jewels, and the seat according to the previous sequence.
One should install the staff as having become manifest (mūrtibhūta), and then perform the ritual of complete integration (sakalīkaraṇa).

On the banner (dhvaja), one should likewise install the partless (niṣkala) form, and there too the limbs (aṅgas); furthermore, one should install the Self-knowledge (ātmavidyā) on the staff and the Śiva-principle (śivatattva) on the banner.
Furthermore, one should worship the lords of the worlds there for the destruction of obstacles and for the attainment of success. || 41 ||
Having properly meditated upon all of them— as self-possessed, belonging to Śambhu, peaceful, and with their forms raised with their own weapons— the Guru should then cause them to ascend.
Having joined it with the *dhvaja-mantra* and the *astra-mantra*, one should place it somewhere;
then [recite] either the *aghora* mantra of Śiva, or the great *pāśupata* mantra. (43)
In the renowned scripture of Īśvara, which destroys the multitude (or onset) of obstacles,
one should offer perfumes and other substances with the Brahmamuṇḍa mantra or with the Vidyādhipa mantra.
One should offer the food offering and the bali-rite with the *puruṣṭuta* mantra, while using the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) for the visualization;
one should meditate [on the deity] as having the brilliance of a thousand suns and the roar of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
With the tips of his fangs ablaze, his cave-like mouth radiant, possessing three eyes, with a tongue like a flash of lightning, and with glowing eyebrows, whiskers, and hair; (46)

He has four arms and four faces, wears a serpent as his sacred thread, and holds a trident, sword, spear, and mallet; he is adorned with a crest of the shimmering crescent moon and is the crusher of the fierce pride of gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas.
The preceptor should perform the hoisting of the banner and the ritual service.

Then, with all the mantras ending in *phaṭ*, according to their respective divisions beginning with the heart-mantra, the Guru, stationed at the tip of the banner, should recite his chosen mantra. (49)
Having performed three circumambulations, he should join the officiant;
then the patron, together with his wife, sons, and family, becomes ready for the auspicious moment.
Having circumambulated the abode three times and bowed down again and again,
he was like a banner atop a palace being shaken by the winds.
Likewise, the performer shall instantly cast off the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes;
there shall be peace in the kingdom, the king shall be victorious, and the subjects shall likewise be happy. (52)

Through the gift of a hundred thousand gold pieces, women give birth easily, as do righteousness, abundance of food, and health; yet the merit from the raising of the flag (dhvaja) is ten million times greater.
When the restoration of what was decayed is performed, at the conclusion of the flag-rite, the performer obtains the fundamental fruit.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Installation of the Banners of Īśāna and the Others," in the Compendium of Characteristics. 20.

Now the twenty-first [chapter]: Now, in this world, beings such as bhūtas, vetālas, and rākṣasas take refuge in shrines and the like that are dilapidated, defiled, abandoned by the gods, and deserted.
Constantly causing great terror and possessing exceedingly cruel forms, they bring about a multitude of evils in those kingdoms where they reside.
Great portents, the destruction of the earth, the rout of armies, defeat, terrible famine, disease, the ruin of subjects, and poverty. || 3 ||
Anxiety, dispute, despondency, and loss regarding one's children and wealth; suffering caused to cows, Brahmins, and others; the king’s own misery, and his lack of virtuous conduct.
There will be a loss of majesty and strength, as well as being possessed by greed, delusion, and other vices;
there will be suffering from the calamities of enemies, and great anxiety shall arise.
When a wicked omen persists in the kingdom, the wise king does not find prosperity among his subjects;
therefore, its removal must be performed according to the prescribed rite preceded by mantras.
A *liṅga* that has been uprooted by non-instructors who lack mantras and disregard the prescribed rites will certainly afflict the kingdom with bile-like fever and destroy the king.
Therefore, for the sake of the increase of cattle, Brahmins, subjects, and his own kingdom, the king should swiftly cause the *liṅga* and other [emblems] to be raised within his realms.

(92) I shall proclaim the restoration of dilapidated [shrines], as it has been taught in the scriptures: on an auspicious lunar mansion, day, and yoga, under a favorable planetary hour, and when the patron is in a state of excellence.
One should construct the previously described pavilion (maṇḍapa) to the south or the northeast;
it should be well-covered, consecrated, beautiful, and provided with a single water-gate and an archway (toraṇa).
Abounding with plantain trees, sandalwood, and garlands, crowded with canopies and banners,
one should construct, as before, a beautiful altar protected by the auspicious pitcher and the weapon-mantra. || 11 ||
Having first properly worshipped those who bear the form of the Guru with golden garments,
one should worship Hara upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on a pedestal filled with sand. (12)
One should feed five bearers of the Śiva-linga with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
O Brahmins, one should thoroughly satisfy eight [priests] beginning with Arkopendra;
one should give sacrificial fees according to one's wealth, and they shall pronounce blessings for the welfare of both the kingdom and the king.
Or else, the instructor should offer a thousand oblations of the terrible great weapon (mahāstra) with the three-sweetened sacrificial ingredients into a circular pit, using dūrvā grass.
The preceptor should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and the performer should offer a cow to him;
thereafter, gifts should be given to those who bear the forms [of the deity], as well as the bali-offering to the spirits and the deities of the directions.
Then, having performed the fierce and peaceful rites and having petitioned Maheśvara,
and having obtained permission from Mahādeva, one should perform the extraction of the liṅga and other elements.
Having struck it with that Flower-Arrow weapon, one should utter the Weapon-mantra by the command of Śiva:
"Whatever being is stationed here, let it depart elsewhere, having abandoned this place. (18)
Thus, by the command of Śiva, one should abandon that principle through the Great Weapon (mahāstra);
then, having consecrated the liṅga and so forth with water over which the weapon-mantra has been recited. || 19 ||
"In some places it has been stated by Śambhu that the *sthāpaka* should tie a golden bracelet upon the hand of the patron (*yajamāna*) at the time of the ritual raising."
Having bound the *liṅga* with the noose called *Svarṇa* and with the *Pāśupata* [noose], and having bound it upon the humps of the two bulls with the *Varman* [noose] made of fine thread; || 21 ||
Facing north, the Guru, using a plough made of gold or iron and smeared with honey,
should dig all the directions starting from the northeast (Īśāna) in sequence, while reciting the *Khādaka* mantra.

In the supreme *tārasāra* [mantra], by virtue of its nature, one should form the pair of noose and goad from another [syllable] by excluding the syllable *māṣa*; likewise, the two bulls should be made strong.
Having dispatched the two bulls with sharp-edged spears, Nandin, by the sound of his conch, [uttered:
"Worn out, shaken, broken, shattered, or damaged by lightning. (24)
That which is possessed of great defects, burnt, with missing limbs, or emaciated;
or that which is too thick, poorly set, or causes pain upon the ground. (25)
(94) One should treat these with various substances and likewise with measures such as weights and so forth, just as one administers medicine to a sick person. (26)
In their case, there is no fault when drawing, dividing, cutting, or likewise uprooting [the plant], because it is performed while devoid of mantras. || 27 ||
One should discard the linga, the pedestal, the stone, the image, the space, the eagle (Tārkṣya), and so forth, as well as the bull,
whether made of baked clay, stone, or gemstone, into the left [hand] during daily rites.
One should burn wood with the Aghora mantra using clarified butter as the fire of Śiva;
having thoroughly melted all metal, one should then place it back in that very same spot.
One should discard a burnt image made of gemstone like a stone that has lost its luster;
as for an image made of plaster, a painting, a cloth-scroll, or a modeled figure, one should refine it with fire and then cast it away.
A tooth that has fallen out and been replaced, one that is crooked, one from a river, one from a person afraid of others, or one from someone who has not received initiation—
provided it is not defective, one should extract it according to the ritual rules and install it preceded by a sacrifice.
One should insert the *liṅga* in such a way that it does not touch the door;
then one should install the *brahma-śilā* and all other components in the sequence as before.
First, the measurement and its form are determined by the material previously prepared;
another [image], such as a *liṅga* and so forth, should be installed, or else there is great fruit in the superior [installation].
As long as the linga, the pedestal, the temple, and the worship remain upon the earth,
for that many thousands of kalpas shall the maker of them dwell in that city.
This is the fruit for those made of clay; for those made of wood, it is even greater than that.
(Note: This reading enclosed within brackets is not present in the original manuscripts *ga* and *gha*)
And for those made of stone, it is double; for those made of lead, it is even greater than that. || 35 ||
The value of those made of tin is double that, while those made of bell-metal (ghoṣaja) are more than that;
those made of brass (rīti) are double that, and those made of copper (sulva) are more than that.
Those made of silver (tāra) are double that, and those made of gold are more than that.
For those made of jewels, however, the merit is double; if there is an abundance of jewels, the fruit is even greater.
One should establish [the deity] after performing a hundred oblations, and cause it to move by means of a thousand; or,
for the movement of the abode, one should perform twice that number with the Ghora or the Mahāstra mantra.
But for those situated in pleasure or pain, by the movement of the *liṅga* and other centers, a living being certainly dies quickly; and having died, he goes to the Raurava hell.

In a dilapidated temple, one should sequentially remove the Īśāna, the jar (ghaṭa), the crest (cūla), the door, the heart, the feet, and so forth, according to the previously mentioned procedure for restoration (jīrṇoddhāra).
One should then worship the body of the temple-mantra, having placed it upon a sword.
Having fashioned a linga covered with wooden plates, one should then construct the temple.
Having superimposed the [mantra] as before upon the door and so forth, ending with the banner,
one should perform the conjunction of the limbs within the perfected abode, having drawn it forth from the sword.

Having removed the worn-out [liṅga] and installed a new one, he should perform oblations for expiation so that there may be flawlessness and fullness by means of a hundred recitations of the Aghora mantra.

And having prostrated before the Lord, he should ask for forgiveness: "By your command, I have extracted the *liṅga* and other [images] that were installed; please forgive me for this act of mine. (44)
May there always be peace for the king who acts as the protector of his subjects;
and may you be well-pleased with us artisans as well, O Bhava! (Gh: ...with you! 45.
Then the performer, having first prostrated like a staff upon the ground before his guru,
should give that sword, the bracelet, the cow, and two bulls along with their equipment.
Thus ends the twenty-first procedure, titled "The Description of the Method for the Restoration of the Worn," within the Compendium of Characteristics.
Now, the twenty-second [chapter]: Regarding non-duality (advaita), the offering of libations (tarpaṇa) into the mandala should be performed for the deities,
beginning with a single cubit and proceeding in sequence up to eight cubits.
The mandala for all the gods consists of a single lotus provided with doorways, corners, and pathways, endowed with doors and [enclosures],
and equipped with the weapons of the world-protectors.
May that divine [mark], known as Mudrālaya, accompanied by divine gestures (mudrās),
and wherein conch-shells are situated at the four corners— known as Śrīvatsa— be for the delight of Hara.
It is provided with the previously mentioned lotuses, a broad-bodied *karṇikā*,
a wide path (*vīthī*) equal to half a lotus, and possesses a neck (*kaṇṭhaka*) and other features;
the door is equal to the lotus-thread and is considered to be outside the lines of the qualities (*guṇarekhā*).
Now, another [type] consisting of nine fortresses and so forth is called the "nine-navelled" (navanābha).
In the center of the thirty-two-paved field, there is a lotus with sixteen parts;
the body [of the mandala] consists of two paths, and there are eight lotuses in the cardinal directions.
And so it is. || 6 ||
The *mekhalā* (fillet) is one part on the exterior; the neck and cheeks are formed by two parts each;
the door should be equal in measure to the lotus-base (*padma*); and the *prativāraṇā* (lintel) is one part.
In the Vaiṣṇava and Bhairava sacrifices, as well as in the installation of a Yoginī,
the mandala known as the nine-navelled (navanābha) bestows an increase in sons, longevity, and wealth. (8)
Or with white powders of rice, sandalwood, wheat, and barley;
or with red minerals, *iṅguda* fruit, vermilion, or beeswax.
It may be yellow by means of *tāla* or with a single portion of powdered *śāli-haridrā*; or it may be white by means of burnt *marmura* (wild rice), charcoal, or husks.
By means of a single portion of black, two portions of yellow— using turmeric and bilva leaves—
and two portions of white along with a portion of black, there shall be a unified smoky color (dhūmra).
One should fill the maṇḍala with these colors so that it shines beautifully;
the lines must be made very elegant, neither deficient nor excessive, and not crooked.
If [the planet] is deficient, there will be the loss of a son; if it is excessive, a great disease;
if it is retrograde, there will be the loss of wealth; and if it is situated in an unfavorable position, there is an enemy. (13)
For the sake of establishing one who desires liberation in non-duality, the mandala is considered the initiation;
therefore, it bestows all virtues, whether it be made of clay or of sand. (14)
Now, for the sake of the dwellings of ascetics and for the construction of palaces, I shall describe their meritorious sites upon the surface of the earth. (15)

On the lord of mountains and on the family-mountains, likewise in the primary fields and secondary fields, in the clusters, on the banks of rivers, and everywhere in the seats of the perfected ones (siddhakṣetra). || 16 ||
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Gandhamādana, Mālyavat, Śṛṅgin, Nīla, and Ṛkṣa—these are the lords of mountains. (17)
Malaya, Vijaya, Sahya, Pāriyātra,
Arbuda, Śrīśaila, Vindhya, and Mahendra are the principal mountain ranges.
Prayāga, Kāśikākolā, Cāṭṭahāsā,
Jayantī, Caritra, Ekāmraka, and Devīkoṭṭa— these are the eight sacred fields (kṣetra).
Kāśmīra, Maru, Pāṭalī, Tumula, Elā, Pusta, Viraja, Ceruḍa, and Puṇḍra—these are the secondary fields (upakṣetra). || 20 ||
Kubjikā, Ujjayinī, Pṛṣṭhapura, Parastrīraṅga, Kuśadvīpa, Ādrika, Māyāpurī, and Jālandhara—these are known as the *sandoha* [congregations]. || 21 ||
The Narmadā, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Pañcanadī, Sindhu, and Sarasvatī are the eight rivers. || 22 ||
Śrāvastī, Kikaṭa, Lāṭa, Kurukṣetra, Ujjihānaka, Antarvedī, and Pratiṣṭhāna are considered the regions of the Yājñikas. (23)
The Dāruvana forest, the cremation ground, Puṣkara, and likewise Naimiṣa; Karavīra, Mahākāla, the Saugandhika grove, and the forest.
And there is the presence of those established at Vaṭaikaliṅgāditya and other sites, as well as of Bāṇaliṅgas, Svayambhūliṅgas, lotus-pools, and ponds. || 25 ||
The hermitages of Vadari, sacred fords (*tīrtha*), confluences of rivers, as well as the abodes of perfected beings and gods, villages, towns, market towns (*kheṭaka*), and cities. (26)
A port, a delightful region, an ordinary mountain, or a river;
furthermore, a sacred site and these various places of the Siddhas. (27)
In these regions, if an ascetic should undertake the stage of life beginning with that of a deity,
he should first acquire land either by royal decree or by purchase.
Nor by force, nor even by obstructing the flow of a river;
for the positions of Īśa and the others are established first from the eastward direction starting with Kūrma, and thereafter from that [starting point].
O Lord of the Gods, those ascetics who dwell in monasteries as abbots—those of evil intellect who, having taken refuge in a monastery, worship the *liṅga*—should not reside there. (30)
They are declared to be greedy; they do not attain liberation. If one wishes to go to hell together with sons, grandsons, and others, [then let them be so]. || 31 ||
Therefore, for one day, the offspring of the monastery (the monks) should perform worship in the temple of Śiva.
Having understood this, he may establish the world of moving and non-moving beings according to his desire.
Now, for the purpose of examining the ground, I shall state what is acceptable and what is unacceptable.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Ambu, Vāyu, Indu, Īśa, Plava, and Mahī. (33)
In sequence, it brings prosperity, burning, death, disease, and poverty;
an enemy, honor, and happiness—thus the middle [line] floats everywhere.
(101) For the deity [presiding over] the East, there is abundant enjoyment, but no worship and destruction;
for the Vajra [deity], fear.
For the Yellow one, there is ruin, wealth, and worship, due to the flooding of the earth starting from the East. (35)
It has been stated that the earth, when submerged in the middle, destroys the lineage; thus the ground may be auspicious or inauspicious.
In sequence, there is fear from fire and enemies, strife, and the destruction of children.

The movement of women, the depletion of garlands, prosperity, and peace result from wells starting in the east and other directions; water entering from the north is auspicious, as are those flowing from the east or even the west.
It should not be joined with the south or the north, nor with water to the east;
nor should there be a forest or a mountain situated to the south, or a forest to the west is auspicious. A temple and a step-well should be to the north, and a lake to the northeast.
The Vaṭa tree is in the east; the Yajñāṅga and Bodhi trees are in the direction of Yama (the south) and the direction of Varuṇa (the west), respectively.
The Plakṣa tree to the north is also praised; these trees—Jayantī, Dāḍimī, Śyāmā, Punnāga, and Ariṣṭa—are auspicious both collectively and individually.
In whichever part of the site there may be auspicious signs, it is favorable for a house; other signs are also auspicious.
O Brahmins, a site abounding in *darbha* grass is suitable for a Brāhmaṇa, while one thick with *śara* reeds is for a Kṣatriya. (41)
The Vaiśya [land] is characterized by glossy dūrvā grass; the Śūdra [land] by uśīra and kāśa grass;
while that which possesses fruits and flowers, as well as glossy shrubs, medicinal herbs, and trees, is [the land of the Kṣatriyas].

Furthermore, where cattle, humans, or horses always find delight, and which is uniform in color, dense, level, and elevated toward the northwestern direction (the direction of Yama and the ocean), [that is a place for a dwelling]. (43)
It should be extensive, firm, praised, and naturally fragrant with auspicious scents;
[such as] sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, moon-lotus, blue lotus, and campaka. || 44 ||
The *pāṭala*, *nāga*, and *jāti* flowers, as well as *mallikā*, wine, and spirituous liquors; rice, barley, meat, curd, clarified butter, and milk—these are fragrant substances. (46)
Possessing distinct and blended fragrances, she bestows prosperity upon the four castes;
she is cool during the summer season and accompanied by warmth in the winter.
In the rainy season, that [wind], which possesses the touch of both [heat and cold], brings happiness to the twice-born and others;
it carries the auspicious sounds of mṛdaṅgas, flutes, lutes, kettledrums, and the like.
The earth, which always brings about the prosperity of the four castes,
is white when she is childless and odorless; but when red, she bears the blessing of sovereignty.
The earth that is yellow is for the Vaiśya, while that which is salty is for the Śūdra; the black earth is the bearer of impurity.
The earth that has the taste of molasses, ginger, myrobalan, and neem belongs to the Brāhmaṇa and the other castes respectively.
Peace, victory, wealth, and long life—these should be granted respectively to the twice-born and others.
Likewise, the asterisms Āṣāḍhā, Kṛttikā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣā are auspicious. (51)
Varuṇa, Agni, Indra, and Vāta are recorded as the deities in sequence;
likewise, a woman of their own caste, or even a Brāhmaṇī, may be accepted according to availability. (51)
One should avoid ground that smells of fat, oil, or wicks;
that which is red, or contains charcoal and stones, or is infested with worms and insects. (52)
Sloping, possessed of pits, rough, saline, full of holes, and muddy;
containing bricks, hair, bones, ashes, anthills, and gravel. (53)

A place where the water and other elements flow counter-clockwise is not praised as it is confused; likewise, a place with many calamities, many castes, and [afflicted by] thunderbolts, fire, enemies, thieves, and diseases [is not praised]. (54)
In that [house] where a woman is unchaste, there is no happiness, no righteousness, no offspring, and no wealth; there shall be only disease and fear of the king. (55)
If it is filled with the sounds of jackals, donkeys, and horses, or has a noise resembling broken pottery,
or the cries of crows, herons, and camels, such a sound portends the arrival of all asuras.
Always hot, always cold, rough, and filled with steam; quickly drying up the water, undesirable, destroying wealth and weapons, and accompanied by craftsmen—[such a well is not auspicious]. (57)

When the pit and the area of one cubit are filled with earth, the ground should be known as inferior, middling, or superior according to whether it is deficient, level, or excessive [in height]. || 58 ||
After filling the pit with water and then walking one hundred paces away,
the ground is classified as inferior, middling, or superior according to whether the water has receded by two, one, or no fingers' breadth.

(p. 104) From the location of the pit, one should carefully pour out flowers of white, red, yellow, and black luster; that ground belonging to the twice-born and others withers. Into small bowls filled with raw-pot-fragrance, clarified butter, and so forth—
And for the twice-born and others, white-colored [clouds] and others appear at night with blazing whirlpools.

Established in their desired locations by means of the mantras of the eastern and other faces, they are to be extinguished; for while blazing, they bestow happiness or suffering according to their own nature.
In the absence of the sequence of characteristics as previously described, one should adopt whatever is available;
having accomplished the arrangement of the syllables by means of their respective innate vowels [or *tīśaśambarai* according to Mūlagh].
Having thus carefully examined the ground and having plowed it, one should sow barley;
according to its growth after seven, five, or three nights, it is of three kinds, beginning with "inferior" (hīna).
The earth, extending eight parts in length, is beneficial for a Brahmin; for a king, it is beneficial when extended by eight parts;
for a Vaiśya, it is beneficial when extending six parts; and for a Śūdra, it is auspicious when merely extended in length.
That which is broad and twice as long, that which has its ears severed and is two-triangular,
that which is curved, that which has a half-moon and two triangles at its center, that which is circular, and that which is six-triangular. || 66 ||
O Brahmin, the earth, by giving a *pala* [of gold] in sequence, bestows the exhaustion of vehicles, fear, the loss of wife, sons, and wealth, as well as death, disease, and sin. (67)
From the mouth of a cow, there is a radiance like a trident; from a snake, the form of the sun; from a *vajrī*, the back of a camel;
and from a *śakaṭa* or a twice-born (*dvija*), the appearance of one who is confused about the directions. (68)
The destruction of subjects, the loss of beloved ones, illness, poverty,
headache, grief, total ruin, and the decay of all the worlds— in this sequence. (69)
Having five corners, resembling the leaves of the Bodhi tree, and like the vulture, the ox, and the camel; with a waist like a barley grain or an ant, and a belly like a drum or a kettledrum. (70)
Those whose backs resemble a fish, the earth, or a woman; and those who are like the belly of an elephant or a camel—these indeed cause various defects and are to be avoided by everyone. (71)
But another maiden, blessed and endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics,
should be accepted according to the prior injunction, provided she is not defiled.
This earth, which is always inhabited by outcasts, the lowest of men, and the base, as well as by flesh-eating beasts and birds, is lukewarm and defiled by blood and vajras.
Even earth mixed with ashes, bricks, bones, stones, gravel,
and dust is acceptable if it is rich in qualities and well-purified for the construction of a house or a temple.
Having ploughed the earth a hundred times with golden-tipped ploughs,
one should establish a herd of cows there for five months for the sake of purification.
Then, one should cause sacrificial rice and sesame seeds and so forth to be sown;
having consecrated them with ripened grain, one should construct a dwelling or a residence.
Having thus leveled the purified ground, one should smear it;
thereafter, one should prepare the orientation for the house and so forth—this is what is taught. (77)
By the piercing of Tiṣya, one should lead [the thread] toward the east;
or by the conjunction of Mīna between Citrā and Svātī, one should lead it toward the north by means of the Dhruva conjunction.
On the equinox, when the sky is clear and a mandala has been drawn upon that ground,
one should place a stake made of khadira wood, twelve finger-breadths in height, in the center of it.
Having a circumference of six finger-breadths and marked all around with lines of Rudra,
one should mark the western direction by the entry of its shadow.
One should lay out the thread for its exit toward the east,
and likewise establish the line suitable for the fish [the diagonal] toward the south and the northern direction.
From the center of the directions, by means of the half-cord of the field itself, four corners are formed;
and by casting four cords there, the quadrangular [mandala] is accomplished.
In the eastern direction there are ten channels; having become [these], I shall state their names:
Śāntā, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Viśālā, and Prāṇavāhinī. (83)
Matī, Vasumatī, Nandā, Subhadrā, and Manoramā—
these ten others in the northern direction constitute the eighty-one *Aṅghrikārikās*. (84)
Hariṇī, Suprabhā, Lakṣmī, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Śriyā, Jayā, Jvālā, and Viśokā—these are remembered as being [established] by the casting of the thread. 85.
One should worship the eight deities beginning with Īśa in the directions, as well as Īśa, Caya, Jaya, Śakra, Arka, Satya, Bhṛśa, and Vyoman in the east. (86)
Havyavāha (or Mātariśvan), Pūṣan, Vitatha, and Saumya;
then Kṛtānta, Gāndharva, Bhṛṅga, and Mṛga on the south. (87)
One should always worship Pitṛ, Dvārapāla, Sugrīva, Puṣpadantaka, Varuṇa, Daitya, Śoṣa, and Yakṣman in the west.

One should worship Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma (or *Somāhi*, which is the correct reading), and Diti—[the latter two] in the northern direction—and Brahmā situated in the ninth final square; the others have two feet. || 89 ||
The one called Āpa is situated in the two squares between Brahmā and Īśa;
likewise, the one called Cāpavatsa is in the six squares within the center.
In the midst of the mirage-fire stands the Sun, situated upon two feet;
below him is Sāvitrī on two legs, and below her is Vivasvat on six feet.
Between Pitṛ and Brahmā, one should worship Indra and Mitra located twice, and Jaya below them; between Varuṇa and Brahmā, one should worship the one named Mitra in six squares.
In the Brahmāntara, Roga is always situated twice, and Rudradāsaka is likewise;
below that, Yakṣman has two feet, and Dharādhara is located in the six [directions], in the north.
One should worship Carakī, Skanda, Vaidārya, Kandarpa, and Pūtanā, as well as Jambha, Pāpa, Pilipiñcha, and others, in the directions starting from the exterior.
The pavilion is a hall of eighty-one squares and possesses a hundred pillars;
as before, the deities ending with Brahmā are to be worshipped within the sixteen-fold portion.
Marīci, Vivasvat, Mitra,
and Pṛthvīdhara are situated in the ten squares in the cardinal directions, while the others occupy the corners beginning with the northeast (Īśa).
The Daityas, Mātṛs, Haris, Kha, Agni, those called Mṛgas, Pitṛs, as well as Pāpas and Anilas—these deities are situated at intervals of one and a half quarters each. (97)

I shall explain, in due order, each of the bali-mantras, the avoidance of piercing the vital points (marmavedha), and all else regarding the ritual for the deity’s dwelling (devavāstu), as well as the extraction of structural defects (śalyoddhṛti).

The construction of cities, watchtowers, palaces, and so forth, as well as the consecration of gateways and villages, the worship of pillars and other rites, and the laying out of residential sites (vāstu) have been described; in some instances, these are distinct, while in others they are like the ritual for a well. 99.
I shall describe the *yatyāṅghrika* [style] in brief and according to its sequence:
it is twenty-one cubits in length and twenty-seven cubits in width. || 100 ||
The hermitage of Śiva belongs to the one named Śikha; it is diminished by four in both cases at all times.
The circumference is doubled from that of Rudra, excluding the three broad lights.

The abode of Sāvitra should be made such that its length is twice the measure of a graha and its width is fifteen units; for those [other deities], the breadth should be one-tenth of the distance between the directions.
The wall [gh: *kuḍyaṃ*] has broad shanks and is high; its height is three times [kh: twice] that [of the width].
The pathway (*vīthī*) is equal in measure to the wall-sutra, and it is of many kinds according to the variations of the pathways.
The Kuvendra [K, Kh, Ṅ: Tadendra] consists of five paths, excluding the hero-path at the front;
it is inferior to the Śrījaya [Kh, Ṅ: Śrīkuśa] behind, and is the Bhadrogra [K, Kh, Ṅ: Rudrogra].
Except for the two sides. || 104 ||

The street (vīthī) should be equal in width to the inner sanctum (garbha), or in some cases half of that, or even a quarter; it is enriched with a secondary street (upavīthī) measuring half the width of the main street, and it may be provided with one, two, or three storeys.
This house is indeed renowned as belonging to ascetics (yatis) according to the distinction of their alms-rounds (gocara).
I shall now describe the common house that grants all desires to everyone: it consists of one, two, three, four, or eight wings (śāla), respectively.
If there is one facing south and two facing north, they should be positioned behind and facing forward.
The four-hall (catuḥśāla) layout is formed by facing those two [directions] joined with Indra and the Moon;
Siddhārtha is in the south-west, and Yamasūryaka is in the north-east.
When situated in the east and north, it is called Daṇḍa; in the east and south, it is named Vāta;
in the west and north, it is called Gṛhacūlī; and between the south and north, it is termed Kāca. (109)
In Siddhārtha, there is the acquisition of wealth; in Yamasūryaka, death occurs;
in the one called Daṇḍa, punishment from the king; and in the one called Vāta, there is constant strife. (110)
In the *gṛhacalya* configuration, wealth is lost; in the *kāca*, there is enmity with kinsmen. However, the *triśāla* known as *saumya-hiraṇya* brings about the increase of wealth. (111)

If it lacks the eastern wing, it bestows an increase in good fields; if the southern wing is missing, there will be a "cūlī" (a painful affliction), and such a three-winged house is supreme at taking away wealth. (112)

I shall describe the eight houses beginning with the banner (dhvaja) in the order starting from Indra: the house of the banner causes the destruction of one's faction; the house of the tortoise is devoid of water; the house of the serpent destroys one's sons; and the house of the bull creates many enemies. (113)
In the east is a mixed dwelling, in the south-east a fire-pit and a kitchen;
