in the south is a place for alchemical work and a bed, and in the southwest are excrement and weapons.
If Venus is in the second house, there will be wealth; if Mercury is there, grain and fragrance;
if Mars is there, cattle; if Jupiter is there, initiation and a temple. (115)
Having made the house measured by the master’s hand-cubit, with its width, length, and height combined,
doubled and joined with the cubit, it is likewise divided by eighth parts.

Whatever remains after that cutting should be used for the crow-mark at the end of the banner and so forth; the measurement of the *tapa* (the penance-line) shall be derived from the wings, fire, Vedas, and flavors, up to the sky (zero). || 117 ||
A house situated both in the middle and at the end causes total destruction;
therefore, it is considered that a dwelling located in the ninth part brings about auspiciousness.

In the middle of that, a pavilion (maṇḍapa) is recommended, either square or twice as long; likewise, a row of houses may be situated toward the east, north, west, or south, with a marketplace (haṭṭa) at the entrance.
In each of the directions, there are eight palaces for each [deity], beginning with Īśa and ending with Diti; their respective fruits follow in due order.
Fear, fickleness of women, victory, growth,
majesty, righteousness, strife, and poverty— these are located at the eastern gates in their respective order.
The eightfold [mantra] is fixed. || 121 ||
Burning, happiness, loss of friends, loss of wealth, death, acquisition of wealth, craftsmanship, and a son—these are the eight results of the southern door. (122)
Longevity, success before renunciation, grain, wealth, peace, and the depletion of one's purpose;
as well as edema, disease, and sin— these are the results from the water gate.

Disease, intoxication, suffering, and the like; loss of wealth, shortness of life, and lack of intelligence; and pride—these are said to occur in succession from the gateway in the northern direction. (124)
It may be constructed of wood, brick, stone, or clay, adorned with lattices and balconies, and provided with beautiful pillar-bands and doors fitted with bolts. (125)
Having thus prepared the site for the ascetic, the Guru should worship the deities of the dwelling;
in the pavilion before him, he should satisfy them all with oblations (*homa*).
Then, having sprinkled the interior of the house along with its doors with water for the guest-offering (argha),
one should gratify the preceptor with devotion at the time of establishing the residence.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the quarters outside, he should then provide food for ascetics;
having given all household utensils, as well as beds, seats, and so forth. || 128 ||
One should establish a hermitage for those aged three, two, or one year, or half of that, or even half of that again;
then one should construct a temple for one's chosen deity, the characteristics of which are now described. (129)
Thus ends the twenty-second rule in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya* concerning the construction of pavilions and the establishment of dwellings.
Now begins the twenty-third:
if the shadow of the Asura (the western quarter) should fall upon the site from east to west, [then...]
Fear, burning, pain, death, and poverty would constantly bring about these effects in succession.
Having set aside a cord twice the height of the two [pillars], one should fashion the northern [side];
some say that the temple (surālaya) should have a single jagatī or even a broad base. || 2 ||
The threefold hand-measure previously mentioned applies to the primary [length] and so forth measured in barley-corns;
among those, however, one may be determined according to the desire of the practitioner.
Another [type of] principal [image] is considered to be made with twenty-four thumb-breadths;
or it should be made as five cubits, which is recorded as being six [or] four finger-breadths [in width].
One should measure all these sites with equal cubits;
if measured with uneven ones, they will not be central, and there would be a great defect in the center.
A wise person should cause it to be given there— either one and a half, or one and a quarter, or three-quarters of an *aṅgula*— for the sake of purifying the defects of the dimensions.
It should be made of solid wood, free from flaws, excellent, straight, and perfectly round;
it should be three finger-breadths in circumference and twenty-four finger-breadths in length.
(114) Endowed with three primary lines and accompanied by two lines at the tip;
the method for establishing the site (vāstusādhana) is thus explained in brief through the proportions of the hand and wood.

The measure of four cubits is said to be a *dhanus* (bow-length); a staff (*daṇḍa*) is one and a half *dhanus*. A *krośa* consists of a thousand *dhanus*, and a *gavyūti* is recorded as being double that.
A *yojana* should be known by calculation as being twice a *gavyūti*. Furthermore, one hundred is known as ten, and a thousand is an *ayuta*. (10)
One should know the niyuta and the prayuta, as well as the arbuda and the nyarbuda;
then the vṛnda, the kharva, the nikharva, the śaṅkha, and that which is designated as the padma.
The ocean, the middle, the end, the beyond, and likewise the supreme;
and the half of the supreme—all these are declared to increase tenfold in each successive stage.
Thus have these numerical places been described by the wise for the city on all sides, in every direction, both externally and internally. (13)
At every gate, in the four directions, one should likewise fashion Śrī and Vaiśravaṇa facing toward the village or the city.
The construction of palaces should be carried out outside the walls and the moats,
either at a distance of one hundred bows or two hundred bows.
In all cases, facing forward is praised; facing away is not praised.
The central lineage comes from the east and west, while [the others] are from the south and north.
On both sides, palaces should be constructed without beams;
those on the west are recommended facing east,
and those in the eastern direction facing west.
Others flow toward the north or the south;
those facing east or west are auspicious, but never those facing north, nor even those facing south. (18)
But having left the assembly hall of the Daityas,
and having seen the Mothers and Vināyakas, he indeed drew this design from the mind of the Goddess.
In whichever divine location the residence of a deity was previously mentioned, that is first proclaimed for the sake of stability, by one desiring auspicious fame for the builder. (20)
Vibhu and Indra [are worshipped] in the eastern quarter; Bhānu, Aindra, Agni, and Bhāskara in the south-eastern portion; and Hanumān, Bhūta, Vetāla, Mātṛkā, and Kālī in the southern quarter.
The ancestors and Bhadrakālī reside in the Daityas and Rākṣasas;
the oceans, Varuṇa, the rivers, Viśvāmitra, and the Apsarases reside in the water.
In the northwest (Māruta), Vāyu, Kātyāyanī, the Nāgas, Satī, and Bhāsya are to be established;
in the north (Saumya), Skanda and Viśākha, as well as the Yakṣas and the Planets (Grahas), are to be installed.
In the northeast are the Bhairavas and Rudras; in the center is the four-faced Brahmā.
The auspicious deities are stationed in their respective places, facing toward the east and other directions. 24.
If one has turned away from one's position without leaving it, or by taking refuge in a river deity,
one should draw a gentle deity on that wall facing forward.

p. 116) Just as in the city, so too in the village, the town, and the capital, the deities should always be installed upon the foundation of the site and within the various parts of the temple. [mū, ṅ:
one's own deities] || 26 ||
The śamī, śokā, āmra, and mālūra trees situated to the north are auspicious;
whereas trees known as piśācas and others that are pungent, thorny, and bitter are inauspicious.
Furthermore, those trees that are sapless, as well as others that are defective according to the scriptures, if situated near a temple, bring about all manner of evils for men. (28)
If [the trees] are beset by demons and spirits, or inhabited by wicked birds,
and are incapable of being cut down, one should plant milky-sap trees among them.
Nāgakesara, punnāga, jambīra, ariṣṭa, and pomegranate; orange, coconut, jackfruit, and campaka. (30)
Jayaṃtī, ketakī, kubjaka (or kuṇḍa), bījaka, mātuluṅgaka, sarala, nandikāvarta, tāla, agastya, and timuktaka. || 31 ||
The *kramuka*, the *karavīra*, and species such as the *pārāvata*—when cruel trees are separated by these, they become givers of happiness. (32)
The rule regarding the directions and locations for the deities has been declared with specific detail; however, there is no such restriction concerning the construction of a temple for Śiva.
Beginningless, all-pervading, and worthy of worship with devotion in all directions,
the Lord bestows liberation effortlessly upon the seeker of liberation wherever he may be.
(117) According to the different directions, the desired fruits for those with longing are said to be:
[attainment of] the powers of Pātāla and the Khecarīs, the burning of enemies, and pacifications. || 35 ||
The destruction of enemies, long life, and the treasury that bestows nourishment—these are the results in sequence.
Gods situated in the northeast, east, and southeast of the village and so forth, facing westward, are auspicious. (36)
Situated in the directions from south to north, facing east, they are beneficial;
however, if they are excessive, equal, or deficient, they cause obstruction to the eastern alignment and so forth. (37)
One should not construct a palace or similar structure; if one should do so, one would meet with death.
One should build it at twice the height of both [the previous structures], leaving space on the ground in front.
I am not [the deity] at the back of both, nor at the tip of their feet, nor on their two sides;
this rule applies when the navel is pierced, but there is no fault when the navel is unpierced.
Because it would cause harm to the principal deity by becoming a subordinate limb within the temple starting from the corner,
one should understand this according to the Bāṇa doctrine and plant [the trees] beginning with the Hari and Sūrya directions.
The self-manifested (svayambhū) [liṅga] ends with the bāṇaliṅga; it cannot be obstructed by others.
In the case of a self-manifested [liṅga], there is one thousand [obstacles] for the great ones and five hundred for others.
The sacred field for a Liṅga installed by a human being shall be one hundred cubits;
for a stationary image, the field extends as far as the Jagatī on the ground of the ascetic.
Indeed, the floral offering (nirmālya) produced there brings liberation when the living being has died.
On a day favorable to the sacrificer and marked by auspicious omens,
the wise one, being composed, enters that ground in the region between the north and the northeast.
(118) When it has been well-concealed under a cloth, one should examine it with great care;
it should be provided with grains, water, and fruits, and well-anointed with sandalwood paste. (44)

One should place there a divine jar with its neck wrapped in cloth, firmly secured, filled with water containing gems and medicinal herbs, amidst the sounding of musical instruments and auspicious chants. (45)

One should worship the axe, the mallet, the measuring cord, and the pegs to the north of that [deity], according to the ritual procedure for the *arghya* offering and so forth, in accordance with the system of Viśvakarman.
Having established [the deity] and bathed it, one should worship it in due order.
The ritual stakes (kīlakas) should be made from the wood of the Punnāga or other excellent trees, all of a single species.
The stakes should be very firm, made from sacrificial wood, round or square,
eight finger-breadths in circumference, and as long as a cubit.
There, one should establish a square using the casting of lines as before;
then, one should fix a gnomon (śaṅku) therein according to the sequence of the movement of the sun.
Their roots were smeared with honey, clarified butter, curd, and milk, along with sandalwood;
they were all wrapped in fine cloths and perfumed with excellent incense. || 50 ||
Adorned with three threads dyed with red lac and worshipped with white flowers,
they should have their roots pointing downward and their tips directed upward, being straight in form and very beautiful.
One should strike the corner-spikes located in the southeast and other directions with iron mallets;
having caused the spikes to be firmly grasped, one should indeed proceed toward the direction of fire (the southeast).
Then the wise Ācārya, wearing white garments, stands facing the east.
Having raised it with the right hand, [one should hold it] with the fist of the left hand. || 53 ||
Having taken the ritual stake (kīlaka), one should hold it straight and upright upon the ground;
while striking [the earth], one should recite the mantra and observe the preliminary signs.
Oṃ! May the Nāgas and the World-Protectors who grant desires enter the surface of the earth;
may they always remain in this house, bestowing long life and strength. 55.
Oṃ skrī/ krī/ hrī/ hū/ svāhā. [This mantra does not appear in the root manuscript; oṃ maṃ vaṃ hrī/ hū/ svāhā kha ṅa | oṃ krī/ hrī/ phaṭ svāhā ka pā0 |].
Thus ends the mantra for the installation of the *kīlaka* according to the system of Bāṇa.
The preceptor, whose very body is the mantra, should himself bestow the eightfold blow;
thereafter, the principal assistant should strike so that [the disciple] may enter.
If that [object] falls to the ground, then its accomplishment is considered destroyed;
if everything enters rapidly, then there is misfortune for the performer. (57)
If it is broken, one would kill one's son; if it is shattered, there is destruction for the performer and his wife.
One would sink gradually downward; thus, one should predict the failure of the undertaking.
When the *śaṅku* (gnomon) falls toward the east and other directions, there will be, respectively: fear, wealth, burning fever, poverty, fear, loss of wealth, disease, happiness, and honor. (59)
If the *kīlaka* (the ritual peg) is bent at the top by the stroke [of the hand], there will be an increase in longevity, sons, and wealth; if it falls from the hand, there will be great danger. (60)
One should fix an auspicious cord— made of kuśa grass, or from the valvaja plant, or muñja grass, or hemp— measuring half a finger's breadth upon the śaṅku peg, so that it does not slip off.
If it is released, the son dies; if it is cut, the performer perishes. Therefore, having tied it with a firm knot, one should wrap it around with the right hand.
Once the field has been made square, one should cause an offering to be given at the stakes;
facing the southeast, one should utter this mantra.
Oṃ! To all the fires, and to those others who have taken refuge in them, I offer this oblation—excellent and meritorious cooked rice. May they all, empowered by mantras, accept it. (64)

[This passage enclosed in brackets is not present in the manuscripts mū, a, k, and kh. And to the lord of the southwest, and to those *rākṣasas* who are in the southwest, I offer this oblation; may they all accept it, empowered by my mantra. (65)
Oṃ, homage to the kings of the wind and to others who depend upon them;
to them I offer this sacrificial oblation of excellent, meritorious rice—may they accept this meritorious rice. (66)
Oṃ! To all the Rudras and to those others who depend upon them, I offer this oblation; may they accept it with joyful minds. (67)
Let all of them, being joyful, receive [the offerings] joined with the utterance of "svāhā";
having kindled the mantras beginning with Dhruva and having performed the breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should present them.
Thus, when the gods beginning with Agni are worshipped in this sequence, they become satisfied in mind and grant the accomplishment of one's rites. (69)
Thus are the mantras for the installation of the *kīlakas* according to the divine tradition.

As for the thread, O inauspicious one, it may be made of sinew, or of skin, or of silk, or from the fibers of the *kaṭuka*, *kaṇṭaki*, *śākhoṭaka*, and *kali* trees. [The reading "or from the fibers of the *koṭṭha*" is correct.]
The spikes. || 70 ||
Then, immediately thereafter, one should worship the Vāstucakra;
a [mandala] that is not larger than this bestows happiness upon the builder, for these defects always arise when it is larger.
Enmity, female spirits, destruction, death, disease, loss of wealth, exile, and fear of thieves occur when the thread begins in the east and other directions respectively. (72)
Knowing this, one should have the sūtras written with gold or jewels, or even with silver, for the sake of increasing the wealth of those twice-born who are destitute. (73)
If the site is marked out with weapons, iron, unstable materials, charcoal, horns, wood, bricks, stone, or even grass, these defects arise. (74)
Death, imprisonment, punishment, burning, ruin, loss of wealth, fear of thieves, then concealment, loss of what is desired, and disease follow in sequence. (75)
Exorcism is achieved by drawing with the foot; epilepsy by drawing with the fingernail;
and disease occurs through the use of a deer-skin; therefore, one should always draw with gold.
Having worshipped with offerings in that place, one should mark out the site and then string the lines for the temple;
at that time, one should specifically observe for any hidden defects (śalya), as this is now being explained. (77)
Thus ends the twenty-third rule, concerning the determination of the characteristics of the sacrificial ground and location within the compendium of defining characteristics. 23.
Now, in the twenty-fourth [chapter], I shall explain the extraction of the thorn (śalyoddhāra) for both the temple and the residence;
when the site has been smeared and well-prepared, and the measuring cord (sūtra) is being stretched according to its dimensions.
If, in the midst of that, at its end, or near it, there should be the sight of sentient beings,
or their praise, or their sound, or even the crossing of the thread (or, according to some versions,
the characteristic mark). || 2 ||
Then indeed, one should recognize the "dart" (śalya) to be where the householder resides;
by means of that dart of the vital marrow and bone, great fear shall arise for the perpetrator. || 3 ||
The impurity residing within the bones breaks through the wall and constantly produces foulness;
therefore, one should extract that thorn, which is produced from that [source] and is of its same dimension.
The bones of a cat, a mongoose, or a donkey, or [the bone] produced from a donkey [placed] at the navel by means of a donkey [mantra],
shall cause the expulsion [of an enemy] and bring fear to the lord.
A dog’s bone is always a thorn [to a dog], and from it constant agitation arises;
for goats and sheep there is the bone of a cow, or indeed the bone of those two themselves. (6)
From the bone of a cow comes extreme poverty; from the bone of a goat, oppression by cattle;
from the bone of a sheep, the destruction of intelligence; and from the bones of a frog or a cow, the same result.
From the birth of a horse, there is the loss of cattle; from a frog, the destruction of dharma and wealth; and from a son [born under such signs], joy arises.
One should know that from a horse comes the buffalo, and likewise from an elephant comes the camel.
(124) From the bone of a horse born from that [mare], one acquires through three [bones] a state of bad character;

from the bone of a jackal, through a buffalo, and from the bones of a deer and a bear [or a cow and a goat], one acquires birth as such [an animal]; through three [bones] one acquires dependence on others; and from the bone of a boar, through Śivā, one acquires disease.
If there is a tiger bone in the portion belonging to a boar, there will be fear from an enemy when one is bitten by it. || 10 ||

An arrow from an elephant [brought by] a tiger causes misfortune and agitation; furthermore, embers [brought] by a camel, as well as white-bodied [objects] and dusty ones, [bring similar results]. (11)
Having seen two men, one should observe frost, embers, ashes, and dust;
through ashes and embers there will be a burning fever, while through dust there will quickly be exile.

If there is husk, there will be the destruction of grain and constant misfortune in the house of the sacrificer; but if the thread is struck while being stretched across the sky, it results from the falling of excrement from the heavens.
The treasure-trove (nidhāna) should be situated beneath the house according to the measurement of the site-plan (vāstu-aṅga);
they know that the treasure is marked by a bull and consists of silver from cow's urine.
Gold found in its dung bestows wealth and sons and causes their increase;
grain found by a child while laughing brings happiness to the house. (15)
With its urine, however, a well shall be formed; by that [urine], death is produced.
With dog's urine, tin is obtained, and with its excrement, lead is always produced.

Copper [is affected] by the impurity of goats and sheep, which causes the excessive destruction of brass; tin [is affected] by the impurity of the wild cat, [causing the loss of] wealth held in the hand.
This is the loss. ||17||
By the mention of "mother-of-pearl" (śukti), mother-of-pearl bestows happiness and peace;
and from the roar of the elephant of the peaceful quarter (Śānta-diggaja), a treasure-trove is situated beneath the performer [of the rite]. (18)
When the Sun is situated in a *kakup* (triangular) configuration, the three [planets] beginning with Mars are then considered malefic;
however, all others become pacified and yield their full results through the rising of a decan (*drekkāṇa*), an exaltation, or a planet's heliacal rising.
From the sweet fragrance of birds situated in a peaceful direction comes a treasure;
and from the mention of carnivorous beasts and birds, there shall be their bones.
If this [mark] is not extracted, death will remain unshaken for these people;
the head will become like a rat's burrow, causing the destruction of sons and wealth. (21)
A thorn originating from a mongoose or an iguana brings about the ruin of one's kinsmen;

that which comes from a serpent is known as "serpentine" (sarpata), and it bestows misfortune and the destruction of wealth. A thorn born from a tortoise should be known as "tortoise-born" (kūrmaja), and it causes the success of sacrifices.
One should make [an object] from conch for the sake of desire; they know that one made from horn serves the same purpose.
With a cow-horn one gains wealth and grain, but with a buffalo-horn there is death;
with a deer-horn there is eye-disease and death, while with an iron [horn] it always brings about destruction by metal.
From the urine of a cat (vṛṣadaṃśa), there is bondage and loss of wealth;
from the sound or sight of hair, bricks, or stones, that which arises from them is considered [the result]. (25)
There would be fear from bricks and stones, and no relief from their dust;
from hair comes a life of suffering, and from grass and leaves, that same state of fear.

From [stealing] a tiger’s skin comes poverty; from [stealing] the leaves of young trees, dependence on others; from [stealing] a man’s arrowhead, one becomes fickle like a woman; and there is no doubt that [stealing] a Brahmin’s property results in the sin of killing a Brahmin. (27)
There are fifty-six types of thorns for sentient beings, both by their gestures and otherwise;
among them, twelve are desirable, while the remainder cause what is undesirable. (28)
At the commencement [of the work], one should observe omens from birds, questions, sounds, or even scratching;
this applies to the artisan, the patron, and others who are employed by them. (29)

One should recognize that whatever name and whatever sound one hears in the body, that is undoubtedly a thorn (śalya) residing therein; it consists of the very essence of that [name and sound]. || 30 ||
When [the ground] is unchanging, or when it is devoid of sounds and so forth, then the ground should be declared "thornless" by the teachers. (31)

If a structural member (*vāstuaṅga*) remains with a flaw (*śalya*), it will bring misfortune to the builder; therefore, one should extract that flaw, and that [procedure] is described in relation to that [member]. (32)
If there is a thorn in the head while scratching, death of sons occurs from the head down to the breast; by that, one shall suffer separation from kinsmen. (33)
On the surface of the eyebrows, gold or glass may bring about good or evil fortune; pearls are obtained from the scratching of the eyes, according to the measurement of those limbs. || 34 ||
(127) By touching the face with wood produced from the top [of a tree], or even by using both hands for those two [actions], poverty and death shall follow respectively. (35)
If he scratches from tooth to tooth with three paws, there will be a loss of fruit [or, according to variant *gh*: a loss of mounts].
If he scratches his ear with coral, gold, or silver, it shall come to pass.
A thorn remaining in that [part] according to its measure brings about health, auspiciousness, and peace;
if it is felt in the neck, it is called *graiya*, or it may be a chain made of iron.
Or one should extract from both hands (or three, according to version gh) a cat's skeleton;
likewise, a "neck-bone" (grai-va) is a thorn that brings death, and a chain is one that destroys one's wife.
Through the cage of a cat, there may be the destruction of one's son and wife;
through the touching of its limbs, one's own limb may be affected; and from measuring it, many diseases arise. (39)
One should know that a mark on the shoulder-blade [arising from the hand] causes the loss of wealth;
however, black iron on both armpits, by its measure, brings intense suffering.
On his arm, the one who brings about supreme prosperity wears that [skull] up to the neck;
and on his right hand or back, he carries a skull or one made of clay.
When the waist is reached, it belongs to the son;
and when the left hand is touched, the foot of the bed arises from that limb. (42)
If it is below the height of the knee, it certainly causes the destruction of wealth and wife;
if it is on the side, one should know it brings itching, but if it is half the size of a man, it brings a woman with loose limbs.
He shall suffer from eye disease and experience agitation again and again;
there will be a foreign object like a beast's bone in his stomach, and it will cause extreme grief in the region of the hips. (44)
In the heart, one should place the heart-born [image], and below it, the image that causes hunger and thirst, according to its proportions;
on the back, the back-born dart, or the Śaukara, or the Kūrpara.
From measuring it [the body] in that manner, one becomes a creator of hatred in the world; a great disease arises from the pig-like [measurement].
An iron [mark] on the waist or back, or one below the neck at two cubits [in length], brings about the destruction of wealth. (46)

A [mirror] of that same size made from copper causes disease of the buttocks; one made of iron from the touch of the penis causes urinary disorders (meha), and one from the lower part of the hand destroys women.
Alternatively, one made from the thighs of an ox or born of wood, measuring a full cubit, [should be used];
for a dart born from the thighs of a woman of ill character causes the loss of wealth through a wooden dart. (48)
The pillars at the knees and shanks, as well as the base-block (*bhaṇḍikā*) for the barber,
should be one cubit in height; if they are lower than that, there will be death and bondage for the kinsmen.
There will be the tools of a barber, suffering, poverty, and dependence on others for one's livelihood;
and by the touch of the shank, there will be bone below eleven finger-breadths.
[This reading enclosed within brackets is not present in the *mū* and *a* manuscripts: And by that, there may be the death of the killer; his own death thereafter is not to be doubted.
With his feet turned backward, he shall have his ankles [visible] eighteen finger-breadths below. (51)
From that, there is the loss of wealth and cattle, living abroad, and a life of suffering;
from the touch of a foot, there may arise the bone of an elephant or even the thorn of a *śālmalī* tree. (52)
Measuring twelve finger-breadths, it bestows, in sequence, prosperity, travel, and death; it may be made of metal, wood, or clay, or decorated with gold leaf, chalk, or other pigments. (53)
Sixteen finger-breadths below [the navel], there is the destruction of grief and desires in due order;
at three finger-breadths, there is the bone of a horse, and at one and a half tālas, the death of a cow.
Bell-metal (kāṃsya) that measures less than eight finger-breadths (aṅgula) from the little toe is known to destroy wealth;
likewise, leather (carma) [measuring less than eight fingers] from the sole of the foot, and gold (rukma), should always [be measured] at eight finger-breadths.
From scratching the heels, from the tāla, kapāla, and abhra [omens], and from the touching of the limbs, a wise man should recognize various thorns (dangers). 56.
[This reading is enclosed within brackets; it does not appear in the root manuscript: Sand, ashes, iron, bone, gems, pearls, and so forth belong to the site;
by constantly touching many parts [of the body], various thorns [are removed]. (57)
Those [measures] and their fruits are according to that specific characteristic, as before; for the maker who is unaltered by rice, they are forty-seven. (58)
Among those, they say five are auspicious and forty-two are otherwise,
if they are found when a pit for the foundation is being dug into the earth.
Gold, coral, stars, and various kinds of gems;
jewels, pearls, cow-horns, conch shells, and oyster shells—these always bestow auspiciousness.
Furthermore, both living and lifeless frogs and tortoises are givers of prosperity.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, one should place a white parasol in the center.
(61) A stake buried to the depth of a man within the house does not cause harm;
however, a stake situated near water within a palace brings misfortune to men. (62)
Therefore, a wise man should dig a pit for the *khādhārikī* fire near water;
even if a thousand *rudra* oblations are offered there at some time, no fault arises.
In a pit equal to the abode of the gods, in a hundred sanctuaries of Bāṇaliṅgas,
or in a sacrificial pavilion below the knees, there shall be no fault if one offers oblations with splinters.
At the beginning of the acquisition of a dwelling site, as well as during the laying of the foundation,
and especially when constructing the walls, one should worship Vāstu at the three times of day.

In an auspicious hour with favorable planetary positions, under a beautiful ascendant, when the strength of the moon and the stars is excellent, and on ground that is level, well-smeared, and endowed with the primary qualities according to the prescribed measurements for the pit (*garta*); || 66 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth procedure in the Compendium of Characteristics, concerning the determination on the extraction of foreign bodies. || 24 ||
Now, the twenty-fifth [chapter]:
The sacrificer should be pure, wise, and dressed in white garments and unguents;
likewise, the preceptor and the architect, as well as the astrologer, should be endowed with excellent qualities.
The patron (yajamāna) should worship all these individuals dressed in white garments:
the architect (sthapati), Viśvakarman, the astrologer (daivajña), and Nandikeśvara. || 2 ||
That very learned Śrīkaṇṭha himself is the establisher upon the surface of the earth;
having worshipped all of them, he should satisfy them and ask for their forgiveness. || 3 ||
Those who perform the preparatory services are also worthy of worship according to one's capacity;
one should satisfy them with gifts of gold and clothing, or by means of pleasant words.
Then, having sipped water according to the rules together with the artisans, the preceptor,
having gathered the sacrificial materials, should enter the ground with a concentrated mind.
Facing north and having performed the ritual purification of his body,
he should perform self-worship and the offering of the arghya vessel, and then purify the ritual substances.

Having delineated the ground on all sides with kusha grass over which the Astra-mantra has been recited, the wise one should sprinkle it with water as well as with fragrant water containing [the water of] the Ganges.
Having fashioned a mandala of the Vedas and hermitages in the center with fragrant water and unbroken grains of rice,
[one should place] a beautiful woman, in the form of a young maiden, adorned with pure ornaments.
Having meditated upon that earth as being composed of those three states, one should worship the ground;
there, one should worship Vāstupuruṣa, who embodies all the gods. (9)
Then, having smeared that site so as to be square on all sides—
either by means of a water-clock and a gnomon, or by observing the stars— [one should proceed].
Having carefully examined [the time], the astrologer should declare a pure *lagna*;
in accordance with the time of the *lagna*, he should cast a thread upon the ground.
Śrī, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Supriyā, Vimalā, Śivā, Suśobhā, Bhānukī, and Cetā—these are the nine channels facing the east. (12)
Dhanā, Dhānyā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Drutāsavā, Niśā, Vidrumā, and Vibhavā—these nine have arisen from the northern face. (13)
Having made the field consist of sixty-four squares (eight times eight) and marked by two diagonal threads, one should worship the nine deities beginning with Earth; half of this belongs to the gods.
In the northeast quarter of the footprint, one should worship Īśvara with unbroken rice grains soaked in ghee;
Parjanya with water-lilies; and Jaya with a banner made of flour. || 15 ||
One should worship Indra with jewels, Ravi with incense, and the Guru with a canopy;
for the two [Ravi and Guru], one should truly offer wheat and the like, and for [the others], meat and curd in abundance.
The deity named Vyoma [is worshipped] with the flesh of birds; thus are the deities in the eastern direction.
In the square below Agni, one should worship Vahni with [an offering] made from flour, using either a ladle (śruva) or [the hand].
One should always worship Pūṣan with gold, and Vitatha with the same two [substances];
one should offer honey to Gṛhakṣata, and chickpea food to Yama.
One should offer two types of fragrances to Gandharva; to Bhṛṅga, the Khagajihvika;
and to Mṛga, one should give blue barley in the southern half of the Koṣṭha.
One should offer sesame and rice to Pitṛ, a tooth-cleansing twig to Nandin,
two yava grains to Sugrīva, and darbha grass to Puṣpadanta.
One should give a lotus to Pracetas, liquor to Asura, and to both of them [liquor];
ghee and water to Ketu; parched grain to Paṅkavardhana, and a cane to the western [direction].
Half of the *maṇḍa* and clarified butter are for Vāyu; *nāgakesara* is for Nāga.
Edible foods are for both Mukhya and Yakṣapa; *mudgānna* (mung bean rice) is for Kṣaya. || 22 ||
For Soma, there is milk-rice and honey; for the two, Śālaka and Mālūka, there is a liṅga;
for Diti, a loaf (lopī); and for Aditi, cakes (pūpa)—half on each side, starting from the quarter of Soma.
And one should place milk in the water-square (āp) located below the northeast (īśa);
then, in the square below that, one should indeed offer curd to Āpavatsa.
An offering should be given to Marīci with four-legged animals;
to Sāvitrī, always in the square below the fire, with sweetmeats and water mixed with *kuśa* grass.
Then, one should cause molasses, cakes, and so forth to be offered to Sāvitra;
to Vivasvat, one should give red sandalwood at the four corners.
In the lower corner square of the Rakṣas, one should offer food with ghee for Indra;
below that, in the corner square, food with clarified butter for Indrajaya.
To Mitra, who has four feet, one should give molasses and milk-rice;
but to Rudra, in the north-eastern corner, one should offer the flesh of birds.
In the corner cell below that, [offer] raw meat to Yakṣa;
likewise, to Mahīdhara, offer black gram food with meat in the four quadrants.
In the center, one should offer sesame seeds and rice to Brahmā seated upon a four-legged throne;
having worshipped these with garments and other offerings, one should then [worship] the group of eight Rakṣas in due order.
Then, outside the pit, the wise one should worship the eight Rakṣasas at the beginning of the directions starting from the northeast;
he should offer meat and ghee to Carakī, and rice-and-sesame mixture (kṛsara) and milk-rice (pāyasa) to Skanda.
One should worship Vidārī with red lotuses, Kandarpa with cooked rice mixed with meat,
Pūtanā with meat and bile, and Jambhaka with flesh and blood.
One should offer the sin consisting of bile, blood, and bones to Pilipiccha;
and with a garland of blood, one should offer it to the hosts of Rākṣasas, Mātṛs, and Īśas, as well as to the Piśācas and others.
One should offer an oblation (bali) to the ancestors and the guardians of the field according to one's desire;
in the absence of these, it may be offered with cooked grain and meat, or even with clarified butter and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).

One should worship with parched grains, or even without guile, or with *kuśa* grass and flowers; yet one should not have temples and such structures built without first satisfying and performing sacrifices for these deities.
Through both non-origination and non-destruction, [there is] the duality of the property and the possessor of the property.
Previously arisen, possessing great power, it brings fear to all beings. (36)
He who was cast upon the earth by the gods is considered the Vāstupuruṣa;
as long as the earth remains stable in the world, so long does the Vāstunara remain. || 37 ||

At the time of withdrawal, however, he goes to dissolution along with the gods, the planets, and the rest. In all matters concerning the site (vāstu), one should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunāyaka).
By the command of Śiva, it exists eternally as the means for that [attainment];
its extent all around is a hundred crore yojanas.
Standing pervading the entire earth, one should worship by mentally conceiving that body;
its head is in the northeast corner, and its shoulder and arm are in the east.
The elbow and knee are in the south-east; the shank and foot are in the south;
the lower arm, thigh, and hand, as well as the side, are from the south-eastern direction. (41)
In this very manner, in the counter-clockwise direction, there are Soma, Anila, Ambu, and Nairṛta;
thus, on the surface of the earth, the Lord of the Vāstu site is situated within a square.
Whatever shape the field may be, it becomes that very form;
when climbing over walls and such, one should not cause pain to the head or other parts [of the body]. (43)
One should mark the head of that thread situated at the northeast (īśa) and rakṣas;
from the water (west) comes Indra, from the host (gaṇa) the sun, and from Sugrīva, Satyaga is considered [to be reached].
From Bhauma comes Soma, from Yama comes Bhalla, and from Gandharva comes Bṛhaspati;
these are the channels situated in the primary branches, while these others are situated in the secondary branches.
From Gṛhakṣata comes Jalādhyakṣa; from Gaṇottama, Niśākara; from Bhallāṭa, as far as Bhāskara; and from Mahendra, Yamadevatā. (46)
The channels situated along the spine have been described; now the abiding of the deities is stated: Īśa and the others always reside in the head, while Āpa and Aditya reside in the two eyes.
Āpa is located in the region of the face, while Āpavatsa is likewise in the throat;
Jaya and Giri are situated in the two eyes, and the five beginning with Soma reside in the arms. (48)
On the left [side] are the five beginning with Indra; Rudra and Yakṣa are on the upper arms.
Likewise, Sāvitrī and Savitṛ are on the forearms, while the two hands are at the heart.
Dharādhara and Marīci are on both breasts;
Brahmā is eternally situated at the navel; Mitra and Vivasvat are stationed on the sides and in the belly; and Indrajaya is at the anus.
Śepha, Sīndra, and Suhṛt are well-known; these seven, beginning with Pāpa, occupy the rows [of the diagram]. (Mūla, A:
Pañjikā) || 51 ||
All seven deities beginning with Brahmā are located in the right knee and shanks;
Pitṛ and Mṛga are situated in the feet— thus are the Vāstu-deities described.

Now, however, the vital points (marmans), secondary vital points (upamarmans), and joints of the horse are being described: the head, the mouth, the heart, the two breasts, and the navel are the five great vital points.
The vital points (marmas) are in the middle of the feet; the remaining lines are the joints.
There are the lines of the primary and secondary bones, as well as the six types of spikes and the thunderbolt.
The group of four is in the four corners, and the tail is above the feet;
Īśa, Agni, Pitṛ, and Vāyu always reside upon the spikes. (55)
Āpavatsa, Sāvitrī, and Jayadāsa occupy the four squares;
if pierced in the vital point (marman), death occurs, and if in the secondary vital point (upamarman), it concerns the sons.
In the *sandhi* (juncture), there is loss of friends; in the *vaṃśa*, likewise, the destruction of the lineage;
in the *upavaṃśa*, there shall be suffering; and in the *triśūlaka*, there is the destruction of the fetus.
In the six [nakṣatras], there is much enmity; in the four, the destruction of vehicles;
in the tail, disease of the head; and during the piercings of the gods, there is affliction.
The destruction of the maker would occur at the top; therefore, one should turn these [proportions] back.
Here, the measurement of the head (śiras) is said to be one-sixteenth part of the foot.
The measurements for the bamboo and other materials shall be determined respectively by twelve, ten, and eight parts;
this has been declared as the gross measurement, and now the subtle measurement is being stated here.
Beginning from one finger-breadth and decreasing by one barley-corn at each step, one should gradually move the thread starting from the north or the east.
In the arrangement of walls, pillars, and so forth, no defect of piercing (vedha) arises;
however, if a piercing of the vital points (marman) should occur, whether through knowledge or ignorance, [it must be avoided]. || 62 ||
"Through the hundredfold oblation to Aghora, peace is then produced.
Thus has the worship of Vāstu for both houses and palaces always been described here. 63.
Īśa is this Rudra Īśāna; Parjanya is the leader of the clouds;
and Jayanta, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, is Mahendra, the leader of the gods.
The Sun, the son of Aditi, the truthful one, the great lord of Dharma,
Vṛṣa, Skanda, the sky, the firmament, and Fire are considered to be Vaiśvānara. (65)
Pūṣan, Pṛṣadeva, Dadhīci, Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, the well-known Kujja, Yama, Kāla, and Rocana; || 66 ||
The Gandharva Viśvāvasu, Bhṛṅgīśa, the weak Gaṇa,
Mṛga [or Yama according to mū, a, g, gh], his sister Mṛṣā, Tṛṣṇā, and the lord of the Rākṣasas shall be his father. || 67 ||
The gatekeepers are known as Nandin, Sugrīva, Caṇḍabhairava, Puṣpadanta—the foremost of the Gaṇas—and Varuṇa, the lord of the waters. || 68 ||
Śukra is said to be the minister of the Daityas; Śoṣa is declared to be Ketu; he who is known as the wicked Manda is called Vega, and Vapu is also proclaimed [as such]. (69)
The nāga Vāsuki is proclaimed as the primary name, and Bṛhaspati is Bhallāṭa;
he is the king of the yakṣas, and Soma is the moon whose essence is nectar.
The physician Śvaraka shall be known as Samākhya; Diti shall be Suramātā (the mother of the gods), and Diti is said to be the mother of the Daityas; and likewise Āpa and Himācala.
Āpavatsa, Umādevī, Marīci, Brahmajottama, Savitṛ, and another, Arka; and Sāvitrī, the wife of Brahmā. (72)
Vivasvān is known as Aryaman, the friend of Indra and Upendra;
Indrajit is the son of the Rakṣasa [Indradāsa], and Bhānu is the third, known as Mitra. (73)
Rudradāsa, the one named Pracāṇḍa, the one named Yakṣman, and Somarudraka; Dharādhara, Ananta, and Brahmā is considered to be Caturmukha. || 74 ||
This method which was proclaimed in the *Pārameśvara* for the *mura*s has been stated here; however, those previously mentioned as *rakṣa*s and others are indeed *rākṣasa*s. (75)

One should worship the directions beginning with Hara (the North-East) using the letters from *ka* to *ha*, mounted upon the *rā* vowel, joined with the bindu, and extending from the feet to the world-measure; and one should conquer with Brahman and Dhruva.

In the rite of offering (balikarma), one should worship Carakī and the other Rākṣasīs with [mantras] consisting of long vowels, eight syllables, and one [syllable], enriched by the bindu, preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with Namaḥ and Svāhā.
When the pit has been filled up to one-quarter less than its full depth, one should place a foundation stone (pada) somewhere at the beginning;
for with mere bricks, stones, and the like alone, there would be instability.
If there is fear of earthquakes, winds, or even the apprehension of a storm,
one should fill that area with soft sand, bricks, or stones from the east.
Then, having filled eight cubits with earth and a full cubit with stones,
and having flooded it with water, it should be leveled by the sacrificial elephant's feet.

From the length, by means of divisions of three, two, four, and one, one should successively fashion the sky, the half-portion, and the pit; then, with cords and wooden pegs, one should construct the level ground, the full cart-shape, and the angles. (81)
Having led [the deity] to that site which is slightly elevated, one should then worship the Vāstu once more in a pit smeared with cow dung,
at the front of its door, and in the pavilion.

On an auspicious day, one should worship the Guru and the others according to the prescribed rite with gold, garments, and other offerings, in a place enriched with plantain and mango groves and adorned with arches and banners.

Having worshipped Śiva in the Śivakumbha, the directional Kumbhas, and likewise the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in their midst, one should then offer the oblation into the desired fire-pit according to the prescribed rule.
One should likewise offer oblations to the deities of the site (vāstudevas), as well as to Aghora and Pāśupata,
together with precious gems, medicinal herbs, metals, grains, and mercury.
One should place pitchers made of gold and other materials, adorned with cloth necks, in sequence;

having first placed Ananta in the center, one should then place the eight treasures (nidhis) in order. (Note: This reading enclosed within brackets is not present in the manuscripts mū, a, g, and gh. || 86 ||
In the four corners starting from the southeast (Agni), and in the four directions starting from the east (Indra), one should place four others:
Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, and likewise Kacchapa.
And the eight treasures (nidhis), namely Mukunda, Nanda, Nīla, and Śaṅkha;
these should be worshipped in their proper order, beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ, with the name placed in the middle.
The Guru should install these treasures, but he must not move them again.
Having installed the deities upon the eight stones—in some traditions, the eight-formed Śiva—[he should proceed]. (89)
Having firmly secured the lords of the treasures within the eight jars, one should place the footprint;
then, in the corners starting from the southeast, one should place either new bricks or stones in due order. (90)
One should place four [lotuses] marked with lions, beginning with Dharma as the feet and so forth;
there, five others marked with lotuses are to be placed, one of which is in the center.
These are known as the Ādhāraśakti (Supporting Power), and the [other] Dharmas and so forth are to be placed starting from the eastern direction.
The deities beginning with Śarva and ending with Bhīma reside within the eight stone slabs.
And by means of the mantras beginning with the first letter of one's own name, preceded by bathing, worship, and so forth,
one should visualize the [deities] starting with Dharma as having the form of feet ending in yellow,
and those starting with the Bull (Vṛṣa).
Having meditated upon a firm seat and the path [or: my arrow], one should fashion it with garlands;
elsewhere, jars and stones are mentioned, as well as five [types]. 94.
One should place a stone in the center toward the east, and then [stones] in the corners starting from the southeast;
likewise, one should place Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, and Kacchapa.
And here, one should deposit the five treasures, beginning with Śaṅkha, according to their respective names;
having laid out the temple, one should do so from the center of the width of the wall.
The procedure for placing the foundation stones (śilānyāsa) is prescribed at a location level with the ear-threads;
the stones should be made square and measured at one cubit on all sides.
They should be raised to a height that is one-third of their width; those made of brick should be constructed of bricks, and in the case of stone structures, they should be made of auspicious stones.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and the fifth, known as Pūrṇā, are considered [the five days].
Having constructed an altar with unbroken grains (akṣata), they are placed upon it. (99)
One should cause Nanda and the others to descend into the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya),
accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and auspicious, beautiful omens.
First, one should establish Nandā by means of the equinox of the body;
then the other [tithis] should be established in their respective directions in due order by the mantra-practitioner.
Having made them steady with equal ears, they should be bathed and worshipped in sequence:
first with water from the *astra* mantra, and then again with clay and other substances.
Having bathed those stones, which were golden-colored and beautiful, they meditated upon them as being the forms of the Vidyās; thus satisfied, their faces were smiling. (103)
Having invoked them, the mantra-practitioner should establish them according to the rite with mantra-consecrated water,
using very sturdy earthen jars or those made of gold for the wealthy.
Having drawn up water with a cloth, one should anoint [the deity] with sandalwood paste;
having performed worship with garments and other offerings, one should present the food offering (naivedya).
Having performed this, the mantra-practitioner should consecrate the stone with the name-mantra (or mantras). || 105 ||
Oṃ! O Nandā, daughter of Nandin, I establish you here for the benefit of virtuous people;
remain here, well-pleased, as long as the moon and stars endure. 106.
O Nanda, grant to men at all times their desired lifespan and prosperity;
you must always provide protection for this temple with great effort. (107)
Oṃ Bhadre! Be always auspicious, ever bringing welfare to men;
O Goddess, grant long life, fulfill desires, and bestow prosperity at all times.
Oṃ Jaye! Stay here forever, for you have been installed by me;
O Goddess, O Sovereign, be eternally victorious and bestow prosperity. 109.

Oṃ! O you who are empty, O destroyer of the defect of emptiness, O bestower of perfection and liberation, O auspicious one, O destroyer of all defects at all times—abide here in this form of the Lord! 110.
Oṃ! You are the fullness, O Great Wisdom, characterized by the gathering of all things;
make everything here in this temple eternally complete. 111.
Above them, five stone slabs are to be placed in sequence;
by the command of Śiva, they— Nanda and the others— are to be installed eternally, just like the liṅgas.
Having thus propitiated Nanda and the others, the wise practitioner should worship Kūrma in the center;
in this arrangement of the jars, the ritual procedure should be performed as in the arrangement of Śiva.
Having thus cast gems, metals, minerals, seeds, medicinal herbs,
and mercury into the interiors of the jars, one should deposit eight or five treasures.

The power of the support (ādhāra-śakti) should be placed upon the stone slab as before; and the presiding deities, up to the intellect (buddhi), are to be established within the construction of the pedestal (pīṭha-bandha). || 115 ||
Having held a great festival at night and offered the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions,
and having given food and gifts to the preceptor and others, one should perform the concluding rites for the task.
The height of the *upajaṅghā* (the upper leg) from the middle of the pinnacle (*śikhara*) is considered the best when it is one-third of the width;
the middling is less by one-quarter; and the lowest is considered to be half of the best measurement. (117)
For Brahmā, Upendra, and the Sun-god, the *jyeṣṭha* and *upajaṅghikā* [measures] should be used; for others, however, the *aghamā*; but for Śiva, it is according to his will.
Having left a cavity in the center, one should fill it all around with half a liṅga as wide as Viṣṇu for the purpose of making stone images of Kūrma and others.

In the center of the pedestal, upon a white lotus, one should meditate on the Vāstu deity as differentiated by the syllables beginning with the vowels and the letters *arkasura* (the consonants), consisting of the primary form and its limbs; then one should worship it again.
Having made the shanks equal in length up to the base of the plinth,
one should there lay out the palace with the sound of musical instruments and auspicious chants.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth procedure, titled "The Establishment of the Sections for the Worship of the Site," within the Compendium of Characteristics. || 25 ||
Now, the twenty-sixth [chapter]: there should be temples with three, two, eight, or six-fold proportions,
and the *liṅgas* should be according to the measurement of the temple.
The walls are extended in width by half the length of the liṅga, respectively.
When the field has been made sixteen squares, the central womb-chamber (garbha) is formed by four parts;
the surrounding walkways (vīthī) shall be equal to those same parts, and the walls shall consist of twelve parts.
Alternatively, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) may be one part out of twenty-five parts of the base;
its interior (garbha) shall consist of eight parts, while the walls (bhittayaḥ) shall consist of two parts.

For the mixed images (miśrārcā) and those with unmanifest emblems (avyaktaliṅga), the inner sanctum (garbha) is determined by parts of three, two, and two-and-a-half [respectively], starting from the smallest; in some cases, however, there is an increase in the thickness of the wall.
The width of the base is twenty-six parts; the walls are twenty parts;
the central void of the womb-chamber is twelve parts; and the pedestal in the middle is four parts.
In some cases, the length of the *liṅga* should be equal to the width of the wall;
in other cases, it is said to be twice that. When the temple has been divided by the six tastes (*rasa*), [the measurement is as follows].
The jagatī is threefold: equal to the dhāma, one-quarter less, or half [of it];
these are to be known as the projections (nirgama) for the largest and other sizes. The rim (nemi) is that same measurement minus one-quarter.
(146) We shall describe the *krama* meter, which is the supreme among meters in the world, consisting of thirty-six syllables divided into feet.
From the middle of the four-footed [verse], there is a *garbha*; with one [syllable] added to that, there is the *piṇḍikā*.
The walls are formed by the division of twelve (the sun), and from the rotation [of the digits],
the wall consisting of twenty-eight parts, including the pillars and pilasters, is established by the divisions of twenty (the nails).
With thirty-four firm pillars in the four directions,
there should be four main pillars in the center, and twelve kumārikā pillars [surrounding them].

One should place three [pillars] in each of the corners, and two pillars at the front in the Kumārikā [shrine]; or one may also construct them on both sides at the front, provided they are joined by a cross-beam (āsāra).
A pavilion (maṇḍapa) is considered to be of three kinds: one with walls, one with corner-walls, and another which is without walls but joined with corner-pillars. || 12 ||

Likewise, the *catuṣkikās* (or *tuṣṭikās*, as read in the Liṅgapurāṇa manuscript) should be constructed on both sides and three times at the back; all of these, in the case of the best class of temples and others, should consist of twelve parts.
One should make the central chariot with six parts, and likewise the upper chariots with three;
one should make the side-chariots with four parts, and similarly the other [chariots] with five parts.
From the middle, having held the jagatī by one part from each of the two intermediate points (the pravelās) in succession, one should omit the encircling part.
The *balabhī* should be established with six parts (*rasāṃśa*) in the four cardinal directions and in the center;
the corner pavilions (*koṇadhāman*) together with the *maṇḍapas* should be established with eight parts (*vasvaṃśa*) in the intermediate directions.
Having given one part on the outside, the remaining middle portions should be removed;
at the intersection of the equal lines, one should rotate from the equal division. (17)
On the ground, for the purpose of circumambulation, and upon the walls of the pavilion,
there were beautiful temple pillars, roof-ridges, and pinnacles.
Skilled artisans should fashion for that deity a wall, a lotus, a figure, a leaf-and-creeper design, or even a rug (kutha).

Having repeatedly understood those [proportions] of the bhaga and the mukta through the walls of increase, that which is known as the measurement of the site (vāstu-māna) is concluded; now, the measurement of the linga is being stated.
The inner sanctum (garbha) is twice the size of the liṅga; the central seat (āsana) is half of that;
the width of the two walls is one-eighth of the pedestal (pīṭha), and from that, two parts each for the two walls. The height of the outer pillar-base (bāhyajaṅghā) is equal to the width of the wall.
The *mañjarī* consists of two parts, and the nose is half of a *mañjarī*.
The half above the nose, which is another half, shall always constitute the shoulder;
its width is five parts, and likewise the neck is three parts high.
The two cheeks and the two *sāra* portions extend out by half of a half-part each;
the height of the neck and the other parts increases in sequence by three parts, two parts, half a part, two parts, and half a part respectively. (24)

The *kapola* (the side wall) should be equal to the pedestal (*vedikā*) according to the measurement of the *liṅga*; the circumambulatory path (*bhramaṇa*) should be made from half the height of the temple (*dhāma*), and the walls (*bhittayaḥ*) should be half of that.
To the east of the temple, the pavilion should always be twice the size [of the main hall].
In front of it, the entrance pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) should be half the measurement of the pavilion. || 26 ||

A quadrangular pavilion (catuṣkikā) should be constructed with half the measurement of the pavilion called the "face" (mukha); in front of this quadrangular pavilion, there should always be a jagatī according to the measurement of the temple (dhāma).
One should construct the corner pavilions with a measurement equal to half that of the main hall;
likewise, the *balabhīs* situated at the cardinal directions should be identical in size and provided with their own pavilions.
There, one should fashion the footstool (padapīṭha) at the midpoint of the upajaṅghikā;
its height should be one-fourth or three-eighths of the temple's total height.
The width of that [structure], which possesses six parts and an additional space, is now described.
Having subtracted the height from that [total], the *khurapaṭṭikā* (the plinth-band) is placed within one part.
The *kumbha* (pitcher) should be two parts; the *kumbhapaṭṭikā* (pitcher-band) one part;
the neck (*kaṇṭha*) should be two parts, and at its front, it should be sixfold in width.
With one part there should be a neck-band (galapaṭṭī); with the second, a decorated collar (valitāṅkikā);
with the third, however, an upper band (upapaṭṭī) which is square due to its proportions.
The portion called *haṃsa* is three-quarters of a unit, and the upper fillet (*paṭṭikā*) is one-quarter of that;
having divided the space between them into eight parts, one should fashion the lotus with those parts.
The entry should be by one part, and the lotus should not occupy six parts (or six limbs).
Now, the pericarp is described according to its width as one part of the moon.
When the half-pīṭha has been made into a *jinī*, one should place eight chariot-ornaments (*rathaka*) in the middle;
for the purpose of constructing a house, there should be an entrance in the center of that with two parts.
Furthermore, the entrance is always situated within a portion of the central chariot;
likewise, the extent of the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) extends as far as the altar (vedikā). || 36 ||

One should fashion an auspicious *balabhī* (pavilion) in the middle of the base of the *jaṅghikā* (the lower wall); or else, one may describe the pinnacle of the temple (*prāsādaśikhara*) and the upper stories (*uparathādika*).
One should construct the upper path with *nāgas* and the corner-binding with *navāṃśas*;
the entrance is said to extend from the pedestal (*pīṭha*) up to the lotus (*abja*) in height.
One should make the entry of the plinth with half [the width], the pitcher with one part, the fillet with half, and the neck-entry with two parts. (39)
The neck-entry, the exit of Śani, and likewise the *balita*-band;
above that, by half a part, the *upapaṭṭikā* should be made. || 40 ||
The rectangular band at the exit is equal to that;
the *haṃsa* [according to manuscript gh: two parts] enters with three-quarters, due to its entry by half of that band.
One should fashion a beautiful lotus with its petals joined at the joints, such that by means of the portion extending outward, the lotus enters half a unit into the east. 42.
By entering half a portion [of the base], the abode situated upon the pericarp (karṇikā) shall have a stone-made footstool;
thus it is also for those made of wood or brick.
The shank is twice the measure of half the back; the *añjarī* is twice the measure of the shank.
Having made the *graha* equal to its height, the shank is [divided] in the middle by the [three] qualities (*guṇa*). (44)
The *mañjarī* should be made with six parts, and the *śukanāsikā* (fronton) half of that;
the *vedī*, *bandha*, *varaṇḍā*, *diṅ*, *nigaḍa*, and *yan* should follow in successive order.

The *jaṅghikā* (the lower part of the wall) should be half as wide as the base; its height should be one and a half parts of the *jināṃśa* (the Jina-measure), with one-sixteenth part extending outward.
In that [height], one-fourth of the height is set aside for the *nidrāṃśaka* (the recessed portion).
One should fashion a square band from those two [parts] and the two [other] parts;
the pitcher (kumbha) should be three and a half [parts], and the pitcher-band (kumbhapaṭṭikā) should be half of that.
This part known as the "hoof" (khura) is said to consist of six parts;
the neck should be half a part, and the pitcher (kalaśa) should be three parts.
The excellent pitcher (kalaśa) is one-fourth of the width of that fillet (paṭṭikā);
from the entrance on one side, the necks are half [the width], and the projecting fillet is likewise half.
The fillet (paṭṭī) of the pitcher (kumbha) is one-fourth [of its height], and the base (pāda) is one-fourth;
the fillet of the pitcher stands at two parts of the neck-ring (kupālī).
In this manner, craftsmen most proficient in the technical treatises should fashion [the image] equipped with the three hooves and so forth, designated as having the pedestal-bond (*vedībandha*).
From one-fourth of the altar's width, there should be a protrusion (badurmi) above that;
when three parts have been made, the recessed sections (praveśikā) should be three-quarters of a part.
From the foot [of the pillar], there is a fillet (paṭṭī) extending from the section of the pitcher's projection;
that fillet known as the square (caturasra) is situated with a width of one and a half parts.
One [pillar] should have two [ornaments] with a fillet (paṭṭi) due to an inward projection of one-third;
the shaft (jaṅghā) of the largest [pillars] should be provided with a base (khuṃra) and a pitcher (kumbha) according to the measurement of a quarter.
From the portion of the *dhāma* (the temple's height) and the sun's parts (*arkāṃśa*), the hanging ornament (*lambinī*) should be placed above the shank by the wise;
it may extend up to nine units, or it may be excellent with leaf-patterns (*patravallī*). 55.
Abounding in the beauty of various tilakas and adorned with strings of pearl necklaces,
the portion above the shanks is divided into eight parts by taking a fourth part.
Holding one part below and behind, one should cause that to be struck;
there, with half of that, one should fashion the plank known as the "entrance" upon the ground.
Likewise, with half of that *niṣkāśikā* portion, there are four *trikās*;
with a quarter-portion less than that, the fillet called *haṃsa* (or *hasta*) arises from that same base.
The molding called varaṇḍa should consist of three parts, while the neck-band (kaṇṭhapaṭṭī) should be one part;
that band should be made with a projection of three-quarters of a part.
In that [layout], there should be a triple-folded band (trikaṭapaṭṭī) consisting of three parts, and a triangle (tryasrikā) from one part;
having divided one part into three, the entrance is made from one part.
The neck-line (kaṇṭhasūtra) should be made straight; likewise, there should be a projection on the second [line].
A fillet (paṭṭikā) should be fashioned with a secondary projection on the second [line].
The *balita* (folding) should be one-quarter less than two parts; from that, the *paṭṭikā* (band) should be one quarter.
The portion called *balitā* should consist of three parts, while the waist (*kaṭi*) should consist of nine parts. || 62 ||
One part is for the portions of the *rasa* (flavor); therein, the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is two parts.
From the neck-thread (*kaṇṭhasūtra*), the collar (*kaṭha*) enters for one part, and above that is the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) for half a part.
The emergence of the *haṃsa* is by one part, and the square is by two parts;
the base, the shank, and the hip of the ground are thus proclaimed according to the eightfold scripture. (64)
One should calculate one-fourth of the maximum portion as the height;
below that, one should construct it with a width of one and a half parts.
There, the shoulder is one and a half parts; the remainder consists of sixteen parts.
From the middle part of the altar and the hip, [one should take] four parts, excluding the feet.
Having divided the parts of the transformation, from the waist upwards to the limit of the shoulders,
one should enter by means of each individual part according to the thread of the throat.
The width of the corner-piṇḍī and so forth is nine units; the space between the water-channels (udakāntara) is one unit.
The *anuratha* is six units; the space between the water-channels is seven units.
One should know that from the middle of the chariot upwards, it is likewise divided by eight parts;
one should divide the ground between the hips and the shoulders into thirty-five parts.
The eastern ground is raised by nine parts, while the others decrease by one part each;
thus is described the entry into the circle for the corners, the chariot, and so forth. (70)
p. 153) The entry into each individual stage (bhūmikā) should always occur by means of the outer half;
likewise, the entry of the chariot-follower (anuratha) occurs by means of a fourth part. 71.
In this way, the wise one should always contract the central chariot, having omitted the respective portions of all the earths in their proper sequence. (72)
Then, having taken one-fourth from the portion of Indra, the wise man should first draw the ground;
the pitcher (kumbha) shall be made from two parts less a quarter, and its band (paṭṭī) shall be one-quarter.
Likewise, a band (paṭṭī) extends halfway down the neck on both sides;
in the middle, occupying three-quarters of a part, is the element called puṭa, which has a circular interior.
From one-third of the sides of that womb, two internal horses are proclaimed;
those two should likewise be made in the shape of a water-jar at the edges of the knife-blade.
The vedāsrā (four-cornered) band should be made, while the kumbhikā (jar-shaped part) is reduced by one-quarter;
the kumbha-band is [reduced] by one-quarter, and the neck-band by half.
From the midpoint of the neck-lotus, the square [pedestal] should be known to be one part;
likewise, the fillet (paṭṭī) is half the height of the pitcher (kumbha), and the neck is half the height of that fillet. || 77 ||
In this very manner, the wise one should proceed with the six parts at the two corners;
from the middle of the two-and-a-half parts, he should fashion the cavity for the inner chamber (puṭa).
On the sides, within the circular boundary, there are two altars (mekhalā) consisting of three parts each, and the full-moon-shaped pinnacle (pūrṇenduśālikā).
One should fashion the height of the three-pronged [structure] there with two [parts] on both sides.
In the center of the *candraśālā*, at the top, there is likewise a *śikharikā* made of three parts; its base is two parts, and the middle should be like the fruit of the *lavalī*. (80)
At its top, the entry of the fillet (paṭṭī) from half of the fillet-width should occur;
the exit, known as the other part, should be from half of the square portion.
One should construct the *kumbhapaṭṭī* from half a part by means of half of that half;
in its center, a *tilaka* should be made, and thus the *varaṇḍikā* is formed with three parts.
Thus, from the eastern part of the *manvaṃśa*, there are four others according to the sequence of lunar days (*tithi*).
Such is the form of the corner chariot; now I shall describe the upper chariot (*uparatha*) after this.
Having made the height sixtieth part [of the total], there the sections are square;
the fillet (paṭṭī) is by one part, and the neck (kaṇṭha) likewise by half a part.
Having divided one part into three, the neck-band (kaṇṭhapaṭṭī) shall consist of one portion; one should fashion the circular band (vṛttapaṭṭī) as projecting by one part.
In the same manner, one should construct the Śikharī from the middle of the side;
in that portion, a gartālaka should be made by the wise, and on its two sides, it should be three parts.
The wise should recognize the Tuharī as having the height of one share, with a peak [shikhara] at the top;
it is occupied by a tilaka mark above and below, and is situated above the central position. 87.
On both sides of the Tuhaṛī, two vedikās should be made;
the remaining portions for the *candraśālikās* shall each be four parts.
The height should be made by three [thirty] units each, increasing by one earth-unit at a time. Thus, fifteen types of *pañcabhūmīnduśālikā* [temples] have been described. (89)
One should divide the width of the middle chariot by three and a half parts;
there, from the center, a half-chariot protrudes by one and a half parts.
One should construct the Ardhendu-śālikā with a width of one and a half parts, two parts on each side,
and a height of sixty parts.
There, one part should be used for the Vedāsras (the corners) and another single part for what is called the *kumbha* (the pot);
likewise, one should fashion the *kumbhapaṭṭī* (the neck-band) and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) with half [a part].
Having divided it into two parts, one part is for the neck-band (*kaṇṭhapaṭṭī*) and the pitcher-shape (*kumbhikā*).
Likewise, it should be made square, constructed with a portion of a portion (*bhāgabhāgena*). (Note: This reading enclosed within brackets is not found in the *mū*, *a*, or *kh* manuscripts.)
In the center of that, there should be half a *puṭa*, with a height of two parts less one-quarter;
it should be provided with a *tilaka* for digging, and outside of that is the *ardhendu-śālikā*.
It should be constructed in the form of a terrace, raised to a height of two and a half [units];
in its center, a pinnacle (śikhara) two parts high, exceedingly beautiful, [should be placed]. (95)
On the side, a beautiful Trikaṇṭhaka should be made, rising to two parts;
likewise, on the side of that half-chariot, an Ardhendūśālikā should be constructed.

In the same way, one should extend another section from the *varaṇḍaka* according to the division of the Veda; three sections should be placed one above the other, and one [should be made] equal to the ground-line (*bhūsūtra*). || 97 ||
(156) And the moon-crescent temple (candrārdhaśālikā), ending with the five elements and the altar (vedikā), is to be constructed;
this is the work for the central chariot (madhyaratha). Now, the altar and so forth are described.
One should cause the height of the previously mentioned pedestal (vedikā) to be two and a half parts;
the recessed fillet (praveśapaṭṭī) should be one quarter [of that], and the projecting fillet (nirgamapaṭṭikā) should be one quarter.
The haṃsapaṭṭī, however, should be one part, and the kapotikā three-quarters of a part;
its square face should be one-quarter [of a part], and its width should be half of the inner sanctum (garbha).
The upper portion of the altar (vedī) is considered to be three parts in width;
its height is six parts, measured from the half-line ending at the so-called haṃsa-mark.
Therein, the width of the neck is one part from the extent of the protrusion of the cheeks;
from the cheeks, by an extraction of one part, is the width of the pure nostrils. || 102 ||
The neck should be one-sixteenth [of the total height] above the lord of the wings (the head);
it should be divided into three parts, with the collarbone (*galapaṭṭī*) occupying half and the lower collarbone (*upapaṭṭī*) the other half.
The part known as the *vṛtta* (circle) is formed by a portion of the *tattva* (essence); from its side, there is a square (*caturasrikā*).
With two [portions], that which is called *āmalasāra* is raised all around the circle.
One should divide that single quality above, joined with the petals of the transformation;
by one [unit] it becomes a square, and by two, a *haṃsakapotikā*.
The head [of the structure] should be formed by means of the joining of the cheeks (or door-panels);
likewise, even for another purpose, one should construct the temple firmly in this very manner.
From the third part of the palace, which is five parts wide, the base known as Amala should be made;
with three parts plus one part of earth, the pitcher (ghaṭa) should be made, its height being double that [of the base].
Aghora should be established in the south, and the one known as Vāma in the north;
likewise, Vāyu and the two parts of the shanks are in the east with joined palms.
The gods should also be stationed on the half-peak and in the middle of the chariot;
in some cases, Bhairava, Nāṭyeśa, Gaurī, and Arka are placed from the south onwards.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be adorned with these [deities] such as Indra and others, stationed in their respective directions.

From the middle of its shaft (jaṅghā)—which has the previously mentioned emergence, back, and nose—the face should be formed, starting from the eldest [side]; and above that, the hip (kaṭi) should be as before.
Having divided the height of that hip-section into eight parts, [one should proceed]. || 111 ||
One should construct chariot-pavilions (*rathaka*) as before using three parts;
with three parts one should make the *candraśālā*, and with two parts the city from the center.
The wise man should fashion the beautiful form of the Jīva situated there;
on both sides of the *candraśālā*, the triple neck (*trikaṇṭha*) shall consist of two parts.
Behind the *candraśālā*, however, there is one circular *bherī*;
at the middle-upper portion of the *candraśālā*, the parts are considered to be the *cinnaraka*.
With one [unit], the upper pinnacle (*śikhara*) should be made in the shape of a *tilaka*;
likewise, on its sides, structures such as the *ardhendu-śālikā* should be constructed. (115)
I shall now describe the ornaments for the site made of stone, pearls, and other materials.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth rule, titled "The Construction of the General Five-Chariot Temple" (*sāmānyapañcarathakaprāsādavartanā*), within the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*, known as the *Talacchanda-vāstubhūṣaṇa*. [The reading "nāma" does not appear in the manuscript copies. 26.
Now begins the twenty-seventh [chapter].

Alternatively, I shall describe the three [planets] beginning with Jupiter, the dwellers of heaven, in their respective order, according to the sequence of the chariots (7), the nine (9), and the seven (7) arrows (5), starting from the Sun. 1.
In the Mañjarī [style], the width at the base shall consist of ninety parts;
the openings and so forth are formed by eight-sevenths, while the middle and half-ratha [sections] are formed by nine [parts].
The water channel should enter evenly with a width of one and a quarter parts;
there should be four chariot-arches (rathaka) and four cross-beams (chalāgama), each measuring one and a half parts.
The ground [of the base] is nine times the height of that cluster [of the pinnacle] divided by thirty.
Then, by omitting one part at a time, there are nine stories with six pillars each.
Having constructed a railing on the outside, adorned with moon-chambers and the like,
and joined by Vidyādharas and immortals— thus indeed is the Jyeṣṭha Khadruma.
When the width is increased by one-sixtieth part, the binding of the corners is formed with jewels;
with one and a quarter arrows (five and a quarter) and seven munis (twenty-one), it becomes the *aṇuka* type.
The Munis (seven) should be placed at the end of the chariot; then one should enter by means of three and a quarter parts respectively;
likewise, there should be three units for the interval between waters, and only one unit for half the water.

There are seven chariots, seven worlds, and seven [levels]; when a third part is established for the height, the first level is formed by the portions of desire through the application of a decrease of one for each.

p. 160) Up to the seventh part, seven very beautiful pavilions (mahya) should be constructed; they are enriched with moon-chambers (candraśālā) and so forth, and outside there is a vedī as before. || 9 ||
Having divided [the width] into nineteen parts,
the wise one should make the corner [of the mandala] with five parts and the path [between the spokes] with four parts.
In the middle is a slender chariot with arrows, and on the outside, it is reduced by one-quarter of its parts;
in this manner, the remaining half should be fashioned, endowed with five earth-chariots.
Having made the eastern earth (Prāktanī) half a hundred parts in height, the other five earths, ending with Vasu, are successively reduced by one part due to the destruction of their form. (12)
Between the two sides of the Vedāstra (the four-armed square), that field is divided into parts according to the yugas;
having made a single entrance there, the first corner-ratha (chariot) is formed.
