The middle half-ratha is two parts; it is excluded from the entrance.
The fifth [part] is the abode of the chariots, and likewise the other is from the portion of the elements (bhūta).
It may consist of seven chariots;
likewise, with six parts, there may be an entrance by one [chariot], while two [chariots] occupy the middle space.
Thus is described the nine-chariot Jyeṣṭha temple as proclaimed by Śaṅkara; its width at the base of the altar, as well as the height of the mañjarikā, should be as follows.

These two, when divided by the lunar-day portions (tithyaṃśa)—Jyeṣṭhā being from the eighth portion (harāṃśa) onwards, the middling, and the inferior consisting of nine portions—are of three kinds: thick, middling, and thin. (17)
The *jaṅghā* (shaft) is half the width in height, excluding the middle part of the foot;
it is equal [in height] in the smallest temple, while the *śikhara* (spire) is double [the height] in all three [temple sizes]. (18)

The flower-cluster (mañjarī) is of three types: shaped like the sunflower, like barley, or like the flame of a lamp; it is respectively two and a half times, one and a half times, or three times the [length of the] stalk. 19.
By rotating [the cord] with three cords measuring one and a half times the width of the shank, a circle should be formed;
when the cord is positioned at half of that half-shank, there arises the beautiful armor-like [pattern].
In some cases, they may be inferior in their characteristics, deficient in their marks, or consist of three chariots and three arrows;
for them, water falls with each single arrow at every two corners.
It should have a moat equal in width to its extent and be adorned on all sides with pavilions; for the central chariot-pavilion (madhyaratha) should be made with a portion consisting of twenty parts.
The first earth [level] should be thirty parts in height, with eleven parts (the Rudra-portion) for its base;
the other levels should be made as before, with ten parts (the direction-graha-portion), O excellent one.
The temple (prāsāda) is one part of its own [total] measure; here, Brahmā and the other three [deities] reside.
Its varieties consist of four-sided, eight-sided, and circular forms, and there are three other types as well. (24)
From a triangle, there arise [diagrams] with four, five, eight, and sixteen sides;
they may be circular, non-circular, or oblong—there are six types. I shall now state their names.
The one called Virāja has eight corners and is long; that same shape is the Puṣpaka.
That which is called Tripiṣṭa has eight corners, while the Himāṃśuka has sixteen corners. || 26 ||
The round sun is that [mandala], and the one called Maṇika is long and located in the west.
There are eighteen others besides these; I shall describe those beginning with the "excellent" (uttama). (27)
The Kāliṅgas, Nāgaras, Lāṭas, Varāṭas, Drāviḍas, and Gauḍas—these six types of temples are provided with decorative lines (rekhakas). || 28 ||
The Latina, the Kuṭṭima, the Śekharī [or Khecarī], the Cakrin, the Gāndhāra, and the Bhaumaja—these six are known as the Prāsādas. || 29 ||
*Dhāman* is masculine, *balabhī* is feminine, and *sthitikṛt* is neuter;
these are, respectively, the designations for the unmanifest, the manifest, and the mixed genders. (30)
The best [height] is two and a half cubits; the middle is increased by one quarter-cubit;
and the lowest is three times that [quarter-cubit], plus a quarter-cubit for the pedestal.
[The Māṇika] || 31 ||
In the science of arrows (bāṇa-śāstra), it is proclaimed that the length [of the bow] should be six parts and its height twice that;
furthermore, for each [type of arrow], there is a threefold range according to the hands of the superior and other [categories].
A linga made of gold or silver, one of great splendor, or an auspicious one from Gandhāra is desirable;
however, one that is inferior in substance, cruel, or exceeds the prescribed measurements is not desired.
Therefore, the tenfold characteristics of the Nāthārathaka temple type— consisting of Mānāṅghri, Chandasya, Vṛtta, Śṛṅga, Indu, and Śālā— are now described.
From fifty [aṅgulas], there are nine [units] less five; from ten cubits, there are nine [units] less than that.
This is the measurement for the Gāndhāra-śuddhadhāma-liṅga.
p. 163) By omitting four parts out of thirty-six hundred, there is an increase up to four cubits;
these ninety-nine types of *bandha* arise from the measurement of the *liṅga*. || 36 ||
Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Vimāna, and Bhadraka (or Rudraka)—
these nine, known as Śrīvatsa, Ukapa, and Nanda, are born from Vairāja.
Balabhī, Vajrapadma, Valayāṅka, and likewise Hari;
ending with Vṛṣa, Ibha, Hasa, and Tārkṣya—these constitute the nine divisions in their respective order.
The abode of Indra is Balabhīcchandaka; the supreme one is born from the Puṣpaka;
Vajra is from the heaven of the three worlds (Tripiṣṭapa); Candra, Padma, and Arka are from Dvālaka; and Hari is from Hari.
The Maṇika, Vṛṣabha, Nāga, Haṃsa, and Tārkṣya—these nine are indeed from the primary [class];
and from the secondary, there are eighteen prāsādas that possess both characteristics.
Other mountains born from these portions will be described in detail according to their sequence:
Mālyavān, Malaya, Supārśva, Meru, and Ambhavān. (41)
Himavat, though possessing a beautiful form, would be split by Meru and Mandara;
and Śrīparvata would be split by Vimāna and Mandara.
The Samudgaka is declared to be accompanied by Kelāsa and Mandara; and from the Vimāna arise the Latā, the Ghaṇṭā, and the Vibhāni.
Always. || 43 ||
From Bhadra arises Mahābhadra; Nalina is the Sarvabhadra [the face].
From Śrīvatsa comes the one called Vardhamāna; the Mālā is designated as Śrīvatsa. (44)
Nandi and Vṛddhi, with Khādhāra as the third, are proclaimed;
the hall and the large house are in the Brahma-mandira (or mandala).

From the lord of the house (gṛhādhipa), there arise the bhuvaja, the śikhika (or śivika), the veśmaprabhava, those born from the valabhī, the ardhagṛha, that which is called the kuṭīra, and the sthitikṛt. (46)
Śrīkaṇṭha, Svastika, Khaḍga, Kuliśa, Svastika, Gadā, and Cakra—these seven, known as the Svastikas, are born from the Vajra. || 47 ||
From the lotus (padma) comes the great lotus (mahāravinda); kumuda, utpala, and the three [others];
dundubhī, mukulī, cakra, uṣṇīṣī, and the one known as śaṅkha. || 48 ||
Drumavṛkṣa and Oghaṭa—these seven were the younger brothers of Valaya;
as well as Ṛkṣaka, Bhūṣaṇa, Bhūdhara, and Śrījaya. (49)
Pṛthvīdhara [is derived] from the sixty-four varieties arising from the bull;
these are the temples (prāsādas) described in the Bāṇaśāstra, though their specific divisions are extremely extensive.
And thirty-two thousand, plus four hundred, are said to be the divisions of the abodes (dhāman) distinguished within the Pārameśvara [Tantra]. (51)
A square, four-faced temple is prescribed for the four-faced Liṅga of Brahmā, but never for any others.
The temple for all the gods, as well as for the three-faced Liṅga, is proclaimed to have a single entrance and four corners. || 53 ||
This circular temple is said to be for the single-faced Liṅga and for the image of Bhava; it belongs to Maheśvara alone and to no one else. (54)
The temple of the four-faced Liṅga likewise has four doors; it is said that the temple of Īśvara is circular, and not that of anyone else.
Likewise, that which has one face and eight sides belongs to Viṣṇu and Bhava;
furthermore, this one with four doors belongs to Bhava as well as Brahmā.
Those that are square and elongated, as well as others that are circular and elongated—
all these *prasāda* temples are traditionally held to have a single door and to be endowed with the proper characteristics.
The *muktā-liṅga* of Maheśa and likewise the *kamalāsana*; indeed, temples are prescribed for all these images. (58)
The eighteen excellent *vāmagas* (leftward-moving) are said to be established in their respective positions;
having divided the number of hands into two parts, one should fashion the *meru* and so forth.
The outer wall is formed by the portions of Hara (*rudra*), and the *randhrakārikā* by the ten-fold parts (*daśāṃśa*).
The Krauḍabhitti [temple] was built by the portions of Rudra, and likewise the Suśira by the portions of the planets.
The half-pedestal consists of nine parts, and the remaining portions are likewise;

thus Meru shall consist of one hundred parts, and Mandara and the others are described in the same way. The outer pedestal is the wall of darkness, and it is exactly half the size of the inner pedestal.
By discarding each part in succession in this manner, it becomes Ānanda (Bliss). || 62 ||
Then, when the field has been divided by snakes (eight), the wall is formed by the parts consisting of pairs of hooves and nails (twenty);
the enclosure wall and the inner sanctum are formed by the pairs (four), while the pedestal is formed by the heat (three).
The wall, the blind-wall, the partition, the delusion (or illusion), and the pedestal (pīṭha) occur in sequence;
[these are determined] by thirty-two, twenty-four, eight, and sixteen parts respectively, within the ninefold division. (64)
In a field of sixty-four squares, the central pedestal (pīṭha) consists of four parts;
the well (suśira) consists of twelve parts, and the walls consist of twenty-seven parts.
From the gradual emergence of external *chandas* through the transformation of the "conqueror of teeth" (*dantajina*), there is a surrounding arrangement;
therefore, no pressure should be applied to the walls there.
Having divided the field into one hundred parts including the sun [six], and taking a transverse multiplier of nine parts, one should draw diagonal threads to the corners;
from the corner, one should remove three parts.
A pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be fashioned with five parts by omitting the planets, the elements, and the fires.
Indeed, from the opening, the arrangement of the chariot-axles (rathakāṇa) occurs at the Rāma portions (9). || 68 ||
In the center, its exit is formed by the divisions of action and the seasons; and there, surrounding it in the four directions, are nine chariot-like structures beginning with Action.

Its height from the base to the top is two and a half times that [width]; however, in some places, having divided the space between the hips and the shoulders by two hundred [parts], [the measurement is adjusted].
One should construct the floors beginning with the *kāryā* and others using parts of the nails, omitting one part at a time from the other;
even including the *candraśālā*, this continues up to sixteen floors.
In some cases, the uneven ground is said to be rough like an uneven chariot;
it possesses four horns, and the four nostrils extend halfway up the peaks.
The altar-ground is the waist, the neck is the throat, and the *āmalasāraka* is the cheek.
As before, there is Mount Meru, which has four faces and a hundred peaks.
In the quarters of Yama, Indra, the Moon, and Śukra [the planets Saturn, Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury], there are Heramba, Āditya, and Maṅgala;
the linga of another [deity] is likewise nine cubits in measurement from the door. (74)
Above the tip of the śukanāsa, there should be a lion with a distorted face;
the length of the lion is said to be half of the protrusion of the neck.
Its height is known to be one-third of that [measurement], and its width is equal to that; the elevation of the head-piece (mastaka) should be made according to the measure of the width and height.
The neck stands three parts high, with the *śukanāsa* (gargoyle) in the middle extending half [the height].
The tip of the nose protrudes by the same amount as the projection of the front neck.

The lion should be depicted with an ant's waist, its tail tucked behind by its hindquarters, possessing broad hips and a large chest, and endowed with a mane. (In this context, the reading "kesarānvitaḥ" found in the manuscripts uses the palatal *s*; it is etymologically correct when analyzed as "that which is scattered (*keśīryate*). ) || 78 ||
The *lelihāna* (tongue-like) part, with its neck turned upwards, is situated upon its own pedestal;
the altar (*vedi*) should serve as the support for the neck, with a width equal to half that of the temple (*prāsāda*). (79)
Upon the railings at the corners, there should be lions with distorted faces; they should be equal in width and length to their own man-lions (mānava), with their tails resting upon their heads.
Their length is proclaimed to be one-third [of the total];
the lions, endowed with their own characteristic features, should be made with flowing manes. || 81 ||
Likewise, upon the altar and in the cardinal directions, there are four figures in human form,
joined with hanging pendants and reaching up to the moon-chambers (candraśālā).

One should adorn the nine levels with the directions, the Vedas, the eight, the lotus, the limbs, the holders of the threefold knowledge, the planets, the *kinnaras*, the Mothers, the Gaṇas, and the Lords of Knowledge. (83)
Since there may be danger of collapse due to that which arises from the *garbhāśma-mañjarī*,
one should therefore make two apertures for the passage of water at each stage of the earth.
Meru: Having divided [the area] into eighty-four parts, one should discard two and a half parts from each corner;
there, the pedestal (piṇḍī) shall be formed by thirty-six parts, consisting of sixty-four divisions.
In that [mandala], the entry and exit occur in the center by means of the earth-lords (bhūpendra) and the suns (bhānu);
the exit occurs in every direction. Thus, nine chariot-arrays (rathaka) are recognized. 86.

In the space between the waist and the navel, having made one hundred sixty-two [units], the ground [of the first square] shall be formed by dividing by eighteen; the others follow in sequence, each minus one.
In this manner, there would be fourteen Bhuvah-worlds, provided with supports for the lotuses;
each having four gates, four nostrils, and endowed with various wonderful cavities.
The wise man should construct the auspicious Mandara mountain, provided with the previously mentioned necks and peaks of the altar, and possessing ninety peaks.

In the Mandara [mandala], within a field divided into thirty-six parts, there are four parts from each corner. One should eliminate the cord, the form, that which is at its front, and the fire-line drawn transversely.
Having established the chariot at the end of the Veda (four) with a portion of three, moon, and fire (313),
one should likewise cut off [the same distance] within the interval and establish the middle half-chariot with the waters (four).
Starting from the corner, one should proceed with the remaining half in this very manner.
Having made the spire (śikhara) twice the height of the hip (kaṭi) plus a half, it should be fashioned as described above for the section above the hip.

Having made one hundred and one parts from the first bhūmi of the kings, she [the earth] was formed; by the successive omission of each remaining part, its height became equal to that of the sun's orb.
One should construct the excellent Kailāsa, which has four nostrils and faces, is endowed with moon-chambers and deities, and is possessed of eighty peaks.
Kailāsa:
When the field is divided into two by the mantra, there are twenty-four ears (śrutis) in the heart of Rudra.
From the left, the corner is formed by the reduction of three; from those two, the pillar is formed by the reduction of one. 95.
The upper chariot should consist of one part water and three parts in the middle;
in this very same manner, the lower half should likewise be formed in all four directions on every side.
In the center, it is adorned with peak-turrets following the columnar spires,
along with moon-crested finials, door-leaves and bolts, water-jars representing the Vedas, and lattice windows shaped like serpents.
Having divided the eastern ground into ninety-five parts above the waist,
one should construct ten levels (bhūmis) starting from Indra’s region, with each subsequent level decreasing by one part.
The ground, the abode, the chariots, the five, and the two chariots marked with arches; the hollows, the gods, and in the center of the small chariot, there are the celestial palaces (vimānas).
Half [of the structure] consists of jar-shaped door-panels that look at one another;
the lord of the primary door has eight feet and seventy horns.

The celestial chariot (*vimāna*): In a field twice the size of that of Śakra, a chariot is situated in the center; it is formed by six parts, with the two lower foundations (*uparadhi*) considered to be constructed from one part each and three parts respectively. (101)

The *anuratha* should be constructed with two [parts], the *koṇabandha* with those consisting of three [parts], the *sāndhāra* and *caturāsya* with four [parts], and the *vedāghra* should be provided with circular enclosures (*bhramaṇa*). || 102 ||
With chariots possessing peaks and turrets, provided with seven-flamed [fires] and moon-chambers, and filled with lovely Vidyādharas, Bhadra would have sixty peaks. (103)
In the Bhadra [type],
there are two small cells (kuṭīs) on each level, and ten pillars made of wood there;
the Mahābhadra is said to be adorned with staircases and the characteristic parts of the Bhadra.
Mahābhadra is equal in extent to Bhadravattala; it is turned downwards at the bottom and upwards at the top, consisting of celestial palaces (vimāna), and in sequence, they are Meru and Mandara. 105.
Kailāsa, Nandana, Śrīvatsa, and that known as Bhadra—
all these should be constructed with peaks, for they constitute the Sarvatobhadra, which is the soul of all.

It is joined with seven chariot-stages, endowed with the Vedas as its feet and faces, and possessed of whirling motion; it has Puṣpaka in its hands, is beautiful with four porticos in the four directions,
provided with four jars, and equipped with staircases and balconies.
The Sarvatobhadra:
On a field divided into thirty-six parts, one should draw a circle at each corner by omitting three parts.
Similarly, Piṇḍāmbu is always without a name, followed by Śara and Ratha in the middle half; elsewhere, however, it is thus increased by Saptaratha.
The hall with a pinnacle and a moon-ornament should have doors facing the cardinal directions, with its feet and mouth possessing a beautiful luster.
The *rucaka* [type]:
when the field has been divided into ten parts, a *rathaka* (chariot-square) is formed in the middle by three parts;
two *anurathas* (smaller chariot-squares) are to be made with one and a half parts each, and the corner is likewise from two parts.
And likewise, the corners according to their divisions. || 110 ||
There are chariots with five-fold ground and one foot, as well as four peaks;
the chariot is marked by the abode (dhāman), and the earth is the chariot situated within the hollow (kuharī). || 111 ||
In the caves, men and women, lions, tigers, elephants, birds, monkeys, and so forth, dwell together;
such is the Śrīvatsa mark, which is dear to Hari.

The Śrīvatsa, the Caturasra, the Sāndhāra, the Bhadra, and the Rudra— these five types of three-storied pavilions (gati) should be constructed for the lord of the house, provided they possess lion-like shoulders and are joined with pure structural supports (amalāsāra). || 113 ||
The King of Houses (gṛharāja): When the Indra [or Nidra] division has been established in the edifice, the corners are formed from the water-carrying (jalahāni) lines;
two [lines] should be made for the side-chariots (anuratha), and the middle chariot is formed by the four parts (vedāṃśa).
With one leg, possessing seven stories, adorned with five lines and the moon,
filled with various gods, delightful, the Nandana grove is the joy of the gods. (115)
Nandana.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh rule, titled "The Construction of the Nine-Tiered Palace with a Central Hall," in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*. [The word "named" (*nāma*) does not appear in the manuscript copies.]

Now, the twenty-eighth [verse]: in the portion of the Vedas (four), with the feet added (eight), and being long (twelve), it is the "pregnant" [meter] consisting of the remaining parts (the nakhas, twenty).
On both sides there should be a wall with five [units], and it should extend behind and in front on all sides—or, according to the Kh manuscript, by half a unit.
When the field is divided into ten parts, the central portion is considered the *madhya-ratha*;
the *upākhyaratha* and the corner (*koṇa*) are each made from four half-parts.
In succession. || 2 ||
From the entry of the fire of the thin wings, the remainder is thus in each city (pura) in front and behind;
it should be in the side-half, in the portion of Rudra, by means of three parts from the center, [measured] by pairs and waters.
The corners of the *ratha* and *atiratha* pavilions are each separated by water;
it is provided with *valabhī*, *candraśālā*, and four *nāsikā*-like projections.
The shank is raised by the planets (nine units) through its qualities; the seven stories occupy three parts.
The drum, the crescent moon, and the *śālikā* are each two units, while the height of the pinnacle is one *meru* (eighteen units).
Having made the portion for the modification the length, and one-third the width,
one should contract the portion for the armor from the right side to form the pinnacle.

Due to the downward extension of the upper thread, the female abode (strīdhāmā) resembles a Śrī-puta. In some cases, six lions with pot-shaped heads, shining like Mount Meru and other peaks, are to be fashioned.
Having divided the four corners eightfold by means of devotion (the reading *bhaktvā* is correct),
one should draw out sixteen [lines]. Two by two should be joined on both sides of the six pairs, and two at the front for the sake of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Maya spoke of the *garbha* (the womb/central part) as the suns; others say it is so because of the destruction of the Jinas.
The nose should be fashioned with the meanings of the Vedas (*vedārtha*), while the nostrils are the Vedas themselves, situated on the peak of the mountain of the nose.
The *valabhī* (pinnacle) is on the exterior; on the eight-cornered [base], there is a vajra-face, while on the single-legged mouths it rests upon the ground.
In the case of the Lord of the Gods (*surādhipa*), the inner sanctum is circular, or has four corners, or eight corners, or is one-eighth [of the total].
The vajra has ten points;
the lotus should have sixteen points according to some views, or it may be circular, joined with a lotus of eight petals. || 11 ||
Likewise, the abode of the gods named Padma is endowed with joints and petals, circular in shape, very beautiful, having one door and one nose. 12.
The lotus [is formed] by a circle drawn from the midpoint of the diagonal line of the square, elevated by one-eighth [of that distance];
being thus circular, it is called a "valaya" (enclosure) as it is surrounded by a rim. || 13 ||
The petals within the enclosures of the *valaya* (encircling bands) are like the interior of armor (*kaṅkaṭa*).
The pure essence of the neck of the altar-platform is as before, except for the absence of the nose.
The Valaya [enclosure]:

from the placement of the nose at the corner of the Yuga-field, extending outward by one and a half [units], it is elevated in the middle like a circle, with its front face adorned by eight lions. || 15 ||

This temple named Siṃha, beloved by Narasiṃha and the gods, is characterized by corner-projections (*karṇa-koṇa*), yoke-pieces (*yuga*), feet (*aṅghri*), and faces (*āsya*), which pierce the frontal globes of elephants.
Homa is dear to the immortals. || 16 ||
The lion [pedestal] is circular at its base; in the [inner] field, it should be provided with pillar-like shanks. The bull [pedestal] has a nose-protrusion, four corners, and a height of five units.
From the corner of the four-angled [mandala] and from the urine-line (mūtra), one should fashion the curved part in the portion of the elephant;
on the back it is circular, with two corners at the tip, and like the interior, it has a prominent nose.
The Gaja [Vimāna]: When a square field of sixteen units is prepared, with a circular interior for the Śuka-nose and the Jaṅghā, it is the Kaṭī of the Vimāna called Bhadra. (19)
And the Mañcaryā of Śrīvatsa is marked by a swan;
it is situated on both sides of the waist, equal to it, and constantly directed upwards.
One should place Brahmā in two parts;
Hari and Śaṅkara are each in two parts.
Or, according to the desire of the patron, another deity who bestows auspiciousness may be installed. (21)
The *haṃsa* [is formed] with eight feet at the corners of the *yuga*, and with the nose and wings like the interior [of the previous figure].
The shank should be made like a pillar, with a high nose and joined by wings. || 22 ||

The womb is a hexagon; Tārkṣya is with the *kuṭās* [the *śaktis*]; the five elements together with the Sun are the hips, neck, and face; and it is established in the sacrificial bricks (*iṣṭakā*) that are well-situated. || 23 ||
In the square known as the "neck-noose" (kaṇṭhapāśa), there is a circumambulation path formed by the corner sanctuaries;
in the cardinal directions, all the [shrines] beginning with Balabhī are provided with stairs and plinths.
Tārkṣya: the height is double the width; in one part of the *jaṅghā* is the *napuṃsaka*; above that, by half [a part], there should be the *haṃsa*; the *vedī* is equal to the *garbha*. (25)
Joined with peaks in all directions, possessing a neck, fillet, and core;
endowed with a pitcher by means of half of Śeṣa— this is like the housework of a eunuch.
It is established that for the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and others, three pairs and one hand are prescribed;
it resembles the hollow of the armpit, with the neck and head adorned by its edge. || 27 ||
The other [type] is characterized as inferior and non-inferior.
Among those beginning with Meru and ending with Garuḍa, the Nāgarī style is said to be produced by the turning of the serpent;
the Lāṭī style is similar to the Nāgarī, but it is fashioned from wood. (28)
When the Nāgarī style is made with increased proportions for the legs, the upper stories (candraśālā), and the floors,
it is proclaimed by the wise as Vārāṭī.
Where the *jaṅghikā* (the lower shaft) supports pillars, plates, and bands of various colors,
and there are leaf-patterns within the *mekhalā* (waistband), that is called the Drāviḍī style.

The girdles at the waist of the vimāna should have a height of three times its width plus one-quarter; they are considered to be provided with projections for the pillars, mouths, bands, and vakulī ornaments.
The Kālindī, the Gauḍikā, the Pañcikā, and the Pādacandrikā—thus have they been described according to the scriptures, by way of a brief indication of their general forms. (32)

The *nāgarī* style is considered to bestow happiness in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*), while the *vārāṭī* and others do so in their own respective regions; in other lands, other styles bring misery.
One who desires prosperity should never employ the *miśrakā* style, which is excessively mixed.
However, according to another school of thought, they must be performed with effort as pure [or auspicious] rites alone. || 34 ||
Having understood [this] again and again, artisans shall fashion [the temple] with subtle works.
The characteristics of the palace have been declared; now the nose-door (nāsādvāra) is described. 35.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Liṅgas, Measures, and Temples," in the Compendium of Characteristics. || 28 ||

Now, the nineteenth [chapter]: Temples are considered to be of three kinds—[those with] one-quarter, one-eighth, or less than one foot [of the base]; they are prescribed with a width for the nose (nāsā) equal to half the thread-line of the inner sanctum (garbha) and its secondary chamber (anugarbha). || 1 ||
Its emergence is fivefold, according to the distinctions of the *uttama* (excellent) and other types;
it is measured by one-eighth, one-sixteenth, one-thirtieth, and one-sixty-fourth parts of the womb's size. || 2 ||
The first [section], beginning with the "chariots" (ratha), consists of seven [parts];
the "grounds" (bhūmikā) are joined with the odd-numbered ones.
Together with the intervening water-spaces, they are divided into three parts like a palace.

The *candraśālās* (dormer windows) should be made with a height equal to half that of the spire (*śikhara*) and adorned [with ornaments]; they should be provided with leaf-patterns, sprouts, and the like, as well as finials (*śṛṅga*) and so forth, and equipped with *bherī*, *icchu*, and *rakā* (or *cchivuka*).
Adorned with crests and forehead marks, and further embellished by Hari above,
one should consecrate them and install the deities within the Candragarbha as before.
From the center, fire (three parts) should be taken; from the revolution (twelve parts), the bherī (nine parts); and from the destruction of the qualities (six parts).
Having subtracted eighteen parts from the circumference, the śukanāsikā (front porch) is formed.
For the sake of accomplishing all desires, one should first have a door constructed in the middle of the eastern side of the hall that is the abode of wealth.
The western [side] is for the sake of attaining accomplishment; the northern [side] bestows peace and nourishment;
and for cruel rites, one should likewise perform it on the southern side or in the intermediate directions.
Liṅgas with one, two, or three faces, as well as the eastern door, are desired first; however,
the northern direction is for both the manifest (vyakta) and the unmanifest (avyakta).
For Surā, Agni, Indra, and for all purposes, it is in the northeast; for the worship of the Liṅga, it is in the west.

Cāmuṇḍā is in the Bhairava [temple], and the door for Yama and the Moon is in the south or in the north for Caṇḍī and Bhadrakālī; or else, [the door for] Indra is in the east and for Varuṇa in the west.
One should construct doors in the four directions for the Brahma-vedāsya and the liṅga.
All those auspicious [deities] stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions face east and west;
they face toward the corner-hall, the moon-pavilion, the southern hall, and the corner-shrine.
The door, measuring one-third of the height (dhāman), should be divided into parts for its width;
the best, middle, and lowest sizes are determined respectively by divisions of four, six, and eight [parts]. 13.
From the end of Rudra up to Viṣṇu, and from the end of Keśava, that [measurement] is broad;
the door for those with one, two, or three hands and so forth shall be according to the measurement of the liṅga.
The lowest [door] should always be in the highest chamber, the middle one in the middle chamber;
the highest door is in the lowest [chamber], as is stated according to the measurement of the womb.

The door for those of inferior status and so forth shall be three, four, or five parts of the total, when the womb and neck (or corner) have been divided into sections corresponding to the superior, middling, and inferior types.
In a small temple, the width of the corner of the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is considered by some to be twice the size of the door; otherwise, the measurement for the height is stated differently. (17)
The ten doors are established with sixty hundred (six thousand) finger-breadths and so forth, decreasing by ten at each step; and among them, four are the foremost. || 18 ||
In this case, three should be of medium size and three indeed of small size;
the width should be half the height, or the height should be three times greater than the width. || 19 ||
Alternatively, the door that brings auspiciousness may be measured by the fingers of Dignāga and others in successive order;
the lintel (śākhā) is wide by half its height and has an odd number of divisions.
Equal to that, or twice that minus eight, is the measurement for the first udumbara;
the width of the branch is considered to be one aṅgula less than the width of the two arms.
The door, which grants desired boons, is adorned with three branches corresponding to the number of mountains and planets;
according to some, it is considered to be endowed with the Rudra-branch within the abode of the Great Image.

Having made the width like that of the nails, the thickness is divided by the lunar days (fifteen). The staff and the branches are each one-sixth part, and the [three] sections of the trunk are each one-third part.

The subtle body (tanu), which is called "form" (rūpa) by its share of the elements (bhūtabhāga), remains as the producer of blindness; from the pair of rays, that which is called "the root" (mūla) should be produced in the form of poison. || 24 ||
Two hundred and two *daṇḍas* each, together with two and a half arrows; thus, the entry of all the *andhakārikās* shall be equal to the root and the branches. || 25 ||
The triple-branch gate:
the width of the thirty-fold part is increased by two parts; having divided those two into halves, the outer portion of the gate shall be the stalk and the branches. (26)
By its breadth, it enters the interior of the moon's darkness by one-sixteenth part;
indeed, its branches extend from the four Vedas with a width of one and a half units of water.
It should be made with a width of three-quarters [of the door], extending to the end of the *andhāra*;
from its two entrances, this pillar-shaft (*stambha-śākhā*) shall have a width equal to the lord [of the measurement]. 28.
The six *veśas* and *Dandhakārī* are reduced by one-quarter of their width;
from the shoulder (*aṃsa*), the width of the *rūpa-śākhā* and so forth is reduced by one-sixth.
The one called Dhvānta (Darkness) has a width of three-quarters of a part from its entrance;
Marīci has a width of two and a quarter parts from its entrance.
On the leaf-patterned branches and at the openings,
the craftsmen should fashion decorative bands and other ornaments with a width equal to one-twelfth part of the thickness, in accordance with the overall beauty of the design.
The door has five branches. The right petal shall have an extent of forty-five parts;
it is named Daṇḍāndhakārikā, while the branch of form is called Śāntā.
*Andhārī* is *patraśākhā*; *dhvāntā* is known as *stambhaśākhikā*. *Andhakārī*, however, is *rūpākhyā*; and *cāndhakārī* is *marīcikā*. (33)
From the nose down to the end of the root-branches, it is held that the divisions increase sequentially by one and a half, four and a half,
two and a half, one, and one and a half [units]. (34)
By her, through the half of two bodies and one quarter of a wing [of the water-born],
the root-branch arises from the fifth part of the arrows; and from the staff, there is the entry of the elements.
The wise should fashion a decorative band (paṭṭikā) on the branch-member (śākhāṅga) for the sake of beauty, using portions of seven, nine, two, and five [units] respectively. 36.
The door has seven branches;
the bolt should be made from a portion of five units, a portion of eleven,
and half of a hundred.
The one named Daṇḍānukārikā is a branch of the pillar called Dhvānta.
Andhakārī is called Mṛṇālā; Andhakārī is also Varuthikā. Dhvāntā is called Patraśākhā, and likewise there is Andhakārikā again. || 38 ||
The pillar is called Andha; the form is named Rūpa; the Andhakārī is like a mirage;
and the leaf-branch should be made in sequence like a half-arrow and a half-moon.
The forms of the single yuga and the five [yugas] are [determined] by the numbers one, four, ten, one, and water (four), which are designated as the Vedas, the single yuga, and so forth. 40.
And the two Aśvins are established by the Vedas, the staffs, the twenty-two, the six, and the two;
together with the five waters.
The seven arrows [pierce] the nine apertures with the Rudras. || 41 ||
Due to the convergence of the root and the branches within all the *andhakārikās*,
one should know that the *paṭṭikā* is the branch once the branches have been condensed.
The door has nine branches. Having divided the width and thickness, [the proportions] are by sixty parts multiplied by seven;
[these constitute] the staff, the blind-panel, the serpent-head, and the pillar-blind-panel.
Patrāndhakārī, Rūpākhyā, Dhvāntanāmikā, Nāgāndhakārīkāhvā, and again Stambhāndhakārikā. || 44 ||
Patratamāṅkikā is the form [of the goddess] Andhakārī;
Mṛṇālikā is known as Andhā, while Marīcyaṅkā is celebrated as Mūlaśākhā. || 45 ||
Together with the *sārdhabhūtas*, with one and a half yugas, one fortnight, and five moons;
and with four Vedas, one and a half, and four again—these constitute the fourth form of the ocean of existence (*bhavāmbu*). || 46 ||
The stability of the two branches and the two doorways should be known, respectively, by means of one, two, one, and a half units of water measured by the moon. (47)
The entry of the Gāndhārīs occurs, as before, at the fourth parts of the lunar days of the Bhūta-pakṣa, namely seven, five, eight, six, twelve, one, and two. || 48 ||
The eleven branches [are placed] on the left. (p. 184) At one-fourth the height of the branch, two door-keepers (pratīhārau) are situated below;
Jāhnavī and Yamunā are also on its sides, as well as the bearer of the burden (bhāravāhikā).
It is adorned with beautiful leafy creepers, pairs of kinnaras and others,
and vidyādharas rich in splendor, as well as with jars and pairs of nāgas [or pāṭala trees].
One should carefully decorate the remaining branches with swastikas, garlands, śrīvatsas, lotuses, and stones, as well as with very beautiful ornaments made of gold.
Śrī, Yakṣeśa, Gaṇeśa, Vyākhyārudra, or Mṛtyujit should first be installed in the Udumbara [tree], adorned with all their limbs. (52)
Beyond Brahmā and Viṣṇu is Rudra; Guha has two faces and the face of an elephant; and the planets, the Mothers, and the Vidyās are established in the activity of eating and so forth. || 53 ||
Above that, the artisan should fashion in sequence a firm and beautiful forehead on the *udumbara* beam, provided with decorative ivory pegs (*nāgadanta*).
The two sages, having made them equal in width to the branches and equal in height to that [door],
[should do so] with a quarter of the door's height, or with two cubits.
The inferior livelihood occurs above;
the portion of the Nāgas is increased by half of a hundred parts (fifty parts) from the portion of Rāma at the junction.
The *khuraka* is made with one part of *yama*, and the *stambhī* with two parts;
the three *guṇa* and three *giri* parts [make up the height], and the two *khuras* each consist of two parts.
The *andhārī* is one part of the body; the *khurajaṅghikā* is six parts;
the *guṇādhāna* is five parts; and the *muṇḍaka* is made with the remaining parts. (58)

The *cūlikā* (finial) should be made with four parts of the measure known as *skandhamālā*, and the *yugala* (pair) with two parts; the *dehalī* (threshold) and the *vyāghrapaṭṭikā* (tiger-stripe molding) should be made with four parts of the *yama* (twofold) measure.
Having well-constructed the door within the middle of the palace wall,
one should place something slightly to the north for the purpose of destroying all piercing.
The defects, such as *kṣaya* and so forth, always exist at the gateway when it is joined with the Vedas (or *veda*, according to the readings *mū*, *a*, *g*, *gh*, *ṅ*).
Therefore, for the purpose of avoiding those, the knowledge of the Guru is declared [by the King, according to *kh*]. || 61 ||
If pierced by a house, there is constant passion; by a crossroads, however, the destruction of intellect.
If pierced by a carriage road, there will be exile; by a four-way junction, there is harshness.
A head with three lines indicates headache; a śṛṅgāṭaka [triangle] indicates great fear;
a tree-shaped mark indicates loss of wealth; and a pillar-shaped mark indicates servitude to others.
Through the archway (toraṇa) there would be hatred; through the decorative band (bhogapaṭṭī), fear of serpents;
through the corner (koṇa), royal punishment; and through the door-leaf (dvāraśākhā), delusion.
By a banner there shall be loss of wealth; by a pit or trench, emaciation;
by a well, fear of an enemy; and by a hole bored by a deity, imprisonment. (65)
If pierced by a pond, epilepsy occurs; by mud, the destruction of desired objects;
by ashes, the loss of cattle; and by a *vardhamāna* (a type of vessel), the piercing of cows.
(186) Loss of sons occurs through *apāka*; poverty through *cuhlībiddha*; loss of wealth through *vaktra*; and fear through *ālindaśravaṇa*. (67)

If pierced by a *sabhā*, there is poverty; if by water, the loss of wealth; if by a chariot, fear; if by a small insect (*kṣaudra*), as it is said, there is danger from swarms of flies; and if by a pit, the loss of one's children. (68)
By one pierced by a shadow there is poverty; by one pierced by a water-vessel, a wicked mind;
by one pierced by a pestle (or ring), loss of wealth; and likewise, by one pierced by a stone, there is disease. (69)
Therefore, with the performer's desire for merit, one should effect the abandonment of the piercing by means of the gift of a high wall or by the removal of that [piercing]. || 70 ||
By abandoning twice the area of that ground, the defect of piercing (vedha) does not arise;
however, a threshold (dehalī) that is set with a stake or is excessively high destroys the builder.
A woman who has risen from a lowly state and is surely destitute of wealth should have her pedestal half the height of the linga;
such is the height of the pedestal for an image.
Greed and anger arise, as does sorrow, when the door is devoid of the measurement;
and if the door is wide at the bottom, there will be disease or an unsteady wife.
One should give [the land] with a narrow middle for a man, or with a broad upper part for female ownership;
a "middle like an ant" (pipīlikāmadhya) leads to ruin, while a "conch-neck" (śaṅkhakaṇṭhaka) destroys the lineage. (74)
A tree with faces [branches] facing cows, buffaloes, or servants brings about their destruction;
when it has split branches, an opening for decay, or is confused in its directions, there is confusion regarding its location. (75)
If it is joined with both old and new [wood], there is poverty and many husbands;
if it is dilapidated or reversed, there is constant loss of wealth for the man. (76)
In a house that is crooked and riddled with the openings caused by disease, there will be strife for the man;
likewise, if it opens by itself, there will be various forms of suffering and harm.
Unmāda, Kulahṛt, Mṛtyu, and Mūla—these are located at the door in the sequence of Pha, Pha, and Pha.
One should always abandon a house where the left door is pierced by these, out of fear for the destruction of the family.

I have described what is called the "general piercing" (sāmānyavedha) for both houses and palaces; this applies when there is a distance of twice the [required] interval between the two sites to be pierced and the piercer.
Whatever auspicious rite for pacification has been performed as desired, which bestows welfare upon all—including the doors and other parts—I shall now describe those [rites]. (80)
Having combined the length and width of the two doors, measured in finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
one should divide that total by three, six, or eight.
Knowledge is its abode, and it is the exhaustion of the fire; hear now its qualities:
stability, nourishment, radiance, movement, and impartiality.
Friends, wealth, a multitude of cattle, renunciation before attaining sovereignty, the non-falling from one's desires,
and despondency— these are the fruits for embodied beings in the seven [sub-periods] within the portion of Ādri.

Whatever remains as the residue of that worship of yours—beginning with the first and ending with the eighth—is always auspicious when it is odd-numbered, while even numbers therein lead to undesirable results. (84)

Those known as the Banner, Lion, Bull, and Elephant are situated in the cardinal directions, beginning with the East; while Smoke, Dog, Donkey, and Crow are likewise situated in the intermediate directions. (85)
The proportions of the flagstaff (*dhvaja*) and so forth for the channels (*nādī*) are as follows:
these qualities bestow fortune, good luck, sons, and long life upon women, and they grant the increase of righteousness (*dharma*).
The banner. || 86 ||
Hari grants victory, health, wealth, friends, and all perfections; Vṛṣa bestows wives, sons, and wealth, granting every happiness and prosperity.
The dog is said to be a constant fire that causes the heat of disease, a smoke that destroys all purposes, a bestower of sickness and death, and a plunderer of wealth and lineage. 88.
The donkey brings about the eradication of the remainder [of one's merit], as well as enmity, separation, death, and punishment;
it causes emaciation, harshness, poverty, and all manner of misfortune. (89)
The Vāyasa [sub-period] brings about the loss of wife, sons, army, wealth, prosperity, and longevity; it causes grief, delusion, strife, disease, bondage, and the like. (90)
Having understood the proportions, one should apply two, four, or even five barley-corns, or even a single finger-breadth, so that the length may become excellent.
Having done this, one should establish the door according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth procedure, titled "The Characteristics for the Installation of the Deity Door," in the Compendium of Characteristics.
Now begins the thirtieth.
Having first performed the Vāstuyāga as previously described for the pavilion,
the construction of the altar and subsequent rites should be carried out above the pedestal (or half of it), just as in the case of the temple.
One should decorate the outer walls with the pillars of the pavilion’s roof-ridges;
for others, [the decoration] should be done with [architectural elements] such as the *karma* (base), but not with *maṇḍapas* for the most excellent [temples].
Likewise, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) may be one and a half times, or twice, the measure of the base;
and there shall be seven, twenty-one, or indeed thirty-seven pillars.
And therein, six pillars are described as preeminent by name and form:
the one called Rucaka, which is four-cornered; and the one named Vajra, which is eight-cornered. (4)
The one called Ativajra has sixteen spokes, while Pralīnaka has ten spokes;
Manthāna has sixty-four spokes, and the one named Manmatha is circular.
It is twelve finger-breadths in width, and its height is equal to the height of the door.
This common pillar should be applied in this manner for the smallest [type].
The height should increase by four finger-breadths, and they also increase in width; in some traditions, the height of the pillar is considered to be three-quarters of the measurement of the temple.
(190) Marked with lotuses, with water-vessels having faces like lotus petals and bearing jars below,
they should be adorned in the middle with strings of pearls and above with pure central pillars (sārakas). || 8 ||
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed from pillars, female pillars, hip-plates, and large, excellent liṅgas; its lower portion should extend downwards from the height of the legs.
The pavilion for others, however, consists of pillars joined in groups of four or eight;
I shall now describe those that are declared as common in all the scriptures. (10)
Susūtra, Apabhadra, Siṃha known as Dvipada,
Karṇikāra, Haryakṣa, Sugrīva, and Maṇibhadraka. || 11 ||
Mānava, Nandana, Tāpa, Śatrundana,
Śuśīla, Viśāla, Yajñabhadra, and Śrutīśvara.
Vāstusaṅkīrṇaka by name, another called Viṣama, Śrīvatsa, Jaya, Jayabhadra, and then Buddhibhṛt. (13)
The Kauśalya, the one named Puṣpananda, the Suvrata, the Puṣpabhadraka,
and the one known as Puṣpakānta— these are the seven [twenty pavilions (maṇḍapa) according to the Liṅgapurāṇa].
They may consist of twelve [pillars] and so on, increasing by two each time, up to a final total of sixty-four.
According to the sequence of the ritual pillar (stambha), the fingers beginning with the little finger are designated as such in accordance with the scriptures. || 15 ||
(191) They should be established with very firm, beautiful, and excellent materials such as stone or wood;
and in their center, likewise, one, two, or three superstructures (*vimāna*) should be placed above.
The necks should be fashioned together with impurities, marrow, and jars;
they are triangular, circular, half-moon-shaped, crescent-like, and sixteen-sided.
The quadrangular [diagram] bestows, in sequence, the attainment of sovereignty, enemies, the anus, sons, and wealth; indeed, it yields all these fruits. (18)
The characteristics of the pavilion:
In the east is the one named Vṛṣa, and in the southeast is Nāyakesarī;
Valabhīcchanda is in the south, and Garuḍa is prescribed for the southwest.
Likewise, the Śrīvṛkṣaka should be in the north-east, or else the sixteen-sided one in the north-west;
the Purāgaja is in the north, and the Sarvabhadraka is in the north-east.
These pavilions (maṇḍapas) are known as mixed; they should be employed in the performance of the rite.
They are fashioned upon various divisions, such as the square and so forth, or upon circular sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). || 21 ||
Those [liṅgas] scattered in the various directions are beneficial for performing their respective functions;
these, along with the half-measures, should be employed in the ritual accomplishment (sādhana), and never otherwise.
Having made it square and equal, with fourteen cubits in its smallest form,
one should divide it according to the desired proportions, increasing by two [cubits] for each subsequent size.
The walls are one part on all sides, and the *vīthikā* (corridor) is three parts;
provided with pillars in front and behind, the sanctum (*garbhaka*) is three parts each. (24)
In the middle of the two houses, an external space should be made for the purpose of a staircase;
likewise, the walls of those two should be one part, and the door in the middle should be three parts.
Above that, on the ground, one should construct four pillars in the middle;
one should fashion the *lopakula* (the central core) as well as the four walls situated at the corners.
It has four walls, four gateways, and a series of pillars all around;
it is provided with *mattavāraṇa* panels and is topped with successive tiers of roofing.
In the center, one should construct a dancing hall called Citra, joined with a pavilion, possessing a beautiful neck and a spotless core, and provided with a lotus and a water-pot.
The characteristics of the dance hall (*nāṭyaśālā*):
Its roof-ridge should be made of thick bricks, it should be treated with smooth clay and mud,
and it should be purified with the powder of *khalī*.
Likewise, with powders made from mung beans. || 29 ||
Having sprinkled it with *āmrātaka* water, one should cover it for three days in succession;
then, having smeared it with powdered mustard and ginger, the wise practitioner should subsequently spread [the covering] over it. (30)
Then, having further pounded it with mallets using the juice of *āmrātaka* fruit,
one should cover it with moss until it becomes as smooth as a mirror.
Having drawn it out from the moss, one should smear it with the paste of oil-cake;
then, after resting for one night, one should smear it with cow dung. (32)
The characteristic of pulverization:
having burnt the stūpa of cow-sugar, one should then diligently sprinkle it with the decoction of *śaṇaphalī* and *aṅghrikā*, or with the juice of the *sthopalatā* creeper. (33)

[The preparation should be made] with water boiled with *āmrātaka* roots and the decoction of *triphalā*, or with water in which black gram (*māṣa*) has been steamed, or even with the water of steamed *bilva*. || 34 ||
Alternatively, one may use the juice of *kolā* fruit, *viḍaṅga*, and *uśīra*, or water from a river of buttermilk, or even plain water;
thereafter, one should have coarse powders made from the mortar and other ingredients. || 35 ||
Having opened it with *sūrya*-flowers and gathered those powders, the wise one should place them inside a vessel and then pour in the liquids.
Then, moist buffalo hide, crushed hemp fibers, sand, cow's milk, resin oil, and linseed oil; 37.
Having prepared [the paste] for ten days with curd,
honey, oil, and water, it should be ground with the juice of *āmrātaka* by one called Sthūlāsyā-dugdhikā.
Another excellent *sudhā* (mortar) is prepared by mixing these same substances with fine flour;
having kneaded them with jaggery and curd, one should smear it over the *dugdhikā* plant.
(39) This is the characteristic of *sudhā*.
The "diamond paste" (vajralepa) is now described here for the purpose of strengthening the joints of the *liṅkha* and other parts.
One should have finely ground powder of smooth stone and well-powdered ram's horn mixed with sand, and then rub it with *umā* oil.
[One should take] linseed powder mixed with a decoction of *meṣaśṛṅga*. || 41 ||
Having thoroughly ground it, one should cook it until it has reached a state of uniform consistency;
this is known as Vajralepa (adamantine cement), likewise when combined with Sarja resin.
Now, the firm binding is described in detail:
with beeswax, and with very strong, fresh pastes made from hemp fibers. (43)
Having ground together guggulu resin mixed with sand and powder derived from stone,
one should thoroughly cook it after mixing it with linseed oil.
That is declared to be the adamantine plaster (vajralepa), and after that, the binding of the ground (bhūmibandha).
The binding of the ground is prescribed for temples, houses, and so forth. (46)

The characteristics of the diamond-paste (*vajralepa*): With powdered clay and bricks, combined with oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), the ground should be made as firm as stagnant water; thus it becomes a level *sutala*. (47)

Having thus leveled the ground, one should thereafter begin the binding of the perimeter (bhūbandha). Taking excellent, smooth, and unbroken grains of sand, the wise practitioner should take the moist bark from a mango tree and grind it to make a paste.
One should prepare a paste from that and, having dried it, form it into a pill in the sun.
Having thus purified that paste seven times over again and again,
one should then knead it with curd and perform the binding of the ground.
Alternatively, the binding of the ground is prescribed by another method:
one should make the ground level, beautiful, well-situated, and filled with water. (50)
One should cause the resin of that very paste mentioned previously to be given;
one should employ the substance in portions commensurate with the time.
The number of portions is stated according to the appropriate season:
in summer there should be five portions, and likewise three in the winter season. (52)
In autumn, three-quarters [of the land] should be given, and two parts at the onset of the rainy season;
having given thus as previously stated, the bond regarding the earth is declared here.
Then, having smeared [the body] with the *kūrca* brush stroke by stroke as it dries,
the wise practitioner should have the *kūrca* removed from the water.
Astringent and slimy substances, as well as resin and bark from the śālmali, tinduka, and similar trees, are recommended for binding the ground. (55)
For as many bricks, pieces of wood, stones, and so forth as there are in the temple of the deity,
for that many thousands of years shall the builder rejoice in that city.

The Characteristics of the Earth-Binding (bhūbandha): (196) By the command of Śiva, five Herambas, who are the forms of obstacles, reside in five locations—at the commencement, on the navel, the nose, the shoulders, and the head—respectively. (57)
Ālasya, Mohana, Vibhrama, and likewise Śāsaka;
the fifth is named Kāladaṇḍa—these, along with their lineages, are the yielders of fruit. || 58 ||
Ālasya causes indolence, and Mohana causes delusion; Vibhrama causes confusion, while Śāsaka always exercises authority. (59)
The extremely fierce Kāladaṇḍa may cause great fear of punishment;
these are obstacles in the abode of the gods as long as they have not been worshipped. (60)

Having performed the ritual on a sacrificial mound or within the city with white and other [colored powders] according to the prescribed form, all [the deities] are surrounded by the six limbs; they destroy obstacles through offerings and oblations.
Those who disregard their preceptor and act contrary to his wishes commit manifold faults;
therefore, at the outset of a śrāddha, the ancestors facing downward (nānvīmukhas) must likewise be first satiated.
For the destruction of obstacles, there is the worship of Gaṇeśa.
In this regard, one should know that the form [of the deity] is twofold: land-born and water-born.
Land-born [images] originate from [specific] lineages (gotra) and are equal in value to various types of stones. (63)
The land-born [variety] is called *vipula* and is of two types: fallen and upward-pointing.
The water-born variety arises from the lotus root (*abjakanda*) and is distinguished by three types: the *tilaka*, the *aṅka*, and the *karṇika*.
It has massive knots as its broad markings, is adorned with buds and sprouts,
is vast with many branches as its limbs, possesses a hundred thousand [leaves], and is tender, born from the mountain.
A strip, a single *tilaka*, a *tribhaṅga* as the second,
and a lotus with a half-moon as the third— this is the characteristic of the *tilaka*. (66)
At the tip, there should be a lotus-like limb, in some places broken yet very delicate;
it is expansive, curved, spreading, elevated, broad, and clearly manifest.
This face, arising from the *kunda* flower, is beautiful and born of water;
it is fivefold by means of ten lines, while the sixth is the form with all parts (*sakala*).
It should be known that there are twelve varieties, both land-born and water-born:
Kalinda (or Kāliṅga), Koladaṣṭrārdra, and those entirely covered with thorns. (69)
The bamboo should be blue and very tender; its joints, lines, and edible parts should be free from defects. Its leaves should resemble the horns of a ram and be produced from young shoots. (70)
Gold that is yellow, crowded with fissures, dense-bodied, spreading,
shaped like the bud of an *agasti* flower, and called "purifying" (*pāvanāhvaka*)— [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a description of defective gold.]
[To] Kaṇṭhaka || 71 ||
One should fashion the Bhāskara [mark] as broad and green with a fine thread,
its tip rounded like a dog's tail and curved like a cat's claw.
The "parrot-mouthed" thorns are said to be blood and ginger; the leaf is called *nāgara*.
The thorn of the *aurvāru* (or *airvāru*) plant, which has the tip of a thread-like coil, is known as *sarpasarpaṇa*.
Mutually joined together, it is a leaf with many veins;
it is broad, with curled tips, white, and adorned by a red face. (74)
It is young, tawny-red, rough, and exceedingly harsh; it is covered with knots, leaves, and sprouts that are distorted and constantly growing upwards.
Its limbs were blossoming with playful grace, densely crowded with sprouts;
in some places it was severed, in some split, and in others encircled by half-leaves. (76)
The Dravidian leaf is like the smoke of straw; it is thus:
richly adorned with the aforementioned creepers, heart-pleasing, beautiful, and well-drawn.
A leaf that is mixed with all characteristics is known as *vaiśaram*;
it is considered old at the base and middle, and young at the tip and on the small branches.
One should draw the entire three-pronged [design], with each petal possessing the characteristics of a petal;
having had it multiplied by the artisans, one should subsequently delineate the petals. (79)
What is there for men to fear from the pillar, the pot, the face, the door, the chariot, or even the side-carriage, once they have emerged from the tail and the flanks of the royal swan?
Thus ends the thirtieth rule, titled "The Characteristics Pertaining to the Maṇḍapa and Other Structures," within the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*. [This word does not appear in the Liṅgapurāṇa.]
Now, the thirty-first [chapter]:

One should always worship the Vāstu deity and the gods in the three [circles] at the beginning of the lotus-pools and so forth when establishing an underground chamber; and in the four-cornered [mandala], one should offer to those who partake of Rudra.
In each of the three compartments [mū, kh, gh, ṅ], one should worship those beginning with Hara;
in the quarters, those beginning with Marīci; and in the center, the creators (Vedhas) within the principles (tattvas).
Then, one should worship Kālāgni upon a white lotus in the Brahma-square, located in the middle between the two pairs of feet at the corners of the eight squares.
Endowed with the six limbs of the Mūrtyaṅga and with the first letter of one's own name,
[one worships] Hāṭakeśa, Baleśa (or Caleśa), and likewise Atibala.
Furthermore, Mahodara, Mahābdhi, and Kumbhārṇava,
as well as Virūpākṣa as the seventh and Bhrukuṭīśa, are on the petals.

One should worship with perfumes and other offerings starting from the east and ending in the northeast, as well as from Ananta (or Nanda) and others on the body, up to Karkoṭaka, using their respective mantras in the chamber located in the northwestern direction.
And in the outer areas, one should satisfy Carakī and the others with offerings and burnt oblations;
likewise, one should satisfy the world-protectors beginning with the Planets, as well as the eight Nāgas.
Anantādya, Mahāpadma, Takṣaka, and likewise Kulika;
Śaṅkha, Vāsuki, Padma, and Karkoṭakāntaka. (8)
Having first performed ablutions and sacrifices on an auspicious day with favorable omens,
one should deposit the medicinal herbs— which remove afflictions— starting from the east and ending in the northeast, and placing the principal ones in the center.
Phalī, uśīra, yaṣṭyāhva, sahā, hilocanā, hrīka, bamboo-hair, and artha;
[according to manuscript gh: rasa-kūrmepu]; gems, lotus, Gaṅgā-water, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). 10.
Then, one should pour water into the pond and place sixty snakes in its center;
they should be twice the height of the pit, or three-quarters of it, or exceeding it by one-eighth.
[The Adhisārdhakām] || 8 ||
Having thoroughly bathed Sālasundarī and the others with fragrant waters, garments, and so forth, one should worship them with the Ananta-mantra, preceded by a firm gaze and mental concentration.
With that very same [staff], one should erect a serpent-staff in the center for protection,
once the entire [structure] has been completed like a banner amidst the sound of the Vedas and musical instruments. || 13 ||
Salutation to the one who possesses the seven types of enjoyments and a beautiful crown, who dwells in all directions and remains as the support;
*hūṃ* *hūṃ*, salutation to Ananta, the lord of the *nāgas*. || 14 ||

With the *anantamantra*, having sprinkled [the victim] with weapon-water (*astrodaka*), one should bind him with the *pāśupata* mantra. Having struck him with a razor-edged blade (*khurika*), this [victim], who is the "Elder" (*jyeṣṭha*), should be cast into water with the secret mantra. || 15 ||
The Guru, the performer of the rite, holding various nooses and reciting the Pāśupata mantra, should remain here; the sacrificer, grasping the tail of a tawny cow, should cross over.
There, the performer shall cross the terrible Vaitaraṇī river;
thereafter, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the Bahurūpa mantra.
One should satisfy the god Varuṇa and the god Soma, or perhaps gratify them by offering something;
one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (caru) with that, and by means of that very same substance, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti). || 18 ||
The Guru, being delighted, should bestow the *pūrṇāhuti* with the [mantra] "Śivenāśivaharīṇā. And he should give that cow to the Guru and satisfy him according to his own means. (19)

In the well, when it has been prepared in this manner, one should likewise worship the Lord situated in the two and a half quarters located in the solar portion (arkāṃśa), as well as the eight Āpādikas starting from the northeast (Īśāna) at intervals of one quarter in each corner. These are: Khāgni, Gogryūṇa, Pitṛ, Rugvā, Yuditī, and Īśa.
In the directions, one should place Marīci and the others, and in the center, upon the six-petaled lotuses, the Unborn (Aja).
In the supreme region of the foot of the well (kūpāṅghri), surrounded by eight Tāra-Nāgas,
one should worship Kālarudreśa in its center with perfumes and other offerings as before.
Having offered oblations, one should give a sacrificial offering (bali) to them; then the preceptor should give a cow to the teacher.
He should then throw the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into the well along with water consecrated by the Gaṅgā-mantra.
Afterwards, the Guru should thoroughly sprinkle the performer with water for pacification (śāntyambu).
Having requested blessings from one another like seekers of wealth, the performer should feed the Brahmins according to his capacity.
In a well made of brick or stone, he should place a firm, thick rope.
With wooden ladles held in their hands, they [carried] a wooden wheel with small jars.
It is proper that a man should draw this water by means of two tubes for the sake of grasping it;
he should place the one who has fallen asleep there, at the midpoint of the tube, preceded by a sacrifice.
In the six types of lotus ponds and so forth, whether constructed of stone or brick, Lord Hari should be installed upon a water-bed; alternatively, he may be named Gaṅgānāga.

For the sake of the ascetic's livelihood, one should construct ponds and other such features in the directions from the east to the northeast; likewise, in gardens or before temples, one should construct a well in the cardinal directions as previously described.
In all excavations, such as wells, the entire procedure—
including the throwing [of earth] and the sowing [of seeds]— should be performed by means of both the left and the right [hands].

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites for trees such as the bilva, as well as their cleansing and worship; one should also perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds situated in the center, using one's own stars (tārakas).

In a grove or garden as well, one should likewise offer oblations to the deity of the trees, who resides in a tree situated in the northeast; or else, the offering should be made in the eastern chamber of the trees.

Having adopted from the Bāṇa-mata the entire sequence beginning with the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship, as well as the feeding of ascetics, it has been written down using those very characters. (32)

Thus ends the thirty-first procedure in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*, titled "The Establishment of Lotuses, Wells, Trees, Groves, and Parks. [The word *nāma* does not appear in the Liṅga-puṣkara manuscript. 31.
Now,

for one performing the four-month vow (cāturmāsya-vrata), the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) must be performed at the beginning of the annual worship and other rites, in order to complete whatever may have been deficient. || 1 ||
In the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, or Nabhasya, and not thereafter; during the fortnights of one's own chosen deities, beginning from the first day of the lunar month (pratipad) dedicated to Fire,
and for those of Jvalana, Brahmā, Gaurī, Heramba, and the Serpents.
And of the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Śaṅkaras, Caṇḍī, Yama, and Viḍaujas. || 3 ||
Furthermore, on the full moon day, the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) is prescribed for Viṣṇu, Manmatha, Śambhu, Sarveśvara, and the ancestors.
Having first examined the place and taken up the tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*).
Earth, ashes, cloth, leaves, and so forth, as well as thread, in seven ways. || 5 ||
The thread may be made of linen, muñja grass, hemp, silk, or even from woven cloth; it may also be made of lotus fiber or cotton, prepared by a daughter of the twice-born or others.
Having tripled [the length] three times according to the measurement of the *liṅga* starting from the *jyeṣṭha* size,
there should be a knot at intervals of ten finger-breadths, with each subsequent interval decreasing by one finger-breadth.

The remaining two [measures] should be two finger-breadths at the end of the hand, starting from nine and so on. With one hundred and eight threads, the largest [measure] is formed; otherwise, it is determined by a reduction of eight by eight.
The knots should be counted according to the number of threads, with some being irregularly placed;
they should be smeared with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron, and marked with "intoxicated moons" (madacandra) as far as possible.
One should further beautify those knots with silver or with metallic minerals.
Three [knots] should be made for the three principles (tattvas), and the fourth is produced from the support (āvalamba).
One should place well-washed purifiers upon the pedestal, the liṅga, and the head;
one bestows the fulfillment of all aims, and the fourth is placed on the back of the pedestal.
From the feet up to the forehead, and from the heart up to the throat within one's own body,
there should be knots of thread corresponding to the syllables of the eight hundred and sixty-four verses, in their respective order.
With the syllables of the mantra located at the tips of one's own arms and palms, and abiding in the true principles,
[one should place them] upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) of Hari and Śambhu, on the petals, filaments, and corners.
The knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others are formed by thirty-two threads with an increase [in number], while for the others, they are formed by ten threads with a decrease of one petal.
The purifier (pavitraka) for images is held to reach up to the head and the knees;
for the bull, the purifier is considered to extend from the tips of the horns to the hooves, just like that of the linga.
One should wrap palaces, monasteries, and houses with a single thread;
however, for other deities, the sacred thread (pavitra) should consist of three threads.
On the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), the knots [of the cord] corresponding to the length of the mobile liṅga should be equal;
in some cases, it is measured by a span (vitasti), with threads [forming] quarters of a quarter of a hundred.
The threads for those who dwell in permanent houses or on sacrificial altars should consist of twenty-one,
twelve, and twenty-four strands respectively, according to the number of feet, syllables, and kalās.
And for the cloth-paintings and the scriptures, there should be a binding with three threads.
For the sake of the teacher and for one's own sake, there are eleven knots respectively according to the [number of] threads;
with the thirty-six principles as the count, there are nine knots of five kinds.
The measurement from the base of the little finger to the armpit, and from the shoulder to the navel, is equal. || 20 ||
One should perform the bath, worship, recitation, fire-oblation, meditation, and the formal petition,
as well as the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa), using the desired mantras according to the three principles (tritattva).
The twice-born situated in the east, south, north, and west should likewise offer the *pavitraka* in those directions; and others should do so in the directions starting from the southeast (Agni).
Having bathed and performed the daily worship— or indeed the occasional worship—
of the Lord, one should [worship] with three or five threads, using the heart-mantra of the All-pervading One.
"You have been addressed, O Lord of Gods; worship has been offered by me.
Accept this, O Mahādeva, you who are the cause of all rites. (24)

Clay, water scented with *sāmalaka*, auspicious ashes, tooth-sticks, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—these are used in sequence for those [materials]: palmyra, sandalwood, and iron. (25)

One should employ a stone or even yellow pigment (rocanā) with one's own mantra, O goddess with the most excellent face, along with all the substances for the fire-oblation (homa) together with kuśa grass. (26)
One should offer collyrium, saffron, oil, a probe, hair-cleansing powder, betel, and sacrificial porridge with clarified butter to the Guhyakas; furthermore, one should offer it to Nara.
To the south, [he should place] the staff, the rosary, the loincloth, and the alms-bowl;
in the northeast, the seat, the umbrella, the sandals, and the yoga-band.
One should mentally conceive of these as being endowed with effort;
having made them into vessels and sprinkled the purifiers with auspicious water, they are consecrated. (29)
Having covered it with a black antelope skin and other materials, one should offer it while reciting the collection of mantras,
along with perfume, flowers, incense and the like, unbroken grains of rice, and a sacred thread.
The wise one should recite the supreme mantra consisting of words along with its introductory invocation;
he should then offer Śiva, rendered immortal by the *recaka* breath, upon his head.
Oṃ, salutation to Vrateśvara; fulfill, fulfill, svāhā!
Having fasted, one should recite this at night, or during the nakta period, or at the very time of the nakṣatra.
Having bathed in the morning, pure and cleansed, one should perform worship according to one's means.
With water filtered through a cloth and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform a bath with devotion;
then, a bath with the five sweet substances (pañcamadhura) and drying with other waters.
Having drawn water with a cloth, one should perform a bath with fragrant water and other substances;
then, having offered the eight-limbed *argha* and anointed [the deity], one should worship.
The protection of the Śiva-pitcher and the ritual weapon (astra), the mandala as prescribed by the scriptures, and the dwelling covered with cloths and adorned with jars and chowries. (35)
With hanging flower garlands and various excellent garments,
and with rows of plantain and mango trees bearing ripe fruit and beautiful blossoms.
One should beautify the house with banners, flags, lamps, and other offerings such as food oblations;
one should pass the night with great festivities consisting of dance, song, and melodious instrumental music.

With devotion, one should satisfy all the teachers, the lords of Śiva-yogins, and those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgins) with one's own wealth, by means of gifts of clothing and the like, as well as food.
Having thus performed the auspicious Pavitrārohaṇa as described, one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 39 ||
A householder should wear the purifying thread for one night or three nights, avoiding beds, lying down, false speech, women, travel, and meat. (40)
If ascetics are unable to perform the Cāturmāsya rites due to illness, fear, or other such causes,
they should perform worship, bow to Śiva, and then dismiss the *pavitra*.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, having performed a great worship— including the mandala and other rites as before—
one should cast the sacred threads (pavitra) either into the Śiva-fire or into pure water.

O Lord, he who has been initiated but does not perform the offering of the *pavitra* to the All-pervading One shall become subject to expiation and go downward, even if he has performed ten million Rudra-rites.
The Ritual for the Ascension of the Pavitra.
209) From the golden liṅga comes the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and from the seed-syllable *tāra* come the Viśvedevas.
Due to his birth in that lineage, Piśāca was like the sun because of his worship of the copper linga.
The Vasus were perfected from the sound [of the bell], the Maruts from the worship of the mountain, all the Guhyakas from lead, and the Rākṣasas and Asuras from iron. || 45 ||
From triloha all the Mothers [arose]; from tvaṣṭaloha, Mārtaṇḍa;
from vajra, Surendra and Mārkaṇḍa; and from pearl, the Lord of the Night (the Moon).
From the ruby (puṣparāga) comes the preceptor, from the cat's-eye (vaidūrya) King Rāghava, from the ruby (padmarāga) the Fire-god, and from the sapphire (indranīla) Hari through worship. (47)

Bāṇa [attains his goal] from a liṅga made of emerald; the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) from one made of crystal; the Nāgas from worship of one made of coral; and Śukra always [attains his] from one made of emerald.
From Palaka arose Vāgīśa; from Rājāvarta came Śanaiścara;
from Paulastya came Jīvajāti; and from Ṛṣṭi came Siddha and Kinnara.
Bali was perfected through contentment; Praśānta through his vow;
the Aśvins from the ripened clay; and the Gandharvas from the production of offspring.
Brahmā is perfected through the stone-born [liṅga], the sages through that made of painted cloth,
Kandarpa through the scent-born, and the sky-clad [Digambara] through the flower-liṅga.
From serving the Śārṅga bow, Dakṣa attained excellence; from the elephant’s tusk, Māruti;
from the tortoise, Kauśika; and from the bull, Vāsuki became the leader of serpents. || 52 ||

Through the worship of Nakula, King Hariścandra attained perfection; and Ambarīṣa likewise achieved complete success through the installation and worship of the Liṅga—just as the gods and others became perfected. (53)
From the eight-fold flour-paste produced from the liṅga, the eight Siddhas and Gaṇeśvaras arose;
and from the butter, Dhanvantari was perfectly accomplished.
The drinkers of Soma. || 54 ||
Tārkṣya [attained his state] from worshipping a rice-offering (odana), and Budha likewise from a liṅga made of molasses;
furthermore, liṅgas produced from various fruits, when served according to the prescribed rite, [yield their respective fruits].
By that [merit], those sages, the Bālakhilyas, became perfected and highly exalted;
from Saikata came Viśvakarman, and from Lavaṇodbhava came Śacīśa.
Vibhīṣaṇa [attained his state] from a linga made of dust; Caraka, from one made of roots through worship; and the king named Sagara, from a linga made of a bamboo sprout. || 57 ||
King Jayadratha arose from the city-dwellers; Rāhu from the worship of *rāmaṭha* (asafetida);
the son of Sumitrā from a water-liṅga; and the Yoginīs from the production of *siktha* (honey-wax).
The goddesses born of clay and born of lotus, as well as the earthen liṅgas and the five Pāṇḍavas—
these have been established through their efficacy in this world and recorded from many scriptures. (59)
Therefore, one should perform rites pertaining to this world even if they lack formal consecration;
by the words of the Lord, through their own mantras ending with the syllable *kṣa*, they shall be granters of desires and bestowers of success.
The *liṅga* consists of all the gods; the *liṅga* is established within all things.
When installed with the mantras of the ritual (or Śiva), it bestows virtue (*dharma*), desire (*kāma*), wealth (*artha*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). (61)
When a single *liṅga* has been installed or worshipped, all the deities become worshipped and established; therefore, that which is to be worshipped and established is [the one *liṅga*] in reality.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred fords, and the gods [or the Vedas],
one obtains a fruit ten million times greater than that by installing a liṅga.
Whoever should install a single *liṅga* according to the prescribed rite, accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
shall obtain merit proclaimed in all the scriptures, multiplied ten million times ten millionfold.
