The beast clearly sees the bracelet on its own hand with a mirror, yet it does not see the entire world marked with the *liṅga* nor even marked with the *bhaga*. 65.
For the sake of the attainment of perfection and liberation, and out of a desire for the welfare of devotees,
take all of this from the scriptures and write down that which was spoken by Śikhin.

Having seen that a complete certainty regarding all things cannot be achieved through a brief and one-pointed [treatment], and fearing that confusion might arise from an extensive one, this has therefore been made of moderate length. (67)
The installation has been described by Sundara and others, and it has also been described by me, though my power is slight;
for if even Garuḍa flies, do not the bees also fly here? (68)

The meanings of many scriptures, clothed in garments of meaning and well-composed in the form of books and aphorisms, have been uttered by the Kaṇṭhācāryas for the destruction of the cold of ignorance. (69)
(212) Through the application of words, syllables, and other means, by means of concealment of designations and gender, one who is unmentioned among the wise is indicated by that [text]. (70)

There was a king named Gopāla, a jewel adorning the entire earth; his son was the high-souled Dhīranātha, free from faults, who exerted himself in serving kings and possessed vast glory. His son, renowned for his eloquence, attained great fame.
In the Bhūmicakra, he— this very one who has compassion for the world called Radhīna— [taught] this most beautiful ritual of consecration (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*),
which is sung by the five-faced one. || 71 ||

Born of the illustrious Mattamayūra lineage, equal to Hara, a devotee of Śiva, and illuminating the [Kaula] tradition, there was a renowned and preeminent teacher, Vimalādi, who was devoted solely to Śiva;
he was honored by King Nirbhaya and was personally consecrated as his guru.
From him was born Jñānīśānaśiva, and from his feet was born the teacher Vairocana. || 72 ||
He who removes the threefold impurities born of illusion, karma, and the like; who has descended into the body of knowledge (*jñānadeha*);
who is non-different in form from Śambhu; who is known by the sages as the "Upward-Facing One" (*ūrdhvavaktra*);
the renowned Lord of Teachers (*ācāryendra*) who benefits all people and abides in the pure Śaiva stage of life— [Please provide the subsequent portion of the text for translation.]
I bow my head to the ground before the lotus feet of that teacher of mine.

He whose two tusks are like the sharp and fierce fangs of the *Siddhāntadvaya-ṭaṅkaśātaka* (or *dṛkca-gāruḍa*), whose tongue is long and possesses a mane, and whose left and right paths are the scriptures (*savyāpasavyāgamau*).
This Vairocana-lion, whose claws are the extensive systems of all beings, who crushes the pride of the intoxicated deer and elephants, wanders about with the roar of the earth. 74.
Independent study is debate, while the observation of others' systems is [the means to] that;
this quality, which produces intelligence and wisdom, belongs to the Śaiva teacher of those sciences. (75)
At the beginning, verses in the Vasantatilakā and Sragdharā meters shine forth;
the remainder are in Anuṣṭubh, and this work, consisting of a thousand qualities, was composed in the middle [of the treatise]. (76)

Whatever has been spoken by me, who possesses but little intelligence, for the benefit of those who show the way, may any ill-spoken words therein be like a *ṭaṅka*— a stone-cutter’s tool— as described in the *Amara-kośa*, or like a *śākaṭa* load, as described in the *Amara-kośa*.
Having understood this well-spoken teaching, the wise will act accordingly.
This scripture should not be given to one who shows no devotion, nor to a non-devotee of Maheśvara;
it should always be given to the followers of Śiva, both in accordance with its meaning and its scriptural tradition.
"Protect me from the thief who begs from others, from affection that loosens one's bonds,
from thorns, anthills, and fire"— thus says the book.
The Rudra named Ananta, situated above, supports the earth by his power of upholding it,
just as Mount Sumeru, surrounded by the best of peaks, stands in the center of Jambūdvīpa.
As long as the sky shines, resplendent with the beautiful light of the moon, the sun, and the stars,
so long may the fame of the Guru Vairocana spread through the world, like a lotus flower.
As long as the glorious Ananta supports the earth upon his upraised power of support (*ādhāra-śakti*), and for as long as the seven oceans endure— (p. 114) — [so long shall this remain].
In the center of the earth, surrounded by the ocean, stands Mount Meru;
as far as the moon, the sun, and the host of stars, this world shines brilliantly with their jewel-like radiance.
Meanwhile, may this fame of his remain for a long time in the world in the form of this book. || 81 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second ritual, titled "The Ascension of the Pavitra," in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*, the Compendium of the Essence of the Characteristics of Consecration. || 32 ||
This work is completed.
Auspiciousness.
